pages.title: Quickstart
pages.description: Install the CLI, start a sandbox, let an agent build something inside it, and open it at a live URL.
pages.markdown:
MIOSA runs isolated Linux sandboxes and full cloud desktops for your code and your AI agents, then publishes the result to a live URL. This page takes you from install to an app that an agent built, in four steps. Video: [Quickstart, explained](https://miosa.ai/videos/quickstart-explained.mp4) (1:35) ## Let your agent drive MIOSA Most people run MIOSA through a coding agent, not by hand. Your agent can run on your laptop and control the whole platform. It has four ways in: | Way in | What to do | |---|---| | CLI | Your agent runs `miosa` commands. Start it with the [Agent operating guide](/docs/guides/agent-operating-guide). | | MCP server | `miosa mcp install --client claude` (also `cursor` and `gemini`). OSA and Hermes use a config file instead: see [MCP](/docs/mcp). | | Skills | Claude Code skills for sandboxes, computers, and deploys. See [Claude Code skills](/docs/guides/skills). | | `llms.txt` | Point any agent at [miosa.ai/llms.txt](https://miosa.ai/llms.txt). It lists every docs page in plain text. | This works with OSA, Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Hermes, Kimi Code, and more. The rest of this page puts an agent inside a sandbox. Already know what you need? - [Sandbox to deployment](/docs/quickstart/sandbox-to-deployment): the recommended first walkthrough. - [Agent-driven build](/docs/quickstart/agent-driven-build): dispatch work, stream events, and collect artifacts from your backend. - [Docker Host](/docs/quickstart/app-engine): run containerized applications on a workspace Docker Host host; check [availability](/docs/availability) first. - [Connect your own server](/docs/opencomputers/connect): run your first command on a Linux machine you operate. ## 1. Install **macOS / Linux** ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Miosa-osa/miosa-cli-go/main/install.sh | sh ``` **Windows** ```powershell npm i -g @miosa/cli ``` The installer does these steps: 1. Detects your OS and CPU. 2. Downloads the matching `miosa` binary and checks its SHA-256. 3. Installs it to `~/.local/bin/miosa` (or `/usr/local/bin` when run as root). Then run `miosa login` to sign in: it opens your browser, and the key for this machine is stored in `~/.miosa/config.toml`. Prefer npm, Homebrew, or a manual download? See [Install the CLI or SDK](/docs/cli/install). ## 2. Start a sandbox ```bash miosa create my-box --wait # provision a sandbox and wait until it is ready miosa list # see all your sandboxes ``` A sandbox is a fast, isolated Linux VM. Your agent writes files into it, runs commands, and opens ports as live preview URLs. Its filesystem persists when the sandbox pauses, so you can resume it later. Read [Sandboxes](/docs/develop/sandboxes) for sizes, limits, and lifecycle. ## 3. Run an agent inside it Pick your agent. MIOSA installs it in the sandbox and runs it there. The agent uses your own model account, so you pay your own provider. MIOSA credits never pay for the model. Each agent has three parts: connect your account, start the agent, and give it a task. **OSA** OSA is MIOSA's own agent. It works with the model you connect. **Connect.** Open the MIOSA console, go to **Agents**, and connect your model key for OSA. **Start it and give it a task.** ```bash miosa prompt --harness osa --sandbox my-box \ "Build a landing page and serve it on port 3000" ``` **Claude Code** **Connect.** Sign in with your Claude plan. The command prints a link and a code. Approve it in your browser, then paste the code back. ```bash miosa connections add models claude --sandbox my-box ``` Or use your own Anthropic key: ```bash miosa connections add models anthropic --key-stdin <<< "$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY" ``` **Start it and give it a task.** ```bash miosa prompt --harness claude-code --sandbox my-box \ "Build a landing page and serve it on port 3000" ``` **Codex** **Connect.** Sign in with your ChatGPT plan. The command prints a link and a code. Approve it in your browser. ```bash miosa connections add models chatgpt --sandbox my-box ``` Or use your own OpenAI key: ```bash miosa connections add models openai --key-stdin <<< "$OPENAI_API_KEY" ``` **Start it and give it a task.** ```bash miosa prompt --harness codex --sandbox my-box \ "Build a landing page and serve it on port 3000" ``` **OpenCode** **Connect.** In the MIOSA console, go to **Agents** and connect one of these for OpenCode: an Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, or Mistral key, or your ChatGPT plan. `miosa connections` does not cover this agent yet. **Start it and give it a task.** ```bash SANDBOX_ID=$(miosa info my-box --json | jq -r .id) RUN=$(miosa api POST /runs -d "{ \"runner\": \"opencode\", \"sandbox_id\": \"$SANDBOX_ID\", \"instruction\": \"Build a landing page and serve it on port 3000\" }" | jq -r .data.id) miosa run follow $RUN ``` **Hermes** Hermes Agent is a first-class runner in the run API. It is not in the CLI `--harness` list yet, so start it with the run API. **Connect.** In the MIOSA console, go to **Agents**, and connect a ChatGPT plan, a Claude plan (Max with extra usage), or an Anthropic, OpenAI, or OpenRouter key. `miosa connections` does not cover this agent yet. **Start it and give it a task.** ```bash SANDBOX_ID=$(miosa info my-box --json | jq -r .id) RUN=$(miosa api POST /runs -d "{ \"runner\": \"hermes\", \"sandbox_id\": \"$SANDBOX_ID\", \"instruction\": \"Build a landing page and serve it on port 3000\" }" | jq -r .data.id) miosa run follow $RUN ``` **Kimi Code** **Connect.** In the MIOSA console, go to **Agents** and connect your Kimi Code plan or your Moonshot key. `miosa connections` does not cover this agent yet. **Start it and give it a task.** ```bash SANDBOX_ID=$(miosa info my-box --json | jq -r .id) RUN=$(miosa api POST /runs -d "{ \"runner\": \"kimi\", \"sandbox_id\": \"$SANDBOX_ID\", \"instruction\": \"Build a landing page and serve it on port 3000\" }" | jq -r .data.id) miosa run follow $RUN ``` **Pi** **Connect.** In the MIOSA console, go to **Agents** and connect one of these for Pi: an Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, or Mistral key, or your Claude or ChatGPT plan. `miosa connections` does not cover this agent yet. **Start it and give it a task.** ```bash SANDBOX_ID=$(miosa info my-box --json | jq -r .id) RUN=$(miosa api POST /runs -d "{ \"runner\": \"pi\", \"sandbox_id\": \"$SANDBOX_ID\", \"instruction\": \"Build a landing page and serve it on port 3000\" }" | jq -r .data.id) miosa run follow $RUN ``` **Mistral** **Connect.** In the MIOSA console, go to **Agents** and connect your Mistral Vibe plan or your Mistral key. `miosa connections` does not cover this agent yet. **Start it and give it a task.** ```bash SANDBOX_ID=$(miosa info my-box --json | jq -r .id) RUN=$(miosa api POST /runs -d "{ \"runner\": \"mistral\", \"sandbox_id\": \"$SANDBOX_ID\", \"instruction\": \"Build a landing page and serve it on port 3000\" }" | jq -r .data.id) miosa run follow $RUN ``` If you have not connected an account, the run is refused or fails. MIOSA never falls back to its own keys. ## 4. See what it built ```bash miosa preview create my-box 3000 --visibility public ``` Open the URL it prints. That is the page your agent built, served from inside the sandbox. If nothing loads, the agent did not leave a server running. Start one yourself: ```bash miosa process start my-box --name web --cwd /workspace -- python3 -m http.server 3000 --bind 0.0.0.0 ``` ## Or do it by hand You do not need an agent for this. Write a file, start a server, and open a preview yourself. **CLI** ```bash miosa exec my-box -- echo "hello from MIOSA" echo "

Hello

" | miosa files write my-box:/workspace/index.html miosa process start my-box --name web --cwd /workspace -- python3 -m http.server 3000 --bind 0.0.0.0 miosa preview create my-box 3000 --visibility public ``` `miosa process start` returns at once and keeps the server running. Do not use `miosa exec` for a server, because `exec` waits for the command to end. **TypeScript** ```typescript import { Miosa } from "@miosa/sdk" const miosa = new Miosa({ apiKey: process.env.MIOSA_API_KEY! }) const sandbox = await miosa.sandboxes.create({ templateId: "miosa-sandbox", workspaceSlug: "default", // the workspace it belongs to; every create names one wait: true, // hold the call until the sandbox is ready }) console.log(sandbox.id, sandbox.state) // sbx_a1b2c3d4e5 running await sandbox.files.write( "/workspace/index.html", ` My App

Hello from MIOSA

Built in a sandbox.

` ) // Start the server in the background. This call returns right away. await sandbox.exec( "nohup python3 -m http.server 3000 --bind 0.0.0.0 > /tmp/web.log 2>&1 &", { cwd: "/workspace" } ) const preview = await sandbox.previews.create(3000) console.log(preview.url) // https://3000-abc12345.sandbox.miosa.ai ``` You can also hand the whole job to an agent: `await sandbox.run("Build a landing page and serve it on port 3000", { runner: "codex" })`. **Python** ```python import os from miosa import Miosa miosa = Miosa(api_key=os.environ["MIOSA_API_KEY"]) sandbox = miosa.sandboxes.create( template_id="miosa-sandbox", workspace_slug="default", # the workspace it belongs to; every create names one wait=True, ) print(sandbox.id, sandbox.state) # sbx_a1b2c3d4e5 running sandbox.files.write( "/workspace/index.html", """ My App

Hello from MIOSA

Built in a sandbox.

""", ) # Start the server in the background. This call returns right away. sandbox.processes.start("python3 -m http.server 3000 --bind 0.0.0.0", name="web") preview = sandbox.previews.create(port=3000) print(preview["url"]) # https://3000-abc12345.sandbox.miosa.ai ``` Open the preview URL MIOSA returns. Your `index.html` is served live from inside the sandbox. ## Pick what you need | You want to | Product | Start here | |---|---|---| | Run code, builds, tests, and dev servers | [Sandbox](/docs/develop/sandboxes) | [Create and connect](/docs/develop/sandboxes/create) | | Drive a browser, a desktop app, screenshots | [Computer](/docs/computers/overview) | [Computers overview](/docs/computers/overview) | | Ship an always-on app at a public URL | [Docker Host](/docs/docker-host/docker-deploy) | [Deploy overview](/docs/docker-host/overview) | | Run an AI agent against a sandbox or computer | [Agent Runs](/docs/api-reference/agent-runs) | [Agent operating guide](/docs/guides/agent-operating-guide) | | Build a white-label product on MIOSA | [Platform builders](/docs/platform/overview) | [Platform overview](/docs/platform/overview) | ## Next - [Sandbox to deployment](/docs/quickstart/sandbox-to-deployment): The full first walkthrough: create a sandbox, write files, preview, publish to production, and prove the deployment is live. - [Agent-driven build](/docs/quickstart/agent-driven-build): Dispatch work to your agent, stream events, and collect artifacts from your backend, with external attribution. - [Docker Host](/docs/quickstart/app-engine): Run containerized applications on a workspace Docker Host host. - [Connect your own server](/docs/opencomputers/connect): Run your first command on a Linux machine you operate. - [Concepts](/docs/concepts): Every MIOSA primitive in one architecture reference. - [API reference](/docs/api-reference): Every endpoint, error code, and webhook.

pages.title: Sandbox to deployment
pages.description: The full first walkthrough: create a sandbox, write code, preview it live, publish to production, and prove the deployment is running.
pages.markdown:
Start with **Track 1: Sandbox to deployment**. The recommended first walkthrough. Your first success is a small site running at the production URL returned by MIOSA, with its deployment verified. Complete that path before adding agent orchestration or another runtime. > **Building a white-label product?** If your goal is to ship a SaaS where your customers never see the MIOSA brand, start with the [White-Label Integrator Guide](/docs/integrations) instead. It covers per-user provisioning, custom domains, iframe embeds, webhooks, and usage billing from scratch. ## Prerequisites ### Account and workspace Create a MIOSA account at [miosa.ai](https://miosa.ai) and a workspace. ### API key Create a key in Settings → API Keys for the intended workspace. See [API keys](/docs/platform/api-keys) for key types and scopes. Export your key in the terminal where you will run the examples: ```bash export MIOSA_API_KEY="msk_u_..." ``` ### Install tooling for your language **TypeScript** ```bash npm install @miosa/cli @miosa/sdk # or: pnpm add @miosa/cli @miosa/sdk ``` **Python** ```bash pip install --upgrade miosa ``` **Elixir** ```elixir # mix.exs - published on Hex.pm: https://hex.pm/packages/miosa {:miosa, "~> 1.1"} ``` Then run `mix deps.get`. **MCP (Claude Code / Cursor / Windsurf)** **Zero-install option - just a URL + API key:** ```json { "mcpServers": { "miosa": { "url": "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer msk_u_..." } } } } ``` Add this to `~/.claude/mcp.json` (Claude Code), Cursor's MCP settings, or Windsurf's `mcp_config.json`. No pip, no npm - the current capability-scoped tool catalog appears immediately after a client restart. This is the easiest way to get started. **Local server (optional):** ```bash pip install git+https://github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa-mcp.git ``` Or via the TypeScript CLI: ```bash npx @miosa/cli mcp serve ``` > **Caution: Never put msk_* in a browser** > > Workspace API keys are server-only. For browser-side preview embedding, your backend mints a short-lived share token. See [Browser Tokens](/docs/platform/browser-tokens). ## Step 1 - Create a sandbox. **TypeScript** ```typescript import { Miosa } from "@miosa/sdk" const miosa = new Miosa({ apiKey: process.env.MIOSA_API_KEY! }) const sandbox = await miosa.sandboxes.create({ templateId: "miosa-sandbox", workspaceSlug: "default", // the workspace it belongs to; every create names one }) console.log(sandbox.id, sandbox.state) // sbx_a1b2c3d4e5 running ``` **Python** ```python import os from miosa import Miosa miosa = Miosa(api_key=os.environ["MIOSA_API_KEY"]) sandbox = miosa.sandboxes.create(template_id="miosa-sandbox", workspace_slug="default") print(sandbox.id, sandbox.state) # sbx_a1b2c3d4e5 running ``` ## Step 2 - Write a small static site into `/workspace`. **TypeScript** ```typescript await sandbox.files.write( "/workspace/index.html", ` My App

Hello from MIOSA

Built in a sandbox.

` ) ``` **Python** ```python sandbox.files.write( "/workspace/index.html", """ My App

Hello from MIOSA

Built in a sandbox.

""", ) ``` ## Step 3 - Start a dev server so you can preview it. **TypeScript** ```typescript // Start the dev server. `exec.stream` keeps the process running and yields its output. const events = sandbox.exec.stream("python3 -m http.server 3000 --bind 0.0.0.0", { cwd: "/workspace" }) for await (const event of events) console.log(event) ``` **Python** ```python # Start the dev server in the background. server = sandbox.commands.run( "python3 -m http.server 3000 --bind 0.0.0.0", cwd="/workspace", background=True, ) ``` ## Step 4 - Create a preview and open it. **TypeScript** ```typescript const preview = await sandbox.previews.create(3000) console.log(preview.url) // https://3000-abc12345.sandbox.miosa.ai ``` **Python** ```python preview = sandbox.previews.create(port=3000) print(preview.url) # https://5173-abc12345.sandbox.miosa.ai ``` Open the URL in your browser. You see your `index.html` served live from inside the sandbox. ## Step 5 - Publish to production. **CLI** ```bash miosa deploy create --from-sandbox \ --name my-app \ --dir /workspace \ --type docker_deploy \ --wait \ --json ``` Use the `deployment.id` and `deployment.public_url` returned by MIOSA. **TypeScript** ```typescript const result = await sandbox.deploy({ name: "my-app", outputPath: "/workspace", }) // Read the production URL from the response; do not construct it. console.log(result) ``` **Python** ```python result = sandbox.deploy( name="my-app", output_path="/workspace", ) # Read the production URL from the response; do not construct it. print(result) ``` MIOSA freezes a source snapshot, runs a Builder to package the files, stores an immutable Release, and routes the Deployment URL to it. The sandbox remains alive and editable. ## Step 6 - Prove the deployment. The production URL is the URL returned by MIOSA. Do not construct it from the slug. Use deployment proof when you need an operator or CI check that the app is live. ```bash miosa deploy get --json ``` For Docker Host deployments, proof checks the deployment row, Docker Host host link, host health, durable app target, container route, and public URL probe. ## Step 7 - Make a change and republish. Edit `/workspace/index.html` again and publish to the existing deployment: ```bash miosa deploy create --from-sandbox \ --name \ --dir /workspace \ --type docker_deploy \ --wait \ --json ``` MIOSA creates a new immutable Version and promotes it only after verification succeeds. The previous healthy version remains available for rollback. ## Step 8 - (Optional) Attach a custom domain. See [Domains](/docs/docker-host/domains) for the DNS setup. Short version: add a `CNAME` from your domain to the generated host, hit the verify endpoint, MIOSA issues a TLS certificate. ## Step 9 - Clean up. **TypeScript** ```typescript await sandbox.destroy() ``` **Python** ```python sandbox.destroy() ``` The sandbox is gone. The published deployment and its domain are unaffected - the Release is immutable and lives in object storage independently of the sandbox. ### What you just did | Step | What happened | |------|--------------| | `sandboxes.create` | Created an isolated sandbox on the sandbox image | | `files.write` | Wrote a file into `/workspace` inside the running VM | | `exec` | Ran a command inside the VM over the exec API | | `previews.create` | Opened a tunnel from a public hostname to port 3000 inside the VM | | `sandbox publish` | Froze source, ran Builder, stored Release, created Version, and made it live | | `deploy prove` | Verified that MIOSA can prove the deployment route and runtime state | | `sandbox.destroy` | Terminated the VM; deployment is unaffected | ## What's next - **Add a real backend.** Move from static to dynamic deploys with [Publishing](/docs/docker-host/publishing) and a managed [Postgres database](/docs/data/postgres). - **Authenticate end users.** [Auth-as-a-service](/docs/data/auth) adds a full JWT signup/login flow with one environment variable. - **Roll back a bad deploy.** [Rollback](/docs/docker-host/rollback) repoints the domain at an older version in seconds. - **Understand every primitive.** [Concepts](/docs/concepts) is the canonical architecture reference. - **Build your own product on MIOSA.** The [Platform / White-label overview](/docs/platform/overview) covers preview tokens, share URLs, tenant branding, per-user quotas, webhook subscriptions, Docker Host domains, and the audit log. - **Drop in UI components.** `@miosa/react`, `@miosa/vue`, and `@miosa/svelte` provide `MiosaPreview`, `MiosaTerminal`, `MiosaFileTree`, and `MiosaUsage`. See [UI Components](/docs/ui-components). - **See a full white-label example.** The [reference integration](https://github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa/tree/main/examples) shows a complete platform embedding. - **Extend Claude Code with MIOSA skills.** 5 pre-built skills at [github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa-skills](https://github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa-skills) give Claude Code sandbox, computer, and deploy primitives. See [Skills](/docs/guides/skills). - **API wire format.** [API Reference](/docs/api-reference) documents every endpoint.

pages.title: Agent-driven build
pages.description: Dispatch work to your agent, stream events, and collect artifacts from your backend, tagging every resource with your own customer IDs.
pages.markdown:
This track treats the sandbox as an agent's tool environment. You can supply the intelligence from your own backend, or use the Agent Runs API when you want MIOSA to dispatch OSA, Claude Code, Codex, or another harness against a sandbox or computer target. For the managed runner path, see [Agent Runs](/docs/api-reference/agent-runs) and [Agent Run Groups](/docs/api-reference/agent-run-groups). To try a harness from the terminal first, follow [Quickstart, step 3](/docs/quickstart#3-run-an-agent-inside-it). ## Pick a harness A harness is the coding agent that MIOSA runs inside the sandbox. You pick it with the `runner` field. The agent uses your own model account, never MIOSA credits. | Agent | `runner` | Connect your account | |---|---|---| | OSA | `osa` | Connect your model key in the console, under **Agents**. | | Claude Code | `claude-code` | `miosa connections add models claude` (your plan) or `anthropic` (your key). | | Codex | `codex` | `miosa connections add models chatgpt` (your plan) or `openai` (your key). | | OpenCode | `opencode` | `miosa connections add models chatgpt`, `openrouter` or `anthropic`, then `miosa connections use opencode --all`. | | Kimi Code | `kimi` | `miosa connections add models kimi` (your plan). | | Pi | `pi` | `miosa connections add models anthropic`, `chatgpt` or `openrouter`, then `miosa connections use pi --all`. | | Mistral | `mistral` | `miosa connections add models vibe` (your plan) or `mistral` (your key). | | Hermes | `hermes` | `miosa connections add models chatgpt` (your plan) or `anthropic` / `openai` / `openrouter` (your key). | Run one from your backend: **TypeScript** ```typescript const run = await sandbox.run("Build a landing page and serve it on port 3000", { runner: "osa", // or "claude-code", "codex", "opencode", "kimi", "pi", "mistral" }) console.log(run.status) ``` **Python** ```python run = sandbox.run_agent( "Build a landing page and serve it on port 3000", runner="osa", # or "claude-code", "codex", "opencode", "kimi", "pi", "mistral" ) print(run["status"]) ``` If the account for that harness is not connected, MIOSA refuses the run and says what to connect. You do not need the console to connect one. Set a key or connect a Claude or ChatGPT plan from your own code, for your workspace or for each of your end users: [Connect agent accounts](/docs/guides/connect-agent-accounts). **TypeScript** ```typescript await miosa.connections.setKey({ provider: "anthropic", key: process.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY! }) // A customer's own Claude plan, used only for runs on their machines const signin = await miosa.connections.connectSubscription({ provider: "claude", externalUserId: "user-456" }) console.log(signin.verificationUrl) // show it in your UI, then: await signin.submitCode(pastedCode) ``` **Python** ```python miosa.connections.set_key("anthropic", key=os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"]) # A customer's own Claude plan, used only for runs on their machines signin = miosa.connections.connect_subscription("claude", external_user_id="user-456") print(signin.verification_url) # show it in your UI, then: signin.submit_code(pasted_code) ``` ### Step 1 - Create a sandbox with external attribution. If you're embedding MIOSA in your own product, pass your user/project IDs so you can filter resources later. **TypeScript** ```typescript const sandbox = await miosa.sandboxes.create({ templateId: "miosa-sandbox", workspaceSlug: "default", // the MIOSA workspace it belongs to wait: true, // hold the call until the sandbox is ready externalWorkspaceId: "acct-123", // your own grouping id, not a MIOSA workspace externalUserId: "user-456", externalProjectId: "intake-portal-789", }) console.log(sandbox.id) // sbx_f6g7h8i9j0 ``` **Python** ```python sandbox = miosa.sandboxes.create( template_id="miosa-sandbox", wait=True, # hold the call until the sandbox is ready external_workspace_id="acct-123", external_user_id="user-456", external_project_id="intake-portal-789", ) print(sandbox.id) # sbx_f6g7h8i9j0 ``` ### Step 2 - Give your agent an exec tool. The pattern below shows the structure. Substitute `callYourLLM` with your actual model call. **TypeScript** ```typescript // Tool the agent can call async function execInSandbox(command: string): Promise { const result = await sandbox.exec(command) return result.stdout + result.stderr } // Example: agent scaffolds a project const output = await execInSandbox("npx create-react-app /workspace/my-app --template minimal 2>&1 | tail -5") console.log(output) // Success! Created /workspace/my-app // Happy hacking! ``` **Python** ```python def exec_in_sandbox(command: str) -> str: result = sandbox.exec(command) return result.stdout + result.stderr # Example: agent scaffolds a project output = exec_in_sandbox( "npx create-react-app /workspace/my-app --template minimal 2>&1 | tail -5" ) print(output) # Success! Created /workspace/my-app # Happy hacking! ``` ### Step 3 - Let the agent write files directly. **TypeScript** ```typescript // Agent writes a component await sandbox.files.write( "/workspace/my-app/src/App.jsx", `export default function App() { return

Generated by my agent

; }` ) ``` **Python** ```python # Agent writes a component sandbox.files.write( "/workspace/my-app/src/App.jsx", """export default function App() { return

Generated by my agent

; }""", ) ``` ### Step 4 - Start the dev server, create a preview, stream it to your user. **TypeScript** ```typescript // Start the dev server in the background. This call returns right away. await sandbox.exec("nohup npm start > /tmp/app.log 2>&1 &", { cwd: "/workspace/my-app" }) const preview = await sandbox.previews.create(3000) const share = await sandbox.previews.share(preview.id as string) console.log("embed this URL in your product's UI:", share.share_url) // https://3000-abc12345.sandbox.miosa.ai?preview_token=miosa_pv_... ``` **Python** ```python # Start the dev server in the background. This call returns right away. sandbox.processes.start("cd /workspace/my-app && npm start", name="app") preview = sandbox.previews.create(port=3000) share = sandbox.previews.share(preview["id"]) print("embed this URL in your product's UI:", share["share_url"]) # https://3000-abc12345.sandbox.miosa.ai?preview_token=miosa_pv_... ``` The `share_url` is safe to put in an `<iframe>` in your end user's browser. It expires after the configured TTL. Your `msk_*` key never leaves your server. ### Step 5 - Take a screenshot of a Computer (optional). If your agent needs to verify GUI output or run browser-based tasks, use a Computer instead of (or alongside) a Sandbox. **TypeScript** ```typescript const computer = await miosa.computers.create({ name: "agent-desktop", template_type: "miosa-desktop", size: "small", }) // Let the agent observe the screen const png = await computer.desktop.screenshot() // → Buffer containing PNG bytes; send to your vision model // Let the agent interact await computer.desktop.click({ x: 800, y: 400 }) await computer.desktop.type("hello world") await computer.destroy() ``` **Python** ```python computer = miosa.computers.create( name="agent-desktop", template_type="miosa-desktop", size="small", ) # Let the agent observe the screen png = computer.desktop.screenshot() # → bytes containing PNG; send to your vision model # Let the agent interact computer.desktop.click(x=800, y=400) computer.desktop.type("hello world") computer.destroy() ``` ### Step 6 - Publish what the agent built. **TypeScript** ```typescript const result = await sandbox.deploy({ name: "intake-portal", outputPath: "/workspace/my-app/build", }) // Read the production URL from the response; do not construct it. console.log(result) ``` **Python** ```python result = sandbox.deploy( name="intake-portal", output_path="/workspace/my-app/build", ) # Read the production URL from the response; do not construct it. print(result) ``` ### Step 7 - Filter all sandboxes for this customer. **TypeScript** ```typescript const allForCustomer = await miosa.sandboxes.list({ externalWorkspaceId: "acct-123", }) console.log(`${allForCustomer.length} sandboxes for acct-123`) // 3 sandboxes for acct-123 ``` **Python** ```python all_for_customer = miosa.sandboxes.list(external_workspace_id="acct-123") print(f"{len(all_for_customer)} sandboxes for acct-123") # 3 sandboxes for acct-123 ``` ### Step 8 - Clean up. **TypeScript** ```typescript await sandbox.destroy() ``` **Python** ```python sandbox.destroy() ``` ### What you just did | Step | What happened | |------|--------------| | External attribution | Tagged every resource with your customer's IDs - no MIOSA accounts needed for your end users | | Exec as agent tool | Ran arbitrary shell commands inside an isolated VM from your agent loop | | `files.write` | Agent wrote generated code directly to the sandbox file system | | Share token | Minted a browser-safe URL for preview embedding - workspace key stays server-side | | Computer screenshot | Optionally gave the agent a real desktop with a vision-accessible screen | | `sandbox.deploy` | Shipped the agent's output to a permanent immutable URL | | `sandboxes.list` with attribution | Queried only resources belonging to one customer - cross-tenant leakage impossible |

pages.title: Docker Host
pages.description: Run containerized applications on a workspace Docker Host host, then confirm the app is live.
pages.markdown:
Use Docker Host when a workspace needs many always-on apps, funnels, APIs, or client sites without provisioning a separate production VM for each deployment.
The visible product name is Docker Host.
The CLI and API still use `docker_deploy` as the internal compatibility value.

## Step 1  -  Ensure the workspace Docker Host host.

```bash
miosa api POST /docker-deploy/hosts/ensure -d '{"workspace_id": "<workspace-id>"}'
miosa api GET /docker-deploy/hosts
```

The host must be active before an Docker Host publish can finish.

## Step 2  -  Publish the sandbox to Docker Host.

```bash
miosa deploy create --from-sandbox <sandbox-id> \
  --name my-app \
  --dir /workspace \
  --run-command "npm run start" \
  --port 3000 \
  --type docker_deploy \
  --wait \
  --wait-timeout 900s \
  --json
```

The response includes the Deployment and its `public_url`.
That URL may be a MIOSA-managed tenant URL, a workspace deployment domain, a tenant deployment domain, or an exact custom domain.
Always show the returned URL.

## Step 3  -  Confirm the app is live.

```bash
miosa deploy get <deployment-id> --json
miosa deploy requests <deployment-id>
```

`deploy get` shows the deployment's status, product and `public_url`.
`deploy requests` shows the recent HTTP requests served, so you can confirm real traffic reaches the app.

## What you just did

| Step | What happened |
|------|--------------|
| `docker-deploy ensure` | Created or returned the workspace Docker Host host |
| `sandbox publish --docker-deploy` | Published the sandbox artifact as a container on that workspace host |
| `docker-deploy doctor` | Proved the container and public URL are real |

> **Note: Read more**
>
> See [Docker Host](/docs/docker-host/docker-deploy) for the full deployment contract, and [Deploy overview](/docs/docker-host/overview) for the rest of the deploy surface.

pages.title: Install and authenticate
pages.description: Install the miosa CLI from npm, Homebrew, the install script or a release archive on macOS, Linux and Windows, verify 2.3, then sign in.
pages.markdown:
`miosa` is the official MIOSA command line tool. There is one `miosa` CLI: version 2.3. It runs on macOS, Linux and Windows.

## 1. Install

**macOS / Linux**

```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Miosa-osa/miosa-cli-go/main/install.sh | sh
```

macOS and Linux. Installs to `~/.local/bin/miosa` for non-root users and `/usr/local/bin/miosa` for root. Override with `INSTALL_DIR=/usr/local/bin`.

**Windows**

```bash
npm i -g @miosa/cli
```

Installs the `miosa` 2.3 CLI. The package resolves the right native build for your platform, including Windows x64. Works the same on macOS, Linux and Windows.

The installer does these steps:

1. Detects your OS and CPU.
2. Downloads the matching `miosa` binary and checks its SHA-256.
3. Installs the binary onto your `$PATH`.

Then sign in with `miosa login` (step 3 below): it opens your browser, and the key for this machine is stored in `~/.miosa/config.toml`.

Prefer another install path?

**Homebrew**

```bash
brew install --cask Miosa-osa/homebrew-tap/miosa
```

macOS only.

**Manual**

Download the archive for your platform from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa-cli-go/releases/latest) and place the binary in a directory on your `$PATH`.

```text
miosa_2.3.1_darwin_arm64.tar.gz
miosa_2.3.1_darwin_amd64.tar.gz
miosa_2.3.1_linux_arm64.tar.gz
miosa_2.3.1_linux_amd64.tar.gz
miosa_2.3.1_windows_amd64.zip
```

## 2. Verify

```bash
miosa --version
miosa version
```

These print `2.3.1`. If they print `1.x`, run `npm i -g @miosa/cli@latest` or `brew upgrade` to move onto the 2.x line.

## Windows

The npm install is the simplest path on Windows: `npm i -g @miosa/cli` resolves the `win32-x64` build (`@miosa/cli-win32-x64`) and puts `miosa` on your PATH.

To install by hand, download `miosa_2.3.1_windows_amd64.zip` from [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa-cli-go/releases/latest), extract `miosa.exe`, and add its folder to your `PATH`. In PowerShell:

```powershell
$dir = "$env:USERPROFILE\miosa"
Expand-Archive -Path "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\miosa_2.3.1_windows_amd64.zip" -DestinationPath $dir
[Environment]::SetEnvironmentVariable("Path", "$env:Path;$dir", "User")

# open a new terminal, then
miosa --version
```

`SetEnvironmentVariable` with the `User` scope makes the change permanent without admin rights; it only affects terminals opened after you run it. For the current session only, use `$env:Path += ";$dir"` instead.

Windows builds are x64 only. There is no windows/arm64 archive.

## Upgrading from 1.x

1.x was the Node CLI. 2.x is the same `miosa` command with a rewritten command surface, and the installs above now all give you 2.3.x.

What changed:

- **Sandbox commands lost the `sandbox` prefix.** `miosa sandbox create` is now `miosa create`.
- **Deployment work moved under `miosa deploy`.** The old `miosa app` and top-level `releases`, `rollback` and `builds` commands are now `miosa deploy` subcommands. New in 2.2: `miosa deploy create` publishes a sandbox, a git repository or a local directory.
- **Contexts became profiles.** `miosa context` is now `miosa profile`, stored in `~/.miosa/config.toml`.
- **Restored in 2.1.** Several 1.x command families came back, renamed: `miosa device` (any runtime kind), `miosa mcp`, and the `miosa host` families for containers, meshes, GitHub Actions runners, backups and tunnels.
- **Still removed from the public CLI:** the internal OSA tooling `actions`, `blueprint`, `changes`, `drift`, `evidence`, `capabilities` and `command-overview`. Action authority is server-side, and `miosa --help` replaces `command-overview`.

Renamed commands:

| 1.x | 2.3 |
|---|---|
| `miosa sandbox create` | `miosa create` |
| `miosa sandbox exec` | `miosa exec` |
| `miosa sandbox stop` / `resume` | `miosa stop` / `miosa resume` |
| `miosa sandbox fork` | `miosa fork` |
| `miosa sandbox wait` | `miosa wait` |
| `miosa sandbox prompt` | `miosa prompt` |
| `miosa sandbox write-file` | `miosa files write` |
| `miosa sandbox dev` | `miosa console` |
| `miosa sandbox doctor` | `miosa doctor` |
| `miosa sandbox publish` | `miosa deploy` |
| `miosa ls` | `miosa list` |
| `miosa rm` | `miosa destroy` |
| `miosa cp` | `miosa files cp` |
| `miosa watch` | `miosa events` |
| `miosa context` | `miosa profile` |
| `miosa app link` / `promote` / `rollback` | `miosa deploy` (`promote`, `rollback`) |
| `miosa releases` | `miosa deploy releases` |
| `miosa rollback` | `miosa deploy rollback` |
| `miosa builds` | `miosa deploy builds` |
| `miosa deploy destroy` | `miosa deploy rm` |
| `miosa deploy domain` | `miosa deploy domains` / `miosa deploy domain-add` |
| `miosa deploy env` | `miosa deploy env` / `miosa deploy env-set` |
| `miosa databases` | `miosa db` |
| `miosa api-keys` | `miosa api-key` |
| `miosa checkpoints` | `miosa checkpoint` |
| `miosa templates` | `miosa template` |
| `miosa schedules` / `miosa cron` | `miosa schedule` |
| `miosa connectors` | `miosa connections` |
| `miosa workspaces` / `miosa teams` | `miosa workspace` |
| `miosa devices` | `miosa device` |
| `miosa opencomputers` | `miosa host` |
| `miosa containers` | `miosa host container` |
| `miosa meshes` | `miosa host mesh` |
| `miosa gha-runners` | `miosa host gha-runner` |
| `miosa backups` | `miosa host backup` (snapshots under `miosa host backup snapshot`) |
| `miosa tunnel open` | `miosa host tunnel` |
| `miosa mcp ...` | `miosa mcp ...` (restored in 2.1) |
| `miosa capabilities` | `miosa catalog` |
| `miosa command-overview` | `miosa --help` |
| `miosa actions ...` | removed (authority is server-side) |

## Update

```bash
miosa update            # download and replace the binary
miosa update --check    # report only
miosa version
```

`miosa update` verifies the SHA-256 of the download against the release `checksums.txt`, and refuses to replace a Homebrew-managed binary (use `brew upgrade` there). A one-line notice appears at most once a day when a newer version exists; silence it with `--no-update-notice` or `MIOSA_NO_UPDATE_NOTICE=1`.

## Shell completion

```bash
miosa completion zsh      # bash, fish, powershell
```

Sandbox names, profiles, templates and agents complete from the live API.

## 3. Sign in

```bash
miosa login               # opens the browser, device-code sign in
miosa whoami              # organization, plan, credits, and the scopes your key holds
```

`miosa whoami` shows the user, organization, workspace, plan and the scopes the key holds.

### Sign in with a key

`miosa login --with-key` asks for a key with hidden input, and `--key-stdin` reads it from stdin. A key is never accepted as an argument.

```bash
miosa login --with-key
echo "$MIOSA_KEY" | miosa login --key-stdin
```

### Credential resolution

Credentials resolve in this order:

1. `--api-key`
2. `MIOSA_API_KEY`
3. the active profile in `~/.miosa/config.toml`

> **Tip**
>
> CI and other non-interactive environments use `MIOSA_API_KEY`. See [Config and profiles](/docs/cli/config) for multi-account setups.

## Sign out

```bash
miosa logout
```

Removes the stored key of the active profile. `miosa logout --all` deletes the config file for every profile.

## Diagnose

```bash
miosa doctor
```

Checks configuration, connectivity and authentication, and prints a fix for each failure.

- [Config and profiles](/docs/cli/config): Named sign-ins, api_url, workspace defaults.
- [Raw API access](/docs/cli/api): miosa api for anything the high-level commands do not cover.

pages.title: Sandboxes or Computers?
pages.description: Pick where your app or agent runs on MIOSA: a Sandbox for code, previews and a built-in browser, a Computer for a full desktop, Docker Host to publish.
pages.markdown:
Most work starts in a **Sandbox**.
Reach for a **Computer** when someone has to see and use a real screen.
When the result should stay online for your users, publish it with **Docker Host**.

- [Sandbox](/docs/develop/sandboxes): A fast, isolated machine for code. Run commands, edit files, install packages, open a live preview URL, and drive the built-in browser. Pauses when idle and wakes on the next request.
- [Computer](/docs/computers/overview): A durable cloud desktop. A real Linux screen with a browser, desktop apps, mouse and keyboard control, a live view a person can take over, and state that stays between sessions.

**Ready to go live?** [Docker Host](/docs/docker-host/docker-deploy) keeps what you built online at a stable URL, with your own domain, versions and rollback.

## Pick by what you need

| You want to | Use |
|---|---|
| Run code, build, test, or install packages | Sandbox |
| Show a live preview of an app while you build it | Sandbox |
| Let an agent browse and fill forms in a browser | Sandbox, with its [built-in browser](/docs/browser-use) |
| Use desktop apps, or anything that needs a full screen | Computer |
| Keep logins, files and a desktop around for days | Computer |
| Let a person watch and take over an agent's screen | Either: the sandbox browser or the computer desktop both have a live view |
| Keep an app online for your users | Docker Host |

> **Tip: Not sure? Start with a Sandbox**
>
> Sandboxes start fastest and cost the least.
> Move to a Computer only when the work truly needs a desktop.

## Create one

**CLI**

```bash
# A sandbox for code and previews
miosa create

# A computer with a full desktop
miosa computer create --size small
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { Miosa } from "@miosa/sdk";

const miosa = new Miosa({ apiKey: process.env.MIOSA_API_KEY! });

const sandbox = await miosa.sandboxes.create({ templateId: "miosa-sandbox" });
const computer = await miosa.computers.create({ name: "research-desk", size: "small" });
```

## Often you use both

A typical agent product writes and runs code in a Sandbox, uses a Computer when a task needs a real desktop, and publishes the finished app with Docker Host.
See [Agent device selection](/docs/guides/agent-device-selection) for the full decision guide, including when an agent needs no machine at all.

## Next steps

- [Quickstart](/docs/quickstart): create your first sandbox in minutes.
- [Computers](/docs/computers/overview): lifecycle, streaming and embedding.
- [Build an app like...](/docs/build): pick a product and get a step-by-step guide.

pages.title: Build and deploy a Next.js app
pages.description: Build a small Next.js app in a Sandbox, preview it, publish it as an immutable Deployment, prove it is live, connect a custom domain, and roll back safely - with the miosa CLI 2.x and the SDKs.
pages.markdown:
This tutorial takes a small Next.js application from an empty Sandbox to a verified production URL. You will create a Sandbox, write the app, review a temporary Preview, publish an immutable Version, verify the stable Deployment URL, connect `app.example.com`, and learn rollback before you need it. Do it now Deploy your first app Turn a repo or a sandbox into a stable production URL with immutable versions and rollback. - [New deployment](https://miosa.ai/deploy/new): (opens the MIOSA console in a new tab) miosa deploy create --from-sandbox my-box --wait Publish a sandbox, a git repo (--git) or a local directory (--dir). Add --type docker_deploy for App Engine. Next [Publishing guide](/docs/docker-host/publishing) > **Note: What this tutorial preserves** > > Publishing does not destroy or convert the Sandbox. > The Sandbox remains a development environment, while the Release and Deployment become independent production resources. ## What you will create | Resource | Example | Purpose | |---|---|---| | Sandbox | `hello-nextjs` | Mutable place to create and test the application. | | Preview | API-returned temporary URL | Review the live development server before publishing. | | Deployment | `hello-nextjs` | Stable production identity and version history. | | Platform URL | API-returned `public_url` | Immediate production access without customer DNS. | | Custom domain | `app.example.com` | Optional customer-owned hostname attached to the Deployment. | ## Before you start You need: - A MIOSA User with access to the intended Organization and Workspace. - A workspace API key stored only in a server or terminal environment. - The MIOSA CLI installed (v2.2 or later). - Permission to create Sandboxes, publish Deployments, and configure domains. - Access to the DNS provider only if you complete the custom-domain section. ```bash export MIOSA_API_KEY="msk_u_..." miosa whoami ``` Confirm that the response identifies the expected Organization and Workspace before creating anything. > **Caution: Do not continue in the wrong Organization** > > Resource IDs are not a substitute for checking the active customer boundary. > If the CLI reports the wrong Organization or Workspace, correct that context before creating the Sandbox or Deployment. ## Step 1: Create the Sandbox **CLI** ```bash miosa create hello-nextjs \ --template nextjs \ --ttl 1h \ --wait \ --json ``` Save the returned Sandbox id: ```bash export SANDBOX_ID="" ``` **TypeScript** ```typescript import { Miosa } from "@miosa/sdk"; const miosa = new Miosa({ apiKey: process.env.MIOSA_API_KEY! }); const sandbox = await miosa.sandboxes.create({ name: "hello-nextjs", templateId: "nextjs", }); console.log(sandbox.id); ``` **Python** ```python import os from miosa import Miosa miosa = Miosa(api_key=os.environ["MIOSA_API_KEY"]) sandbox = miosa.sandboxes.create(name="hello-nextjs", template_id="nextjs") print(sandbox.id) ``` **Expected result:** the Sandbox reaches a usable running state. If creation remains pending, inspect the returned capacity or readiness reason before retrying. Do not create repeated Sandboxes while the first request is still progressing. ## Step 2: Create the Next.js application Scaffold the app inside the Sandbox, then replace `app/page.tsx`. **CLI** ```bash miosa exec hello-nextjs --cwd /workspace -- bash -lc 'pnpm create next-app@latest hello-nextjs --typescript --eslint --app --no-tailwind --use-pnpm --yes' ``` Write the page file locally, then copy it into the Sandbox: ```bash miosa files cp ./page.tsx hello-nextjs:/workspace/hello-nextjs/app/page.tsx ``` Build it: ```bash miosa exec hello-nextjs --cwd /workspace/hello-nextjs --timeout 300 -- pnpm build ``` **TypeScript** ```typescript const page = `export default function Home() { return (

Deployed with MIOSA

Hello from MIOSA

); }`; await sandbox.exec.run( "cd /workspace && pnpm create next-app@latest hello-nextjs --typescript --eslint --app --no-tailwind --use-pnpm --yes", ); await sandbox.files.write("/workspace/hello-nextjs/app/page.tsx", page); for await (const event of sandbox.exec.stream( "cd /workspace/hello-nextjs && pnpm build", )) { console.log(event); } ``` **Python** ```python page = '''export default function Home() { return (

Hello from MIOSA

); }''' sandbox.exec.run( "cd /workspace && pnpm create next-app@latest hello-nextjs --typescript --eslint --app --no-tailwind --use-pnpm --yes", ) sandbox.files.write_file("/workspace/hello-nextjs/app/page.tsx", page) for event in sandbox.exec_stream("cd /workspace/hello-nextjs && pnpm build"): print(event) ``` **Expected result:** the build command exits with status `0` and Next.js reports a successful build. ## Step 3: Start and preview the application Start the server as a background process so it keeps running after the CLI disconnects, then expose port 3000. **CLI** ```bash miosa process start hello-nextjs \ --name web \ --cwd /workspace/hello-nextjs \ -- pnpm start --hostname 0.0.0.0 --port 3000 miosa preview create hello-nextjs 3000 --name web --json ``` **TypeScript** ```typescript const preview = await sandbox.previews.create(3000); console.log(preview.url); ``` **Python** ```python preview = sandbox.previews.create(port=3000, label="app") print(preview["url"]) ``` Open the exact Preview URL returned by MIOSA. **Expected result:** the page displays "Hello from MIOSA." > **Tip: Preview is not production** > > The Preview reflects the current Sandbox process and files. > It can change immediately and can disappear when the Sandbox stops. > The stable production URL is created during publishing. ## Step 4: Publish a Deployment `miosa deploy create` publishes a new Deployment and makes it live. Give it the Sandbox as its source, the path the app lives at inside the Sandbox, and the command that serves it. **CLI** ```bash miosa deploy create \ --from-sandbox hello-nextjs \ --name hello-nextjs \ --dir /workspace/hello-nextjs \ --port 3000 \ --run-command "pnpm start --hostname 0.0.0.0 --port 3000" \ --wait \ --json ``` Add `--type docker_deploy` to publish through Docker Host instead of the default runtime. Save these values from the response: ```bash export DEPLOYMENT_ID="" export PUBLIC_URL="" ``` **TypeScript** ```typescript const result = await sandbox.deploy({ name: "hello-nextjs", path: "/workspace/hello-nextjs", port: 3000, runCommand: "pnpm start --hostname 0.0.0.0 --port 3000", }); // Read public_url from the response. Do not construct a production hostname. console.log(result); ``` **Python** ```python result = sandbox.deploy( name="hello-nextjs", path="/workspace/hello-nextjs", port=3000, run_command="pnpm start --hostname 0.0.0.0 --port 3000", ) # Read public_url from the response. Do not construct a production hostname. print(result) ``` Always use the returned `public_url`. Do not construct a production hostname from the slug, Organization name, or Workspace name. **Expected result:** the response identifies the Deployment, candidate Release, promoted Version, and `public_url`. ## Step 5: Prove production A successful build is not enough. Confirm the Deployment resolved to a live Version and that the public URL answers. ```bash miosa deploy get hello-nextjs --json curl --fail --silent --show-error "$PUBLIC_URL" | grep "Hello from MIOSA" miosa deploy observe hello-nextjs ``` **Expected result:** the Deployment reports a running state with a `public_url`, the public response contains "Hello from MIOSA", and `observe` shows the request. ## Step 6: Connect a custom domain This step is optional. The platform URL remains valid while DNS is being configured. ```bash miosa deploy domain-add hello-nextjs app.example.com ``` MIOSA displays the required DNS record and verification target. Copy those values exactly into the DNS provider. For a normal subdomain, the record generally has this shape: | Type | Host | Value | Proxying | |---|---|---|---| | `CNAME` | `app` | The target shown by MIOSA | Disabled until verification completes | Do not copy `example.com` literally. Use a hostname controlled by the customer and the target displayed in the live MIOSA domain flow. Check public DNS, then verify: ```bash dig app.example.com CNAME +short miosa deploy domain-verify hello-nextjs ``` **Expected result:** the domain moves through DNS verification, certificate issuance, and routing until HTTPS is active. > **Caution: Wildcard and exact domains are different** > > An Organization-level deployment domain can generate many application hostnames beneath one parent domain. > An exact custom domain attaches one chosen hostname directly to one Deployment. > Follow the record shown for the domain type you selected. > See [Domains](/docs/docker-host/domains). ## Step 7: Publish an update safely Change the heading in `app/page.tsx`, rebuild in the Sandbox, and publish again. ```bash miosa exec hello-nextjs --cwd /workspace/hello-nextjs --timeout 300 -- pnpm build miosa deploy create \ --from-sandbox hello-nextjs \ --name hello-nextjs \ --dir /workspace/hello-nextjs \ --port 3000 \ --run-command "pnpm start --hostname 0.0.0.0 --port 3000" \ --wait \ --json ``` Reusing `--name` targets the existing Deployment, so its identity, stable URL, domains, bindings, and release history are preserved while a new Version is promoted. Run the proof steps again after the new Version is promoted. ## Step 8: Understand rollback before you need it List the Deployment versions: ```bash miosa deploy versions hello-nextjs --json ``` If the new Version is unhealthy, return to the earlier ready one: ```bash miosa deploy rollback hello-nextjs --to ``` Rollback repoints the active Version in seconds without a rebuild. It does not change the Deployment identity or require a new domain. See [Rollback](/docs/docker-host/rollback). ## Common failures and recovery | Symptom | Likely cause | Safe action | Proof after repair | |---|---|---|---| | Sandbox creation remains pending | Requested capacity is not ready or the request is still progressing. | Inspect the readiness reason and wait or select compatible capacity. | The original Sandbox reaches a usable state. | | Preview returns an error | The Next.js process is stopped, bound to the wrong interface, or using another port. | Start it on `0.0.0.0:3000` with `miosa process start` and recreate the Preview. | The Preview returns "Hello from MIOSA." | | Publish reports Docker Host is unavailable | The Workspace Docker Host Host is not active. | Confirm the Workspace has an active Docker Host Host, then retry the same `miosa deploy create ... --type docker_deploy`. | Publish returns a Deployment and `public_url`. | | Build succeeds but the application is not live | Promotion, container health, or routing proof has not completed. | Inspect the publish result and run `miosa deploy get` and `miosa deploy observe`. | The public URL responds with the expected content. | | DNS remains pending | The record has not propagated, uses the wrong host, or points to the wrong target. | Compare public DNS with the exact record shown by MIOSA and keep proxying disabled during verification. | `miosa deploy domain-verify` reports DNS verified and TLS active. | | The custom hostname opens another application | The hostname was attached in the wrong Organization or to the wrong Deployment. | Stop and inspect ownership and route bindings before changing DNS again. | The domain resolves to the intended Deployment id and active Version. | | A new publish causes a regression | The candidate passed build but application behavior is incorrect. | Roll back to the earlier ready Version. | The stable URL serves the previous known-good content. | ## Completion checklist - [ ] The Sandbox exists in the intended Organization and Workspace. - [ ] The Next.js production build exits successfully. - [ ] The Preview displays "Hello from MIOSA." - [ ] Publishing returns a Deployment id and API-selected `public_url`. - [ ] The public URL returns the expected content. - [ ] The custom domain is verified and TLS-active, if configured. - [ ] An earlier ready Version is identifiable for rollback. - [ ] The Sandbox can be removed without deleting the Deployment. ## Continue from here - [Add Postgres](/docs/data/postgres): Bind durable application data without putting a database inside the application container. - [Add secrets](/docs/security/secrets): Provide sensitive runtime configuration without committing it to source. - [Understand publishing](/docs/docker-host/publishing): Learn the full Release, Version, promotion, proof, and retry contract. - [Operate domains](/docs/docker-host/domains): Configure deployment domains, exact custom domains, verification, TLS, and recovery. ## Next steps - [Publish from a sandbox](/docs/docker-host/publishing): Static, dynamic, and App Engine publishes with proof. - [Attach a custom domain](/docs/docker-host/domains): DNS verification, TLS, and route caching. - [Roll back in seconds](/docs/docker-host/rollback): Re-point a deployment at an older version with no rebuild. - [Return to Learning Paths](/docs/learn): Choose the agent, desktop, or white-label journey next.

pages.title: What you can build with MIOSA
pages.description: Concrete product patterns for MIOSA sandboxes, computers, agent runtimes, generated artifacts, previews, and deployments.
pages.markdown:
MIOSA is the infrastructure underneath AI products. Your product, or your agent, gets real machines and real URLs:

- **Sandboxes** for code, files, builds, and previews.
- **Computers** for browsers and full desktops, with human handoff.
- **Agents** you dispatch, stream, and collect artifacts from.
- **Deployments and Docker Host** for immutable releases on stable URLs, with custom domains and rollback.
- **Platform features** for white-label products: organizations, workspaces, scoped keys, domains, and usage metering.

```text
User request
  -> agent plans work
  -> sandbox does code, files, builds, tests, artifacts
  -> computer does browser, desktop, screenshots, manual-style tasks
  -> MIOSA streams events and previews
  -> deployment ships the finished app
```

MIOSA is not just a remote shell. It is the execution layer for products that need AI agents to do real work safely.

## Browse the Build gallery

Every product shape below has a step-by-step guide in the [Build gallery](/docs/build): the primitives you need, an architecture diagram, six steps from API key to custom domain, and a prompt you can hand to your coding agent.

- [AI app builders](/docs/build#bg-app-builders): Lovable, Bolt, v0, Replit-style: prompt to a deployed app.
- [Run coding agents](/docs/build#bg-run-coding-agents): Claude Code, Codex, Cursor in the cloud.
- [Autonomous agents](/docs/build#bg-autonomous-agents): Agents with their own machine that finish work.
- [Browser and computer-use agents](/docs/build#bg-browser-computer-agents): Agents that drive a real browser or desktop.
- [AI chat and companions](/docs/build#bg-chat-companions): Assistants and always-on companions.
- [Answer engines](/docs/build#bg-answer-engines): Research products that cite their sources.
- [Multi-agent](/docs/build#bg-multi-agent): One request, many agents in parallel.
- [Voice agents](/docs/build#bg-voice-agents): Agents that talk and act on calls.
- [AI design tools](/docs/build#bg-design-tools): Prompt to a designed UI or asset.
- [AI video and creative](/docs/build#bg-video-creative): Generate, edit, and produce media.
- [Vertical AI apps](/docs/build#bg-vertical-ai): Agents for a specific industry workflow.
- [Internal tools](/docs/build#bg-internal-tools): A company OS where agents, apps, and data live together.

---

## Builders and developers

- **Prompt-to-app builders**: Lovable and v0-style products where an agent turns a prompt into a live app, then fixes and republishes it.

  `Sandbox`
  `Preview`
  `Deployment`

  [Start here: build a Lovable-style app](/docs/build/lovable)
- **Coding agents in sandboxes**: Run Claude Code, Codex, or OSA inside a persistent sandbox with the files, packages, and shell a real repo needs.

  `Sandbox`
  `Agent runs`
  `Snapshots`

  [Start here: run coding agents](/docs/build/run-agents)
- **Code execution products**: Run untrusted user code in an isolated microVM, stream stdout, and collect the artifacts it produces.

  `Sandbox`
  `Events`
  `Artifacts`

  [Start here: streaming code execution](/docs/cookbook/streaming-code-execution)
- **Evaluation and benchmarking harnesses**: Run repeatable evals and benchmark bursts on real runtimes, with per-run evidence instead of mocks.

  `Sandbox`
  `Benchmarks`
  `Events`

  [Start here: evaluations](/docs/evaluations) and [benchmarks](/docs/benchmarks)

## Agent product teams

- **Always-on agents with their own computer**: dots and Grok Bot-style agents that keep a device, files, a browser, and long-running jobs across sessions.

  `Sandbox`
  `Computer`
  `Agent devices`

  [Start here: agent devices](/docs/guides/agent-devices)
- **Browser automation agents**: Browser use runs inside every sandbox: an agent drives a real browser over CDP while a human can watch.

  `Sandbox`
  `Browser use`
  `Live viewer`

  [Start here: browser use](/docs/browser-use)
- **Desktop and computer-use agents**: Agents that screenshot, click, and type on a durable Linux desktop, with human takeover when they get stuck.

  `Computer`
  `Computer use`
  `Embedding`

  [Start here: computer use](/docs/computer-use)

## Platform and agency teams

- **White-label agent platforms**: Lumen-style platforms with your brand, your domains, and your end users, while MIOSA runs behind them.

  `Org and workspaces`
  `Branding`
  `Attribution`

  [Start here: Platform builder guide](/docs/platform/overview)
- **Agency client platforms**: Northwind-style agencies that give each client an isolated workspace, build their apps, and hand over domains.

  `Multi-tenant`
  `Quotas`
  `Custom domains`

  [Start here: Platform builder guide](/docs/platform/overview#northwind-agency-client-work)
- **Internal Business OS for teams**: An Acme Corp-style internal platform where your team agents, apps, and data live together on MIOSA.

  `Sandbox`
  `Connectors`
  `Data`

  [Start here: internal Business OS](/docs/build/business-os)

## Infrastructure and enterprise

- **Bring-your-own machines**: OpenComputers enrolls machines you own so agents can run commands and files on your own hardware.

  `OpenComputers`
  `Hosts`
  `Meshes`

  [Start here: OpenComputers](/docs/opencomputers)
- **Enterprise data with Fractal**: Fractal gives enterprise data a governed home, so agents work against your systems with the right controls.

  `Fractal`
  `Data`
  `Governance`

  [Start here: Fractal enterprise data](/docs/data/fractal)

> **Note: Capability labels matter**
>
> MIOSA can host the application, data, workflow, customer boundary, and deployment for these products today.
> Specialized model and media execution may use connected providers.
> Managed GPU execution and customer-cloud placement remain gated until the availability page marks them shipped.
> See [Availability and roadmap](/docs/availability).

---

## Product primitives

| Primitive | Use it for | Not for |
|---|---|---|
| **Sandbox** | Code, files, commands, package installs, builds, tests, generated artifacts, preview servers | GUI/browser interaction |
| **Computer** | Browser automation, screenshots, mouse/keyboard, desktop apps, visual QA, user handoff | Headless code builds that do not need a desktop |
| **Deployment** | Stable public app/site/API URLs, versions, releases, rollback | Active development iteration |
| **Docker Host** | Many customer apps running as isolated containers on one workspace Docker Host host | Generic sandbox development |
| **Artifacts** | Files created by agents: PDFs, docs, images, reports, exports, screenshots | Hidden temporary state |
| **Events** | Real-time UI updates: tool calls, stdout, file writes, preview readiness, deployment status | Long-term storage |

## Build an agent-company product

Several modern AI products package the same high-level pattern: an agent, a
persistent workspace, connected apps, a browser or cloud device, jobs, files,
and generated deliverables. MIOSA exposes those primitives directly, so you can
build your own version inside your product.

```text
Your product UI
  -> agent configuration
  -> device policy
  -> sandbox/computer/local device
  -> connected accounts and managed connectors
  -> streamed tool calls and events
  -> files, artifacts, previews, jobs, and deployments
```

| Product shape | MIOSA primitives |
|---|---|
| Always-on virtual device | Persistent sandbox or computer, primary device policy, snapshots, jobs |
| Agent team | Orchestrator, child sandboxes, child computers, shared artifacts, event stream |
| Mini-app builder | Next.js sandbox, preview URL, artifact panel, publish flow |
| Operator agent | Browser computer, connected apps, schedules, approvals, memory |
| Design/research agent | Web research, a managed research connector, files, browser screenshots |
| 24/7 monitoring job | Scheduled trigger, persistent device, app connector, notifications |

The important architecture point is that the agent should work in a MIOSA
device. The local CLI, MCP client, or your backend orchestrates, but files,
commands, browser actions, previews, and artifacts live in the assigned runtime.

See [Build an agent-company platform](/docs/guides/build-agent-company),
[What MIOSA agents can do](/docs/guides/agent-capabilities),
[Agent devices](/docs/guides/agent-devices), and
[Agent orchestration](/docs/guides/agent-orchestration) for the full model.

> **Tip: Default agent loop**
>
> For AI coding products, the default loop should be sandbox-first: create or
> resume a sandbox, write files inside `/workspace`, run commands inside the
> sandbox, show the preview, snapshot progress, then publish.

---

## Example: generated app builder

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant User
  participant Product as Your product
  participant Agent
  participant S as MIOSA Sandbox
  participant D as MIOSA Deploy

  User->>Product: Build a landing page for my customer
  Product->>Agent: Start build task
  Agent->>S: get_or_create(name, template_id=nextjs)
  Agent->>S: write /workspace/app/page.tsx
  Agent->>S: exec npm install && npm run build
  S-->>Product: stream stdout, stderr, file events
  Agent->>S: start preview on port 3000
  S-->>Product: preview_url
  User->>Product: Make the hero more premium
  Agent->>S: patch files and rerun checks
  User->>Product: Ship it
  Agent->>D: publish /workspace
  D-->>Product: public_url
```

Your frontend can show the same work stream users expect from modern AI
builders: tool calls, command output, generated files, preview links, screenshots,
and final deployment URLs.

---

## Example: artifact workspace

Use a sandbox when the output is a file, not a deployed app.

```text
User asks for a proposal
  -> agent writes Python or Node generator
  -> sandbox creates proposal.html
  -> sandbox renders proposal.pdf
  -> sandbox creates proposal.docx
  -> product shows artifacts in a side panel
  -> user downloads or asks for edits
```

Good artifact outputs:

- client proposals
- pitch decks
- data reports
- PDF invoices
- SVG diagrams
- PNG charts
- HTML previews
- ZIP bundles
- code archives

---

## Two sandbox choices, and both cover the jobs

| Choice | Intended job |
|---|---|
| The default sandbox (`miosa-sandbox`) | Everything in one place: Python and Node execution, generated web apps, reports and artifacts, browser testing, and database-backed apps. |
| The desktop (`miosa-desktop`) | GUI work and human takeover, when a person needs to see and drive the screen. |

The product shape stays the same: start the default sandbox, let the agent work inside it.

---

## What to show users in your product

Users should not have to understand VM internals. Show them useful work:

- current task and plan
- tool calls
- command output
- files created or edited
- artifacts generated
- preview URL
- screenshots from browser checks
- deployment URL
- rollback/version history
- credits and runtime usage

The message should be: "Your agent is working in a real cloud workspace. You can
watch it, inspect the files, preview the result, and ship when ready."

---

## See also

- [See apps you can build](/docs/build): Step-by-step guides for 20+ product shapes, from Lovable and Bolt to Devin and an internal Business OS.
- [Build an agent-company platform](/docs/guides/build-agent-company): Map always-on devices and operator agents onto MIOSA primitives.
- [Backend orchestration](/docs/integrations/backend-orchestration): Build the API layer that dispatches prompts into sandboxes, computers, and local devices.
- [Agent orchestration](/docs/guides/agent-orchestration): Coordinate sandbox agents, computer agents, artifacts, events, and deployments.
- [Sandboxes](/docs/develop/sandboxes): Persistent code workspaces for files, commands, previews, snapshots, and publishing.
- [Computers](/docs/computers/overview): Desktop/browser runtimes for screenshots, clicks, uploads, visual QA, and handoff.

pages.description: Learn MIOSA your way - read the basics, learn the words, or play the games - then follow five steps from zero to production.
pages.markdown:
We know our docs are a lot. MIOSA is essentially an AWS-class cloud, made as simple as we could make it. AWS and GCP have twenty sidebars and a hundred services; we have a handful of building blocks.

Not everything is AI, and using AI doesn't mean you understand what you're building. Learn how MIOSA actually works, step by step, so you can build, connect and ship with confidence.

Four steps, in order. Your progress is saved as you go.

1. [Learn the words](/docs/glossary)

   A 7-unit path from the words to building a product. Real puzzles with no timers, and every unit is open from the start.

   Put it to work: add your brand, tenants, domains and billing, and ship a product on MIOSA.

pages.title: MIOSA Glossary
pages.description: Plain-language definitions for MIOSA resources, services, deployment stages, domains, on-premises infrastructure, OpenComputers, Optimal, agent workflows, data, and billing. Search by topic, study with flashcards, and link straight to any term.
pages.markdown:
Plain-language definitions for every MIOSA resource, API field, and billing term, with a shareable link for each. See how they fit together in the [Product model](/docs/concepts).

## Core primitives

The things you create, build, publish and run.

### App Engine Host

An App Engine Host is an always-on machine for one Workspace that runs many of its apps as separate containers.

Use it when a Workspace publishes lots of small apps, funnels, or client sites and a new production VM for each would be wasteful. MIOSA still routes, secures, and meters each Deployment individually.

In MIOSA, a Northwind Agency workspace with fifteen client sites runs them all on one App Engine Host. The host is capacity, not an access boundary.

Related: Deployment, Workspace, Runtime Instance, Host, App Engine

### Artifact

An Artifact is a file or result worth keeping from a build, command, evaluation, or Agent Run: a report, a screenshot, a build folder, a CSV.

Use Artifacts to hand outputs to people. The Sandbox stays the working surface; you export exactly the paths a user should receive instead of asking them to scrape terminal output.

In MIOSA, an agent writes `/workspace/artifacts/report.pdf`, your backend calls an export for that path, and your user clicks Download. A saved Sandbox state is a Snapshot, and a published app is a Release.

Related: Snapshot, Release, Agent Run

### Background process

A Background process is a command you start in a sandbox that keeps running on its own, such as a dev server or a long job. Its output is kept, so you can read it later.

Use `exec` for a command whose result you wait for, and a background process for servers and anything long.

In MIOSA, `miosa process start my-box --name api -- node server.js` starts one, and `miosa ps` lists what is running.

Related: Exec, Sandbox, Streaming exec, Preview, Logs

### Build

A Build installs dependencies and compiles or packages your source into something that can run. MIOSA does it in an isolated Builder from the frozen source snapshot.

You mostly let MIOSA pick: it detects a Dockerfile, a language manifest, or plain static files. Override with a build command when the defaults are not right.

In MIOSA, `miosa deploy builds team-portal` lists a deployment's builds, and a failed build leaves the old Version live.

Related: Builder, Publish, Release, Dockerfile, BuildSpec

### Builder

A Builder is the isolated worker that handles one publish. It takes the frozen source, runs the build, stores the result, and exits.

You rarely touch it directly. It is why a build cannot be influenced by whatever you are doing in the Sandbox at the same time, and why builds are repeatable.

In MIOSA, a publish for Lumen's team portal starts a Builder, which installs dependencies, runs the build command, and produces the Release. Builder time is billed in seconds during the publish.

Related: Publish, Release, Build, BuildSpec

### BuildSpec

A BuildSpec is a small JSON document that overrides MIOSA's default install, build, and start commands for a Sandbox or Deployment.

Use it when auto-detect guesses wrong, for example a monorepo with an unusual build step.

In MIOSA, a BuildSpec can set `install` to `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `build` to `pnpm build`, and `start` to your server command, plus environment variables.

Related: Build, Builder, Dynamic deployment, Template

### Checkpoint

A Checkpoint is a fast, sandbox-local restore point. Take one before a risky step, such as upgrading dependencies, and restore from it if the step goes wrong.

Snapshots are the portable history of a machine and the basis for forking. Checkpoints are the quick, in-place kind. Use a Snapshot when you want to move or copy a machine, and a Checkpoint for a fast undo.

In MIOSA, `miosa checkpoint create my-box --comment "before deps"` takes one.

Related: Snapshot, Restore, Named snapshot, Sandbox

### Computer

A Computer is a durable cloud desktop: a real Linux machine with a screen, a browser, files, and a shell that you or an agent can operate, and that keeps its state when stopped.

Use one when the work depends on pixels or sessions: clicking through a website, a logged-in browser, desktop apps, or a human taking over where an agent stopped. For code and builds, a Sandbox is cheaper and faster.

In MIOSA, a Northwind Agency operator watches an agent fill in a client's web form on a Computer, then takes over the same desktop to finish. Sizes run from `xs` to `xl`, and `small` is the default.

Related: Desktop session, MIOSA-managed Computer, OpenComputer, Readiness, Capability, Computer use

### Container image

A Container image is an app that is already built and packaged, published to a registry like GitHub Container Registry or Docker Hub.

Use it when you build your app elsewhere and only want MIOSA to run it. MIOSA pulls the image and starts it without a build step. A private registry needs a registry secret.

In MIOSA, `miosa service deploy shop API --image ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4 --port 8080` deploys an image.

Related: Service, Container, Dockerfile, Build, Release

### Cron job

A Cron job runs one command on a schedule you write as a cron expression, for example every five minutes or every night at 3 am.

Use it for work nobody should have to remember: a health check, a nightly export, a cleanup. The command runs in the Sandbox you attach it to, so that Sandbox needs the script and the credentials it uses. You can also trigger a run right now to test it.

In MIOSA, cron jobs are created through the MCP `cron_create` tool, and agents can also be started on a schedule with `miosa agent triggers add`.

Related: Sandbox, Job, Webhook

### Deployment

A Deployment is the durable production identity of your app: its name, URL, history of Versions, domains, settings, and attached data. The Deployment stays put while the code behind it changes.

Use it as "the live app". When you publish and promote a new Version, the same Deployment and URL serve the new code. Databases and storage attach to the Deployment, not to each Release.

In MIOSA, Lumen's `team-portal` Deployment keeps `team-portal.example-org.miosa.app` and the custom domain `portal.example.net` stable across every Version.

Related: Version, Release, Promotion, Domain, Binding, Environment, Runtime Instance, Static deployment, Dynamic deployment, App Engine, Service

### Desired state

Desired state is what MIOSA has been told a resource should look like: running, stopped, on this size, with this configuration.

It matters because MIOSA keeps comparing the world with that record. If a host restarts and a Computer you wanted running is not, MIOSA brings it back instead of waiting for you.

In MIOSA, you stop a Computer on purpose and its desired state is stopped, so it stays stopped through host maintenance. A Computer that was running is restored and verified.

Related: Reconciliation, Control plane

### Desktop session

A desktop session is the live connection you use to see and control a Computer's screen. It is the window onto the machine, not the machine itself.

Use it when you or an agent need to watch, click, and type. Closing the session leaves the Computer running or stopped exactly as it was, and you can open a new one later.

In MIOSA, a support lead opens a live viewer onto the Computer an agent was using at Acme Corp, takes over to finish a task, and closes the viewer without ending anything.

Related: Computer, Readiness, Agent Run

### Dockerfile

A Dockerfile is a text recipe that says how to assemble a container image: the base system, the files to copy, and the command to run.

If one exists in your app's output folder, MIOSA builds your app from it. You can also use it to build a custom Sandbox template.

In MIOSA, sandboxes include Docker Engine, so you can test a Dockerfile inside a Sandbox first, then publish through App Engine.

Related: Container, Build, Template, App Engine

### Dynamic deployment

A Dynamic deployment runs code on a server: APIs, server-rendered pages, WebSockets, and background workers. MIOSA starts it, checks it, and keeps it running.

Choose it when the app must do work per request. You give a run command and a port so MIOSA knows how to start and reach it.

In MIOSA, `miosa deploy create --from-sandbox my-box --port 3000 --run-command "npm start" --wait` publishes a running server.

Related: Static deployment, Runtime Instance, Health check, Replica

### Environment

An environment is a named starting setup for new machines: which repositories to clone, which variables and secret files to inject, and which of your credentials the machine may use.

Use environments so every new Sandbox or Computer starts ready, and so staging and production do not share settings. Every Workspace has a default named `base`.

For Deployments, a Deployment Environment is the scope where variables, secrets, and data bindings apply. Every Project gets `production` and `staging`, and you can add others such as `preview/pr-42`.

Related: Template, Environment variable, Secret, Deployment, Workspace

### Exec

Exec runs one command inside a Sandbox and returns its output and exit code. Examples are `npm install`, `python app.py`, or `npm run build`.

It is how agents and scripts do the work: install, build, test, start a server. The CLI exits with the remote command's exit code, so it drops straight into scripts and CI.

In MIOSA, a Lumen agent runs the build through Exec and reads the output to decide what to fix next. A command has 30 seconds by default and 300 at most; run anything longer as a background process.

Related: Sandbox, Job, Event stream (SSE), Computer, Logs, Background process, Streaming exec

### Fork

A Fork creates a new Sandbox from a copy of an existing one's current state, leaving the original running. After the fork they are independent.

Use it to try something risky on a copy, or to give each customer a fresh copy of a prepared setup.

In MIOSA, `miosa fork my-box --ttl 2h` forks a running Sandbox. Forking from a named snapshot also works after the original machine is gone.

Related: Snapshot, Sandbox, Pause and resume

### Health check

A Health check is a quick request to a URL path in your running app. A success response (2xx) says it is healthy, so MIOSA sends it traffic.

Add one so a broken release never takes over. MIOSA only moves traffic to a new Version once its instances pass, and removes instances that stop passing.

In MIOSA, set `health_check_path` on a dynamic publish. Static sites skip it because there is no app process to check.

Related: Runtime Instance, Dynamic deployment, Promotion, Heartbeat

### Idle sleep

Idle sleep stops a Service that has had no requests for a while, so it does not run when nobody uses it. The next request wakes it and waits for it to start.

It applies only to services with a public address, because a request is what wakes them. Workers and private services never sleep. On the Free plan, services always sleep.

In MIOSA, set it with the `sleep` setting: `{enabled, idle_s}`. A sleeping release shows the state `sleeping`.

Related: Service, Public address, Release, Idle timeout

### Idle timeout

An Idle timeout pauses a persistent Sandbox after it has been inactive for a period, instead of waiting for the fixed Timeout.

Turn it on to save money on Sandboxes people forget about. Commands, file writes, preview traffic, and terminal input all count as activity and reset the clock.

In MIOSA, `miosa create my-box --idle-timeout 15m` pauses it after fifteen quiet minutes. It only applies when you set it, and a paused Sandbox wakes on request.

Related: Timeout, Pause and resume, Preview

### Job
