Related: Placement, Data residency, Sandbox, Computer, Customer-cloud region

### Replica

A Replica is one of several identical copies of a dynamic app running at the same time. More replicas handle more visitors and keep the app up if one fails.

By default a dynamic service has one. Raise it when you need more capacity or resilience.

In MIOSA, you set `desired_replicas`, and the reconciler spreads copies across hosts, and across zones where possible. Traffic is shared among healthy replicas.

Related: Runtime Instance, Dynamic deployment, Reconciliation

### runtime_profile (sandbox field)

A field on the create-sandbox request body that selects the engine. `standard` is Firecracker (the default, no extra approval), `soma` is SOMA (needs an enabled policy and capacity), and `auto` lets policy decide and may pick Firecracker. Omitting the field is treated exactly as `standard`.

Related: Firecracker, SOMA, Sandbox, Runtime Profile

### Shared responsibility

Shared responsibility is the written split of who looks after what: MIOSA, you, or a cloud provider, depending on where your workload runs.

Read it before choosing infrastructure. With MIOSA-managed compute, MIOSA runs the machines. With OpenComputers, you own the hardware and OS. With BYOC, you own the cloud account and MIOSA runs the control plane.

In every model, the application owner owns application data and backup policy.

Related: MIOSA-managed infrastructure, Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC), OpenComputers

### SOMA

SOMA, the Secure Optimized Machine Architecture, is MIOSA's own open-source virtual machine monitor, written in Rust under Apache 2.0. It gives a Sandbox its own hardware-isolated Linux machine.

You do not run it. MIOSA operates SOMA for you, and it is in early access, enabled per Organization. It exists so MIOSA owns the exact moment a machine becomes ready to run commands.

In MIOSA, SOMA starts a sandbox by restoring a certified snapshot, then proves the guest is alive before calling it ready.

Related: Firecracker, Isolation, Sandbox, Snapshot, microVM, runtime_profile (sandbox field)

### Warm capacity

Warm capacity is compute kept ready in advance so a new Computer or Sandbox can start faster instead of cold booting.

It is why a managed Computer can be handed over in under a second on the warm path. It is not a guarantee that every size is available instantly.

In MIOSA, the managed fleet keeps ready desktop and sandbox slots on every host.

Related: Computer, Sandbox, MIOSA-managed Computer

### Worker pool

A Worker pool is a group of compatible hosts that may run a certain kind of workload under placement policy.

It gives MIOSA a set of machines to schedule onto. Mere registration is not enough: members must be compatible and able to do the job.

In MIOSA, a Bring Your Own Cloud region is a pool of worker capacity inside your AWS account or Google Cloud project.

Related: Host, Placement, Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC), Capability

## Keep learning

- [Core concepts](/docs/concepts): Understand the complete resource hierarchy and immutable production model.

- [Quickstart](/docs/quickstart): Create, preview, publish, verify, and promote an application.

- [Deployment domains](/docs/docker-host/domains): Choose between platform URLs, deployment domains, and custom domains.

- [Customer infrastructure](/docs/infrastructure/overview): Compare MIOSA-managed compute, on-premises servers, OpenComputers, BYOC, and hybrid placement.

pages.title: Core Concepts
pages.description: The canonical MIOSA product model, from mutable sandboxes to immutable releases, stable deployments, persistent data, and customer-owned infrastructure.
pages.markdown:
MIOSA gives developers and agents a safe development loop without making production mutable.
You work in a Sandbox, inspect the result through a Preview, and publish a frozen candidate Release.
After MIOSA verifies that candidate, promotion moves the Deployment's stable URL to the new Version.

If you read only one line, remember this:

**Sandbox (mutable) → Preview → Publish → Release (immutable) → Verify → Promote → Deployment (stable URL).**

The old Version remains available for rollback.
Databases, storage, secrets, and domains remain attached to the Deployment instead of being copied into each release.

> **Note: The central boundary**
>
> Changing a Sandbox changes development state.
> It does not change production.
> Production changes only when an exact immutable candidate is promoted.

This page is the **resource model**: what the MIOSA resources are and how they relate.
For the **API protocol** - authentication, token types, idempotency, rate limits, errors, and events - see [API fundamentals](/docs/fundamentals).

pages.title: Resource model
pages.description: The MIOSA ownership chain and the mutable development resources - Organization, Workspace, Project, Sandbox, and Preview.
pages.markdown:
This page is the **resource model** of the mutable side of MIOSA: the ownership chain and the development resources.
For the production resources and the publish pipeline, see [The publish pipeline](/docs/concepts/publish-pipeline).

## The resource hierarchy

MIOSA resolves every operation through a clear ownership chain:

```text
Organization → Workspace → Project → Sandbox or Deployment
```

- An **Organization** is the top-level customer or platform account.
- A **Workspace** isolates a team, customer, or business boundary.
- A **Project** groups the development and production resources for one product.
- A **Sandbox** is the mutable place where work happens.
- A **Deployment** is the durable production identity that owns versions, routes, and bindings.

Every mutation must resolve one unambiguous organization, workspace, project, and target resource.
This prevents an agent or CLI command from publishing into the wrong customer or environment.

## Development resources

### Sandbox

A **Sandbox** is a mutable, isolated environment where an agent or developer builds an app.
It includes a complete development environment with Node, Python, git, package managers, file APIs, and a terminal.

Key properties:

- **Mutable and stateful.** Files in `/workspace` persist across commands until the sandbox is destroyed or suspended.
- **Executable.** Run commands such as `npm install`, `python app.py`, or `git clone`, with structured stdout, stderr, and exit status.
- **Agent-friendly file access.** Read, write, and synchronize source, configuration, and assets.
- **Previewable.** Expose a running port through a temporary Preview URL.
- **Snapshot-aware.** Save, fork, and restore development state without treating that snapshot as a production release.
- **Suspendable.** Idle compute can pause and later resume from durable state.

A Sandbox is not production.
Its files can change at any time, its process can stop, and its Preview can disappear while suspended.
Use it to create and test the source that will become a production candidate.

```bash
miosa create my-box --wait     # provision a sandbox and wait until it is ready
miosa exec my-box -- echo "hello from MIOSA"
```

Deep-dive on Sandboxes, file I/O, exec, previews, and the dev loop.
[Sandboxes reference →](/docs/develop/sandboxes)

### Preview

A **Preview** is a temporary public URL that tunnels to one port inside a running Sandbox.

```text
https://5173-abc12345.sandbox.miosa.ai
```

When you create a Preview, you specify the port, usually `3000` or `5173`.
MIOSA routes that hostname to the Sandbox process.
As files change and the development server reloads, the Preview changes too.

Key properties:

- **Mutable.** Every request reflects the current Sandbox process and files.
- **Ephemeral.** The URL depends on a running Sandbox and is not a durable customer URL.
- **Shareable.** Short-lived tokens allow browser access without exposing a workspace API key.

```bash
miosa preview create my-box 3000 --visibility public
```

[Previews reference →](/docs/develop/previews)

## Next

- [The publish pipeline](/docs/concepts/publish-pipeline): Builder, Release, Runtime Instance, Domain, Deployment, and Version.
- [Data and bindings](/docs/concepts/data-and-bindings): durable resources that outlive a Sandbox.
- [Core Concepts](/docs/concepts): the one-screen overview.

pages.markdown:
This page is the **production side** of MIOSA: the resources a publish creates and how they relate. For the ownership chain and the mutable Sandbox, see [Resource model](/docs/concepts/resource-model). ## Production resources ### Builder A **Builder** is the isolated worker for one publish operation. It freezes the Sandbox source, runs the selected build pipeline, stores the result, and exits. Later edits to the Sandbox cannot change that build. Three build modes: | Mode | Trigger | Output | |------|---------|--------| | Static packager | `/workspace` has only static files | Tarball served from MIOSA's edge | | Auto-detect | Node/Python/Ruby/Go project detected | Dynamic release served by production runtimes | | Dockerfile | `Dockerfile` present in `/workspace` | Dynamic release served by production runtimes | The Builder is internal and short-lived. Its job is to make production builds reproducible while the mutable Sandbox remains available for continued work. ### Release A **Release** is the immutable artifact produced by a successful Builder run. Its content is addressed by a SHA-256 digest and stored outside the Sandbox. The same bytes can be started repeatedly, placed on different hosts, and verified independently. MIOSA never edits a Release in place. Publishing changed source creates a new Release. That rule prevents a URL from silently serving bytes that do not match its release record. Two shapes: - **Static release** - a tarball of files (`index.html`, `app.js`, assets). MIOSA's edge serves them directly. No Runtime Instances required. - **Dynamic release** - a server app artifact. Served by production runtimes. [Releases reference →](/docs/docker-host/releases) ### Runtime Instance A **Runtime Instance** runs a dynamic Release in production. MIOSA's scheduler places it, the health system checks it, and the reconciler replaces it when the actual runtime no longer matches the desired state. Key properties: - **Placement.** The scheduler selects a compatible host using capacity, region, and policy. - **Scaling.** Multiple instances can serve the same Version. - **Recovery.** Failed instances can be replaced from the immutable Release. - **Isolation.** Production runtimes are isolated from other tenants and from the build Sandbox. Static deployments do not need Runtime Instances. MIOSA serves their immutable files from the edge. [Runtime Instances reference →](/docs/docker-host/runtime-instances) ### Domain A **Domain** is a hostname routed to a Deployment's active Version. The Deployment owns the route, so a new Version does not require a new customer-facing URL. - `my-app.my-workspace.miosa.app` - MIOSA-managed fallback URL, instant, no DNS change needed. - `my-app.apps.yourplatform.com` - tenant deployment domain for generated apps. - `app.yourcustomer.com` - custom domain your customer brings; MIOSA auto-provisions a TLS certificate via Let's Encrypt. Changing a route does not rebuild an application. Promotion and rollback change which verified Version receives traffic behind the same Deployment URL. [Domains reference →](/docs/docker-host/domains) ## The immutable publish pipeline A **Deployment** is the durable identity of a production app. It owns the stable URL, version history, routes, environment configuration, and data bindings. A **Version** connects one Deployment to one immutable Release plus the configuration needed to run it. Publishing creates a candidate Version. It does not make that candidate live merely because the build finished. Promotion must prove that the candidate is ready, its required configuration is present, its runtime is healthy, and its route serves the expected artifact. Only then does MIOSA update `active_version_id`. ```mermaid flowchart LR S["Sandbox
mutable"] -->|publish| B["Builder
isolated job"] B -->|produces| R["Release
immutable bytes"] R -->|creates| V["Candidate Version"] V -->|verify| G{"Promotion gates pass?"} G -->|yes| D["Deployment
stable identity"] G -->|no| F["Candidate remains inactive"] Dom["Domain"] -->|routes to| D D -->|runs| RI["Runtime Instances"] ``` The production transition is intentionally narrow: 1. Freeze the exact Sandbox source. 2. Build an immutable Release. 3. Create a candidate Version. 4. Verify health, routes, secrets, data bindings, and declared requirements. 5. Promote that exact Version. 6. Prove the public URL serves it. 7. Keep the previous Version available for rollback. The object relationship remains stable across releases: ```mermaid graph TD Proj["Project"] Dep["Deployment
team-portal"] V17["Version 17
(active)"] V16["Version 16
(archived)"] V15["Version 15
(archived)"] Rel["Release sha:abc"] RI["Runtime Instances"] D1["team-portal.miosa.app"] D2["example.net"] Proj --> Dep Dep -->|active_version_id| V17 Dep --> V16 Dep --> V15 V17 --> Rel Rel --> RI Dep --> D1 Dep --> D2 ``` Rollback selects an earlier ready Version as `active_version_id`. The Deployment and its domains do not change identity. For dynamic applications, MIOSA routes traffic to healthy instances of the selected Version and retires instances that no longer belong to the active state. > **Caution: A healthy process is not enough** > > A production update is accepted only when the release record, running artifact, public route, required bindings, and declared capabilities agree. > A successful build by itself is only a candidate. ```bash miosa deploy create --from-sandbox \ --name my-app \ --dir /workspace \ --type docker_deploy \ --wait \ --json ``` Builder, Release, Runtime Instance, Domains - the full publish pipeline. [Deploy overview →](/docs/docker-host/overview) ## Next - [Data and bindings](/docs/concepts/data-and-bindings): the durable resources a Deployment attaches to. - [Deploy overview](/docs/docker-host/overview): the full pipeline in the deploy section. - [Core Concepts](/docs/concepts): the one-screen overview.

pages.title: Computers (desktop product)
pages.description: The MIOSA cloud desktop product: full GUI environments with screenshot, click, type, and keyboard APIs, and how they differ from Sandboxes.
pages.markdown:
**Computers** are full desktop environments running in the cloud with screenshot, click, type, and keyboard APIs. They are a separate product surface from Sandboxes  -  different lifecycle, different use cases.

| | Sandbox | Computer |
|---|---|---|
| Primary use | Code execution, file I/O, dev servers, agent tool-use | Desktop GUI, browser automation, computer-use agents |
| Display | None (headless) | Desktop stream |
| Accessibility tree | No | Yes |
| Lifecycle | Short-to-medium lived, auto-suspend | Session-oriented |
| Template | `miosa-sandbox` (the default) | `miosa-desktop` |

Use Sandboxes for building apps. Use Computers when your agent or workflow needs a real screen.

You can also bring your own hardware (Mac, Linux, Windows) and register it as a Computer host via BYOC.

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/computers \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"my-computer","template_type":"miosa-desktop","size":"small"}'
```

[Computers overview →](/docs/computers/overview)

## Three naming layers

One thing trips up every new reader: "Computer" has a specific meaning in MIOSA.

| Layer | Term | Meaning |
|-------|------|---------|
| Brand | **MIOSA** | The wordmark and platform. |
| Resource | **Computer** | The desktop GUI product. Not a generic synonym for "VM." |
| AI agent | **OSA agent** | The agent runtime. Optional; installable inside a Sandbox or Computer. |

Sandboxes are not Computers. Runtime Instances are not Computers. Computers are Computers. When you encounter older docs or code that uses "Computer" generically, substitute "Sandbox" or "Runtime Instance" based on context.

## Next

- [Resource model](/docs/concepts/resource-model): what a Sandbox is.
- [Computers overview](/docs/computers/overview): the full Computers reference.
- [Core Concepts](/docs/concepts): the one-screen overview.

pages.title: Tenancy
pages.description: White-label tenancy and external attribution - how platforms build a product on MIOSA and map MIOSA resources to their own customers.
pages.markdown:
MIOSA is designed for platforms - you build a product on top of MIOSA, and your customers never know MIOSA exists. The tenancy model: - **One MIOSA organization per customer platform.** A platform account has one organization slug and server-side `msk_*` keys. - **Workspaces and projects for downstream customers.** Use MIOSA workspaces for clients and projects for the apps, sites, documents, and workflows they create. - **External attribution for your IDs.** Pass `external_workspace_id`, `external_user_id`, and `external_project_id` when you need your database IDs on usage, audit, and list filters. - **Server-side key, never in the browser.** For browser-side access (embedding a preview, opening a terminal), your backend mints a short-lived scoped token. The `msk_*` key stays server-side. ```mermaid graph TD Plat["Your Platform"] Org["MIOSA Organization
one slug · one bill"] WS["Workspace
Acme Corp"] Proj["Project
Lead Magnet"] Sbx["Sandbox"] Dep["Deployment"] Plat --> Org Org --> WS WS --> Proj Proj --> Sbx Proj --> Dep ``` Filters are always organization-scoped server-side. You cannot cross organizations by passing different workspace, project, or external IDs. White-label tenancy, browser tokens, attribution, and API keys. [Platform / White-label overview →](/docs/platform/overview) ## External attribution **External attribution** is how you map MIOSA resources to your own users, projects, and tenants without creating MIOSA accounts for them. Three opaque string fields are accepted on every resource that supports creation: | Field | Purpose | |-------|---------| | `external_user_id` | The end-user inside your system who owns or triggered this resource | | `external_project_id` | The project, document, or workflow in your database that this resource belongs to | | `metadata` | Arbitrary key-value map for any additional context your platform needs | MIOSA never interprets or validates the content of external attribution fields. They are always stored as-is. ```python sandbox = client.sandboxes.create( template_id="miosa-sandbox", external_workspace_id="acme-co", external_user_id="alice@example.net", external_project_id="invoice-bot", ) ``` For the request fields, list filters, and per-customer chargeback rollup, see [Ownership and attribution](/docs/fundamentals/attribution) and the [Attribution reference](/docs/platform/attribution). ## Next - [Preview and share tokens](/docs/concepts/tokens): browser access without exposing a workspace key. - [Attribution reference](/docs/platform/attribution): the full filter spec and billing split. - [Core Concepts](/docs/concepts): the one-screen overview.

pages.title: Tenant configuration
pages.description: Tenant preview domain and tenant branding - the apex hostname that replaces the MIOSA fallback preview domain and the error pages your end users see.
pages.markdown:
## Tenant preview domain

A **tenant preview domain** is an apex hostname that replaces the MIOSA fallback preview domain in every sandbox preview URL your end users see. It is set per tenant.

When you set and verify a preview domain (for example, `yourproduct.com`), sandbox previews for your tenant are served at:

```text
https://<sandbox-slug>.yourproduct.com
```

Setup is a two-step DNS verification: add a wildcard CNAME (`*.yourproduct.com`) pointing to `proxy.miosa.ai`, then call `POST /api/v1/tenant/preview-domain/verify`. MIOSA auto-provisions a wildcard TLS certificate once the CNAME resolves. Only apex domains are accepted  -  subdomains and protocol prefixes are rejected.

One preview domain per tenant. The domain applies to all sandboxes under that tenant.

```bash
# Set
curl -X PUT https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/tenant/preview-domain \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer msk_u_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"preview_domain": "yourproduct.com"}'

# Verify
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/tenant/preview-domain/verify \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer msk_u_..."
```

[Tenant Preview Domain API →](/docs/api-reference/tenant-preview-domain)

## Tenant branding

**Tenant branding** controls what your end users see on MIOSA-rendered error pages  -  the 404, 502, and gateway-timeout pages displayed when a sandbox is unavailable, a preview URL is invalid, or a custom domain is not yet verified.

Configurable fields:

| Field | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| `logo_url` | HTTPS URL to your logo image |
| `name` | Product or company name |
| `support_url` | Optional link shown on error pages for end-user support |
| `primary_color` | Hex color for CTA buttons (for example `#0066FF`) |

Branding is set via `PUT /api/v1/tenant/branding` and served immediately from cache  -  there is no propagation delay. Deleting it resets the error pages to the MIOSA defaults.

```bash
# Set branding
curl -X PUT https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/tenant/branding \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer msk_u_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "branding": {
      "logo_url": "https://cdn.example.com/logo.png",
      "name": "Lumen",
      "primary_color": "#0066FF"
    }
  }'
```

[Tenant Branding API →](/docs/api-reference/tenant-branding)

## Next

- [Preview and share tokens](/docs/concepts/tokens): browser access to a sandbox preview.
- [Tenant Preview Domain API](/docs/api-reference/tenant-preview-domain): the full request schema.
- [Core Concepts](/docs/concepts): the one-screen overview.

pages.title: Data and bindings
pages.description: Managed Postgres, Redis, object storage, volumes, and auth - the durable resources a Deployment attaches to, and how bindings inject credentials.
pages.markdown:
Sandboxes and Runtime Instances are replaceable.
Data Services are durable resources with an independent lifecycle.
Replacing a Sandbox, publishing a Release, or rolling back a Version does not delete the Deployment's database or object storage.

| Service | What it is |
|---------|-----------|
| Managed Postgres | Fully managed PostgreSQL database. Schema migrations are yours to run; MIOSA provides the connection string. |
| Managed Redis | Persistent Redis cluster for caching, queues, pub/sub. |
| Object Storage | S3-compatible bucket. Useful for uploads, assets, generated files. |
| Volumes | Block storage mounted into Runtime Instances. Persists across restarts. |
| Auth | JWT-based signup/login as a service. One env var gives your project a full auth system. |

Bindings connect a Sandbox or Deployment to those durable resources.
MIOSA resolves the binding and injects the appropriate credentials at runtime.

```bash
DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:pass@host/dbname
REDIS_URL=redis://host:6379
STORAGE_BUCKET=miosa-ws123-uploads
AUTH_URL=https://auth.miosa.app/proj_abc
AUTH_JWT_SECRET=...
```

Destroying a Sandbox does not destroy its database.
Publishing a Version does not automatically make an incompatible schema safe.
Use backward-compatible expand, migrate, and contract changes so the active and previous Versions can both operate during promotion or rollback.

> **Note: Phase status**
>
> Managed Postgres and Auth are part of the platform Phase 6-8 rollout. The doc surface is published now so you can plan integration; some endpoints are still being wired in production.

```bash
miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"app-production","engine":"postgresql"}'
```

[Data overview →](/docs/data/overview)

## Next

- [The publish pipeline](/docs/concepts/publish-pipeline): how a Release attaches to these resources.
- [Data overview](/docs/data/overview): the full data-services reference.
- [Core Concepts](/docs/concepts): the one-screen overview.

pages.title: Preview and share tokens
pages.description: Short-lived preview tokens (mp_*) and revocable share tokens (ms_*) for loading a sandbox preview in a browser without exposing a workspace key.
pages.markdown:
## Preview tokens

A **preview token** (prefix `mp_*`) is a short-lived signed token that authorizes a browser to load a sandbox preview without receiving the workspace API key.

The typical flow:

1. Your backend calls `POST /api/v1/sandboxes/{id}/preview-token` with the sandbox ID and a TTL (max 24 hours).
2. MIOSA returns an iframe-ready URL with the token embedded.
3. The browser loads that URL, for example `https://<slug>.sandbox.miosa.ai?mt=mp_...`.
4. MIOSA's edge verifies the token server-side and proxies the request to the sandbox port. The token value never grants broader access.

Preview tokens are non-renewable and non-transferable. When the TTL expires the URL returns `401`. Your backend mints a new token to restore access.

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/sandboxes/$SBX/previews/$PREVIEW/share \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{"ttl_seconds": 3600}'
```

[Browser Tokens reference →](/docs/platform/browser-tokens)

## Share tokens

A **share token** (prefix `ms_*`) is a revocable public share URL for a sandbox preview  -  analogous to a "share link" in a document editor.

Key differences from preview tokens:

| | Preview token (`mp_*`) | Share token (`ms_*`) |
|--|------------------------|----------------------|
| Intended recipient | Your authenticated user | Anyone with the link |
| Minted by | Your backend | Your backend |
| Revocable | Yes (delete the token) | Yes (delete the token) |
| Password protection | No | Optional |
| Expiry | Required TTL | Optional |

Share tokens are useful for demos, client reviews, or collaborative previews where the recipient does not have a user account in your system. The link can be embedded as a plain URL  -  no `Authorization` header needed.

[Previews reference →](/docs/develop/previews)

## Next

- [Tenant configuration](/docs/concepts/tenant-config): preview domains and error-page branding.
- [Browser Tokens reference](/docs/platform/browser-tokens): minting, scopes, and revocation.
- [Core Concepts](/docs/concepts): the one-screen overview.

pages.title: Projects
pages.description: Group the resources for one app, site, or deliverable inside a Workspace, without becoming a runtime.
pages.markdown:
A **Project** is the durable product boundary inside one Workspace.
It groups the resources for one application, site, workflow, or customer deliverable, and it never runs code itself.
Every resource that belongs to the product carries the project's `project_id`, so ownership, deployment history, domains, members, and usage all roll up to one boundary.

A Project always belongs to exactly one Workspace, and a Workspace belongs to one Organization.
The Workspace is required: creating a Project with no workspace fails with `WORKSPACE_REQUIRED`.

## 1. Create a project

```bash
miosa project create "Lead Magnet" \
  --workspace-id "$MIOSA_WORKSPACE_ID" \
  --description "Customer lead capture app"

miosa project list
miosa project get lead-magnet
```

## 2. Add resources

```bash
# Create a sandbox in the workspace, then publish its output.
miosa create lead-magnet-dev --workspace acme-corp --wait
miosa deploy create --from-sandbox lead-magnet-dev --wait
```

## 3. Deploy

```bash
miosa deploy create --git https://github.com/me/lead-magnet --branch main --wait
```

Publishing creates an immutable version under the Deployment and prints the URL.
Display the URL the API returns; never rebuild it from a slug.

## Pick what you need

| You want to | Page |
|---|---|
| See the project record, fields, and what lives inside it | [Project resources](/docs/projects/resources) |
| Run the full create, configure, deploy, and retire path | [Project lifecycle](/docs/projects/lifecycle) |
| Manage members, permissions, and billing attribution | [Members and usage](/docs/projects/members-and-usage) |

## Next

- [Project resources](/docs/projects/resources): The project record, what attaches to it, and how it maps to your own platform.
- [Project lifecycle](/docs/projects/lifecycle): Create, add resources, configure environments and secrets, deploy, and retire.
- [Members and usage](/docs/projects/members-and-usage): Members, permissions, usage attribution, and common mistakes.

## Related

- [Projects API](/docs/api-reference/projects): Create, resolve, update, and inspect Projects.
- [Publishing](/docs/docker-host/publishing): Move from mutable source to an immutable candidate.
- [Domains](/docs/docker-host/domains): Configure previews, generated app URLs, and exact hostnames.
- [Product model](/docs/concepts): How the Organization, Workspace, and Project layers relate.

Organizations, workspaces, and projects form one hierarchy: [Open the product model →](/docs/concepts).

pages.title: Project lifecycle
pages.description: Create a project, add resources, configure environments and secrets, deploy, then retire it.
pages.markdown:
The five steps below are the whole path: create, add resources, configure environments and secrets, deploy, then retire.

## 1. Create a project

**CLI**

```bash
miosa project create "Lead Magnet" \
  --workspace-id "$MIOSA_WORKSPACE_ID" \
  --description "Customer lead capture app"

miosa project list
miosa project get lead-magnet
```

**REST**

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/projects \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "workspace_id": "'"$MIOSA_WORKSPACE_ID"'",
    "name": "Lead Magnet",
    "slug": "lead-magnet",
    "external_project_id": "project_789"
  }'
```

The response is `201` with the project record.
`workspace_slug` or `external_workspace_id` also resolve the workspace; `slug` is derived from `name` when you omit it.

## 2. Add resources

**CLI**

```bash
# Create a sandbox in the workspace, then publish its output.
miosa create lead-magnet-dev --workspace acme-corp --wait
miosa deploy create --from-sandbox lead-magnet-dev --wait
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
import { Miosa } from "@miosa/sdk";

const miosa = new Miosa({ apiKey: process.env.MIOSA_API_KEY });

// Project CRUD is REST and CLI only; the SDK lists projects per workspace.
const projects = await miosa.workspaces.listProjects(workspaceId);
const project = projects.find((p) => p.slug === "lead-magnet");

const sandbox = await miosa.sandboxes.create({
  projectId: project.id as string,
  projectSlug: "lead-magnet",
});
```

**Python**

```python
from miosa import Miosa

client = Miosa(api_key=os.environ["MIOSA_API_KEY"])

projects = client.workspaces.list_projects(workspace_id)
project = next(p for p in projects if p["slug"] == "lead-magnet")

sandbox = client.sandboxes.create(
    project_id=project["id"],
    project_slug="lead-magnet",
)
```

**REST**

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/sandboxes \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "project_id": "'"$PROJECT_ID"'", "name": "lead-magnet-dev" }'
```

Sandboxes, computers, deployments, databases, storage, functions, jobs, and domains all accept `project_id`.
When you only have your own identifier, pass `external_project_id` and MIOSA resolves or creates the project for you.
Machine commands in the CLI take `--workspace`, not a project, so the project resolves from the workspace default; use the API or an SDK when a resource must land in a named project.

## 3. Environments and secrets

Runtime environment variables resolve narrowest-wins:

```text
tenant defaults < workspace defaults < project defaults < resource env < request env
```

A project-scoped variable reaches every resource in the project without copying values into each one.

**CLI**

```bash
# CLI environments belong to a workspace or the organization.
echo "$STRIPE_SECRET_KEY" | miosa env set --env staging STRIPE_KEY
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
await miosa.runtimeEnv.set({
  scope: "project",
  projectId: project.id as string,
  name: "STRIPE_SECRET_KEY",
  value: process.env.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY!,
});
```

**Python**

```python
client.runtime_env.set(
    scope="project",
    project_id=project["id"],
    name="STRIPE_SECRET_KEY",
    value=os.environ["STRIPE_SECRET_KEY"],
)
```

**REST**

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/runtime-env \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "scope": "project",
    "project_id": "'"$PROJECT_ID"'",
    "target": "all",
    "name": "STRIPE_SECRET_KEY",
    "value": "sk_live_..."
  }'
```

Values are encrypted at rest and never returned in plaintext.
Production configuration for a single deployment is separate: a Deployment owns its own environments (`production`, `staging`, `preview`, `development`) with their own config.

## 4. Deploy

**CLI**

```bash
miosa deploy create --git https://github.com/me/lead-magnet --branch main --wait
```

**TypeScript**

```ts
// The sandbox already carries the project, so its deployment inherits it.
const deployment = await sandbox.deploy({ name: "lead-magnet" });
```

**Python**

```python
# The sandbox already carries the project, so its deployment inherits it.
deployment = sandbox.deploy(name="lead-magnet")
```

**REST**

```bash
# Create the deployment inside the project, then publish a version.
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/deployments \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "name": "lead-magnet", "project_id": "'"$PROJECT_ID"'", "repo_url": "https://github.com/me/lead-magnet", "branch": "main" }'

curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/deployments/"$DEPLOYMENT_ID"/publish \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

Publishing creates an immutable version under the Deployment and prints the URL.
Display the URL the API returns; never rebuild it from a slug.

## 5. Archive or delete

A project row has no state, so there is no project archive.
Archive is a resource concept: a Product is `active` or `archived`, and a deployment environment is `active`, `inactive`, or `archived`.
To retire a project, move or delete its resources first, then delete the project.

**CLI**

```bash
# The CLI creates, lists, and shows projects.
# Moving and deleting a project are REST operations.
miosa project list
miosa project get lead-magnet
```

**REST**

```bash
# Move the project and its children to another workspace.
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/projects/"$PROJECT_ID"/move \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{ "target_workspace_id": "'"$TARGET_WORKSPACE_ID"'" }'

# Delete the project once it owns nothing.
curl -X DELETE https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/projects/"$PROJECT_ID" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

Delete returns `204`.
It returns `409 PROJECT_HAS_RESOURCES` with a `details.impact` document listing what still blocks the delete, and `409 DEFAULT_PROJECT_PROTECTED` for a workspace's Default project.
Move is refused for the Default project and for a caller who is not a workspace admin.

pages.title: Project resources
pages.description: The project record, everything that attaches to a project, and how a project maps to your own platform.
pages.markdown:
The project record itself holds only identity and attribution: | Field | Purpose | |---|---| | `id` | Canonical UUID. Store this after the first resolution. | | `tenant_id` | The Organization that owns the project. | | `workspace_id` | The Workspace the project lives in. Required. | | `name` | Display name, 1 to 120 characters. | | `slug` | URL-safe key, 1 to 80 characters, unique per workspace. Derived from the name when omitted. | | `description` | Optional free text. | | `metadata` | Arbitrary key-value map. | | `is_default` | True for the workspace's Default project. A client cannot set this. | | `external_project_id` | Your own project id, unique per Organization. Attribution only. | | `external_workspace_id` | Your own workspace id, inherited from the Workspace. Attribution only. | ## Where a project fits ```mermaid flowchart TD O["Organization
billing, plan, policy"] --> W["Workspace
team, customer, or business boundary"] W --> P["Project
one app or deliverable"] P --> S["Sandboxes"] P --> C["Computers"] P --> D["Deployments"] P --> DATA["Data services"] P --> DOM["Domains"] D --> V["Versions and releases"] ``` > **Note: Project is not another runtime** > > A Sandbox, Computer, or Runtime Instance executes work. > A Project provides ownership and organization around those resources. Every Workspace also has one **Default project**, created on demand and marked `is_default`. It is the home for resources created without an explicit project, and it can neither be deleted nor moved. ## What lives in a project Resources attach to a project through a canonical `project_id` column, and most also carry `workspace_id` and your `external_project_id`. A resource create call can resolve the project for you: pass `project_id`, `project_slug`, `project_name`, or `external_project_id` and MIOSA resolves or creates the project before inserting the resource. | Resource | In a project | Notes | |---|---|---| | Sandbox | Yes | The mutable development environment. Carries `project_id` and `workspace_id`. | | Sandbox preview | Yes | Generated preview URL for a sandbox. | | Computer | Yes | The desktop runtime. Carries `project_id`; computers have no `workspace_id` column. | | Deployment | Yes | Durable production identity. It owns versions, releases, services, environments, builds, runtime instances, and preview environments, and every one of those children carries the same `project_id`. | | Managed database | Yes | Project-scoped with no workspace column. One is auto-provisioned when the project is created. | | Database | Yes | Database attached to a sandbox. | | Managed service | Yes | Project-scoped with no workspace column. | | Storage bucket | Yes | S3-compatible object storage. | | Volume | Yes | Durable filesystem. A `/data` volume is auto-created with the project. | | Custom domain | Yes | An exact hostname attached to a sandbox, computer, or deployment. | | Edge function | Yes | Code that runs at the edge. | | Cron job | Yes | Scheduled executions. | | Workflow | Yes | Carries `project_id` with no workspace column. | | Project auth | Yes | Built-in auth for one sandbox or deployment, with an encrypted JWT secret. | | Project integration | Yes | Provider credentials such as Stripe, Resend, and Twilio. | | Runtime env var | Yes | `scope` is `tenant`, `workspace`, or `project`. Values are encrypted at rest. | | Agent definition and runtime profile | Yes | Agent configuration scoped to the project. | | Usage meter | Yes | The billing dimension a resource is metered under. | | Run | Yes | Detached when the project is deleted: `project_id` is set to null, the run is not deleted. | | Project member | Yes | Cascades on project delete. | | Product link | Yes | A Product groups one or more projects inside a workspace. | | Audit, usage, and platform events | Attribution only | Immutable history. It keeps the project it was recorded under and is never rewritten. | | Workspace | No | The parent boundary. A project has exactly one. | | Organization | No | Two levels above the project. It owns billing and policy. | For the live counts, health roll-up, last deploy, and linked repository of one project, call `GET /api/v1/projects/{id}/summary`. ## Project, workspace, or organization? | Need | Use | |---|---| | Separate company billing and policy | Organization | | Separate team, customer, or business boundary | Workspace | | Group one app and its resources | Project | | Develop mutable source | Sandbox | | Operate one stable production app | Deployment | | Keep a persistent interactive desktop | Computer | Create separate Projects when applications need independent deployment history, domains, environments, or usage attribution. Do not create a new Project for every build, preview, or release. Previews and releases belong to the Deployment inside the project, not to a new project. ## Domains Preview domains are an organization-level setting, not a per-project one. A tenant preview domain white-labels generated preview links for the whole organization; an exact custom hostname attaches to one Deployment or Computer. The effective order is: ```text Exact deployment/computer hostname -> Organization preview domain -> MIOSA-managed fallback ``` Always display URLs returned by MIOSA instead of rebuilding them from slugs. Every custom domain row carries `project_id` and `workspace_id` alongside the resource it points at, so a hostname is scoped and attributed the same way the resource is. ## Mapping your own platform onto projects | Your platform | MIOSA | |---|---| | Company account | Organization | | Customer or team | Workspace | | App, site, document, or product | Project | | Editable build environment | Sandbox | | Live application | Deployment | Three worked examples: | Platform | Shape | Why | |---|---|---| | Lumen | One Project per customer app, inside one Workspace | Each app gets its own deployment history, domains, and usage line while the whole platform stays on one billing account. | | Acme Corp | One Project per internal tool, inside one Workspace per department | Tools share the company's Organization and policy but roll up their usage and members separately. | | Northwind Agency | One Workspace per client, one Project per deliverable | The client boundary is the Workspace, so isolating clients never leaks into a per-deliverable project. | Store the canonical `workspace_id` and `project_id` after the first resolution. Use `external_workspace_id`, `external_project_id`, and `external_user_id` for correlation, not as substitutes for MIOSA ownership.

pages.title: Members and usage
pages.description: Project members, permissions, usage attribution, the operating checklist, and common mistakes.
pages.markdown:
Access follows the hierarchy and narrows at the project:

- Every Workspace member inherits access to every project in that workspace.
- A **project member** row narrows one user's role for one project. Roles are `owner`, `admin`, `developer`, and `viewer`, and the user must already belong to the parent workspace.
- Project endpoints are gated by the `projects:read` and `projects:write` scopes. An API key bound to a workspace pins `workspace_id` for you, so you do not repeat it in the body.
- Member management lives at `GET` and `POST /api/v1/projects/{id}/members` and `PATCH` and `DELETE /api/v1/projects/{id}/members/{user_id}`.

Usage is attributed by the `project_id` on every metered row.
The project roll-up is available at `GET /api/v1/projects/{id}/usage`, and `GET /api/v1/usage/projects` groups settled cost and runtime hours by project or by workspace.
Usage that carries no project is reported in an explicit `unattributed` bucket rather than merged into a named project, so a total that is short is visibly short.
Your `external_project_id` flows through to usage, audit, and list filters.

## Operating checklist

- Every resource resolves to exactly one Organization and Workspace.
- Every product resource has the intended `project_id`.
- Development happens in a Sandbox, not the live Deployment.
- Production changes only through publish, verify, and promote.
- Data survives Sandbox replacement and application rollback.
- The UI displays the authoritative URL returned by the API.
- The project is not the Default project if you plan to delete or move it.

## Common mistakes

| Symptom | Likely cause | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| Resources appear under the wrong customer | Workspace or Project was inferred from stale UI state | Send the canonical IDs explicitly |
| A new app overwrites an older app's history | Both products share one Project and Deployment | Create a separate Project and Deployment |
| A domain change does not affect Sandbox previews | A production hostname was changed | Configure the Project preview domain separately |
| Deleting a Sandbox appears to delete the app | Development and production were treated as one resource | Publish to a Deployment before removing development state |
| A delete returns `409 PROJECT_HAS_RESOURCES` | Sandboxes, deployments, or data still carry the `project_id` | Move or delete the listed resources first, then delete |
| A delete or move returns `409 DEFAULT_PROJECT_PROTECTED` | The target is the workspace's Default project | Create a named project and move the resources into it |

## Next

- [Projects API](/docs/api-reference/projects): Create, resolve, update, and inspect Projects.
- [Workspaces](/docs/api-reference/workspaces): The team, customer, or business boundary above the project.
- [Usage and billing](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing): Per-customer usage and chargeback on a single MIOSA bill.

pages.title: Services
pages.description: Run web services, workers, private services and static sites in a project, with releases, variables, domains and rollback.
pages.markdown:
Services are the apps a project runs.
A service is one of four common types, plus cron jobs and database services:

| Type | What it is |
|---|---|
| Web service | A process that serves HTTP on a public address. |
| Worker | A process with no port and no address. It runs until it stops. |
| Private service | A process with no public address. Private networking between services is not available yet, so nothing else reaches it by name; it can reach managed databases through their connection variables. |
| Static site | Pre-built files served from the edge. |
| Cron job | A command on a five-field cron schedule, with run history and output. |
| Database service | A managed Postgres or Redis bound to the project. |

Every service belongs to a project and an environment.
A project starts with a `production` environment; add `staging` or anything else you need.

## What a service has

- **Releases.** Every deploy is an immutable release with a number, a state and a reason when it fails.
- **Variables.** Sealed at rest, masked on read, and able to reference another service, a shared variable or a generated secret.
- **An address.** Every service is assigned a private name. A web service or static site can also have a public address.
- **Settings.** Replicas, region, start command, health check, restart policy, volumes and idle sleep.

## The lifecycle

1. Create the service with a source: a git repository, a container image or an uploaded archive.
2. Deploy it. MIOSA builds it and starts a release.
3. The release becomes `active` when its replicas pass their health checks.
4. Deploy again to change it, or roll back to an earlier release. Rollback serves the earlier built image, so nothing is rebuilt.

## Where to go next

- [Quick start](/docs/services/quickstart): a repository to a live URL, then Postgres, a worker, a domain and a rollback.
- [Services and types](/docs/services/services): the source, settings and address of each type.
- [Variables](/docs/services/variables): references between services and generated secrets.
- [Releases](/docs/services/releases): deploy, promote, roll back and cancel.
- [CLI](/docs/services/cli) and [SDKs](/docs/services/sdk): the same operations from a terminal or code.

## Migrating from Railway

The model maps directly:

| Railway | MIOSA |
|---|---|
| Project | Project |
| Service | Service (web service, worker, private service or static site) |
| Environment | Environment |
| Deployment | Release |
| Variables and shared variables | Variables and shared variables |
| Custom domain | Public address |

`miosa service` operates Services.
Services use `/projects/:id/services` and `/services/:id`; the separate Deploy product keeps its own `/deployments` routes.

pages.title: Services quick start
pages.description: Take a repository to a live URL, add Postgres and Redis, add a worker, attach a domain, read a failed release and roll back.
pages.markdown:
This walkthrough takes a repository to a live URL, then adds a database, a worker and a domain.
Every step has a CLI form and an SDK form.

## Before you start

- A MIOSA account with an API key (`msk_...`) or a signed-in CLI.
- A project. `miosa project create shop --workspace-id <workspace>` creates one; `miosa project list` shows the others.
- A repository MIOSA can clone, or a container image.

Export the key once:

```bash
export MIOSA_API_KEY=msk_your_key
```

## 1. Create a web service

```bash
miosa service create shop API --type web \
  --repo https://github.com/acme/api \
  --branch main \
  --start-command "node server.js" \
  --replicas 2 \
  --env NODE_ENV=production
```

`--type web` stores the API's `server` kind, which can have a public address.
`--type private` stores the same kind but never gets one.
The command prints the service, its private address and, once enabled, its public address.

TypeScript:

```typescript
const service = await miosa.services.create(projectId, {
  name: "API",
  type: "web",
  source: { type: "git", ref: "https://github.com/acme/api", branch: "main" },
  settings: { start_command: "node server.js", replicas: 2 },
});
const address = await miosa.services.enablePublicAddress(service.id);
console.log(address.url); // https://api.acme.miosa.app
```

Python:

```python
service = miosa.services.create(
    project_id,
    "API",
    type="web",
    source={"type": "git", "ref": "https://github.com/acme/api", "branch": "main"},
    settings={"start_command": "node server.js", "replicas": 2},
)
address = miosa.services.enable_public_address(service["id"])
print(address["url"])
```

## 2. Deploy it

```bash
miosa service deploy shop API --message "first deploy" --wait
```

`--wait` polls the release until it is live or fails.
Without it you get the queued release and can check it with `miosa service releases shop API`.

```typescript
const release = await miosa.services.deploy(service.id, { message: "first deploy" });
let current = release;
while (!["active", "sleeping", "failed", "canceled", "stopped", "removed"].includes(current.state)) {
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 3000));
  current = await miosa.services.release(service.id, release.id);
}
console.log(current.state);
```

The Python SDK ships `wait_for_release(service_id, release_id)`, which polls and raises on a failed release.

A release goes `queued -> building -> built -> starting -> health_check -> active`.
Any step can fail; the release carries a `reason.code` such as `build_failed`, `healthcheck_timeout` or `no_capacity`.

## 3. Add Postgres and Redis

Templates create the service, its variables and the references between them in one change set:

```bash
miosa service templates                       # the catalog
miosa service templates apply shop nextjs-postgres
miosa service templates apply shop redis
```

The Postgres template creates a database service and a web service whose `DATABASE_URL` is the reference `${{Postgres.DATABASE_URL}}`.
Applying a template stages one change set and deploys every service it creates; pass `--no-deploy` to create them without deploying.

To read the connection string later:

```bash
miosa service connection shop Postgres
```

That call needs `databases:read` and is audited, because the URL holds the password.

## 4. Add a worker

A worker has no port and no address.

```bash
miosa service create shop Worker --type worker \
  --repo https://github.com/acme/api \
  --start-command "node worker.js" \
  --replicas 1
miosa service deploy shop Worker
```

The worker can read the same database with the same reference:

```bash
miosa service vars set shop Worker DATABASE_URL='${{Postgres.DATABASE_URL}}'
```

## 5. Attach a domain

A web service or static site gets a public address on `miosa.app`:

```bash
miosa service domains shop API
miosa service domains enable shop API --label api
```

The result is `https://api.<your-org>.miosa.app`, served from the active release's healthy replicas.
To stop serving publicly without deleting the service, remove the address:

```bash
miosa service domains disable shop API
```

Private networking between services is not available yet, so other services call it at its public address; databases are reached through their connection variables, see [addresses and domains](/docs/services/domains).

## 6. Read a failed release

```bash
miosa service releases shop API
miosa service logs shop API
```

`logs` prints the newest release's state transitions and its failure reason.
Pass `--release <number>` to look at an older one.
The console's Logs tab shows each replica's runtime lines and the build log; see [Logs](/docs/services/logs).

## 7. Roll back

Rollback serves an earlier release's built image with its frozen source and settings.
Nothing is rebuilt, so it is fast.

```bash
miosa service rollback shop API 3 --yes
```

`miosa service promote shop API 3` is the same call: the Services API calls the operation rollback.

## 8. Tear down

```bash
miosa service stop shop API --yes      # stop now, keep the service
miosa service delete shop API --yes    # remove it and stop its replicas
```

Deleting a database service also deletes its data, so it takes `--confirm <exact name>` instead of `--yes`.
See [Deleting a database service](/docs/services/cli#deleting-a-database-service).

## Where to go next

- [Services and types](/docs/services/services): every source and setting.
- [Variables](/docs/services/variables): references and generated secrets.
- [Releases](/docs/services/releases): the state machine and what each reason means.
- [CLI](/docs/services/cli) and [SDKs](/docs/services/sdk): the full command and method list.

pages.title: Services and types
pages.description: The source, settings, address and limits of a web service, worker, private service, static site, cron job and database service.
pages.markdown:
A service's `kind` is what the API stores.
It is one of `server`, `worker`, `cron`, `static` or `database`.
The product types map onto it:

| Product type | `kind` | Public address |
|---|---|---|
| Web service | `server` | Yes, when enabled |
| Private service | `server` | No |
| Worker | `worker` | No |
| Static site | `static` | Yes, when enabled |
| Cron job | `cron` | No |
| Database service | `database` | No (use `connection`) |

There is no `web` or `private` kind.
The CLI and both SDKs take `type: web` or `type: private`, and store `kind: server`.
A private service is a server service with no public address.

## Source

A service builds from one source.

| `source.type` | What it needs | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `git` | `ref` (repository URL), optional `branch` and `root_dir` | Built on a Services build cell |
| `image` | `ref` (OCI image), optional `port`, optional `registry_secret` | The image is run as-is |
| `upload` | `upload_id` | PUT a `.tar.gz`, `.tar.zst`, `.tar` or `.zip` archive first |
| `forge` | `ref` | A repository hosted by MIOSA Forge |

Dockerfile builds run on the Services build cells and are detected in the source.
While the build cells are off, a Dockerfile service does not build; use a git build or an image source.

Uploading a directory is one command:

```bash
miosa service deploy shop API --dir . --wait
```

The CLI packs the directory (skipping `.git`, `node_modules` and `.env*`), records the archive with `POST /uploads`, PUTs it to the returned URL and deploys `{source: {type: "upload", upload_id}}`.
Archives are single use and expire after an hour.

## Settings

Settings are validated strictly: an unknown key is refused, so a typo never silently stays.

| Setting | Applies to | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `start_command` | all | Replaces the image entrypoint when a replica starts. |
| `pre_deploy_command` | all | Runs once in the new replica before the app starts. A non-zero exit fails the release. |
| `healthcheck_path` | `server` | The path probed before a new release becomes active. |
| `healthcheck_timeout_s` | `server` | How long a release may take to pass. |
| `restart_policy` | all | `always`, `on_failure` or `never`. |
| `max_retries` | all | Restarts before an `on_failure` replica is left stopped. |
| `replicas` | all | 1 to 50. A writable volume forces 1. |
| `region` | all | `us-west`, `us-east` or `us-mia`. |
| `limits` | all | `{vcpu, memory_mb}`. Above 4 vCPU or 8192 MB the release fails. |
| `sleep` | services with a public address | `{enabled, idle_s}`. The next request wakes the service. |
| `cron_schedule` | `cron` | Required. Five-field cron, UTC. |
| `overlap_s` | all | Extra time before the previous release is stopped. |
| `terminate_grace_s` | all | Extra time before the previous release is stopped, like `overlap_s`. |
| `volumes` | `server`, `worker` | Up to four `{volume, mount_path, read_only}`. |

Read what each setting actually does on your platform:

```bash
miosa service settings shop
```

Each entry is `enforced` (it takes effect), `stored` (kept but not applied yet) or `unsupported`.
Never present a `stored` setting as if it took effect.

## Create and change

```bash
miosa service create shop API --type web --repo https://github.com/acme/api --replicas 2
miosa service update shop API --replicas 4
miosa service scale  shop API --replicas 4        # also queues a release
```

`update` merges settings: only the flags you pass change.
It sends the `lock_version` it read; a stale value is refused with `STALE_SERVICE` so two editors cannot overwrite each other.
`scale` changes replicas, region or limits and queues a release that applies them.

## Cron jobs

```bash
miosa service create shop Nightly --type schedule \
  --repo https://github.com/acme/api \
  --start-command "node jobs/nightly.js" \
  --schedule "0 3 * * *"
miosa service runs shop Nightly --output
```

`runs` shows the newest 20 runs with state, exit code, times and output.
A run is limited to five minutes.

## Database services

A database service is a managed Postgres or Redis bound to the project.
Apply a template to create one with its variables wired, or attach an existing managed database.
The connection string is only available through `connection`, which is audited:

```bash
miosa service connection shop Postgres
```

## Limits and errors

| Error | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `SERVICE_NOT_FOUND` | No service with that id in the project. The API resolves services by id only. |
| `STALE_SERVICE` | The `lock_version` you sent is older than the stored one. Re-read and retry. |
| `SERVICE_CONFLICT` | `start` on a service that is already running or starting. |
| `SERVICES_NOT_STOPPED` | `stop` could not stop a replica; the service stays running. |
| `INGRESS_DISABLED` | Public addresses are off for this platform; the service runs but has no address to reach it on. |
| `PLAN_LIMIT_REACHED` | The plan's service limit is reached. |

pages.title: Static sites from Git
pages.description: Build a static site from a repository and serve it from the static lane, with an optional build command and output directory.
pages.markdown:
A static service takes a git source like a web service does, and is served from
the static lane instead of a container.

```bash
miosa service create shop site --type static \
  --repo https://github.com/acme/site --branch main
miosa service update shop site --build-command "npm run build" --output-dir dist
```

## How the site is built

The build runs on a build cell: Railpack detects the framework, or a Dockerfile
in the repository is used when there is one. `build_command` replaces the build
command Railpack would use (Railpack builds only), and `output_dir` says which
folder to serve.

With neither set, the output folder is discovered: Railpack's own static root
first, then `dist`, `build`, `out`, `public` and `_site`, taking the first one
with an `index.html` at its top. A Dockerfile build also tries the image's own
document root (`nginx`, `httpd`, `caddy`).

## When the build fails

- `reason_code: build_failed` with `reason_detail` starting
  `static_output_missing:` means no `index.html` was found in any candidate
  folder. Set `output_dir` to the folder your build writes.
- `static_site_too_large:` means the site is over 500 MiB or over 20,000 files.

> **Note: Framework example**
>
> A Vite site needs nothing: Railpack detects Vite, builds it, and the output is
> `dist`. Single-page-app fallback routing is a separate change; until then a deep
> link into a client-side route should be handled by the app.

pages.title: Service settings as code
pages.description: Put a service's settings in a file at the repository root, so the repository says how the service runs and the console shows where each value came from.
pages.markdown:
A service can carry its settings in a file at the repository root. The same file
works for Docker Host and for Services:

- `miosa.app.yml`, `miosa.app.yaml` or `miosa.app.json`, and
- `miosa.json`.

`railway.json` is read as a compatible fallback, so a project imported from
Railway needs no edit first.

## Rules

**Only the fields the file names change.** A file with one key leaves every other
setting as the project has it. A file is an addition, not a replacement.

**The API still validates.** The merged settings go through the same validation
as a console save, so a file cannot write a value the API would refuse.

**The file wins over the console for the fields it names.** The console shows
which fields came from the file.

## Fields

| File key | Setting | Applies to |
|---|---|---|
| `deploy.start` / `startCommand` / `start_command` | Start command | all |
| `deploy.preDeploy` / `preDeployCommand` | Pre-deploy command | all |
| `deploy.healthcheckPath` / `healthcheck_path` | Health check path | web services |
| `deploy.healthcheckTimeout` | Health check timeout, seconds | web services |
| `deploy.restartPolicy` / `restartPolicyType` | `always`, `on_failure` or `never` | all |
| `deploy.maxRetries` / `restartPolicyMaxRetries` | Retries before giving up | all |
| `deploy.replicas` / `numReplicas` | Replicas | all |
| `deploy.cron` / `cronSchedule` | Five-field schedule | cron services |
| `deploy.region` | `us-east`, `us-west` or `us-mia` | all |
| `deploy.sleep` / `sleepApplication` | Sleep when idle, five minutes by default | web services with a public address |
| `build_command` | Build command, Railpack builds only | static services |
| `output_dir` | Directory to serve, relative to the app | static services |

`variables` are read as names; values are not taken from the file.

## What the file cannot carry

Keys with no equivalent are reported in the plan and in the console rather than
dropped quietly: `build.builder`, `build.dockerfilePath`, and anything unknown.

> **Note: Where the value came from**
>
> Every field the file sets is recorded against the file and key that set it, so
> "why is the start command this?" has an answer months later.

pages.title: Services variables
pages.description: Set a service's variables, reference another service's, share variables across an environment, and generate secrets.
pages.markdown:
Variables are stored sealed at rest.
A read returns a masked preview, never the value.
The only plaintext read is `reveal`, which needs `env:reveal` and a person's own credential, and which refuses a sealed variable.

## Set a variable

```bash
miosa service vars set shop API NODE_ENV=production
miosa service vars list shop API
```

TypeScript:

```typescript
await miosa.services.setVariables(serviceId, { NODE_ENV: "production" });
const variables = await miosa.services.variables(serviceId);
```

Python:

```python
miosa.services.set_variables(service_id, {"NODE_ENV": "production"})
variables = miosa.services.variables(service_id)
```

A write merges by name. Deleting takes names:

```bash
miosa service vars unset shop API NODE_ENV,OLD_FLAG
```

## References

A value may be a reference.
MIOSA resolves it when the release starts, so the service always sees the current value.

| Expression | Resolves to |
|---|---|
| `${{Postgres.DATABASE_URL}}` | A variable of another service in the same environment |
| `${{shared.API_BASE}}` | An environment shared variable |
| `${{NAME}}` | Another variable of the same service |
| `${{secret(32)}}` | A generated random secret of 32 characters |

```bash
miosa service vars set shop API DATABASE_URL='${{Postgres.DATABASE_URL}}'
```

Quote the value in a shell so `${{...}}` reaches MIOSA unchanged.

A cycle or a malformed expression is refused with every problem at once, and nothing is written.
A reference to a service or variable that does not exist yet is allowed to be saved, but it blocks the deploy and shows up under `problems`.

## Shared variables

Shared variables belong to the environment and are visible to every service in it.

```bash
miosa project vars set shop API_BASE=https://api.acme.dev
miosa project vars list shop
miosa project vars unset shop API_BASE
```

A service reads one with `${{shared.API_BASE}}`.

## When a change needs a release

Writing a variable does not change the running release.
MIOSA records what the write made stale on the service document as `pending_changes`:

```json
{"needs": "rebuild", "variables": ["DATABASE_URL"], "because": "Web.DATABASE_URL", "at": "..."}
```

- `needs: rebuild` when a build-visible variable changed, because a redeploy alone would ship the value inlined at build time.
- `needs: redeploy` for every other variable, which is read when the release starts.
- `because` is `own`, `shared`, or the reference that carried the change: changing `Web.DATABASE_URL` marks every service whose expression uses it, and changing a shared variable marks every service that reads it.

```bash
miosa service get shop API
```

A deploy clears the mark, and a rebuild is never downgraded by a later runtime change:

```bash
miosa service deploy shop API
```

## Check what a deploy will receive

```bash
miosa service vars effective shop API
```

This shows every variable the release will receive, with references resolved and values still masked, plus a `problems` list.
A release is refused while that list is not empty.

## Read one value

```bash
miosa service vars reveal shop API DATABASE_URL
```

Reveal is for a person acting as themselves.
A sealed variable never reveals, and every reveal is audited with the variable's name and never its value.

## Build-time variables

A variable can be marked build-visible, so the build sees it too.
Platform-provided values are never sent to a build.
Names starting with `MIOSA_` or `RAILPACK_` are reserved.

pages.title: Services environments
pages.description: Every project starts with a production environment. Fork it into staging or a preview, and switch between environments on the canvas.
pages.markdown:
An environment is a copy of a project that runs on its own.
Every project starts with a `production` environment.
Add `staging`, a preview, or anything else you need.

Each environment has its own services, variables and releases.
A change in staging does not touch production.

## Switch and fork on the canvas

The environment name sits in the canvas top bar, next to the project name.
Open it to see every environment of the project and to switch between them.
The canvas reloads for the environment you pick, and the address carries it as `?env=<name>`.

Choose **Fork** to create a new environment from the one you are looking at.
Give it a name.
MIOSA copies the services and variables, then shows a summary of what was copied and what was skipped.

## From the API

```text
GET  /api/v1/projects/:id/environments
POST /api/v1/projects/:id/environments/:env/duplicate   {"name": "staging"}
```

`duplicate` returns the new environment, the services and variables it copied, and the entries it skipped.
The project's service routes accept `?env=<name>`; without it they use `production`.

## Where to go next

- [Variables](/docs/services/variables): variables and references are per environment.
- [Releases and rollback](/docs/services/releases): each environment has its own releases.
- Docker Host has its own [environments](/docs/docker-host/environments) for the former Docker Host deployments.

pages.title: Preview environments
pages.description: Open a pull request and MIOSA deploys it to its own environment with its own addresses, then removes it when the pull request closes.
pages.markdown:
A preview environment is a copy of your project's default environment that runs a pull request.
Open a pull request and MIOSA creates the environment, deploys the pull request's branch, and comments the addresses on the pull request.
Close or merge it and the environment is deleted.

## What happens

| Pull request event | What MIOSA does |
|---|---|
| Opened or reopened | Forks the default environment as `pr-<number>`, deploys every service from the pull request's branch, and comments the addresses |
| New commit pushed | Redeploys the services of `pr-<number>` |
| Closed or merged | Deletes `pr-<number>` and nothing else |

Each server service in the preview is named `<service>-pr-<number>`.
Variables are copied from the environment it was forked from.
A preview never changes the environment it came from.

## Turn it on

Open the project's **Settings** in the console and choose **Previews**.
Set the repository as `owner/name`, switch previews on, and save.
The page shows the webhook URL and the secret to paste into GitHub.

In the GitHub repository, add a webhook:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Payload URL | The URL shown in Previews, `https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/hooks/git/<project id>` |
| Content type | `application/json` |
| Secret | The secret from Previews |
| Events | Pull requests only |

The repository you set must match GitHub's `full_name` exactly, or deliveries are ignored.
A delivery is accepted only when its signature matches the secret.
The secret is write-only: it is never shown again, so keep a copy or set a new one.

## Cost control

| Setting | Default | Range |
|---|---|---|
| `max_open` | 3 | 1 to 20 |
| `ttl_hours` | 72 | 1 to 720 |

A fourth preview is refused while three are open.
A preview for a pull request nobody closed is deleted after 72 hours.
Raise or lower both in Previews.

## From the API

```text
GET    /api/v1/projects/:id/previews
PUT    /api/v1/projects/:id/previews
DELETE /api/v1/projects/:id/previews/:preview_id
```

`PUT` replaces the row, so send the whole object: `{repository, enabled, max_open, ttl_hours, secret}`.
A blank or absent `secret` keeps the one already stored.
The row you get back reports `has_secret`, never the secret, and the `webhook_path` to use.
These routes need the `projects:read` and `projects:write` scopes.

## Where to go next

- [Environments](/docs/services/environments): fork an environment by hand.
- [Variables](/docs/services/variables): what a preview copies.

pages.title: Services releases
pages.description: Deploy a service, follow the release state machine, read a failure reason, promote or roll back, and cancel a release.
pages.markdown:
A release is one build-and-serve attempt of a service.
It is immutable: it freezes the source, the settings and the built image it ran with.

## Deploy

```bash
miosa service deploy shop API                        # rebuild the service's own source
miosa service deploy shop API --dir . --wait         # upload a directory
miosa service deploy shop API --repo https://github.com/acme/api --branch main
miosa service deploy shop API --image ghcr.io/acme/api:1.4 --port 8080
```

Every release takes an `Idempotency-Key`; the CLI sends one so a retried command returns the first release instead of starting a second.

`--wait` follows the release and exits non-zero if it fails, printing the reason.

## The state machine

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `queued` | Accepted, waiting for a worker. |
| `building` | The source is being built. |
| `built` | The image exists; the release is about to start replicas. |
| `pre_deploy` | `pre_deploy_command` is running in the new replica. |
| `starting` | Replicas are booting. |
| `health_check` | The health path is being probed. |
| `active` | Serving. |
| `sleeping` | Idle sleep stopped the replicas; the next request wakes them. |
| `draining` | An earlier release is stopping. |
| `crashed` | A replica crashed and the restart policy did not recover it. |
| `failed` | Terminal failure, with a reason. |
| `canceled` | Canceled by a user. |
| `stopped` | Stopped by `stop`. |

A release that never leaves a state before its deadline is settled by the reaper with `deadline_exceeded`.

## Read a failure

```bash
miosa service releases shop API
miosa service logs shop API
miosa service logs shop API --release 6
```

`logs` prints every transition and the failure reason of the newest release, or of the release you name.
The release events carry the reason a release failed.
The build log and each replica's runtime lines are in the console's Logs tab; see [Logs](/docs/services/logs). The CLI does not stream them.

What a running replica printed is a separate read:

```text
GET /projects/:id/services/:sid/logs                    # the active release
GET /projects/:id/services/:sid/deployments/:did/logs   # one release
```

Each returns the last lines of every replica's output, with your secret values masked.
`tail` sets the number of lines (1 to 1000, default 200) and `replica` narrows it to one replica.
A replica that cannot be read says so in its own entry and does not hide the others.
It is a snapshot, not a stream.

Common reason codes:

| Code | What to do |
|---|---|
| `build_failed` | Read the build output; the command exited non-zero. |
| `clone_failed` | The repository or branch was not reachable, or the credential is wrong. |
| `image_pull_failed` | The image reference is wrong, or the registry secret is missing. |
| `healthcheck_timeout` | The app did not answer its health path in time. Check `start_command` and the port. |
| `pre_deploy_failed` | `pre_deploy_command` exited non-zero; nothing serves. |
| `no_capacity` | No host had room for the shape in that region. Try another region or a smaller `limits`. |
| `reference_missing` | A variable references something that does not exist. `miosa service vars effective` lists them. |
| `reference_cycle` | Two variables reference each other. |
| `deadline_exceeded` | The release sat in one state too long and the reaper settled it. |
| `quota_exceeded` | A plan limit was reached. |

## Promote and roll back

Rollback serves an earlier release's built image with its frozen source and settings.
Nothing is rebuilt, so it is fast.

```bash
miosa service rollback shop API 3 --yes
miosa service promote  shop API 3 --yes   # the same call
```

The Services API has one operation for this and calls it rollback.
The CLI accepts `promote` as its name for "serve this release again"; there is no separate promote route.

## Cancel and remove

```bash
miosa service cancel shop API 7     # a queued or building release
miosa service release shop API 3    # one release
```

A release that already finished can be removed from the history; one that is still running cannot.

## Stop, start, restart

```bash
miosa service stop    shop API --yes   # stop every active release now
miosa service start   shop API         # start a stopped service
miosa service restart shop API         # queue a release that restarts it
```

`stop` fails with `SERVICES_NOT_STOPPED` if a replica cannot be stopped, so a service is never reported stopped while it still runs.
`start` on a service that is already running or starting is `SERVICE_CONFLICT`.

## Rollout and rollback of several services

Each service releases independently.
For a coordinated change, apply a template or a change set, which stages every service's change and deploys them together.

pages.title: Moving from Railway
pages.description: Bring a Railway project to MIOSA with one reviewed plan, every environment in its own Deploy target, services created stopped, and an exact list of what carries over and what you finish by hand.
pages.markdown:
`miosa import railway` reads a Railway project through Railway's public API and writes a plan.
The plan lists the MIOSA project, one Deploy target per Railway environment, and in each target the services, databases, variable names and shared variables it would create.
It also lists everything it cannot carry across.
Nothing is created until you review the plan and apply it, and an apply starts nothing unless you ask.

This page is the reference for what carries over, what does not, and what to do about the secrets.

## Before you start

- A Railway token: an account, workspace or project token from Railway's account settings.
  `--project` takes the project's id, or its name when the login can list it; if Railway refuses, the import prints Railway's message and asks for the id.
  MIOSA reads it, never stores it, and never writes it to the plan.
  If you are logged in with the Railway CLI, `--via railway-cli` reads through that session instead, so no token passes through MIOSA.
- The MIOSA CLI, `@miosa/cli` 2.13.4 or newer:

```bash
npm install -g @miosa/cli
miosa --version
```

- GitHub connected to MIOSA, when your services build from GitHub repositories:

```bash
miosa connections add apps github
```

- Assume every secret in the Railway project is compromised.
  Railway disclosed on 2026-10-21 that its secrets were exposed, so the import copies names, not values, unless you explicitly ask otherwise.

## The steps

```bash
export RAILWAY_TOKEN=...                                          # or --token-file, or a prompt
miosa import railway --project acme-api --environment all         # review only; nothing is created
miosa import railway --project acme-api --environment all --out plan.json
miosa import railway --apply --plan plan.json --region us-east    # creates everything, stopped
miosa service vars set acme-api api STRIPE_KEY=<new value> --deploy-target production
miosa service deploy acme-api api --deploy-target production
```

`--environment` takes one environment, several (`production,staging`), or `all`.
The default is `production`.

The review prints what will be created in each Deploy target, where each setting came from, which variables need a value, and a "Finish by hand" list with the next step for each item.
Every field that cannot be carried appears there; nothing is dropped silently.

## What apply does

- It creates the project, then one Deploy target per Railway environment, reusing a target that already exists.
- It creates every service in the Deploy target of its environment, so `production` and `development` keep separate services, variables and settings.
- It creates every service **stopped**.
  Nothing builds or runs until you deploy it with `miosa service deploy`, or apply with `--deploy`.
- `--deploy` starts every service that has a source, after the GitHub copies are ready.
  It refuses while any variable has no value, so a service never starts with an empty secret.
- It does **not** attach custom domains unless you pass `--attach-domains`.
  Attaching a live domain during the import would move its traffic before the MIOSA services run.
  Without the flag, the review lists each domain as skipped and the summary prints the command that attaches it later.
- It links a GitHub repository, private or public, through your GitHub connection.
  MIOSA copies the repository into Forge and builds from the copy, so no credential is stored on the service.
- It checks everything before creating anything.
  If GitHub is not connected, it stops with `Connect GitHub first: miosa connections add apps github`.
  If your connection cannot read a repository, it names the repository and stops.
