```text
preview/pr-42: version 19 active  ← single-feature preview
```

## Env vars
```http
POST /api/v1/deployments/:id/env
GET  /api/v1/deployments/:id/env
```

Env vars are stored encrypted at rest (ChaCha20-Poly1305) and injected into the sandbox during development and into runtime instances at boot. The list endpoint returns previews of values, not the raw values, by default.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
await miosa.deployments.env.set(deploymentId, {
  environment: "production",
  vars: {
    STRIPE_KEY: "sk_live_...",
    NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: "https://api.example.net",
  },
})

const preview = await miosa.deployments.env.list(deploymentId, {
  environment: "production",
})
// preview returns: { STRIPE_KEY: "sk_live_••••", NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL: "https://api…" }
```

**cURL**

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/deployments/$DEP/env \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "environment": "production",
    "vars": { "STRIPE_KEY": "sk_live_..." }
  }'
```

## Secrets vs env vars

There's no strict UI distinction today: env vars are encrypted at rest regardless. The convention is:

- **Env vars**: configuration that can be retrieved as preview (truncated value).
- **Secrets**: same encryption, but marked `is_secret: true` so previews always show `••••` even to your own admins.

Future-state, secrets will support rotation and access-event audit logging.

## Data service bindings

When you create a Postgres / Redis / bucket via [Data](/docs/data/overview), you bind it to a specific deployment environment. MIOSA injects the credential into env at boot:
```text

production env:    DATABASE_URL=postgres://prod...
staging env:       DATABASE_URL=postgres://staging...
```

You don't ship two database URLs for one app; you ship one connection string variable, and MIOSA picks the right value based on which environment the runtime is booted in.

## Where to go next

- [Publishing](/docs/docker-host/publishing): environments are picked at publish time
- [Domains](/docs/docker-host/domains): attach a staging subdomain
- [Data](/docs/data/overview): environment-scoped credentials

pages.title: Dynamic Runtimes
pages.description: Dynamic deployments: production runtimes started from a release, health-checked, and reconciled by MIOSA.
pages.markdown:
A **Runtime Instance** is a running production runtime that serves a dynamic deployment. Static deployments do not have runtime instances; they are served from immutable static artifacts.

> **Note: Phase status**
>
> The caller-facing contract is stable: dynamic deployments start production runtimes, wait for health checks, and only promote when the new version is ready. You do not need to know how MIOSA places or reconciles those runtimes.

## What a runtime instance is

A runtime started from the customer's release. The release is the customer's app, fully packaged. The runtime:

1. Boots in under a few seconds.
2. Receives `PORT` (the release port, unless you set your own), `DATABASE_URL`, `AUTH_URL`, and other env vars injected by MIOSA at boot.
3. Starts the configured `run_command`.
4. Listens on `port`.
5. Responds to `GET health_check_path` with 2xx.
6. Joins the deployment's backend pool; the router starts sending it traffic.

When a runtime instance dies (crash, host failure, configured restart), MIOSA's reconciler notices and schedules a replacement on another healthy host.

## Where it runs

Each runtime instance runs in its own microVM on a MIOSA-managed host.
Runtimes of different customers are segmented from each other on the network, and a runtime can reach only the services you have linked to it plus the public internet.
A restart of the host's agent does not stop a running instance.
The agent reattaches to it when it comes back.

## The port your app must use

MIOSA sets `PORT` to the release's port (the service `port`, `8080` by default) unless you set `PORT` yourself in the deployment's env vars.
Your app must listen on that port on all interfaces (`0.0.0.0`), not only on `127.0.0.1`.
MIOSA reaches it from inside the microVM and publishes it at the instance's address.
The address and port the API reports for an instance are where MIOSA's router reaches it, and are not always the runtime's private address.

## Next.js apps

Set `output: "standalone"` in `next.config`.
When the build produces `.next/standalone/server.js`, MIOSA copies `public` and `.next/static` beside it and runs:

```bash
HOSTNAME=0.0.0.0 node .next/standalone/server.js
```

A standalone release carries its own traced `node_modules`, so MIOSA does not reinstall dependencies in the runtime.
Without standalone output, a Next.js app starts with `next start` and needs the full build.

## Build output is required

A Next.js release must contain its production build: `.next/BUILD_ID` has to exist in the release.
A release that is only the source tree cannot run, because `next start` stops at once with `Could not find a production build`.
MIOSA refuses such a release at publish time and again at start time, with the error `build_output_missing`.
Fix it by running the build before the release is created, or by letting MIOSA build the app, and publish again.

## When a start fails

A runtime instance start fails, and the instance is removed, when any of these happens:

| Error | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `release_install_failed` | Downloading, verifying or unpacking the release failed. The error carries the exit code and the last output of the step. |
| `build_output_missing` | A Next.js release has no production build (see above). |
| `app_launch_failed` | The start command could not be launched. |
| `app_not_listening` | The app started but did not answer its health check on its port. |

For `release_install_failed`, `app_launch_failed` and `app_not_listening`, the deployment's error message includes the tail of the app's log, the processes running in the runtime, and the ports it is listening on, so you can see why it did not come up.
Read it first: the usual causes are an app that binds `127.0.0.1` instead of `0.0.0.0`, a wrong `port`, a missing dependency, or a missing build.
Because the failed instance is removed, a start that fails never serves traffic and the previous version stays live.

## What you control vs what MIOSA controls

| You | MIOSA |
|---|---|
| Release contents (your code + dependencies) | Where to schedule instances |
| `run_command` and `port` | When to start / stop / replace instances |
| `health_check_path` | Routing healthy instances to traffic |
| Desired replica count (eventually; defaults to 1) | Boot-time env var injection |
| Env vars set on the deployment | Telemetry, logs streaming |

You don't pick a host directly. MIOSA's scheduler matches your workload's requirements (CPU, RAM, region) against the fleet's free capacity.

## Lifecycle

pending goes to starting on scheduled; starting goes to healthy on checks pass; healthy goes to stopping on tear down; stopping goes to stopped.

starting goes to unhealthy on checks fail; unhealthy goes to stopping on replaced.

starting goes to failed on crashloop budget spent.

- `pending`: scheduled, not yet booting.
- `starting`: VM is booting; health check not yet passing.
- `healthy`: serving traffic.
- `unhealthy`: failing health checks; router has removed it from the pool. Reconciler decides whether to restart or replace.
- `stopping` / `stopped`: deliberately torn down.
- `failed`: terminal, having exceeded the crashloop budget. Reconciler stops trying.

## Health checks and the grace period

When a runtime instance starts, it has a configurable grace period (default 60s) to become healthy. During grace, repeated 5xx / connection-refused are tolerated.

After grace, the health check is enforced strictly:

- 3 consecutive failures → instance marked `unhealthy`, removed from routing.
- If a replacement is needed and starts healthily, the old instance is torn down.
- Repeated rapid failures invoke crashloop backoff: 1s → 2s → 5s → 30s → 5min between restart attempts.

## Blue/green during publish

When you publish a new dynamic version, MIOSA does NOT terminate the existing healthy instances first. The sequence is:

1. Start new runtime instances from the new release.
2. Wait until enough new instances pass health checks.
3. Update the router so the deployment's hostname points at the new instances.
4. Drain (stop accepting new connections) and tear down old instances after old in-flight requests complete.

If step 2 never succeeds, step 3 never runs. The old version stays live, the new version is marked `failed`.

## Replicas

By default, a dynamic service has 1 replica. Increase by setting `desired_replicas` on the service. The reconciler spreads replicas across hosts and across availability zones where possible.
```typescript
await miosa.services.update(serviceId, { desiredReplicas: 3 })
```

Traffic load-balances across all healthy replicas in round-robin (or hash-based if sticky sessions are configured).

## Resource sizing

| Spec | Default | Tunable per service |
|---|---|---|
| CPU | 1 vCPU | yes |
| Memory | 512 MB | yes |
| Disk | 1 GB ephemeral | yes |
| GPU | none | not available (GPU is not productized) |
| Outbound bandwidth | metered | yes |

Sizing is per-service, per-deployment. A worker service can be smaller than a web service.

## Logs

Runtime instances stream stdout/stderr to MIOSA's log plane. Logs are retained per the tenant's plan (default 7 days). Access them through:

- `GET /api/v1/deployments/:id/logs`: deployment-scoped, all services
- `GET /api/v1/services/:id/logs`: per-service
- `GET /api/v1/runtime-instances/:id/logs`: per-instance

Logs include structured metadata: `service_id`, `runtime_instance_id`, `version_id`, `host_id`. Filter by `external_workspace_id` to scope to a white-label customer.

## See also

- [Releases](/docs/docker-host/releases): what runtime instances boot from
- [Environments](/docs/docker-host/environments): variable / secret scope
- [Domains](/docs/docker-host/domains): how traffic finds your instances
- [Rollback](/docs/docker-host/rollback): what happens to old instances on rollback

pages.title: Deployment Domains
pages.description: Preview domains, tenant deployment domains, managed fallback URLs, exact custom domains, DNS verification, automatic TLS, and route changes.
pages.markdown:
A **Domain** is a hostname that routes to a preview, a deployment, a computer, or an exact custom resource. For production deployments, always use the `public_url` returned by the API. Do not reconstruct hostnames in SDKs, CLIs, or frontends.

## Domain layers

MIOSA keeps these layers separate:

| Layer | URL shape | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Sandbox preview domain | `https://{port}-{sandbox_slug}.sandbox.{preview_domain}` | Mutable live previews while an agent/user is editing |
| Tenant deployment domain | `https://{deployment_slug}.{deployment_domain}` | Branded durable URLs for generated production apps |
| Managed fallback domain | `https://{deployment_slug}.{organization_slug}.miosa.app` | Always-available MIOSA-managed fallback |
| Exact custom domain | `https://customer-owned.example.com` | A customer's chosen production domain attached to one deployment |
| Computer custom domain | `https://desktop.customer-owned.example.com` | A customer-owned hostname attached to one computer service |

Lumen is a made-up company, and `example.com` and `example.net` are reserved example domains.
Replace them with your own.

Lumen example:

```text
Sandbox preview:   https://5173-abc123.sandbox.example.com
Deployment domain: https://lead-magnet.apps.example.com
Managed fallback:  https://lead-magnet.example-org.miosa.app
Custom domain:     https://portal.example.net
```

Preview domains do not imply production deployment domains. Configure both if you want both surfaces branded.

## Tenant deployment domains

Tenant deployment domains are configured separately from preview domains. The backend resolves `settings["deployment_domain"]` for durable app URLs and falls back to `{organization_slug}.miosa.app` when no deployment domain is configured.

Public tenant-level management routes for deployment domains are not exposed yet. Operators can configure the tenant setting; SDKs and CLIs should treat deployment `public_url` / `url` as authoritative.

Recommended white-label DNS:

| Record type | Name | Value | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `CNAME` | `*` | `proxy.miosa.ai` | Preview domain, including sandbox port previews |
| `CNAME` | `*.apps` | `proxy.miosa.ai` | Durable generated apps |

## Exact custom domains

Exact custom domains attach a customer-owned hostname to one deployment.
Exact custom domains are enabled by plan: Developer includes 3, Business 100 and Enterprise 500, with no support ticket. A Developer plan that has used all three gets `PLAN_LIMIT_REACHED` from the same check as any other cap.

| Kind | Example | DNS record |
|---|---|---|
| Subdomain | `app.example.net` | `CNAME` to the verification target |
| Apex | `example.net` | `A`/`AAAA`, `ALIAS`, `ANAME`, or flattened `CNAME` depending on DNS provider |
| WWW alias | `www.example.net` | `CNAME` to the verification target |

## The attach flow

**TypeScript**

```typescript
// 1. Register the exact domain. MIOSA returns DNS instructions.
const domain = await miosa.deployments.domains.add(deploymentId, {
  domain: "portal.example.net",
})

console.log(domain.dns_records)

// 2. After records are set, ask MIOSA to verify.
await miosa.deployments.domains.verify(deploymentId, domain.id)

// 3. Use the deployment public_url returned by the API.
const deployment = await miosa.deployments.get(deploymentId)
console.log(deployment.public_url)
```

**Python**

```python
from miosa import Miosa

miosa = Miosa(api_key="msk_u_...")

domain = miosa.deployments.domains(deployment_id).add(
    domain="portal.example.net",
)

for record in domain.get("dns_records", []):
    print(record["type"], record["name"], record["value"])

miosa.deployments.domains(deployment_id).verify(domain["id"])

deployment = miosa.deployments.get(deployment_id)
print(deployment["public_url"])
```

**cURL**

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/deployments/$DEP/domains \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"domain":"portal.example.net"}'

curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/deployments/$DEP/domains/$DOMAIN_ID/verify \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

Once verified and TLS-active, MIOSA routes the exact domain to the deployment's active version. Exact custom domains take precedence over tenant deployment domains and MIOSA fallback URLs.

## Redirect policy

For apex + www domains, set the redirect policy:

| Policy | Result |
|---|---|
| `none` | Both apex and www serve independently |
| `apex_to_www` | `example.net` redirects to `www.example.net` |
| `www_to_apex` | `www.example.net` redirects to `example.net` |

Configure at attach time or update later via `PATCH /deployments/:id/domains/:domain_id`.

## What changing a domain does

Changing a domain mapping:

- Updates MIOSA's route table.
- Takes effect within seconds.
- Does **not** rebuild the app.
- Does **not** involve the source sandbox.
- Does **not** require users to change the deployment ID.

This is why rollback is fast: only the deployment's active version/route changes.

## DNS verification edge cases

| Situation | Behavior |
|---|---|
| CNAME points to the wrong host | Verification fails with `dns_target_mismatch`. Show the expected target. |
| TXT record not propagated yet | Verification fails with `dns_propagation_pending`. Retry after a few minutes. |
| User typos the domain | Verification fails with `dns_resolution_error`. Domain stays pending. |
| Domain already attached to another deployment in your tenant | `409 Conflict`. Detach from the other deployment first. |
| Domain attached to a different tenant | `403 Forbidden`. Contact support for transfer. |

## Provider input fields

DNS providers label the same fields differently.

Use the exact values MIOSA returns and translate only the field name:

| MIOSA instruction | Common provider labels | Example for `*.apps.example.com` |
|---|---|---|
| Record type | Type | `CNAME` |
| Host | Name, Host, Alias | `*.apps` |
| Target | Value, Points to, Destination | `proxy.miosa.ai` |
| TTL | TTL, Cache time | Automatic or 300 seconds |

Do not enter `https://`, a path, or a trailing slash in a DNS target.

Disable provider proxying until MIOSA reports that ownership and TLS verification are complete.

## Verification sequence

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A["Register hostname"] --> B["Copy exact DNS records"]
  B --> C["Authoritative DNS answers"]
  C --> D["MIOSA verifies ownership"]
  D --> E["Certificate becomes active"]
  E --> F["Route serves active Version"]
```

If DNS resolves but the page still fails, continue with the [Recovery Playbooks](/docs/operations/recovery) instead of changing records repeatedly.

## White-label checklist

For a platform like Lumen:

1. Configure the organization slug (`lumen`).
2. Configure preview DNS: a wildcard `CNAME` named `*` on `example.com`, pointing to `proxy.miosa.ai`.
3. Configure tenant deployment DNS, for example `*.apps.example.com`.
4. Publish generated apps and display the returned deployment `public_url`.
5. Attach exact customer domains only when a customer brings its own domain.

> **Note: Current V1 rule**
>
> Preview domains, deployment domains, computer URLs, and exact custom domains are separate. Use the URL returned by the backend for each resource: `preview_url`, `desktop_url`, or deployment `public_url`.

## Set up a custom domain in the dashboard

Connect your own domain - for example `app.example.com` - so users land on your brand rather than a MIOSA fallback URL.

Go to **Settings → Domains** and click **+ Add custom domain**. The wizard walks you through three steps:

1. Enter your domain (`app.example.com`  -  no `https://`, no trailing path).
2. Add the DNS records shown to your domain provider.
3. Click **Continue to verify**  -  MIOSA checks your DNS and activates the domain.

You can also register the domain through the exact deployment or computer domain APIs before sending traffic; MIOSA returns the DNS records and verification status.

### Required DNS records

For wildcard preview or app domains, delegate traffic to MIOSA:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Type | `CNAME` |
| Host | `*` (wildcard) |
| Value | `proxy.miosa.ai` |
| TTL | `300` - `600` seconds |
| Proxy status (Cloudflare only) | **DNS only**  -  gray cloud |

Replace `yourdomain.com` with the apex domain you own (e.g. `example.com` if your custom domain is `app.example.com`).

> **Apex domains** (no subdomain, e.g. `example.com` directly) additionally require an A/ALIAS record  -  add `_miosa-verify.example.com TXT <token>` as shown in the wizard.

> **Caution: Important if you use Cloudflare DNS**
>
> If you're using Cloudflare as your DNS provider, make sure the wildcard CNAME has the proxy status set to **DNS only** (gray cloud), not **Proxied** (orange cloud). When proxied, Cloudflare terminates TLS itself and MIOSA never receives the request to issue a certificate  -  your sandbox URLs will fail with a TLS error. Other DNS providers (Route 53, Namecheap, GoDaddy, Porkbun) don't have this issue.

### TLS certificates and propagation

Certificates are provisioned automatically once DNS propagates. There is nothing to upload. You will see a valid `https://` certificate on first browser visit.

DNS changes typically take **5-30 minutes** but can take up to 48 hours depending on your provider's TTL settings.

To check current propagation status:

```bash
dig *.yourdomain.com CNAME +short
```

The expected result is `proxy.miosa.ai.`

Once configured and verified, MIOSA's router confirms the hostname belongs to your tenant, workspace, project, computer, or deployment, issues or reuses the TLS certificate, and routes the request to the current sandbox, computer, standard deployment, or Docker Host container. Domain ownership and tenant scope are checked before MIOSA routes traffic.

## Troubleshooting a routed domain

**Verification fails immediately after adding records**  -  DNS propagation is not instant. Wait a few minutes and click **Retry verification** in the wizard. The wizard polls every 5 seconds while open.

**`dig` shows the right value but verification still fails**  -  Some DNS providers add extra trailing dots or spaces. Ensure the CNAME value is exactly `proxy.miosa.ai` with no extra characters.

**Cache flush**  -  If the record still shows the old value, flush your local DNS cache:

```bash
# macOS
sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder

# Linux (systemd-resolved)
sudo systemd-resolve --flush-caches
```

Or check propagation from a neutral vantage point using [dnschecker.org](https://dnschecker.org/).

**My sandbox URL returns a TLS error or cert warning**  -  DNS hasn't propagated yet, or (on Cloudflare) the proxy status is not **DNS only**. Confirm the record with `dig +short "*.your-domain.com" CNAME` (expected `proxy.miosa.ai.`).

**My sandbox URL returns 502 or 503**  -  Your sandbox isn't running, or no HTTP server is listening on the port you're requesting. The DNS chain is correct; the sandbox just needs to serve traffic.

**My sandbox URL returns 400 or "URL not connected"**  -  The slug doesn't match any sandbox in your tenant. Confirm the sandbox is in `running` state and that the slug (first 8 hex chars of the sandbox UUID) matches the leftmost label of the hostname.

## Branding

Once your domain is connected, customize the app name, logo, accent color, and favicon at **Settings → General → Branding**. The Domains page shows a live preview of what your users will see.

## Disconnecting

To stop using your custom domain: remove the CNAME from your DNS provider, or open **Settings → Domains** in MIOSA and click **Disconnect**. After disconnecting, the next request to `<slug>.<your-domain>` will fail to issue a certificate. The domain becomes available to bind to a different tenant after the cache expires.

## White-label checklist

- [Publishing](/docs/docker-host/publishing): how `public_url` is returned
- [Versions](/docs/docker-host/versions): what the domain points at
- [Rollback](/docs/docker-host/rollback): repointing the deployment at an older version
- [White-label setup](/docs/platform/white-label): setup order for platforms

pages.title: Forge
pages.description: Git hosting built into MIOSA: a home for code written by you, your sandboxes and your agents, with deploys, pull request previews and merge rules.
pages.markdown:
Forge is Git hosting that is part of MIOSA.
Every organization has it, and every repository lives next to the sandboxes, agents and deployments that use it.

## Why Forge exists

Most code on MIOSA is not typed on a laptop.
It is written inside a sandbox, by you or by an agent such as Optimal, and it needs somewhere to go when the sandbox is done.
Forge is that place.

- **One account.** Your MIOSA API key is your Git credential. There is no separate Git host account and no access token to copy around.
- **Deploy from a branch.** Point a deployment at a branch and every push builds and ships a new version.
- **A preview for every pull request.** Each pull request on a linked repository gets its own preview version and a `deploy` check.
- **Merge rules you can enforce.** Branch policy decides how many approvals and which checks a pull request needs before it can merge.
- **Agents are first-class.** The same repositories are reachable from the CLI, the REST API and the SDKs, under the same permissions.

```mermaid
graph TD
    Sandbox["Sandbox or agent writes code"] -->|git push| Repo["Forge repository"]
    Repo -->|pull request| Preview["Preview version + deploy check"]
    Repo -->|push to main| Deploy["Deployment: new version live"]
    Preview -->|policy met, merge| Deploy
```

## What a repository gives you

| Area | What you get |
|---|---|
| Git | Clone, fetch and push over HTTPS at `https://forge.miosa.ai/<org>/<repo>.git` |
| Pull requests | Open, review, comment, diff, close, reopen and merge |
| Checks | Results reported against a commit, with evidence, that branch policy can require |
| Branch policy | Required approvals, independent reviewers, required checks, code owners |
| Releases | Tags with notes and downloadable assets, including a source archive |

Repositories are private by default.
Access follows your organization's roles, and each repository can grant extra roles to people.

## Where to start

- [Quickstart](/docs/forge/quickstart): a repository, a push and a pull request in five minutes.
- [Pull requests and checks](/docs/forge/pull-requests): reviews, checks, branch policy and merging.
- [From a sandbox](/docs/forge/sandboxes): plain `git push` from inside a sandbox.
- [Agents and the API](/docs/forge/agents): Forge from the SDKs and the REST API.
- [CLI reference](/docs/forge/cli): every `miosa forge` command with an example.
- [Limits and FAQ](/docs/forge/faq): what Forge does not do yet.

> **Note: Forge permissions**
>
> Forge uses your MIOSA login: `miosa login` gives the CLI a key that can read and write Forge.
> A key you create yourself under **API keys** needs the `forge:read` and `forge:write` permissions.

pages.title: Forge quickstart
pages.description: Create a Forge repository, push to it with plain git and open your first pull request, in five minutes.
pages.markdown:
This takes about five minutes. You need the `miosa` CLI (version 2.3.10 or later) and `git`. ## 1. Sign in ```bash miosa login miosa whoami ``` `miosa login` gives the CLI a key with the Forge permissions, `forge:read` and `forge:write`. If you use an API key you created yourself instead, tick both permissions when you create it under **API keys** in the console, then `export MIOSA_API_KEY=msk_...`. Without them every `miosa forge` command answers `insufficient scope`. ## 2. Let git use your MIOSA login ```bash miosa forge auth setup-git ``` ```text ok git now uses your MIOSA login for https://forge.miosa.ai ``` This adds a credential helper for `forge.miosa.ai` to your global git config. Git then signs in with your MIOSA key, so you never paste a password or token. ## 3. Create a repository and clone it ```bash miosa forge repo create hello-forge miosa forge repo clone hello-forge cd hello-forge ``` ```text ok Created repository "hello-forge" in the current organization Visibility: private Clone URL: https://forge.miosa.ai//hello-forge.git ``` A new repository is private and starts empty, so git warns that you cloned an empty repository. ## 4. Commit and push ```bash mkdir -p public printf '\nHello from Forge\n

Hello from Forge

\n' > public/index.html git add . git commit -m "First page" git push -u origin main ``` That is plain git: any client, editor or tool that speaks Git over HTTPS works the same way. ## 5. Open a pull request ```bash git checkout -b greeting sed -i.bak 's/Hello from Forge/Hello again from Forge/' public/index.html && rm public/index.html.bak git commit -am "Change the greeting" git push -u origin greeting miosa forge pr new hello-forge --head greeting --title "Change the greeting" miosa forge pr merge hello-forge 1 ``` ```text ok Merged pull request #1 into main as 0d4d9eebbc76 ``` An organization with one member can merge its own pull requests. Once a teammate joins, a pull request needs their approval first; see [branch policy](/docs/forge/pull-requests#branch-policy). ## Clean up ```bash miosa forge repo list miosa forge repo delete --yes ``` `repo delete` takes the repository id that `repo list` shows, and it is permanent. ## Next - [Pull requests, checks and branch policy](/docs/forge/pull-requests) - [Every forge command](/docs/forge/cli)

pages.title: Pull requests and checks
pages.description: Open a pull request on Forge, report checks, set branch policy and merge.
pages.markdown:
A pull request on a Forge repository works the way you expect from other Git hosts.
Checks report results against its commits, and branch policy decides when it can merge.

## Open a pull request

Push a branch, then open the pull request against the default branch:

```bash
git checkout -b greeting
sed -i.bak 's/Hello from Forge/Hello again from Forge/' public/index.html && rm public/index.html.bak
git commit -am "Change the greeting"
git push -u origin greeting
miosa forge pr new hello-forge --head greeting --title "Change the greeting" --body "Says hello again."
```

```text
Number:  1
Title:   Change the greeting
State:   open
From:    greeting
Into:    main
```

Read it back, see what changed and talk about it:

```bash
miosa forge pr list hello-forge
miosa forge pr show hello-forge 1
miosa forge pr diff hello-forge 1 --name-only
miosa forge pr comment hello-forge 1 --body "Looks good to me."
miosa forge pr comments hello-forge 1
```

## Branch policy

Branch policy decides what a pull request needs before it can merge into a branch.

```bash
miosa forge policy show hello-forge
```

```text
Policy:         main v1 (default policy)
Merging needs:  no approval needed (solo organization; the default policy tightens when a second member joins)
Approvals:      1
Independent:    yes
Self-merge:     yes
Checks:         none
```

An organization with one member merges without approvals.
Once a second person joins, the default policy asks for one approval from someone other than the author.

Set your own rules with `policy set`:

```bash
miosa forge policy set hello-forge --approvals 1 --check unit-tests
```

| Flag | What it does |
|---|---|
| `--approvals N` | How many approvals a pull request needs |
| `--independent` | The approver must be someone other than the author (default on) |
| `--check NAME` | A check that must pass; repeat it for several |
| `--code-owners` | Require a code owner's approval |
| `--dismiss-stale` | New commits dismiss earlier approvals (default on) |
| `--branch NAME` | The branch the policy covers (default: the default branch) |

### Working alone

An organization with one member can turn off the approval requirement so the author merges their own pull requests:

```bash
miosa forge policy set hello-forge --branch main --approvals 0 --independent=false
```

Required checks still apply.

## Report your own checks

Any tool can report a check against a commit, for example a test run.
A completed check needs evidence: a JSON file with an `evidence` object of up to 64 KB.

```bash
echo '{"evidence": {"runner": "npm test", "passed": 12, "failed": 0}}' > check.json
miosa forge check report hello-forge --commit "$(git rev-parse HEAD)" --name unit-tests --conclusion passed --summary "12 tests passed" --file check.json
miosa forge check list hello-forge --commit "$(git rev-parse HEAD)"
```

> **Note: A required check comes from someone else**
>
> A check that branch policy requires must be reported by someone other than the pull request's author: MIOSA itself, a CI identity or another member of your organization.
> That way an author can never pass their own gate.
> A check the author reports still shows on the pull request, but it does not count toward the policy, and `miosa forge pr check` refuses it with `CHECK_SEPARATION_REQUIRED`.

## Review and merge

A teammate reviews the pull request; the author cannot approve their own:

```bash
miosa forge pr review hello-forge 1 --decision approved --body "Ship it."
```

When the branch policy is met, anyone with write access merges it:

```bash
miosa forge pr merge hello-forge 1
```

```text
ok  Merged pull request #1 into main as 0d4d9eebbc76
```

> **Note: Merge methods**
>
> Today a merge always creates a merge commit.
> The CLI already has `--squash`, `--rebase` and `--auto`, but the server refuses them with `this MIOSA server does not support --squash yet; nothing was merged`.
> Nothing is merged when that happens.

## Fix "needs approval"

When a pull request does not meet its branch policy, the merge is refused and nothing changes:

```text
miosa: pull request #3 cannot merge: policy main v5 needs 1 approval from someone other than the author [REQUIRED_APPROVALS_MISSING]
  Ask someone with write access to approve:  miosa forge pr review hello-forge 3 --decision approved
  Working alone? Let the author merge:      miosa forge policy set hello-forge --branch main --approvals 0 --independent=false
```

Either ask a member with write access to approve, or, if you work alone, lower the policy with the second command.
A missing required check fails the same way with `REQUIRED_CHECK_EVIDENCE_UNAVAILABLE`; run `miosa forge pr show` to see which check is missing.

## Work on someone else's pull request

```bash
miosa forge pr checkout hello-forge 2 --branch review-2
miosa forge pr close hello-forge 2
miosa forge pr reopen hello-forge 2
```

pages.title: Forge from a sandbox
pages.description: Clone and push to Forge from inside a sandbox with plain git, using the sandbox's own identity.
pages.markdown:
Code written inside a sandbox, by you or by an agent, should land in a Forge repository with a plain `git push`. No API key is copied into the sandbox for that. > **Note: Rolling out** > > Everything on this page is rolling out now. > Until it reaches your organization, a `git clone` or `git push` to Forge from inside a sandbox answers `Authentication failed`. ## How it works A sandbox already carries its own token, scoped to its organization and workspace. Forge accepts that token for the repositories of the sandbox's own workspace, and the sandbox writes a git credential helper for `forge.miosa.ai` when it boots. So inside the sandbox, git just works: ```bash git clone https://forge.miosa.ai//.git cd git checkout -b from-sandbox echo "

Written in a sandbox.

" >> public/index.html git commit -am "Edit from a sandbox" git push -u origin from-sandbox ``` The sandbox reaches only the repositories of its own workspace, with the same branch policy as everyone else. Then open a pull request from your machine, the CLI or the API, as in [pull requests](/docs/forge/pull-requests). ## Today, before it reaches you Do not copy a personal API key into a sandbox to work around it: anyone and any agent that can read the sandbox can read the key. If you need the files now, copy them out with `miosa files cp -r my-box:/workspace/site ./site` and push from your machine.

pages.title: Agents and the Forge API
pages.description: Use Forge from the TypeScript and Python SDKs and the REST API: repositories, files, branches, pull requests, checks and releases.
pages.markdown:
Agents reach Forge the same way you do: with a MIOSA API key, under the same organization roles and branch policy. Nothing an agent does can skip a policy that would stop you. ## From the TypeScript SDK ```bash npm install @miosa/sdk ``` ```ts import { Miosa } from "@miosa/sdk"; const miosa = new Miosa({ apiKey: process.env.MIOSA_API_KEY }); // Every repository in your organization. const repos = await miosa.forge.repositories.list(); console.log(repos.map((repo) => repo.name)); // Read a file from the default branch. const repo = repos.find((r) => r.slug === "hello-forge"); const file = await miosa.forge.repositories.blob(repo.id, { path: "public/index.html" }); console.log(file.content); ``` `miosa.forge.repositories` also has `create`, `get`, `refs`, `tree`, `readme`, `commits`, `putFile`, `deleteFile`, `update` and `delete`. The Python SDK has the same surface as `client.forge`. ## The REST API All routes are under `https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/forge/repositories` and take your key as `Authorization: Bearer `. `:id` is the repository id. | Method | Path | What it does | |---|---|---| | `GET` | `/` | List repositories | | `POST` | `/` | Create a repository | | `GET` | `/:id` | Show a repository | | `GET` | `/:id/refs` | Branches and tags | | `GET` | `/:id/tree?ref=main&path=` | A directory listing | | `GET` | `/:id/blob?ref=main&path=README.md` | A file's content | | `GET` | `/:id/commits?ref=main` | Commit history | | `POST` | `/:id/branches` | Create a branch: `{"name": "...", "from": "main"}` | | `PUT` | `/:id/files/:path` | Write a file as a commit on a branch | | `GET` | `/:id/pull-requests` | List pull requests | | `POST` | `/:id/pull-requests` | Open a pull request: `{"title", "head", "base"}` | | `POST` | `/:id/pull-requests/:number/reviews` | Review a pull request | | `POST` | `/:id/pull-requests/:number/merge` | Merge a pull request | | `POST` | `/:id/pull-requests/:number/close` | Close a pull request | | `GET` | `/:id/check-suites` | Checks reported against commits | | `GET` | `/:id/releases` | List releases | | `POST` | `/:id/releases` | Publish a release | > **Note: Every write needs an Idempotency-Key** > > Each `POST` and `PUT` needs an `Idempotency-Key` header. > Repeating a request with the same key returns the first result instead of acting twice, so an agent can retry safely. > Without the header the API answers `IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REQUIRED`. ### Write a file to a branch A file write is a commit. It needs the branch's current head commit as `expected_head`, so two writers never overwrite each other silently: ```bash curl -X PUT "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/forge/repositories/$REPO_ID/files/public%2Fapi.html" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \ -H "Idempotency-Key: $(uuidgen)" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d "{\"path\": \"public/api.html\", \"content\": \"

From the API.

\\n\", \"message\": \"Add a page from the API\", \"branch\": \"api-branch\", \"expected_head\": \"$HEAD_SHA\"}" ``` The answer has the new commit and the policy decision that allowed it. Without `expected_head` the API answers `EXPECTED_HEAD_REQUIRED`; get the head from `GET /:id/refs`.

pages.title: Forge CLI reference
pages.description: Every miosa forge command with an example: auth, repositories, pull requests, checks, branch policy, grants, forks and releases.
pages.markdown:
Every command takes a repository by name, `org/name` or id, except `repo show`, `repo update` and `repo delete`, which take the id.
Add `--json` to any command for a stable JSON envelope.
Commands that change something take `--idempotency-key`, so a retry never acts twice.

> **Note: Version**
>
> These examples use CLI 2.3.10.
> Run `miosa update` to get the latest.

## auth

| Command | Example |
|---|---|
| `auth setup-git` | `miosa forge auth setup-git` |

Makes git use your MIOSA key for `https://forge.miosa.ai`.
`--host` points it at another Forge host.

## repo

| Command | Example |
|---|---|
| `repo create` | `miosa forge repo create hello-forge --visibility private --default-branch main` |
| `repo list` | `miosa forge repo list` |
| `repo show` | `miosa forge repo show <repository-id>` |
| `repo clone` | `miosa forge repo clone hello-forge` |
| `repo update` | `miosa forge repo update <repository-id> --name "Hello Forge"` |
| `repo delete` | `miosa forge repo delete <repository-id> --yes` |

`repo create` also takes `--slug` and `--project-id`.
`repo delete` is permanent.

## pr

| Command | Example |
|---|---|
| `pr new` | `miosa forge pr new hello-forge --head greeting --title "Change the greeting"` |
| `pr list` | `miosa forge pr list hello-forge --state all` |
| `pr show` | `miosa forge pr show hello-forge 1` |
| `pr diff` | `miosa forge pr diff hello-forge 1 --name-only` |
| `pr comment` | `miosa forge pr comment hello-forge 1 --body "Looks good to me."` |
| `pr comments` | `miosa forge pr comments hello-forge 1` |
| `pr review` | `miosa forge pr review hello-forge 1 --decision approved --body "Ship it."` |
| `pr merge` | `miosa forge pr merge hello-forge 1` |
| `pr check` | `miosa forge pr check hello-forge 1 --name lint --conclusion passed --head-sha <sha> --file check.json` |
| `pr checkout` | `miosa forge pr checkout hello-forge 2 --branch review-2` |
| `pr close` | `miosa forge pr close hello-forge 2` |
| `pr reopen` | `miosa forge pr reopen hello-forge 2` |

`pr new` takes `--base`, `--body`, `--draft` and `--head-repo` for a pull request from a fork.
`pr list` filters with `--state open|closed|merged|all`, `--author` and `--base`.
`pr review --decision` is `approved`, `changes_requested` or `commented`.
`pr check` reports a check on the pull request's head commit and is refused for the pull request's own author.

## check

| Command | Example |
|---|---|
| `check report` | `miosa forge check report hello-forge --commit <sha> --name unit-tests --conclusion passed --file check.json` |
| `check list` | `miosa forge check list hello-forge --commit <sha>` |
| `check suite` | `miosa forge check suite hello-forge <sha>` |
| `check show` | `miosa forge check show hello-forge <check-id>` |
| `check evidence` | `miosa forge check evidence hello-forge <check-id>` |

A completed check needs `{"evidence": {...}}` in `--file`, up to 64 KB.
`--status queued` or `in_progress` reports a check that is still running.

## policy

| Command | Example |
|---|---|
| `policy show` | `miosa forge policy show hello-forge` |
| `policy set` | `miosa forge policy set hello-forge --approvals 1 --check unit-tests` |
| `policy owners` | `miosa forge policy owners hello-forge` |

See [branch policy](/docs/forge/pull-requests#branch-policy) for every flag.

## grant

| Command | Example |
|---|---|
| `grant set` | `miosa forge grant set hello-forge <user-id> --role write` |

Roles are `read`, `write`, `maintain` and `admin`.

## fork

| Command | Example |
|---|---|
| `fork` | `miosa forge fork hello-forge --name hello-forge-fork` |

## release

| Command | Example |
|---|---|
| `release tag` | `miosa forge release tag hello-forge --name v0.1.0 --message "First tag"` |
| `release new` | `miosa forge release new hello-forge --tag v0.1.0 --name "First release" --body "Hello from Forge."` |
| `release upload` | `miosa forge release upload hello-forge v0.1.0 --source-archive` |
| `release list` | `miosa forge release list hello-forge` |
| `release show` | `miosa forge release show hello-forge v0.1.0` |

`release new` creates the tag if it does not exist; `--commit` picks what it points at and `--prerelease` marks it.
`release upload` attaches files, or a `.tar.gz` of the tagged commit with `--source-archive`.

pages.title: Forge limits and FAQ
pages.description: What Forge does and does not do yet: visibility, permissions, merge methods, issues, repository secrets and CI.
pages.markdown:
## Are repositories private?

Yes, by default.
A repository is `private`, `internal` or `public`, set with `repo create --visibility` or changed later with `repo update`.
Members of your organization get access through their organization role, and `grant set` gives one person an extra role on one repository.

## Which permissions does my API key need?

`forge:read` to clone, fetch and read, and `forge:write` to push, open and merge pull requests, report checks and publish releases.
`miosa login` gives a key with both.
A key without them gets `insufficient scope` and the name of the permission it needs.

## Can I use the GitHub CLI or another Git host?

Forge speaks standard Git over HTTPS, so any Git client works once `miosa forge auth setup-git` has run.
Pull requests, checks, policy and releases use `miosa forge`, the API or the SDKs.

## Can I import a repository from GitHub?

Yes, from the console.
An import copies the history once; a GitHub App connection keeps a repository mirrored.

## What Forge does not do

| Not supported | What to do |
|---|---|
| Issues | Track work in your own tool, or in pull request comments |
| Repository secrets | Set them on the deployment with `miosa deploy env-set` |
| CI that runs on push | Run your tests elsewhere and report the result with `miosa forge check report` |
| Squash, rebase and auto merge | Merges create a merge commit; the server refuses the other methods without merging |
| Pushing from a sandbox with its own identity | See [Forge from a sandbox](/docs/forge/sandboxes) |
| Raw file download, blame and Git LFS | Clone the repository |

> **Note**
>
> Forge does not do these today.

## Why was my merge refused?

The pull request does not meet the branch policy yet, and nothing was merged.
The error names what is missing and the command that fixes it; see [Fix "needs approval"](/docs/forge/pull-requests#fix-needs-approval).

pages.title: CI on MIOSA
pages.description: Run GitHub Actions jobs on MIOSA. Connect the MIOSA CI app, use runs-on miosa in a workflow, and each job runs in its own sandbox, billed per second.
pages.markdown:
CI on MIOSA runs your GitHub Actions jobs in MIOSA sandboxes.
You connect the MIOSA CI GitHub app, give it your repositories, change `runs-on: ubuntu-latest` to `runs-on: miosa` in a workflow and push.
Each job then runs in a new sandbox, billed per second, and the sandbox is deleted when the job ends.

The same state is in the console under **CI on MIOSA**, in the `miosa ci` commands and at `GET /api/v1/ci`.

## Set up

There are four steps.
The console page and `miosa ci status` show which are done.

1. **Install the MIOSA CI app on GitHub.**
   In the console, open **CI on MIOSA** and select **Connect GitHub**.
   From a terminal, run `miosa ci connect`; it opens the same link and waits until the connection appears.
2. **Give it access to your repositories.**
   On GitHub, choose all repositories or the ones that should run on MIOSA.
   You can change this later in the app's settings on GitHub.
3. **Use `runs-on: miosa` in a workflow.**
4. **A job passes on MIOSA.**

One GitHub account belongs to one MIOSA organization at a time.
If it is already connected to another organization, disconnect it there first.

The link GitHub returns you through is valid for 30 minutes.
If it expires, select **Connect GitHub** again.

## Change the workflow

Set the label of the job to `miosa`:

```yaml
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: miosa
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm test
```

The label must be exactly `miosa`.
Jobs with other labels keep running where they ran before.
You can move one job at a time.

## Isolation

A CI sandbox is created with none of your organization's MIOSA environment variables, secret files, database links, Git keys or model keys.
It has only what the runner image contains and what GitHub sends the runner.

Keep job secrets in GitHub Actions secrets and pass them to a step the way you do today:

```yaml
- run: ./deploy.sh
  env:
    API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.API_TOKEN }}
```

Each job gets its own sandbox.
Nothing carries over from one job to the next.

> **Note: Public repositories**
>
> MIOSA refuses jobs from public repositories by default.
> Anyone can open a pull request on a public repository, and the job it starts would run on your organization's bill.
> The job is shown in **Recent jobs** with the reason.

## Billing

A CI sandbox is billed per second, like any other sandbox, from when it is created until it is deleted.
The bill shows this usage as **CI**, separate from your other sandboxes.

## Troubleshooting

### The job stays "Queued" on GitHub

- The workflow must say exactly `runs-on: miosa`.
- The MIOSA CI app must have access to that repository.
  Add it in the app's settings on GitHub.
- Run `miosa ci status` to see which setup step is not done, and `miosa ci jobs` to see whether the job reached MIOSA.
- A public repository is refused by default.

### The repository is public

Public repositories are refused unless MIOSA has allowed them for your organization.
Run public repositories on GitHub's own runners, or ask support.

### A step cannot see a MIOSA environment variable

That is intended.
Put the value in a GitHub Actions secret and pass it to the step with `env:`.

### Jobs start slowly or wait

Every job gets a new sandbox, and the runner registers in it before the first step starts.
In **Recent jobs**, **Queued** means MIOSA has not started the sandbox yet and **Starting** means it is being prepared.
If a job stays in either state or fails, the row shows the reason.
A sandbox limit or an empty credit balance on the organization can stop new sandboxes.

### A step needs a tool that `ubuntu-latest` has

The runner image has the GitHub Actions runner and the common tools from `ubuntu-latest`, not every one.
Install what is missing in a step, for languages with `actions/setup-node`, `actions/setup-python` or `actions/setup-go`.

### Debug a failing job

Open the run from the link in **Recent jobs**; the step logs are on GitHub.
The sandbox is deleted when the job ends, so there is nothing to open afterwards.
On GitHub, choose **Re-run jobs** and enable debug logging for more output.
`miosa ci jobs --json` gives the status, conclusion, duration and failure reason of each job.

## CLI

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `miosa ci connect` | Opens the GitHub install link and waits until the connection appears |
| `miosa ci status` | Shows the four setup steps and the isolation note |
| `miosa ci jobs` | Lists recent jobs |
| `miosa ci disconnect <installation>` | Disconnects a GitHub account; running jobs finish |

Every command takes `--json`.

## API

| Request | What it does |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/v1/ci` | Setup state: `available`, connected installations, the four `steps`, the `last_job` and the `isolation` note |
| `POST /api/v1/ci/connect-intents` | Returns the GitHub `install_url`, valid for 30 minutes |
| `GET /api/v1/ci/jobs?limit=20` | Recent jobs with `status`, `conclusion`, `duration_seconds`, `run_url` and `failure_reason` |
| `DELETE /api/v1/ci/installations/:installation_id` | Disconnects a GitHub account; running jobs finish |

A job `status` is `queued`, `starting`, `running`, `completed`, `failed` or `cancelled`.
Errors use the platform error shape.
The codes are `CI_NOT_AVAILABLE`, `CI_INSTALLATION_NOT_FOUND`, `CI_INSTALLATION_OWNED_ELSEWHERE` and `CI_STATE_INVALID`.

```bash
curl -s https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/ci \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

pages.title: Sandboxes
pages.description: Fast, isolated Linux VMs for code execution, builds, tests, and dev servers, with live preview URLs and snapshots.
pages.markdown:
A **Sandbox** is MIOSA's fast code execution environment. Your agent writes files into it, executes commands, exposes ports as live preview URLs, and snapshots state for branching or rollback. Use it for build loops, tests, scripts, package installs, code generation, preview servers, and short-lived automation. Sandboxes are persistent by default, which means they survive a stop. When you stop one or its timeout expires, MIOSA preserves the disk and moves the sandbox to `stopped` so it can resume later. Running processes do not survive a stop. Persistent does not mean the sandbox survives the loss of its host; see [Sandbox lifecycle](/docs/develop/sandboxes/lifecycle). SOMA does not support persistence yet. Destroy only when the saved state should be removed. ## 1. Create a sandbox **CLI** ```bash miosa create my-box --wait # provision a sandbox and wait until it is ready ``` **TypeScript** ```typescript import { Miosa } from "@miosa/sdk" const miosa = new Miosa({ apiKey: process.env.MIOSA_API_KEY! }) const sandbox = await miosa.sandboxes.create() console.log(sandbox.id, sandbox.state) // sbx_a1b2c3d4e5 running ``` **Python** ```python import os from miosa import Miosa miosa = Miosa(api_key=os.environ["MIOSA_API_KEY"]) sandbox = miosa.sandboxes.create() print(sandbox.id, sandbox.state) # sbx_a1b2c3d4e5 running ``` ## 2. Run a command **CLI** ```bash miosa exec my-box -- echo "hello from MIOSA" ``` **TypeScript** ```typescript const result = await sandbox.exec("echo hello from MIOSA") console.log(result.stdout) // hello from MIOSA ``` **Python** ```python result = sandbox.exec("echo hello from MIOSA") print(result.stdout) # hello from MIOSA ``` ## 3. Write a file and open a preview **CLI** ```bash echo "

Hello

" | miosa files write my-box:/workspace/index.html miosa preview create my-box 3000 --visibility public ``` **TypeScript** ```typescript await sandbox.files.write("/workspace/index.html", "

Hello

") const preview = await sandbox.previews.create(3000) console.log(preview.url) // https://3000-abc12345.sandbox.miosa.ai ``` **Python** ```python sandbox.files.write("/workspace/index.html", "

Hello

") preview = sandbox.previews.create(port=3000) print(preview.url) # https://5173-abc12345.sandbox.miosa.ai ``` Open the preview URL MIOSA returns. Only the port you exposed is reachable, and only through the MIOSA proxy. > **Note: The rule** > > Use a Sandbox for code and processes. > Use a [Computer](/docs/computers/overview) for a visible GUI, browser login, or human takeover. > Use [Docker Host](/docs/docker-host/docker-deploy) when the result should be a durable 24/7 deployment URL with custom domains. > Every sandbox boots the same main image, which ships Docker with the `docker compose` and `docker buildx` plugins, and a live browser with CDP on a virtual display (`Xvfb :99`), so you can build and run containers, and drive a browser, while you develop. > A SOMA sandbox does not have that display yet, so the live viewer is not available there. ## Image, template, and runtime Three different things decide what a sandbox boots with, and they are not the same choice. | | What it is | Where you set it | |---|---|---| | **Image** | The one main image, with Node, Python, Docker Engine 29.9 with Compose and Buildx, a live browser with CDP, and the code interpreter already inside. | Nothing to choose: every sandbox boots it. | | **Template** | Optional content staged inside that image at create time: files, a scaffold, packages, and the start command. | `template_id`, for example `nextjs`, `static-html`, or a custom template. | | **Runtime** | Which virtual machine monitor runs the sandbox. | `runtime`: `firecracker` (the default), `soma`, or `auto`. | A template is never a separate image. An older image id passed as `template_id` still works and boots the main image; see the [Sandbox Templates API](/docs/api-reference/sandbox-templates). See [Templates](/docs/develop/templates) for the app starters, and [Choosing a runtime](/docs/soma/choosing-a-runtime) for the runtime option. ## Pick what you need | Need | Product | Result | |---|---|---| | Run commands, edit files, install packages, test code | **Sandbox** | Isolated runtime with exec, files, snapshots, and preview URLs | | Use a browser login, desktop app, screenshots, mouse, keyboard | **Computer** | Durable GUI machine with streaming and desktop control | | Publish a 24/7 app for users | **Docker Host** | Always-on deployment URL with custom domain support | Sandboxes are excellent for building and previewing. They are not the final production hosting layer. When a preview becomes a user-facing app, publish it through Docker Host so it gets the right routing, domains, lifecycle, and billing behavior. ## Next - [Create and connect](/docs/develop/sandboxes/create): Fused run, full create, context managers, and connecting to an existing sandbox. - [Lifecycle](/docs/develop/sandboxes/lifecycle): The state machine, what each state means, and how to pause and resume. - [Sizing and limits](/docs/develop/sandboxes/sizing): Named resource contracts, billing notes, and the opt-in runner fast path. - [Timeouts and auto-stop](/docs/develop/sandboxes/timeouts): Default TTL, extending it, and how usage is measured. - [Sandbox events](/docs/develop/sandboxes/events): Subscribe to lifecycle and activity events over SSE. - [Production checklist](/docs/develop/sandboxes/production-checklist): The defaults to set before relying on sandboxes in production. - [Environment variables](/docs/develop/sandboxes/environments): Set and read env vars at create time, and where secrets should live instead. - [Capabilities](/docs/develop/sandboxes/capabilities): What sandboxes are for, what one is, and the core capabilities. - [Docker in sandboxes](/docs/develop/sandboxes/docker): Docker Engine, Compose, and Buildx inside the sandbox. - [Connecting to a running sandbox](/docs/develop/sandboxes/connect): SDK, CLI, SSH over a tunnel, and preview URLs. - [Internet access and egress](/docs/develop/sandboxes/internet-access): Default network behavior and allowlists. - [Long-running tasks](/docs/develop/sandboxes/long-running-tasks): Background processes and always-on sandboxes. - [Metadata and labels](/docs/develop/sandboxes/metadata): Attach and read arbitrary metadata. ## Related - [Files & Exec](/docs/develop/files-and-exec): Full filesystem and process API: recursive operations, watch, detached jobs. - [Previews](/docs/develop/previews): Live HTTPS URLs proxied to a sandbox port with share tokens and visibility controls. - [Templates](/docs/develop/templates): Built-in images and custom BuildSpec reference. - [Snapshots & persistence](/docs/develop/snapshots): Pause, resume, fork, and the current public snapshot boundary.

pages.title: Capabilities
pages.description: What sandboxes are for, what a sandbox is concretely, and the core exec, files, preview, snapshot, and lifecycle capabilities.
pages.markdown:
This page is the reference behind the [Sandboxes overview](/docs/develop/sandboxes): what people build with sandboxes, what one actually is, and the capabilities every sandbox exposes. ## What Sandboxes are for - **Agent build loops**: Generate code, edit files, install dependencies, run tests, and stream logs back to the agent. - **Preview servers**: Run a web server in the sandbox and expose only the needed port as an HTTPS preview URL. - **Safe execution**: Isolate untrusted commands from your backend while keeping filesystem state scoped to the sandbox. - **Reproducible state**: Snapshot working state, resume later, or fork from a known point for parallel agent work. ## What a Sandbox is, concretely - Isolated compute for code generation, builds, tests, and dev servers. - Named, versioned CPU, memory, and disk contracts plus per-sandbox timeout and environment parameters. - `/workspace` is the editable filesystem root. - Boots from a versioned template, usually `miosa-sandbox`. - Persistent by default, so `timeout_sec` stops compute and preserves state instead of deleting the workspace. - Network-isolated by default. - Preview URLs open only the specific ports you expose. - Destroy is permanent and removes the saved state. ## Core capabilities | Capability | What it gives you | |---|---| | `exec.run` | Blocking command execution with stdout, stderr, exit code, and duration | | `exec.stream` | Real-time stdout/stderr events for long builds or installs | | `files.write/read/list/stat` | Direct filesystem access under `/workspace` and other allowed paths | | `previews.create` | Public HTTPS URL for a running process on a specific sandbox port | | `snapshot` | Durable checkpoint for resume, fork, or rollback | | `pause` / `resume` | Stop compute without discarding saved state | ## See it work **TypeScript** ```typescript const sandbox = await miosa.sandboxes.create({ templateId: "miosa-sandbox" }) await sandbox.files.write( "/workspace/index.html", ` My App

Hello from MIOSA

Built in a sandbox.

` ) const result = await sandbox.exec("python3 --version") console.log(result.stdout) const preview = await sandbox.previews.create(3000) console.log(preview.url) // https://3000-abc12345.sandbox.miosa.ai ``` **Python** ```python sandbox = miosa.sandboxes.create(template_id="miosa-sandbox") sandbox.files.write( "/workspace/index.html", """ My App

Hello from MIOSA

Built in a sandbox.

""", ) result = sandbox.exec("python3 --version") print(result.stdout) preview = sandbox.previews.create(port=3000) print(preview.url) # https://5173-abc12345.sandbox.miosa.ai ```

pages.title: Create and connect
pages.description: Create a sandbox with the fused run endpoint or a full create, manage its lifetime in Python context managers, and connect to an existing sandbox by id or name.
pages.markdown:
Two ways to get a running sandbox: the fused **run** endpoint when you want a sandbox and an immediate first command, and a full **create** when you need to provision first, write files, start a preview server, or keep the ID for a longer session.

## Fast path: create and run

For agents that need a sandbox and immediately run the first command, use the fused run endpoint. It is faster because MIOSA owns the readiness wait on the server and avoids an extra client poll loop plus a second public exec request.

**Python**

```python
import os
import requests

response = requests.post(
    "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/sandboxes/run",
    headers={
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['MIOSA_API_KEY']}",
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
        "Idempotency-Key": "run-2026-06-09-001",
    },
    json={
        "template_id": "miosa-sandbox",
        "command": "python3 -c \"print('ready')\"",
        "size": "small",
        "timeout_sec": 300,
        "wait_timeout_ms": 30000,
        "env": {"NODE_ENV": "production"},
        "metadata": {"agent_run": "abc123"},
    },
)
response.raise_for_status()

run = response.json()
print(run["data"]["id"], run["data"]["state"])
print(run["exec"]["stdout"])
print(run["timings"]["server_wait_and_exec_ms"])
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const response = await fetch("https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/sandboxes/run", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.MIOSA_API_KEY!}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
    "Idempotency-Key": "run-2026-06-09-001"
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    template_id: "miosa-sandbox",
    command: "node -e \"console.log('ready')\"",
    size: "small",
    timeout_sec: 300,
    wait_timeout_ms: 30000,
    env: { NODE_ENV: "production" },
    metadata: { agent_run: "abc123" }
  })
});

if (!response.ok) throw new Error(await response.text());

const run = await response.json();
console.log(run.data.id, run.data.state);
console.log(run.exec.stdout);
console.log(run.timings.server_wait_and_exec_ms);
```

**cURL**

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/sandboxes/run \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: run-2026-06-09-001" \
  -d '{
    "template_id": "miosa-sandbox",
    "command": "python3 -c \"print(1+1)\"",
    "size": "small",
    "timeout_sec": 300,
    "wait_timeout_ms": 30000,
    "metadata": { "agent_run": "abc123" }
  }'
```

Response shape:

```json
{
  "data": {
    "id": "sbx_a1b2c3d4",
    "state": "running",
    "template_id": "miosa-sandbox",
    "ready": true
  },
  "exec": {
    "stdout": "2\n",
    "stderr": "",
    "exit_code": 0
  },
  "timings": {
    "server_wait_and_exec_ms": 512
  }
}
```

## Create with full options

Use full create when you need to provision the sandbox first, write files, start a preview server, attach databases, or keep the ID for a longer session.

**Python**

```python
import os
from miosa import Miosa

miosa = Miosa(api_key=os.environ["MIOSA_API_KEY"])

sbx = miosa.sandboxes.create(
    "miosa-sandbox",              # template_id (positional); default if omitted
    cpu_count=2,
    memory_mb=4096,
    disk_size_mb=10240,
    timeout_sec=3600,             # idle-anchored; resets on activity; default 3600
    env={"NODE_ENV": "production"},
    metadata={"agent_run": "abc123"},
    external_workspace_id="acme-corp",   # white-label attribution
    external_user_id="user_123",
    external_project_id="project_456",
    idempotency_key="run-2026-06-09-001",
)

print(sbx.id)
print(sbx.state)
print(sbx.ready)
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
import { Miosa } from "@miosa/sdk";

const miosa = new Miosa({ apiKey: process.env.MIOSA_API_KEY! });

const sbx = await miosa.sandboxes.create({
  templateId: "miosa-sandbox",
  cpuCount: 2,
  memoryMb: 4096,
  diskSizeMb: 10240,
  timeoutSec: 3600,
  env: { NODE_ENV: "production" },
  metadata: { agentRun: "abc123" },
  externalWorkspaceId: "acme-corp",
  externalUserId: "user_123",
  externalProjectId: "project_456",
  idempotencyKey: "run-2026-06-09-001",
});

console.log(sbx.id, sbx.state, sbx.boot_ms);
```

**cURL**

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/sandboxes \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: run-2026-06-09-001" \
  -d '{
    "template_id": "miosa-sandbox",
    "cpu_count": 2,
    "memory_mb": 4096,
    "disk_size_mb": 10240,
    "timeout_sec": 3600,
    "env": { "NODE_ENV": "production" },
    "metadata": { "agent_run": "abc123" },
    "external_workspace_id": "acme-corp",
    "external_user_id": "user_123",
    "external_project_id": "project_456"
  }'
```

The response body contains `id`, `state`, `template_id`, `size`, `resource_contract`,
`cpu_count`, `memory_mb`, and `created_at`. Save the `id`; every
subsequent call needs it.

### Context manager (auto-destroy)

The Python SDK supports `with` / `async with`; the sandbox is destroyed on exit
even if an exception is raised:

**Python**

```python
with miosa.sandboxes.create("miosa-sandbox") as sbx:
    sbx.files.write("/workspace/hello.py", "print('hello')")
    result = sbx.exec.run("python3 /workspace/hello.py")
    print(result.stdout)
# sbx.destroy() called automatically here
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
// TypeScript: manual cleanup with try/finally
const sbx = await miosa.sandboxes.create({ templateId: "miosa-sandbox" });
try {
  await sbx.files.write("/workspace/hello.py", "print('hello')");
  const result = await sbx.exec.run("python3 /workspace/hello.py");
  console.log(result.stdout);
} finally {
  await sbx.destroy();
}
```

### Connect to an existing sandbox

**Python**

```python
# By ID
sbx = miosa.sandboxes.get("sbx_a1b2c3d4")

# By name (if you set name= at create time)
sbx = miosa.sandboxes.get_by_name("my-dev-env")

# connect() is an alias for get()
sbx = miosa.sandboxes.connect("sbx_a1b2c3d4")
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const sbx = await miosa.sandboxes.get("sbx_a1b2c3d4");
// or
const sbx = await miosa.sandboxes.getByName("my-dev-env");
```

**cURL**

```bash
curl https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/sandboxes/sbx_a1b2c3d4 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"

# By name
curl https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/sandboxes/by-name/my-dev-env \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

## List and filter sandboxes

**Python**

```python
# All running sandboxes
running = miosa.sandboxes.list(status="running")  # status: "running" | "paused" | "destroyed"

# Filter by name (prefix match)
named = miosa.sandboxes.list(name="my-dev")

# Filter by white-label workspace
ws_sandboxes = miosa.sandboxes.list(external_workspace_id="acme-corp")

# Filter by tags
tagged = miosa.sandboxes.list(tags=["pr-preview", "staging"])
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const running = await miosa.sandboxes.list({ status: "running" });  // status: "running" | "paused" | "destroyed"
const named   = await miosa.sandboxes.list({ name: "my-dev" });
const byCorp  = await miosa.sandboxes.list({ externalWorkspaceId: "acme-corp" });
```

**cURL**

```bash
curl "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/sandboxes?status=running" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"

curl "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/sandboxes?name=my-dev" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

> **Note: Related**
>
> See [Lifecycle](/docs/develop/sandboxes/lifecycle) for the state machine these calls move through, [Environment variables](/docs/develop/sandboxes/environments) for create-time and exec-level env, and [Sizing and limits](/docs/develop/sandboxes/sizing) for the resource contracts referenced above.

pages.title: Docker in sandboxes
pages.description: Run containers inside MIOSA sandboxes, publish ports, and reach them through preview URLs. Which templates ship Docker Engine, Compose, and Buildx.
pages.markdown:
Docker is preinstalled in the sandbox image. There is nothing to enable, and no separate template to pick.

```bash
docker run --rm alpine echo hello
docker compose up -d
docker buildx build --load -t myapp .
```

What each template ships today:

| Template | Docker Engine | Compose and Buildx | Runs as `sandbox` user |
|---|---|---|---|
| `miosa-sandbox` (the default) | 29.9 | Yes | As `root` |
| SOMA runtime (`runtime_profile: "soma"`) | 29.9 | Yes | As `root` |

Commands run through `exec` run as `root`, so `docker` works there on every template above that includes it.
Check what a sandbox has with `docker version`, `docker compose version`, and `docker buildx version`.

## What works

| Task | Works |
|---|---|
| `docker run`, `docker exec`, `docker logs`, volumes, bind mounts | Yes |
| `docker compose up` with several services and service-name DNS between them | Yes |
| `docker buildx build` | Yes |
| `docker build` | Yes |
| Pulling from Docker Hub and other public registries | Yes |
| Publishing a port with `-p 8080:80` and opening it through a preview URL | Yes |
| Running as `root` | Yes |
| Running as the `sandbox` user | Yes, when you `exec` as that user |
| Pausing and resuming a sandbox with containers running | Yes, containers keep running |

## Startup behavior

The Docker engine starts the first time you use it, not when the sandbox boots, so sandbox creation stays fast. The first `docker` command in a fresh sandbox takes about 0.6 seconds longer while the engine starts; after that, running an image that is already pulled takes about 0.15 seconds.

If you start containers with `--restart always`, they come back when the engine next starts, which happens on your next `docker` command.

## Open a container port in your browser

Publish the port on the sandbox, then expose it as a [preview](/docs/develop/previews).

```bash
docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:alpine
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const sbx = await miosa.sandboxes.create({ templateId: "miosa-sandbox" });
await sbx.exec.run("docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:alpine");
const preview = await sbx.previews.create({ port: 8080 });
console.log(preview.url);
```

**Python**

```python
with miosa.sandboxes.create("miosa-sandbox") as sbx:
    sbx.exec.run("docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:alpine")
    print(sbx.get_url(8080))
```

The preview URL forwards to the published port. Bind to `0.0.0.0` inside the container, which `-p` does for you.

## Disk and memory

Images, layers, and volumes live on the sandbox disk, so they count against its size. The default `small` sandbox has 10 GiB of disk. When the disk is full, a pull or build fails with `no space left on device` and the sandbox keeps running. Free space with `docker system prune -af` and retry.

The engine uses about 40 MiB of memory when idle. Containers share the sandbox's CPU and memory.

## Docker in a sandbox vs Docker Host

| You want | Use |
|---|---|
| Run, build, or test containers while you develop, or let an agent do it | Docker in a sandbox |
| A durable 24/7 deployment URL, custom domains, and rollback for a containerized app | [Docker Host](/docs/docker-host/docker-deploy) |
| A sandbox whose only job is to be a Docker host with a long-lived disk | A sandbox with `always_on` set |

Docker in a sandbox is for development and automation. It is not a production runtime.

## Templates

- Every sandbox image includes Docker Engine 29.9 with Compose and Buildx, on Firecracker and on SOMA.
- There is no separate Docker template to pick: the sandbox image already includes Docker.

## Limits

- No nested virtualization. KVM and QEMU do not run inside a sandbox.
- Image builds for other CPU architectures need emulation that is not included.
- Docker Swarm ingress is not supported.

## See also

- [Previews](/docs/develop/previews): Expose a sandbox port on a public URL.
- [Templates](/docs/develop/templates): Choose or build a sandbox image.
- [Docker Host](/docs/docker-host/docker-deploy): Publish a containerized app to a durable, always-on URL.

pages.title: Sandbox lifecycle
pages.description: The sandbox state machine from creating to destroyed, what each state means, what stop keeps, what resets the idle clock, and how to stop, pause, resume, and restart.
pages.markdown:
A sandbox moves through a small set of states.
This page is the map: what each state means, what triggers a transition, and how to stop and restart compute without discarding the disk.

## Lifecycle

create() creates creating; creating goes to running on ready.

running goes to stopped on stop(), and back to running on resume().

running goes to paused on pause(), and back to running on resume().

running, stopped or paused goes to destroyed on destroy().

creating or running goes to error on failure; error goes to destroyed on cleanup.

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `creating` | VM is being claimed, restored, and prepared to accept commands |
| `running` | Command-ready: exec, files, previews, terminal, and port exposure work |
| `stopped` | The machine is released and the disk is saved; files survive, processes do not |
| `paused` | The machine is suspended in place with memory and processes intact; only on a runtime that advertises pause |
| `destroyed` | Terminal: resources freed, ID unusable, saved state removed |
| `error` | Boot or runtime failure; check `sbx.data["metadata"]` for `last_error` |

`paused` exists only on a runtime that advertises pause.
Firecracker advertises it today.
SOMA does not: it has no pause, and it does not keep state across a stop yet, so a SOMA sandbox is never `paused`, and a disposable SOMA sandbox is deleted when its timeout expires.
Snapshots are a separate resource, not a sandbox state.

Activity that resets the idle clock: exec calls, file operations, preview HTTP traffic, terminal stdin.
The timeout is idle-anchored: it counts from the last activity.
Once `timeout_sec` elapses with no activity, a persistent sandbox is stopped.
A non-persistent sandbox (`persistent: false`) is destroyed, and its disk is discarded.

`idle_timeout_sec` stops a persistent sandbox after a period of inactivity.
New accounts (created on or after October 11, 2026): sandboxes without `idle_timeout_sec` stop after 30 minutes idle and wake on the next request.
Set `idle_timeout_sec` to `0` to disable.
Existing accounts keep their current behavior (idle timeout off unless set).

`resume()` is not the only way back out of `stopped` or `paused`: a persistent sandbox **wakes on request**.
A request that arrives while it is stopped or paused (for example, to its preview URL) resumes it and is held for up to 10 seconds, then answers `503` with `Retry-After` if it is not running yet.
Exec, file operations, and deploys on a stopped or paused persistent sandbox resume it first and then run.
A non-persistent sandbox is never auto-resumed: the call returns `409`.

## What stop keeps

Stop saves the disk and releases the machine, and moves the sandbox to `stopped`.
Files, installed packages, Docker data, and enabled services survive a stop.
Running processes never survive a stop, on any runtime.
Resume after a stop behaves like a server that restarts: start your processes again, or make them declared services.

Pause is the explicit verb for keeping processes.
It is available on Firecracker only.
A paused sandbox stays resident for at most 30 minutes, with memory and processes intact.
After 30 minutes it behaves like a stop: the disk is kept and processes are not.
A memory checkpoint is an accelerator, never the truth: if it cannot be restored, resume falls back to the disk.

Disk size is a fixed class (10, 20, or 40 GiB) chosen at create.
It can grow only as a parameter of `resume` or `fork`.
A request to shrink is refused with `409` and the sandbox is left untouched.
Disk growth is not available yet on every runtime.

Persistent means the sandbox survives a stop.
It does not mean the sandbox survives the loss of its host.
The `durability` field on the sandbox record states how many hosts hold the saved state: `local_only`, `replicating`, or `replicated`.
Every Firecracker sandbox exposes `durability`.
It is `local_only` until a stopped sandbox's copy has been verified off-host, and then `replicated`.
Off-host replication is rolling out on a QA canary first, so expect `local_only` for most sandboxes today.

See [Persistence, pause, and forks](/docs/develop/snapshots) for the full pause/resume/fork flow.

## Readiness and billing

A sandbox is command-ready only in the `running` state. Two signals tell you when it gets there:

- The `ready` boolean on the sandbox record. `true` means the VM session is prepared to accept exec, files, previews, and terminal calls.
- The `state` field. Poll `GET /api/v1/sandboxes/{id}` until `state` leaves `creating` and becomes `running` (or surfaces `error`).

The fused [run endpoint](/docs/develop/sandboxes/create) owns this wait on the server, so agents that create-and-exec do not need a client poll loop.

Which states cost what:

| State | Billing |
|---|---|
| `creating` | Preparing resources; not yet command-ready |
| `running` | Billed per second at the price of its size (the same on every plan) |
| `stopped` | No compute; cold storage rate only (disk GiB-second) |
| `paused` | No compute; storage rate only (disk GiB-second) |
| `destroyed` | Billing stops immediately |

See [Sizing and limits](/docs/develop/sandboxes/sizing) for the full billing notes and [Timeouts and auto-stop](/docs/develop/sandboxes/timeouts) for what happens at the deadline.

## Pause and resume

`POST /stop` and `resume()` release the machine and bring it back on the same disk.
`pause()` and `resume()` suspend the machine in place and keep its processes, on a runtime that advertises pause (Firecracker only, for at most 30 minutes before it behaves like a stop).

**Python**

```python
sbx.pause()
# Firecracker only: state is "paused" and processes are kept for up to 30 minutes

sbx.resume()
# state returns to "running"
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
// Firecracker only: keeps processes for up to 30 minutes
await sbx.pause();
await sbx.resume();
```

**cURL**

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/sandboxes/$SBX/stop \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{}'

curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/sandboxes/$SBX/resume \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{}'
```

## Restart

`POST /sandboxes/{id}/restart` (`miosa restart`) is a stop followed by a resume of the same disk, under the same id.
Files, packages, Docker data and enabled services survive; running processes do not, and the guest boots on a fresh kernel.
Reach for it when a running sandbox stops answering commands.
A sandbox that is not running answers `409 SANDBOX_NOT_RUNNING`: resume it instead.

> **Note: Related**
>
> [Timeouts and auto-stop](/docs/develop/sandboxes/timeouts) covers what happens when `timeout_sec` elapses, [Snapshots and persistence](/docs/develop/snapshots) covers snapshots and forks, and [Sizing and limits](/docs/develop/sandboxes/sizing) covers what each state costs.

pages.title: Files & Exec
pages.description: Read, write, watch files inside a sandbox. Run commands, stream stdout/stderr, manage processes.
pages.markdown:
The Files and Exec APIs are how you (or an AI agent) interact with a Sandbox. Together they're the substrate for everything else: generating code, running builds, starting servers.

## Files

### Write

**TypeScript**

```typescript
await sandbox.files.write("/workspace/src/index.ts", `
  console.log("Hello from MIOSA")
`)

// Binary
await sandbox.files.write("/workspace/logo.png", pngBuffer, {
  encoding: "binary",
})
```

**cURL**

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/sandboxes/$SBX/files/write \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{
    "path": "/workspace/src/index.ts",
    "content": "console.log(\"Hello from MIOSA\")"
  }'
```
