| Customer data operations | White-label product, webhooks | Client-wide structured data plane |

## Next

- [Data overview](/docs/data/overview): Managed databases, storage, auth, Redis, Qdrant, and volumes.
- [Backend orchestration](/docs/integrations/backend-orchestration): Build the server-side control plane around MIOSA runtimes.
- [White-label SaaS](/docs/platform/white-label): Expose MIOSA-powered experiences under your own product and domain.

pages.title: Services addresses and domains
pages.description: How services reach databases while private networking is not available, the public miosa.app address a web service or static site can have, and how TLS is handled.
pages.markdown:
Services reach managed databases through their connection variables.
A web service or a static site can also have a public address.

## Private networking

Private networking between services is not available yet.
One service cannot reach another by a private name, and `private_network` reads `{"enabled": false}`.
The older `private_domain` field (`<service-slug>.miosa.internal`) and the `MIOSA_PRIVATE_DOMAIN` variable do not resolve; do not build on them.

Managed databases connect automatically from any host.
Reference a database's connection in the service's Variables:

```text
DATABASE_URL=${{Postgres.DATABASE_URL}}
REDIS_URL=${{Redis.REDIS_URL}}
```

To call another service of the project, give it a public address and call that.
The service's Networking tab in the console shows the same.

## Public address

```bash
miosa service domains shop API
miosa service domains enable shop API --label api
miosa service domains disable shop API
```

`enable` gives the service:

```text
https://<label>.<your-org>.miosa.app
```

The label defaults to the service's slug and must be lowercase a-z, 0-9 and `-`.
The label is unique across your organization.
TLS is issued and renewed by the platform; there is no certificate to install.

`disable` removes the public address and leaves the private one in place.
The service keeps running; it just stops being reachable from the internet.

## What serves a public address

The public address routes to the healthy replicas of the service's active release.
A release that is not `active` does not receive traffic.

If the service has idle sleep enabled, a request to a sleeping service wakes it and waits for it.
A service without a public address has no request signal, so it never sleeps.

## Reading the address in code

TypeScript:

```typescript
const service = await miosa.services.get(serviceId);
console.log(service.private_network);       // { enabled: false } while private networking is not available
console.log(service.public_address.url);    // null until enabled
```

Python:

```python
service = miosa.services.get(service_id)
print(service["private_network"])
print(service["public_address"]["url"])
```

## Custom domains

The public address is on `miosa.app`.
A custom domain on your own DNS zone is a separate product: register it, add the CNAME it shows and let MIOSA verify it.
That flow lives under Domains, not under a service, so one domain can outlive a service.

## When ingress is off

If public addresses are not switched on for the platform, `enable` answers `INGRESS_DISABLED` (404).
The service still runs, but has no address to reach it on, and `miosa service settings shop` reports `public_address` as `unsupported`.

pages.title: Previews
pages.description: Live URLs that proxy into a sandbox port. Public, private, embeddable, share-tokenized.
pages.markdown:
A **Preview** is a URL that routes to a port inside a running Sandbox. The agent writes code, starts a dev server, the preview updates live in the browser. This is the build loop of AI app builders.

## Quick create

**TypeScript**

```typescript
// Make sure something is listening on the port first
const preview = await sandbox.previews.create({
  port: 3000,
  visibility: "private",   // or "public"
})

console.log(preview.url)
// → https://3000-abc12345.sandbox.miosa.ai
```

**cURL**

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/sandboxes/$SBX/previews \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{"port":3000,"visibility":"private"}'
```

The URL follows the pattern `https://{port}-{slug}.sandbox.miosa.ai` where `{slug}` is the first 8 characters of the sandbox UUID. For the template default port, the URL is `https://{slug}.sandbox.miosa.ai` (no port prefix). For white-label platforms, this can be `https://{port}-{slug}.sandbox.{your-domain}` once DNS delegation is set up.

## Visibility

| Mode | Access |
|---|---|
| `public` | Anyone with the URL can view (and is rate-limited by IP). No auth required. |
| `private` | Requires either an authenticated MIOSA session OR a valid share token. |

For most white-label use cases, **always use `private`**. Then mint a share token to hand to the end user's browser.

## Share tokens

A share token is a short-lived, scoped credential that lets a specific browser access a private preview without exposing your MIOSA workspace API key.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const share = await sandbox.previews.share(preview.id, {
  expiresInSec: 3600,  // 1 hour default; max varies by plan
})

console.log(share.share_url)
// → https://3000-abc12345.sandbox.miosa.ai?preview_token=<one-time raw token>

// In your end-user's frontend:
//   <iframe src={shareUrl} sandbox="allow-same-origin allow-scripts" />
```

**cURL**

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/sandboxes/$SBX/previews/$PREVIEW/share \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -d '{"ttl_seconds": 3600}'
```

Response:
```json
{
  "data": {
    "id": "preview_...",
    "share_token_prefix": "first12chars",
    "share_token_expires_at": "2026-05-14T19:30:00Z"
  },
  "preview_token": "miosa_pv_<one-time-raw-token>",
  "share_url": "https://3000-abc12345.sandbox.miosa.ai?preview_token=miosa_pv_<one-time-raw-token>"
}
```

> **Caution: `preview_token` is returned once**
>
> The raw `preview_token` value is only in the create-share response. Persist it server-side if you need to re-display, or re-mint a new one. Subsequent reads of the preview return only the `share_token_prefix` (for matching to log entries) and the expiry timestamp.

The token can be passed two ways:
- As `?preview_token=...` query string in the URL (most common; works for iframes).
- As `x-miosa-preview-token: <token>` HTTP header (when you control the request).

MIOSA's proxy strips the credential before forwarding to your sandbox app  -  your app never sees the token. The proxy authenticates the request, then forwards a clean HTTP request to your dev server on the sandbox.

## Iframe embedding

Previews are designed to be embedded in iframes:
```html
<iframe src="https://3000-abc12345.sandbox.miosa.ai?preview_token=miosa_pv_..."
        sandbox="allow-same-origin allow-scripts allow-forms"
        style="width:100%; height:600px; border:0;"></iframe>
```

The preview proxy emits CSP `frame-ancestors` for `*.sandbox.miosa.ai`, `*.miosa.ai`, and `localhost:4000` by default. For white-label embedding into your own domain, contact support  -  the production proxy CSP is configurable per tenant.

## How it works
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Agent / SDK
    participant S as Sandbox
    participant P as Preview proxy
    participant B as Browser

    A->>S: exec("node server.js", detached)
    A->>S: previews.create(port: 3000)
    S-->>A: { url: "https://3000-abc12345.sandbox.miosa.ai" }
    A->>S: previews.share(id, expiresInSec: 3600)
    S-->>A: { share_url: "...?preview_token=..." }
    B->>P: GET share_url
    P->>P: verify preview_token
    P->>S: proxy request to port 3000
    S-->>P: HTTP response
    P-->>B: response (token stripped)
```

## Lifecycle

active goes to expired on token TTL elapses; expired goes to deleted on delete.

- `active` while the underlying sandbox is running and the preview hasn't been explicitly deleted.
- `expired` once the share token TTL (if set) elapses.
- `deleted` when you delete it, or automatically a short time after the sandbox is destroyed.

Re-creating a preview on the same port returns a new preview record with a new slug. Old preview URLs do not automatically transfer.

## Preview vs Deployment URL

| | Preview | Deployment URL |
|---|---|---|
| What it points at | A live sandbox port | An immutable deployment version |
| Updates live? | Yes  -  sandbox edits reflect immediately | No  -  only changes on rollback / re-promote |
| Lifetime | Tied to the sandbox | Persistent |
| Use it for | Build loop, sharing in-progress work | Production traffic |

You don't promote a preview to a deployment. You publish from a sandbox (which produces a deployment version with its own URL). The preview keeps living until the sandbox dies.

## Abuse limits

Public previews are aggressively rate-limited by IP at the edge. Private previews are rate-limited per share token. If you're embedding into a high-traffic site, use a custom domain and a dedicated tenant plan  -  preview hosts are not designed to serve production traffic.

## Why preview tokens exist

Sandbox previews are live HTTP services running inside isolated VMs. To embed one in your product UI, the browser needs to make an authenticated request to the MIOSA preview proxy.

The wrong approach - passing your API key to the browser - would let any user call the MIOSA API as your account. Preview tokens are the correct boundary: scoped to one sandbox, one port, and a short TTL.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant Browser
  participant YourBackend
  participant MiosaAPI
  participant PreviewProxy

  Browser->>YourBackend: GET /embed-url?sandbox_id=sbx_...
  YourBackend->>MiosaAPI: POST /sandboxes/{id}/previews (msk_ key)
  MiosaAPI-->>YourBackend: preview_id
  YourBackend->>MiosaAPI: POST /sandboxes/{id}/previews/{preview_id}/share
  MiosaAPI-->>YourBackend: { share_url, token }
  YourBackend-->>Browser: { embed_url: share_url, expires_in: 3600 }
  Browser->>PreviewProxy: iframe src = share_url (token in URL)
  PreviewProxy-->>Browser: proxied sandbox content
```

## Server-side mint flow

**Python**

```python
from miosa import Miosa

client = Miosa(api_key="msk_u_...")

# 1. Get or create a preview record for the port your app listens on.
previews = client.sandboxes.get("sbx_abc123").preview.list()
preview = next((p for p in previews if p["port"] == 3000), None)
if not preview:
    preview = client.sandboxes.get("sbx_abc123").preview.create(port=3000)

# 2. Mint a time-limited share token.
share = client.sandboxes.get("sbx_abc123").preview.share(
    preview["id"],
    ttl_seconds=3600,
)

embed_url = share["share_url"]   # pass this to the browser
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
import Miosa from "@miosa/sdk";

const client = new Miosa({ apiKey: "msk_u_..." });

// 1. Get or create a preview record for the port your app listens on.
const previews = await client.sandboxes.preview.list("sbx_abc123");
let preview = previews.find((p) => p.port === 3000);
if (!preview) {
  preview = await client.sandboxes.preview.create("sbx_abc123", { port: 3000 });
}

// 2. Mint a time-limited share token.
const share = await client.sandboxes.preview.share("sbx_abc123", preview.id, {
  ttlSeconds: 3600,
});

const embedUrl = share.shareUrl; // pass this to the browser
```

### TTL strategy

| Use case | Recommended TTL |
|---|---|
| Interactive work session | 3 600 s (1 hour) - refresh when the user returns |
| Short demo or share link | 900 s (15 minutes) |
| Public share with explicit expiry | Up to 86 400 s (24 hours) |
| Permanent share | No TTL - use `sandbox.share.create()` with no expiry, manage revocation manually |

When a token expires, the iframe shows a "session expired" message from the preview proxy. Your UI should catch the `message` event from the iframe and re-mint a token transparently.

### Iframe sandbox flags

```html
<iframe
  src="https://preview.example.com/p/sbx_abc123?preview_token=miosa_pv_..."
  allow="clipboard-read; clipboard-write"
  sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-forms allow-popups"
  style="width: 100%; height: 600px; border: none;"
  title="Design workspace"
></iframe>
```

| Flag | Required? | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| `allow-scripts` | Yes | Preview content runs JavaScript. |
| `allow-same-origin` | Yes | Lets the preview proxy set session cookies. |
| `allow-forms` | Recommended | Many sandbox apps submit forms. |
| `allow-popups` | Optional | Only if your sandbox app opens new windows. |
| `allow-downloads` | Optional | Only if your sandbox app serves file downloads. |

Do not add `allow-top-navigation` - it would let sandbox content redirect your top-level page.

### Token refresh

Detect expiry by listening for the `message` event from the iframe:

```javascript
window.addEventListener("message", async (event) => {
  // The preview proxy emits this message when the token expires.
  if (event.data?.type === "miosa:preview:expired") {
    const res = await fetch(`/api/embed-url?sandbox_id=${sandboxId}`);
    const { embed_url } = await res.json();
    document.getElementById("sandbox-frame").src = embed_url;
  }
});
```

### Permission scoping

When you mint a token for an end user, scope it to the minimum permissions they need:

**Python**

```python
token = client.browser_tokens.create(
    workspace_id="550e8400-...",
    project_id="660e8400-...",
    external_user_id="user_42",
    permissions=["sandbox:read", "preview:read"],
    ttl_seconds=3600,
)
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const token = await client.browserTokens.create({
  workspaceId: "550e8400-...",
  projectId: "660e8400-...",
  externalUserId: "user_42",
  permissions: ["sandbox:read", "preview:read"],
  ttlSeconds: 3600,
});
```

Available permission scopes:

| Scope | Grants |
|---|---|
| `sandbox:read` | Read sandbox metadata and state |
| `sandbox:exec` | Run commands inside the sandbox |
| `preview:read` | Embed and view previews |
| `preview:share` | Create public share links |
| `files:read` | Read the sandbox filesystem |
| `files:write` | Write files to the sandbox |

> **Caution: Never mint tokens with sandbox:admin**
>
> Admin-scoped tokens can delete sandboxes and modify configuration. Reserve those operations for your server-side API key.

### Early revocation

Revoke a preview token before it expires - for example, when a user logs out or loses access:

**Python**

```python
client.sandboxes.get("sbx_abc123").preview.revoke_share(preview_id="prev_xyz")
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
await client.sandboxes.preview.revokeShare("sbx_abc123", "prev_xyz");
```

## See also

- [Sandboxes](/docs/develop/sandboxes)  -  what a preview proxies to
- [Browser Tokens](/docs/platform/browser-tokens)  -  share-token patterns for white-label embedding
- [Publishing](/docs/docker-host/publishing)  -  turn a previewable sandbox into a production deployment

pages.title: Internet access and egress
pages.description: Whether a sandbox can reach the internet by default, the two layers of egress control, how to lock a sandbox to an allowlist, and how to debug a blocked call.
pages.markdown:
## Default network behavior

- **Inbound.** A sandbox is not reachable from the internet. Only the ports you expose as a [preview](/docs/develop/previews) accept traffic, and only through the MIOSA proxy.
- **Outbound.** A new sandbox can reach the internet. It starts in **audit-only** mode: no outbound call is blocked. Egress audit capture is not yet enabled in the current release, so calls are not recorded yet. A Computer's network policy defaults to `unrestricted`.

So by default your code can install packages, call APIs, and clone repos. Nothing is blocked until you choose to enforce an allowlist.

### What a sandbox cannot reach

A sandbox cannot reach the platform's own internal network.
The only exception is the managed-database proxy range, which is what a managed Postgres, MySQL, or Redis connection uses inside the sandbox.
This is a mesh-level deny, checked before the egress allowlist, so adding an internal host to an allowlist does not open it.
It is enforced on both runtimes.

`169.254.169.254` is not an egress destination on MIOSA.
It is Firecracker's metadata service (MMDS), the guest-side channel the host uses to hand a sandbox its identity and configuration, and it is answered inside the machine rather than on the host network.
Leave it denied, as the examples below do.

## Two layers of control

MIOSA gives you two ways to constrain outbound traffic. They compose.

| Layer | Scope | What it decides |
|---|---|---|
| Egress policy + allowlist | Computers and Sandboxes | The hosts a resource may reach, in `audit_only` or `enforce` mode |
| Network policy | Computers | A microVM-level mode: `unrestricted`, `allowlist`, `denylist`, or `isolated` |

A Computer or Sandbox resolves its egress policy as: resource override, then tenant default. The tenant default starts in `audit_only` mode.

## Watch, then enforce

The intended path for a sandbox is to observe real traffic, then lock it down to what it actually uses. This is the same flow documented in full on the [network allowlist reference](/docs/security/network):

1. **Observe.** Let the sandbox run normally. Every outbound host is recorded.
2. **Review.** Pull the hosts it contacted, ranked by frequency.
3. **Enforce.** Apply those hosts as the allowlist and switch the policy to `enforce`. Unlisted hosts are then blocked.
4. **Operate.** Blocked hosts land in a pending queue with one-click allow or deny. Revert to audit-only at any time without losing the allowlist.

**Python**

```python
# Suggested allowlist from observed traffic
for h in sandbox.network.suggestions(since="7d"):
    print(h.host, h.request_count)

# Allow, deny, and enforce
sandbox.network.allow("api.openai.com")
sandbox.network.allow("*.anthropic.com", methods=["POST"])
sandbox.network.deny("169.254.169.254")   # Firecracker metadata service (MMDS)
sandbox.network.lockdown()

# Revert, or inspect
sandbox.network.observe()
print(sandbox.network.get_policy().mode)
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const hosts = await sandbox.network.suggestions({ since: '7d' });
await sandbox.network.allow('api.openai.com');
await sandbox.network.allow('*.anthropic.com', { methods: ['POST'] });
await sandbox.network.deny('169.254.169.254');  // Firecracker metadata service (MMDS)
await sandbox.network.lockdown();
await sandbox.network.observe();
const policy = await sandbox.network.getPolicy();
```

### Allowlist rules

| Kind | Example | Matches |
|---|---|---|
| Exact host | `api.openai.com` | Only this hostname |
| Wildcard | `*.openai.com` | Any subdomain of `openai.com` |
| CIDR | `10.0.0.0/8` | Any IP in this range, when the target is an IP literal |

Rules are matched in priority order: exact beats wildcard, wildcard beats CIDR, and an explicit `deny` always beats an `allow`. A rule can be scoped to a method and a path, and marked `warn_only` to let the request through while flagging it in the audit log.

Rules attach at two levels: per-resource (one sandbox or computer) and tenant-wide (every resource unless overridden).

## Restrict a Computer at the microVM level

Computers also accept a network policy that takes effect within seconds, without a restart.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
await client.networkPolicy.update(computerId, {
  mode: 'allowlist',
  rules: [
    { host: 'registry.npmjs.org', port: 443, protocol: 'tcp' },
    { host: 'pypi.org',          port: 443, protocol: 'tcp' },
  ],
});
```

**curl**

```bash
curl -X PUT https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/computers/$COMPUTER_ID/network-policy \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"mode": "allowlist", "rules": [{"host": "github.com", "port": 443, "protocol": "tcp"}]}'
```

| Mode | Description |
|---|---|
| `unrestricted` | Default. All outbound traffic allowed |
| `allowlist` | Only listed hosts and ports permitted |
| `denylist` | All traffic allowed except listed rules |
| `isolated` | All outbound blocked (DNS and MIOSA internal excluded) |

A `PUT` replaces the whole policy; send every rule on every call. `DELETE` resets it to `unrestricted`.

## Credentials on the way out

Egress is also where MIOSA swaps placeholders for real credentials. Your workload sees an opaque `miosa-tok-...` value in its environment; the proxy substitutes the real secret on the outbound request, so the value never lives inside the sandbox. See [Secrets](/docs/security/secrets) and the [Egress API](/docs/api-reference/egress).

## Debug a blocked call

**Python**

```python
# What is being blocked right now
for p in sandbox.network.pending():
    print(p.host, p.request_count, "blocked")

# Or filter the audit log for rejects
for e in sandbox.audit.list(since="1h", action="reject", limit=50):
    print(e.host, e.rejected_by)
```

Common allowlist gaps:

- **`pip install`** needs `pypi.org`, `files.pythonhosted.org`, and `pythonhosted.org`.
- **`npm install`** needs `registry.npmjs.org`; some postinstall scripts also reach `*.github.com`.
- **CDNs and dynamic subdomains** are usually not covered by an exact rule. Use a wildcard like `*.openai.com`.

Every blocked row carries a `rejected_by` field naming the rule that fired. For the full list of fixes, see [Security troubleshooting](/docs/security/troubleshooting).

> **Note: Lockdown does not affect inbound traffic**
>
> Enforcing an allowlist restricts outbound calls only. Preview URLs into your sandbox keep working exactly as before.

## See also

- [Network allowlist reference](/docs/security/network): The watch-then-enforce flow, the SDK methods, and the pending queue.
- [Egress API](/docs/api-reference/egress): Policies, allowlist rules, the audit log, and the vault.
- [Network policy API](/docs/api-reference/network-policy): The microVM-level policy for Computers.

pages.title: Network Allowlist
pages.description: Watch what your sandbox calls. When you're ready, lock it down with a one-click allowlist. Reversible.
pages.markdown:
By default, every new MIOSA sandbox is configured in **audit-only mode**: outbound calls are not blocked. Audit-only mode logs every outbound request, so you can see which hosts your sandbox calls before you lock down.

> **Note: Opt-in, always reversible**
>
> Lockdown is never applied automatically. You explicitly click "Lock Down"  -  and you can revert to audit-only at any time with one click. No data is lost in either direction.

## The two modes

| Mode | What it does | Default? |
|---|---|---|
| **Audit-only** | Logs every outbound request; nothing is blocked. | ✅ yes  -  every new sandbox starts here |
| **Enforce** | Applies the allowlist. Requests to unlisted hosts are blocked. | opt-in |

## The "watch then enforce" flow

### Day 0  -  Sandbox is created

No setup. Audit-only is on by default. Your sandbox makes outbound calls exactly like it did before MIOSA Egress existed. Outbound calls are logged, and the hosts they reach build your allowlist.

### Day 0-7  -  Use your sandbox normally

Build, deploy, run your agent  -  whatever. MIOSA collects audit data.

### Day 7+  -  Visit the Network tab

The Network tab shows you:

```text
HOSTS CONTACTED IN THE LAST 7 DAYS                  REQUESTS

api.openai.com                                        1,247
*.anthropic.com                                          83
github.com                                               412
pypi.org                                                  29
files.pythonhosted.org                                   161
api.github.com                                          1,053
```

Click "Lock Down". A confirmation modal appears showing the checkboxes for each host. You uncheck anything you don't want. Click Confirm.

Mode flips to **enforce**. The proxy now blocks anything not on the list.

### After lockdown  -  New hosts go to Pending

If your sandbox tries to reach a host that isn't on the allowlist, the request is blocked AND the host appears in the **Pending Requests** section of the Network tab. One click → Allow or Block.

You're never stuck  -  denied requests are visible, attributable, and one click away from resolution.

## SDK  -  Network controls

**Python**

```python
# Allow a host (audit-only or enforce  -  doesn't matter; allow is allow)
sandbox.network.allow("api.openai.com")
sandbox.network.allow("*.anthropic.com", methods=["POST"])

# Explicit deny  -  overrides any allow
sandbox.network.deny("169.254.169.254")

# Switch to enforce mode using the current allowlist
sandbox.network.lockdown()

# Switch back to audit-only
sandbox.network.observe()

# Auto-suggested allowlist from observed traffic
hosts = sandbox.network.suggestions(since="7d")
for h in hosts:
    print(h.host, h.request_count, h.last_seen)

# Inspect the current policy
policy = sandbox.network.get_policy()
print(policy.mode, policy.allow_rules, policy.deny_rules)

# Pending blocked requests
pending = sandbox.network.pending()
for p in pending:
    print(p.host, p.request_count, "blocked")
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
await sandbox.network.allow('api.openai.com');
await sandbox.network.allow('*.anthropic.com', { methods: ['POST'] });
await sandbox.network.deny('169.254.169.254');
await sandbox.network.lockdown();
await sandbox.network.observe();

const hosts = await sandbox.network.suggestions({ since: '7d' });
const policy = await sandbox.network.getPolicy();
const pending = await sandbox.network.pending();
```

**Go**

```go
sandbox.Network.Allow(ctx, "api.openai.com", miosa.AllowOpts{})
sandbox.Network.Allow(ctx, "*.anthropic.com", miosa.AllowOpts{Methods: []string{"POST"}})
sandbox.Network.Deny(ctx, "169.254.169.254")
sandbox.Network.Lockdown(ctx)
sandbox.Network.Observe(ctx)

hosts, _ := sandbox.Network.Suggestions(ctx, miosa.SuggestionsOpts{Since: "7d"})
policy, _ := sandbox.Network.GetPolicy(ctx)
pending, _ := sandbox.Network.Pending(ctx)
```

**Java**

```java
sandbox.network().allow("api.openai.com");
sandbox.network().allow("*.anthropic.com", AllowOpts.builder().methods(List.of("POST")).build());
sandbox.network().deny("169.254.169.254");
sandbox.network().lockdown();
sandbox.network().observe();

List<HostSuggestion> hosts = sandbox.network().suggestions(
    SuggestionsOpts.builder().since("7d").build());
NetworkPolicy policy = sandbox.network().getPolicy();
List<PendingHost> pending = sandbox.network().pending();
```

**Elixir**

```elixir
{:ok, _} = Miosa.Network.allow(sandbox.id, "api.openai.com")
{:ok, _} = Miosa.Network.allow(sandbox.id, "*.anthropic.com", methods: ["POST"])
{:ok, _} = Miosa.Network.deny(sandbox.id, "169.254.169.254")
{:ok, _} = Miosa.Network.lockdown(sandbox.id)
{:ok, _} = Miosa.Network.observe(sandbox.id)

{:ok, hosts}   = Miosa.Network.suggestions(sandbox.id, since: "7d")
{:ok, policy}  = Miosa.Network.get_policy(sandbox.id)
{:ok, pending} = Miosa.Network.pending(sandbox.id)
```

## Pattern matching

| Kind | Example | Matches |
|---|---|---|
| Exact host | `api.openai.com` | only this hostname |
| Wildcard | `*.openai.com` | any subdomain of openai.com |
| CIDR (IP only) | `10.0.0.0/8` | any IP in this range, only when the request target is an IP literal (not a hostname) |

Precedence at request time:

1. Exact match wins over wildcard
2. Wildcard wins over CIDR
3. Explicit `deny` rules always win over `allow`

## Per-resource vs tenant-wide rules

You can attach allowlist rules at two levels:

- **Per-resource**  -  applies to just one sandbox or computer
- **Tenant-wide**  -  applies to every resource in your tenant unless a resource has its own override

This means you can have a tenant default of "only allow our internal API + npm" and per-sandbox additions on top.

## When to use warn-mode rules

You can mark a rule as `warn_only`:

```python
sandbox.network.allow("api.experimental.example.com", warn_only=True)
```

In enforce mode, a `warn_only` allow rule still lets the request through but flags it in the audit log. Useful for trial-running a new third-party integration before committing to it.

## Rolling back

If lockdown breaks something:

```python
sandbox.network.observe()
```

You're back to audit-only. Allowlist rules are preserved (so you can re-lockdown later) but they're no longer enforcing.

## Real-world example  -  Python data pipeline locked to its upstream services

A Python sandbox that fetches data from a REST API, processes it, and writes results to an S3-compatible endpoint. Locked down to exactly those three hosts.

**Python**

```python
import os
from miosa import Miosa

client = Miosa(api_key=os.environ["MIOSA_API_KEY"])
sandbox = client.sandboxes.create(template_id="python-ds")

# Store credentials in the vault
sandbox.secrets.set(name="data_api_key", value=os.environ["DATA_API_KEY"], expose_as_env="DATA_API_KEY")
sandbox.secrets.set(name="s3_key", value=os.environ["S3_SECRET_KEY"], expose_as_env="AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY")

# Let it run for a minute to observe traffic
import time
pipeline = """
import os, requests, boto3

resp = requests.get(
    "https://data.example.com/api/v1/events?limit=100",
    headers={"X-Api-Key": os.environ["DATA_API_KEY"]},
)
events = resp.json()

# Process…
summary = {"count": len(events), "total_value": sum(e["value"] for e in events)}

s3 = boto3.client(
    "s3",
    endpoint_url="https://storage.example.com",
    aws_access_key_id="access",
    aws_secret_access_key=os.environ["AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"],
)
import json
s3.put_object(Bucket="results", Key="summary.json", Body=json.dumps(summary))
print("Done:", summary)
"""
sandbox.files.write("/workspace/pipeline.py", pipeline)
sandbox.exec("pip install boto3 -q")
sandbox.exec("python /workspace/pipeline.py")   # observe this run

# Now lock down based on what we observed
suggestions = sandbox.network.suggestions(since="1h")
print("Observed hosts:")
for h in suggestions:
    print(f"  {h.host} ({h.request_count} requests)")

# Allow only the three we expect
sandbox.network.allow("data.example.com")
sandbox.network.allow("storage.example.com")
sandbox.network.allow("pypi.org")          # for the pip install above
sandbox.network.allow("files.pythonhosted.org")
sandbox.network.lockdown()
print("Locked. Mode:", sandbox.network.get_policy().mode)

# Run again  -  still works, nothing else reachable
result = sandbox.exec("python /workspace/pipeline.py")
print(result.stdout)
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
import { Miosa } from '@miosa/sdk';

const client = new Miosa({ apiKey: process.env.MIOSA_API_KEY! });
const sandbox = await client.sandboxes.create({ template: 'python-ds' });

await sandbox.secrets.set({ name: 'data_api_key', value: process.env.DATA_API_KEY!, exposeAsEnv: 'DATA_API_KEY' });

// Observe one run, then lock down
const suggestions = await sandbox.network.suggestions({ since: '1h' });
for (const h of suggestions) {
  await sandbox.network.allow(h.host);
}
await sandbox.network.lockdown();
console.log('Locked to:', suggestions.map(h => h.host).join(', '));
```

## Reuse a policy across sandboxes

Export a locked policy and apply it to a new sandbox:

```python
# Export the policy from a locked sandbox
policy = sandbox.network.get_policy()

# Apply it to a new sandbox
new_sandbox = client.sandboxes.create(template_id="python-ds")
for rule in policy.allow_rules:
    new_sandbox.network.allow(rule.host, methods=rule.methods)
for rule in policy.deny_rules:
    new_sandbox.network.deny(rule.host)
new_sandbox.network.lockdown()
print(f"Policy cloned to {new_sandbox.id}.")
```

For the same policy on every new sandbox, apply rules at the tenant level with `client.network.allow(...)` and `client.network.lockdown()`; they become the default for all resources unless a sandbox overrides them.

> **Caution: Templates carry the policy**
>
> A sandbox created from a template inherits the template's network policy. If the template was snapshotted in enforce mode, new sandboxes start locked down. Call `new_sandbox.network.observe()` right after create to return it to audit-only.

## Full script

End-to-end: observe, review, lock down, and check the pending queue.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""lockdown_workflow.py  -  audit-only to enforce in one pass"""

import os, time
from miosa import Miosa

client = Miosa(api_key=os.environ["MIOSA_API_KEY"])
sandbox = client.sandboxes.create(template_id="python-ds")
print(f"Sandbox {sandbox.id}  -  mode: {sandbox.network.get_policy().mode}")

# 1. Observe (use 7d in production)
time.sleep(10)

# 2. Review observed hosts
suggestions = sandbox.network.suggestions(since="1h")
for h in suggestions:
    print(f"  {h.host}  ({h.request_count} requests)")

# 3. Lock down with the observed hosts as the allowlist
for h in suggestions:
    sandbox.network.allow(h.host)
sandbox.network.lockdown()
print(f"Locked. Mode: {sandbox.network.get_policy().mode}")

# 4. Check what is still being blocked
pending = sandbox.network.pending()
for p in pending:
    print(f"  {p.host}  ({p.request_count} blocked)")
```

## Troubleshooting

**`pip install` fails after lockdown  -  "Could not find a version that satisfies the requirement".**
Three domains are needed: `pypi.org`, `files.pythonhosted.org`, and `pythonhosted.org`. Allow all three before locking down.

**An agent stopped working after lockdown and I cannot tell what is blocked.**
Open the Network tab -> Pending Requests, or call `sandbox.network.pending()`. Each blocked row has a `rejected_by` field naming the rule that fired.

**`npm install` fails after lockdown.**
Allow `registry.npmjs.org`. Some packages also fetch from `*.github.com` during postinstall scripts  -  check the Pending queue for exact hosts.

**My sandbox is in enforce mode but I see unexpected hosts in the audit log.**
Audit-only log entries always appear even in enforce mode (blocked calls still get logged with `action=reject`). Filter by `action=reject` to see what's being blocked.

**I want the same policy on every new sandbox without configuring each one.**
Apply rules at the tenant level using `client.network.allow(...)` and `client.network.lockdown()`  -  these become the default for all resources in the tenant unless overridden per sandbox.

**After `observe()`, my rules are gone when I call `lockdown()` again.**
Rules are never deleted by `observe()`. If they appear missing, check `sandbox.network.get_policy().allow_rules`  -  they'll be listed there. The only way rules disappear is if you called `sandbox.network.clear_rules()` explicitly.

For more issues, see the [Security troubleshooting hub](/docs/security/troubleshooting).

## Frequently asked

**Will lockdown block npm install or pip install?**
Only if you don't allow `pypi.org`, `files.pythonhosted.org`, `registry.npmjs.org`, etc. The 7-day audit data will have already shown you these  -  they're on the suggested list.

**My agent suddenly stopped working after I locked down.**
Open the Network tab → Pending Requests. You'll see exactly what got blocked. One-click allow, or revert with `observe()`.

**Can I share allowlists across sandboxes?**
Yes  -  apply them at the tenant or workspace scope, or copy a "policy template" from another resource (Phase 5).

**Does lockdown affect inbound (preview) traffic?**
No. Lockdown is for outbound only. Preview URLs into your sandbox keep working exactly as before.

pages.title: Edge middleware
pages.description: Ordered path rules and an optional function that run at the edge, in front of a server service.
pages.markdown:
Edge middleware runs in front of a server service, before the request reaches
your process: redirects, rewrites, header changes, and optionally a published
function that can answer, continue or rewrite the request.

It is a structured rule set, so it is written as a file rather than a pile of
flags:

```bash
miosa middleware shop API --from middleware.json
miosa middleware shop API           # what is configured now
miosa middleware shop API --off     # remove the rules and the function
```

```json
{
  "rules": [
    { "path": "/old/*", "redirect": { "to": "/new", "status": 308 } },
    { "path": "/api/*", "request_headers": { "set": { "x-plan": "pro" } } }
  ],
  "function": { "slug": "gate", "paths": ["/app/*"], "timeout_ms": 250, "on_error": "closed" }
}
```

Rules run in order and there can be up to fifty of them. A `path` is either an
exact path or a prefix ending in `/*`, where `$1` is the rest of the path. Each
rule carries exactly one of a `redirect` (with an optional `301`, `302`, `303`,
`307` or `308`, default `307`), a `rewrite`, and/or header changes.

The function answers `x-miosa-middleware: next` to let the request continue, and
may add `x-miosa-middleware-request-<name>` or `x-miosa-middleware-rewrite`. Any
other answer is returned to the client. With `on_error: "closed"`, a failing
function answers `503 edge_middleware_unavailable`; with `open`, the request
continues.

Protected header names are refused, including `host`, `content-length`,
`transfer-encoding`, `connection`, `upgrade`, `x-internal-*`, `x-miosa-*` and
`x-forwarded-*`.

> **Note: It applies in seconds**
>
> A change applies within about five seconds at every edge node. Validation errors
> name the field (`settings.edge_middleware.<path>`), so a typo in a rule is easy to
> find.

pages.title: Protection and WAF
pages.description: Put a password in front of a service, mint share links, and set the web application firewall rules the proxy enforces.
pages.markdown:
Protection and the WAF are enforced at the edge, in front of the service, so they
apply before a request reaches your process.

## Password and share links

```bash
miosa protection shop API                            # is it protected?
miosa protection shop API --password 'open-sesame'
miosa protection shop API --share-link --expires 3600
miosa protection shop API --revoke <link-id>
miosa protection shop API --off
```

The password is never shown again. A share link is a way past it for one person:
the `msl_...` token is shown once, and expires after `--expires` seconds (seven
days by default, at most ninety). A visitor uses it as `?miosa_share=<token>` or
with an `x-miosa-share-token` header.

Protection can also be set on a Deploy target or on an environment kind, and the
rows resolve service over environment over kind. That is why a preview environment
can be protected without touching each service in it.

## WAF

```bash
miosa waf shop API
miosa waf shop API --mode enforce --deny 203.0.113.0/24 --rate 120
miosa waf shop API --allow 198.51.100.0/24
miosa waf shop API --attack-mode on
miosa waf shop API --off
```

- `--mode` is `off`, `observe` or `enforce`.
- `--allow`/`--deny` take IPs or CIDRs (`ip_allow`/`ip_deny` on the wire).
- `--rate` is requests per minute per source; `0` clears the limit.
- `--attack-mode` serves a JavaScript challenge to browsers and `403` to
  everything else.

**Country rules read only the trusted `x-miosa-country` header that the edge
sets.** There is no GeoIP lookup of our own: if a request arrives without that
header the country rules are skipped, and the WAF document says whether they can
act at all with `country_rules_active`.

> **Note: Observe before enforce**
>
> Run `--mode observe` for a day first. The WAF reports what it would have blocked,
> so you can see a wrong CIDR before it turns into a page full of 403s.

pages.title: Public database endpoint
pages.description: Open a TLS-only TCP endpoint for one managed database, with an allowlist, so a laptop or an outside service can connect.
pages.markdown:
A managed database is reachable from inside the platform by its private URL. Turn
on public networking when something outside needs to connect: a laptop, a
migration tool, an analytics job in another cloud.

```bash
miosa db public app-db                       # off or on, and the address
miosa db public app-db on                    # any source
miosa db public app-db on --allow 203.0.113.0/24 --allow 198.51.100.7
miosa db public app-db off                  # close it and free the port
```

The same calls are `GET`, `POST` and `DELETE /api/v1/databases/:id/public-networking`.

## What you get

- A host and a port from **30000-39999**, one port per database. The host is the
  edge's public address, so it does not change when the database moves host.
- `public_url` in the credentials response while it is on, and
  `DATABASE_PUBLIC_URL` in the database service's variables, so
  `${{db.DATABASE_PUBLIC_URL}}` resolves for anything that needs it.

## Security

- **TLS only.** Postgres needs `sslmode=require`; MySQL needs
  `--ssl-mode=REQUIRED` and refuses a plaintext login with error 3159. The
  certificate is self-signed, so `require` encrypts without verifying the name.
- **The allowlist closes disallowed sources before any TLS handshake.** `--allow`
  replaces the stored list, so `on` with no `--allow` means any source. Entries
  are IPs or CIDRs, at most 32.
- Limits: 100 connections per database, 20 new connections per 10 seconds per
  source IP, at most 32 TLS handshakes at once, and 2,000 public connections
  across your databases.

## Engines

Postgres, MySQL, Redis and MongoDB. Other engines answer `ENGINE_NOT_SUPPORTED`.

## Turning it off

`off`, or deleting the database, closes the port within about fifteen seconds.
Both are recorded in the audit log as `database.public_networking_enable` and
`database.public_networking_disable`.

> **Note: Prefer the private URL**
>
> Anything inside the platform should use the private URL. The public endpoint
> exists for clients that cannot reach the private network, not as the default way
> to connect.

pages.title: Agent operating guide
pages.description: The CLI and release workflow for AI agents using MIOSA.
pages.markdown:
Use this page when an AI agent, coding assistant, CI worker, or operator needs to build and release software through MIOSA.
The CLI is the authoritative happy path - prefer its `--json` output over reconstructing lower-level API calls.

## 1. Discover the current inventory

```bash
miosa catalog --json
miosa deploy list --json
miosa deploy get <deployment> --json
```

`catalog` reports the canonical compute products, templates, sizes, and readiness the platform offers right now.
`deploy list` and `deploy get` return the deployments you already own.
Do not guess a resource id from an old transcript when these commands can return the current inventory.

## 2. Develop in a persistent sandbox

```bash
miosa create my-dev-box --template nextjs --wait
miosa console my-dev-box --cwd /workspace
miosa doctor
miosa preview create my-dev-box 3000 --name candidate
```

`create` provisions the sandbox and, with `--wait`, blocks until it is ready.
`console` opens an interactive shell and resumes the same machine on a later run.
`doctor` checks configuration, connectivity and authentication.
Preview publishes a port at a public URL and never promotes production.

## 3. Publish the exact release

**CLI**

```bash
miosa deploy create my-app --from-sandbox my-dev-box --port 3000 --wait --json
miosa deploy releases <deployment>
miosa deploy promote <deployment> <release>
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const result = await miosa.deployments.publish(deploymentId, {
  sourceSandboxId: sandbox.id,
  kind: "auto",                       // "static" | "dynamic" | "auto"
  environment: "production",
  outputPath: "/workspace",
  runCommand: "npm start",            // dynamic deployments only
  port: 3000,                         // dynamic only
})

console.log(result.deployment.public_url)
```

**Python**

```python
result = miosa.deployments.publish(
    deployment_id,
    source_sandbox_id=sandbox_id,
    kind="auto",              # "static" | "dynamic" | "auto"
    environment="production",
    output_path="/workspace",
    run_command="npm start",         # dynamic only
    port=3000,                       # dynamic only
)

print(result.deployment.public_url)
```

A candidate is not production merely because its build succeeded.
Promotion targets one exact immutable release, and the production URL stays stable while the active release changes.

## Pick what you need

| You want to | Start here |
|---|---|
| The full CLI workflow | [Agent CLI workflow](/docs/guides/agent-cli-workflow) |
| Interpret status and protect durable resources | [Agent safety and status](/docs/guides/agent-safety) |
| What agents can do | [What MIOSA agents can do](/docs/guides/agent-capabilities) |
| Configure an agent | [Configure an agent](/docs/guides/configure-agent) |
| Understand the deploy objects | [The deployment model](/docs/docker-host/deployment-model) |

## Next

pages.title: What MIOSA agents can do
pages.description: Built-in tools, connected app actions, device execution, artifacts, browser work, and the permission model for agents running on MIOSA.
pages.markdown:
MIOSA agents are workers that can use real cloud execution. They can research,
write code, run commands, edit files, control a browser or desktop, call
connected apps, create artifacts, start previews, and publish finished apps.

These are the primitives behind products such as Polsia-style autonomous
company operators, Cofounder / Co-Founder AI-style business agents, and
Nebula-style shared virtual devices.

The core rule is simple: the agent should do the work inside a MIOSA device,
not only on the user's laptop and then upload the result later.

Do it now

Create your first agent

A named worker with instructions, a model harness, tools and devices.

- [Create agent](https://miosa.ai/agents/new): (opens the MIOSA console in a new tab)

miosa agent new reviewer --harness claude-code --instructions "Review pull requests and report risks"

Next [Configure an agent](/docs/guides/configure-agent)

```text
User request
  -> agent plans
  -> MIOSA device executes
  -> events stream back to the UI
  -> files, previews, artifacts, screenshots, or deployments are saved
```

---

## Built-in toolkits

| Toolkit | What it does | Primary runtime |
|---|---|---|
| Web research | Search, retrieve pages, summarize sources, gather current context | Agent loop or sandbox |
| Filesystem | Read, write, rename, delete, list, and generate files in `/workspace` | Sandbox or computer |
| Code execution | Run Bash, Python, Node, package managers, tests, builds, linters | Sandbox |
| Live server | Start a dev server and expose a preview URL for review | Sandbox |
| Browser | Navigate pages, click, fill forms, extract data, log in to dashboards | Computer or browser-capable sandbox |
| Desktop | Screenshot, click, type, scroll, clipboard, windows, shell | Computer |
| Media and artifacts | Generate PDFs, DOCX, images, diagrams, charts, HTML reports, ZIPs | Sandbox |
| Deployment | Publish a verified workspace to MIOSA Deploy or Docker Host | Deployment pipeline |
| App actions | GitHub, Slack, Google, Refero, or tenant-provided tools | Managed connectors |
| Sub-agent delegation | Split tasks across child sandboxes, computers, or local workers | Orchestrator |

> **Tip: Default for app builders**
>
> For generated apps, start in a sandbox. Let the agent write files into
> `/workspace`, run `npm install`, start the dev server, show the preview, fix
> errors in place, snapshot, and then publish.

---

## Tools in action

### Web research

An agent can gather current market examples, inspect docs, compare product
flows, and save notes into the workspace before writing code.

```text
research/
  onboarding-patterns.md
  pricing-pages.md
  competitor-notes.md
```

### Code execution on a workspace device

The agent writes code and runs it inside the sandbox.

```bash
miosa exec <sandbox-id> --cwd /workspace -- npm run test
miosa exec <sandbox-id> --cwd /workspace -- npm run build
```

The UI should stream stdout, stderr, exit status, and file events while the
command runs.

### Browser automation

Use a computer when the agent needs a real browser session:

- open a preview
- log in to a dashboard
- fill forms
- click buttons
- capture screenshots
- verify responsive layouts
- extract data from pages that need a browser

### Artifact generation

Use a sandbox when the agent needs to produce downloadable work:

- proposals
- DOCX/PDF files
- pitch decks
- CSV exports
- charts
- SVG/PNG diagrams
- ZIP bundles
- HTML previews

Generated files should be saved as MIOSA artifacts so the product UI can show
them in an artifacts panel with version history.

### App actions

Connected apps become tools. For example:

- GitHub issues and pull requests
- Slack messages
- Google Drive files
- Gmail drafts
- Refero design research
- tenant-provided APIs

App actions should use managed connectors or scoped tenant credentials, not
secrets pasted into chat.

### Sub-agent delegation

One orchestrator can delegate work to multiple runtime workers:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  O[Orchestrator agent] --> C[Coder sandbox]
  O --> T[Test sandbox]
  O --> B[Browser computer]
  O --> A[Artifact sandbox]
  C --> R[Run events and files]
  T --> R
  B --> R
  A --> R
```

Use this for large jobs, QA sweeps, parallel tests, research clusters, and
agent-company products.

---

## Device execution

Agents run against a device. MIOSA has three device classes:

| Device | Use it when | Preserves state |
|---|---|---|
| Sandbox Worker | Code, files, commands, previews, artifacts, publish prep | Yes, through pause/resume and snapshots |
| Computer | Browser/desktop automation, screenshots, visual QA, manual handoff | Yes, through persistent computer storage |
| Local Device | User-owned network/files/apps are required | On the user's machine |

Docker Host is not an agent device. It is the durable hosting target after a
sandbox-built app is ready.

See [Agent devices](/docs/guides/agent-devices) for the full model.

---

## Permissions

Permissions decide what an agent is allowed to do.

| Permission surface | Controls |
|---|---|
| Visibility | Private agent, workspace agent, or platform-managed agent |
| Device access | Which sandboxes, computers, local devices, or pools the agent can use |
| Tool access | Files, exec, browser, deployments, connectors, artifacts |
| Connected accounts | OAuth grants, API keys, managed connectors, tenant-provided integrations |
| Secret exposure | Which environment variables are injected into the runtime |
| Approval policy | Which actions require a human confirmation |
| Quotas | Max child sandboxes, computers, runtime minutes, spend, or concurrency |

Credential rule:

- tenant admin keys stay server-side
- browser code never receives `msk_*` keys
- sandboxes receive scoped runtime tokens
- managed provider tokens stay encrypted in MIOSA
- egress swaps brokered placeholders only for the provider endpoint they belong to

---

## Product surfaces to expose

If you are building an agent platform on MIOSA, show users these things:

- the current plan or task graph
- tool calls as they happen
- command output
- files created or edited
- artifacts with download buttons
- browser screenshots and preview URLs
- connected accounts and missing credentials
- approval prompts for risky actions
- snapshots, forks, and version history
- deployment status and public URL
- usage, credits, and runtime cost

This is the product layer on top of the primitives. The user should understand
that an agent is working in a real device and producing durable outputs.

---

## Related

- [Configure an agent](/docs/guides/configure-agent): Set instructions, model, tools, memory, devices, variables, triggers, and approval policy.
- [Agent devices](/docs/guides/agent-devices): Understand sandboxes, computers, local devices, primary devices, and device selection.
- [Managed connectors](/docs/guides/managed-connectors): Attach MIOSA-managed or tenant-provided provider tools without exposing vendor tokens.
- [Agent orchestration](/docs/guides/agent-orchestration): Coordinate one agent, many sub-agents, or large device pools.
- [Build an agent-company platform](/docs/guides/build-agent-company): Package these primitives into Polsia, Cofounder, or Nebula-style products.

## Next steps

- [Configure an agent](/docs/guides/configure-agent): Instructions, model, tools, devices, memory and approvals.
- [Choose its devices](/docs/guides/agent-devices): Sandboxes, computers, and local devices for agent work.
- [Integrate your own agent](/docs/guides/agent): Drive MIOSA primitives from your own agent loop.

pages.title: Agent CLI workflow
pages.description: The full CLI release workflow for agents: discovery, scope, sandbox development, preview, publish, promote, recovery, and rollback.
pages.markdown:
Use this page when an AI agent, coding assistant, CI worker, or operator needs the full build-and-release path through MIOSA.
The CLI is the authoritative happy path. Prefer its `--json` output over reconstructing lower-level API calls.

## Start with discovery

```bash
miosa catalog --json
miosa deploy list --json
miosa deploy get <deployment> --json
```

`catalog` reports the canonical compute products, templates, sizes, and readiness the platform offers right now.

`deploy list` and `deploy get` return the deployments you already own, with their status, active release and public URL.

Do not guess a resource id from an old transcript when these commands can return the current inventory.

## Resolve scope before mutation

Every mutation must resolve one unambiguous organization, workspace, application, and environment.

Do not create a replacement sandbox, deployment, database, or Docker Host host just because an identifier was not resolved.

Inspect the intended resource first.

```bash
miosa deploy get <deployment> --json
miosa deploy releases <deployment> --json
```

`deploy get` shows the deployment's identity, environment, active release and route.

`deploy releases` lists the immutable releases already published to it.

Do not commit credentials or secrets to a repository.

Secrets belong in encrypted MIOSA environment storage, not in the manifest or shell history.

## Develop in a persistent sandbox

Use the sandbox development flow for mutable work.

```bash
miosa create my-dev-box --template nextjs --wait
miosa console my-dev-box --cwd /workspace
miosa doctor
```

`create` provisions the sandbox and, with `--wait`, blocks until it is ready for commands.

`console` opens an interactive shell on the sandbox and resumes the same machine on a later run.

`doctor` checks configuration, connectivity and authentication, and reports what it finds.

Dependency installation must use a lockfile-strict command such as `npm ci`.

## Preview before production

```bash
miosa preview create my-dev-box 3000 --name candidate
miosa preview status my-dev-box <preview-id>
```

`preview create` publishes a port on the sandbox at a public URL and prints the URL.

`preview status` reports whether it is serving.

Preview never promotes production.

Read the returned `url` and `status` from the JSON response.

Use the returned URL.

Do not construct a sandbox, deployment, or custom-domain hostname.

## Publish the candidate

```bash
miosa deploy create my-app --from-sandbox my-dev-box --port 3000 --wait --json
```

`deploy create` publishes a sandbox, a git repository or a local directory as a new deployment and, with `--wait`, blocks until it is live and prints its URL.

Each publish produces an immutable release that can be promoted or rolled back to.

A candidate is not production merely because its build succeeded.

## Promote the exact release

```bash
miosa deploy releases <deployment>
miosa deploy promote <deployment> <release>
```

Promotion targets one exact immutable release.

It must not select "latest" by timestamp or rely on a mutable version label.

The production URL stays stable while the active immutable release changes.

If the candidate fails to build, the currently active release remains live.

## Recover an interrupted publish

An HTTP timeout does not prove the backend operation failed.

Re-read the deployment before retrying, and only republish when the previous attempt is proven terminal.

```bash
miosa deploy get <deployment> --json
miosa deploy builds <deployment>
```

Do not start a duplicate publish or promotion while an earlier operation may still be active.

## Roll back deliberately

```bash
miosa deploy rollback <deployment> --to <release-id> --yes --json
```

Rollback also targets one exact immutable release.

Use a known-good release and verify the same route, artifact, data, and configuration contract after activation.

Database migrations must remain backward compatible when an older application release may run against newer data.

## See also

- [Agent safety and status](/docs/guides/agent-safety): Interpret composite health signals and protect durable resources.
- [Agent operating guide](/docs/guides/agent-operating-guide): The three-step entry path for agents.
- [Publishing](/docs/docker-host/publishing): Candidate creation, verification, exact promotion, and receipts.
- [Rollback](/docs/docker-host/rollback): Re-point a deployment at an older version with no rebuild.

pages.title: Agent safety and status
pages.description: How agents interpret deployment health, preserve durable resources, and respect current capability boundaries.
pages.markdown:
An agent must not treat a single signal as proof that production is healthy, and must not replace durable resources on a guess.
This page covers status interpretation, durable-resource handling, and the current capability boundaries.

## Interpret status correctly

> **Caution: Healthy is a composite result**
>
> A deployment is not proven healthy from one database row, one HTTP response, or one host heartbeat.
> The active release, running artifact, public route, data bindings, required capabilities, and runtime placement must agree.

| Signal | What it proves |
|---|---|
| Release status is `ready` | The immutable artifact can be considered for promotion |
| Build status is `succeeded` | The build step completed for this release |
| `active_release_id` matches | The control plane selected the expected release |
| The public route responds | Users can reach the deployed application surface |
| Runtime logs show healthy startup | The process bound its port and is serving |

## Preserve durable resources

A sandbox is a mutable development workspace.

A deployment is the durable production identity.

A managed database and its volume are durable data resources.

An Docker Host host can run multiple deployments and should not be replaced for an application-level failure without host-level evidence.

Pause, resume, recover, and reconcile existing resources before creating replacements.

Create a replacement only when the original resource is proven terminal and its state, bindings, and ownership have been preserved.

## Capability boundaries

MIOSA currently supports sandboxes, computers, previews, immutable application releases, managed data, workspace attribution, domains, integrations, and OpenComputers.

Specialized model APIs can be connected today.

CPU-compatible open-source applications can be self-hosted when their runtime requirements fit the selected compute.

Managed GPU execution and built-in managed agent orchestration remain planned until the availability page marks them shipped.

AWS and Google Cloud customer-region packages exist, but production activation remains gated on provider canary and host-acceptance evidence.

## See also

- [Agent CLI workflow](/docs/guides/agent-cli-workflow): Discovery, scope, sandbox development, publish, promote, and rollback.
- [Agent operating guide](/docs/guides/agent-operating-guide): The three-step entry path for agents.
- [Availability](/docs/availability): Check whether a capability is available, integrated, self-hostable, gated, or planned.
