The agent should edit files in `/workspace`, not build everything locally and
upload a finished repo at the end.

```text
bad:
  local agent builds repo on laptop
  upload after the fact
  remote sandbox only previews the result

good:
  agent writes files into sandbox
  sandbox installs dependencies
  sandbox runs tests/builds
  sandbox serves preview
  user sees events and artifacts as work happens
```

### 5. Stream progress into the product UI

Show users the work surface:

- plan created
- device created or resumed
- file written
- command started
- stdout/stderr chunk
- preview ready
- screenshot captured
- artifact generated
- approval required
- deployment ready

This is the difference between "the agent disappeared" and "the agent is
working in a real machine."

### 6. Attach connectors and secrets safely

Use managed connectors, scoped tokens, and runtime variables. Do not paste
provider keys into chat.

```text
Tenant key
  -> stays server-side
  -> mints scoped runtime token
  -> sandbox receives only the scoped token
  -> managed provider token is brokered only to the allowed provider endpoint
```

This is how a platform can provide a managed design-research connector while
still preventing arbitrary token exfiltration.

### 7. Save checkpoints and publish

Use snapshots and versioned deployments:

```text
checkpoint after dependencies install
checkpoint after first working preview
checkpoint before risky refactor
publish after tests and browser QA
rollback through deployment versions
```

For many small customer apps in one workspace, publish to
[Docker Host](/docs/docker-host/docker-deploy). For normal production apps,
publish through MIOSA Deploy.

---

## What your frontend should show

| Surface | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Chat or task stream | User request, agent status, tool calls, command output |
| Device panel | Sandbox preview, computer desktop, logs, screenshots |
| Files panel | Workspace files, diffs, generated code, editable artifacts |
| Artifacts panel | PDFs, DOCX, images, ZIPs, screenshots, downloads |
| Approvals panel | Risky actions waiting for human confirmation |
| Jobs panel | Scheduled and background work |
| Deployment panel | Public URL, versions, rollback, domains |
| Usage panel | Credits, runtime minutes, sandbox/computer cost |

This is how to make MIOSA feel like an agent workspace, not just an API.

---

## Architecture rules

1. **Do not merge sandboxes and computers into one vague concept.** Sandboxes
   are for headless code, files, previews, and artifacts. Computers are for GUI
   and browser automation.
2. **Make persistence the default for agent work.** Idle compute can stop, but
   the workspace state should survive through snapshots or persistent storage.
3. **Use scoped runtime credentials.** Tenant admin keys stay server-side.
4. **Treat the orchestrator as your product.** MIOSA executes; your product
   decides roles, prompts, permissions, retries, approvals, and UI.
5. **Expose run events.** Users need to see code, commands, files, previews,
   artifacts, screenshots, and deploys as they happen.
6. **Dispatch prompts into assigned devices.** A user prompt should become a
   sandbox/computer/local-device run, not a detached local-only script.
7. **Separate development from hosting.** Agents build in sandboxes and
   computers. Finished apps run on deployments or Docker Host.
8. **Keep runtimes replaceable.** A workspace should be executable by OSA,
   Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, Aider, OpenClaw, or a custom runtime without
   rewriting the customer's company knowledge.

---

## See also

- [What MIOSA agents can do](/docs/guides/agent-capabilities): Built-in toolkits, app actions, permissions, artifacts, and product surfaces.
- [Agent devices](/docs/guides/agent-devices): Sandboxes, computers, local devices, persistence, and primary device policy.
- [Agent orchestration](/docs/guides/agent-orchestration): Coordinate one agent, many agents, queues, subagents, and device pools.
- [Managed connectors](/docs/guides/managed-connectors): Provide hosted provider tools without exposing provider secrets.

pages.title: Agent workflow patterns
pages.description: Simple-to-complex workflows for using MIOSA agents, devices, events, artifacts, and deployments.
pages.markdown:
MIOSA workflows scale from a single prompt to a fleet of long-running agents.
The same primitives apply at every level:

```text
prompt -> agent runtime -> assigned device -> event stream -> durable output
```

Use this page to choose the right workflow for your product.

---

## Pattern 1: one-shot run

Use this for quick checks, small scripts, inspections, summaries, and health
tests.

```bash
miosa prompt --sandbox <sandbox-id> "check if the preview server is healthy"
```

Expected behavior:

1. CLI sends the prompt to MIOSA.
2. MIOSA validates the target sandbox.
3. Runtime executes a short task.
4. CLI prints the answer and any structured output.
5. Credits are charged for model usage and device time.

Use this when the user does not need a long-lived session.

---

## Pattern 2: prompt into a sandbox

Use this when the agent should code, generate artifacts, run tests, or start a
preview.

```bash
miosa prompt --sandbox <sandbox-id> \
  --harness codex \
  "Build a Next.js landing page, run it on port 3000, and fix any errors."
```

The agent should work inside `/workspace`:

- write files
- install dependencies
- run tests
- start dev server
- inspect errors
- save artifacts
- snapshot checkpoints
- publish when approved

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant CLI
  participant API as MIOSA API
  participant R as Agent runtime
  participant S as Sandbox

  CLI->>API: sandbox prompt
  API->>S: resume sandbox
  API->>R: start run with sandbox tools
  R->>S: write files, exec commands
  S-->>API: events and preview URL
  API-->>CLI: stream events
```

> **Tip: Do not upload as the default**
>
> Uploading a local repo is useful for import and sync. It should not be the only
> agent workflow. The normal agent-builder path is to let the agent create and
> modify files inside the sandbox.

---

## Pattern 3: prompt into a computer

Use this when the task requires a real browser, GUI, login flow, or visual QA.

```bash
miosa prompt \
  --computer <computer-id> \
  --harness claude-code \
  "Open the app preview, test signup, capture screenshots, and report issues."
```

The computer device can:

- open URLs
- click buttons
- type into forms
- scroll
- log in to dashboards
- inspect UI states
- take screenshots
- use terminal or desktop apps

Use a computer after a sandbox creates a preview, or as the primary runtime for
browser-heavy automation products.

---

## Pattern 4: detached agent session

Use this for tasks that continue after the first command returns.

```bash
miosa agent run builder \
  --sandbox <sandbox-id> \
  --no-follow \
  --json
```

Then inspect and continue the session:

```bash
miosa run events <run-id>
miosa run steer "Now add authentication and update the README." --sandbox <sandbox-id>
miosa run files <run-id>
miosa run stop <run-id>
```

Detached sessions should not require a terminal UI to keep running. A TUI is a
view, not the execution model.

Detached run requirements:

- run id returned immediately (`--no-follow`)
- events available over API and CLI
- reconnectable stream
- durable transcript (`miosa run messages`)
- artifacts linked to the run (`miosa run files`)
- clean stop/cancel (`miosa run stop`)
- typed failure state
- clear credit usage

---

## Pattern 5: app-builder loop

Use this for Lovable, Replit, v0, or Lumen-style app generation.

```text
User prompt
  -> create/resume sandbox
  -> agent edits files in /workspace
  -> run install/build/test
  -> start preview
  -> stream files and preview URL to UI
  -> user asks for edits
  -> agent patches same sandbox
  -> snapshot stable state
  -> publish to deployment
```

Recommended UI:

- chat
- file tree
- command log
- preview frame
- artifacts panel
- deployment status
- version history
- credit usage

Recommended backend records:

```sql
projects
  current_sandbox_id
  current_deployment_id
  latest_snapshot_id

agent_runs
  project_id
  sandbox_id
  prompt
  status
  idempotency_key
```

---

## Pattern 6: artifact workspace

Use this for Claude Desktop-style work where the agent creates documents,
images, diagrams, or data files.

Examples:

- proposals
- DOCX files
- PDFs
- pitch decks
- diagrams
- brand assets
- CSV reports
- HTML previews
- ZIP bundles

Flow:

```text
prompt -> sandbox -> generate file -> render/validate -> artifact -> version
```

The UI should show:

- live text/code generation
- generated file cards
- preview pane
- download button
- revision history
- "make changes" prompt attached to the artifact

---

## Pattern 7: browser operator

Use this for Nebula-style browser work or RPA-like workflows.

```text
prompt -> computer -> browser session -> screenshots/events -> report/action
```

Examples:

- fill onboarding forms
- verify checkout
- inspect admin dashboards
- scrape authenticated data
- test browser UI
- run visual QA on previews

Human approval should be required before:

- submitting external forms
- sending messages
- spending money
- deleting data
- changing account settings
- using admin credentials

---

## Pattern 8: orchestrated agent team

Use this for Cofounder (cofounder.co), Polsia, Agentfounder, or internal
operator products.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  O[Orchestrator] --> Eng[Engineering sandbox]
  O --> Design[Design/browser computer]
  O --> Research[Research sandbox]
  O --> Sales[Sales connector worker]
  O --> QA[QA computer]
  Eng --> Out[Artifacts and run events]
  Design --> Out
  Research --> Out
  Sales --> Out
  QA --> Out
```

The orchestrator should:

- break the prompt into tasks
- assign devices and runtimes
- enforce budget and approvals
- stream each child run
- merge artifacts
- ask for human approval on risky actions
- produce one final status

Use child devices only when they create real leverage. Not every task needs a
new sandbox.

---

## Pattern 9: agent fleet

Use this when the product launches tens, hundreds, or thousands of workers.

Examples:

- large test matrices
- lead enrichment
- website audits
- browser QA sweeps
- benchmark runs
- research crawls
- parallel code migrations

Fleet requirements:

| Requirement | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Queue | Avoid unbounded device creation |
| Idempotency | Retry without duplicate resources |
| Budget cap | Stop runaway spend |
| Concurrency limit | Protect user plan and platform capacity |
| Child-run events | Show progress without opening every worker |
| Aggregation | Merge output into one report |
| Cancellation | Stop the fleet fast |
| Partial results | Preserve useful work after failures |

---

## Choosing the pattern

| User asks for | Use |
|---|---|
| Quick check | One-shot run |
| Generate code | Sandbox prompt |
| Test browser flow | Computer prompt |
| Keep working after disconnect | Detached session |
| Build and preview app | App-builder loop |
| Make a document/image/report | Artifact workspace |
| Operate a website/dashboard | Browser operator |
| Run a company/project | Orchestrated agent team |
| Scale many workers | Agent fleet |

---

## See also

- [Agent product model](/docs/guides/agent-product-model): The canonical vocabulary for agents, devices, runs, events, artifacts, and credits.
- [Runtime routing](/docs/guides/agent-runtime-routing): Route prompts to OSA, Codex, Claude Code, Hermes, Pi, or custom runtimes.
- [Virtual device product](/docs/cookbook/build-virtual-device-product): Build a Nebula-style persistent workspace with files, browser, jobs, and artifacts.
- [Backend orchestration](/docs/integrations/backend-orchestration): Build the product backend that dispatches prompts into MIOSA devices.

pages.title: Agent device selection
pages.description: Decide when an agent needs no device, a sandbox, a computer, a local device, or a deployment target.
pages.markdown:
Not every agent needs a sandbox. The right question is:

```text
Does this agent need an execution environment, durable state, files, browser,
private network access, or deployable output?
```

If the answer is yes, assign a device. If the answer is no, the agent can run
as a lightweight orchestration or reasoning step in your backend.

---

## The short rule

| Agent task | Device |
|---|---|
| Pure reasoning, classification, routing, summarization | No device required |
| Write files, run code, install packages, generate artifacts | Sandbox |
| Browse websites, log in, click buttons, capture screenshots | Computer |
| Use customer-owned files, apps, VPNs, or private network | Local device |
| Serve production traffic | Deployment or Docker Host |

> **Note: No device is still a product decision**
>
> An agent can run without a sandbox when it only needs model reasoning and
> backend-provided context. That is cheaper and faster. Give it a device only when
> the work requires one.

---

## When no device is required

Use no device for agents that only need to think, classify, plan, or transform
text already available to your backend.

Examples:

- route a user prompt to the right department agent
- summarize a short transcript
- classify support tickets
- draft a simple sales email from provided context
- decide whether a run needs human approval
- select the best device for a task
- produce a task plan without touching files
- score leads using fields already in your database

This work can run in the product backend or in a managed MIOSA agent runtime
without creating a sandbox.

Billing is usually model/runtime usage only.

---

## When a sandbox is required

Use a sandbox when the agent needs a workspace.

Examples:

- write or edit code
- run tests or builds
- install npm, Python, Go, or system packages
- generate PDFs, DOCX, images, reports, CSVs, or ZIPs
- keep files between sessions
- run scripts or notebooks
- start a dev server
- expose a preview URL
- snapshot or fork state
- prepare a deployable app
- run a crawler, parser, or data pipeline

Research agents need a sandbox when they move beyond "read and summarize" into
work such as crawling, extracting, transforming, storing, charting, or producing
downloadable research artifacts.

Sales copy agents need a sandbox when they generate landing pages, proposals,
brand assets, email sequence files, spreadsheet exports, or versioned campaign
artifacts.

---

## When a computer is required

Use a computer when the agent needs a real browser or desktop.

Examples:

- log in to a dashboard
- test signup or checkout
- click through a SaaS UI
- fill forms
- inspect visual layout
- capture screenshots
- use a browser extension
- access a desktop-only workflow
- verify a preview like a human

Computers are more expensive than pure model runs and usually more expensive
than lightweight sandbox work. Use them when browser or desktop state matters.

---

## When a local device is required

Use a local device when the agent must work with customer-controlled resources
that should not move into the cloud.

Examples:

- local files that cannot be uploaded
- private network or VPN access
- installed desktop applications
- hardware-attached workflows
- local credential stores
- customer-controlled browser profiles

Local devices should be opt-in and visible. Users should know which workspace,
agent, and session can access their machine.

---

## When deployment is required

Deployment is not an agent workspace. It is the durable target after development
work is complete.

| Need | Target |
|---|---|
| Share a live dev preview | Sandbox preview |
| Serve a production app | MIOSA Deploy |
| Host many small apps for one workspace | Docker Host |
| Run an always-on agent workspace | Persistent sandbox or computer, not deployment |

Docker Host is where a verified app container runs. It is not where the agent
should be editing files.

---

## Examples by agent role

### Research agent

| Research task | Device |
|---|---|
| Summarize provided notes | No device |
| Search public web and write a brief answer | No device or sandbox, depending on tool policy |
| Crawl many pages and dedupe results | Sandbox |
| Generate charts and CSV report | Sandbox |
| Log in to a private analytics dashboard | Computer |
| Use a customer VPN-only database | Local device |

### Sales copy agent

| Sales task | Device |
|---|---|
| Draft email copy from CRM fields | No device |
| Generate a campaign brief artifact | Sandbox |
| Build a landing page | Sandbox |
| Preview and visually QA page | Sandbox plus computer |
| Send campaign through CRM/email tool | Connector with approval |
| Log in to ad platform and configure campaign | Computer with approval |

### Engineering agent

| Engineering task | Device |
|---|---|
| Explain a stack trace pasted into chat | No device |
| Edit code and run tests | Sandbox |
| Start a dev server | Sandbox |
| Verify browser UI | Computer |
| Publish production app | Deployment after approval |

### Support agent

| Support task | Device |
|---|---|
| Draft reply from ticket text | No device |
| Search internal docs and produce answer | No device or sandbox |
| Inspect account in web admin dashboard | Computer |
| Generate customer export file | Sandbox |
| Send reply | Connector with approval or policy |

---

## Decision tree

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[New agent task] --> B{Needs files, code, packages, artifacts, or preview?}
  B -- yes --> S[Use sandbox]
  B -- no --> C{Needs real browser, GUI, login, screenshots, or form fill?}
  C -- yes --> D[Use computer]
  C -- no --> L{Needs customer local files, apps, or private network?}
  L -- yes --> LD[Use local device]
  L -- no --> N[No device required]
  S --> P{Needs production URL?}
  P -- yes --> DEP[Publish to deploy target]
  P -- no --> OUT[Return artifact or result]
```

---

## Cost and performance guidance

| Choice | Startup | Cost | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| No device | Fastest | Lowest | Routing, planning, summarization |
| Sandbox | Fast | Medium | Code, files, artifacts, previews |
| Computer | Slower | Higher | Browser/desktop automation |
| Local device | Depends on user machine | Relay/model/tool cost | Private resources |
| Deployment | Build/publish dependent | Hosting cost | Durable production apps |

Start with the cheapest runtime that can safely complete the job. Escalate to a
sandbox, computer, or local device only when the task requires it.

---

## Backend routing policy

Your backend should make device selection explicit:

```typescript
type DeviceDecision = {
  required: boolean;
  deviceType?: "sandbox" | "computer" | "local";
  reason: string;
  needsApproval: boolean;
  estimatedCredits: number;
};
```

Record the decision with the run. If a run fails because the wrong device was
chosen, the recovery path should say which device class to retry with.

---

## See also

- [Agent product model](/docs/guides/agent-product-model): The canonical vocabulary for agents, devices, runs, events, and credits.
- [Agent devices](/docs/guides/agent-devices): Understand sandboxes, computers, local devices, persistence, and deploy boundaries.
- [Agent workflow patterns](/docs/guides/agent-workflow-patterns): Map device decisions to simple and complex workflows.
- [Agent credit metering](/docs/platform/agent-credit-metering): Understand the cost impact of each device choice.

pages.title: Connect agent accounts (keys and subscriptions)
pages.description: Connect a model key, a Claude or ChatGPT plan, or a tool-server key to your workspace, or to one of your end users, from your own code. No console visit needed.
pages.markdown:
An agent run thinks with an account that belongs to its owner.
MIOSA never powers your agents with its own model keys.
So before a run can start, a model provider has to be connected: an API key, or a subscription plan such as Claude or ChatGPT.

You can do that in the console.
You can also do it from your own code, for your own workspace or for each of your end users.
That second case is what a platform needs: your customer connects their own Claude plan inside your product, and every run on their machines uses it.

This guide covers both.

## What you can connect

| Connection | What it is | How you connect it | Name in the SDK |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude plan | A Claude Pro or Max subscription. | Sign-in, the user pastes a code back. | `claude` |
| ChatGPT plan | A ChatGPT Plus, Pro or Team subscription (Codex). | Sign-in, the user enters a code. | `chatgpt` |
| Kimi plan | A Kimi Code subscription. | Sign-in, the user enters a code. | `kimi` |
| Mistral Vibe plan | A Mistral Vibe subscription. | Sign-in in the browser. | `mistral` |
| Anthropic key | An Anthropic API key. | Set it. | `anthropic` |
| OpenAI key | An OpenAI API key. | Set it. | `openai` |
| OpenRouter key | An OpenRouter API key. | Set it. | `openrouter` |
| Other keys | DeepSeek, LLM Gateway, Moonshot, Mistral, Amazon Bedrock. | Set it. | `deepseek`, `llmgateway`, `moonshot`, `mistral`, `bedrock` |
| Tool-server keys | The key a tool server needs: Apify, Refero, any MCP server. | Set it. | `toolKeys` |

A key never leaves the platform.
Every read returns a status, a redacted preview such as `sk-ant...1234`, and for a plan the account email and plan name.
Never the secret.

> **Note**
>
> One connected plan can power several harnesses where the vendor supports it.
> A ChatGPT plan powers Codex and OpenCode, for example.
> Connect it once, and any run on a compatible harness picks it up.
> See [which harness uses which connection](/docs/guides/connect-agent-accounts#which-harness-uses-which-connection).

## Who the connection belongs to

Every call takes the same two optional identifiers.

| You pass | The connection belongs to | A run uses it |
|---|---|---|
| Nothing | Your organization. | In every workspace, unless a narrower one exists. |
| `workspaceId` | One workspace. | For runs in that workspace. |
| `externalUserId` | One of your end users: your own id for them. | For runs on that end user's machines, before the workspace's. |

A run looks for the account in this order, and stops at the first one it finds:

1. The end user's own connection.
2. The workspace's connection.
3. The organization's connection.

The end user is the one on the machine the run uses.
You tag a machine with `externalUserId` when you create it, the same id you use everywhere else in your platform ([Ownership and attribution](/docs/platform/attribution)).

Writes and deletes always touch exactly the scope you name.
Setting a key for one end user never changes the workspace's key, and removing it falls back to the workspace's.
An end user's connection is never visible to another end user, to the workspace, or to another organization.

## Your own workspace

**TypeScript**

```typescript
import { Miosa } from "@miosa/sdk"

const miosa = new Miosa({ apiKey: process.env.MIOSA_API_KEY! })

// An API key
await miosa.connections.setKey({
  provider: "anthropic",
  key: process.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY!,
  workspaceId,
})

// Check that it works
const check = await miosa.connections.test({ provider: "anthropic", workspaceId })
console.log(check.ok, check.httpStatus) // true 200
```

**Python**

```python
import os
from miosa import Miosa

miosa = Miosa(api_key=os.environ["MIOSA_API_KEY"])

# An API key
miosa.connections.set_key(
    "anthropic",
    key=os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"],
    workspace_id=workspace_id,
)

# Check that it works
check = miosa.connections.test("anthropic", workspace_id=workspace_id)
print(check["ok"], check["http_status"])  # True 200
```

**CLI**

```bash
# The key comes from standard input, never from an argument
miosa connections add models anthropic --workspace-id "$WORKSPACE_ID" --key-stdin <<< "$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"

miosa connections test models anthropic --workspace-id "$WORKSPACE_ID"
```

Setting a key again replaces it.
That is how you rotate one.

## Your end users

Pass `externalUserId` and the connection is theirs.

### An API key

**TypeScript**

```typescript
await miosa.connections.setKey({
  provider: "openrouter",
  key: userSuppliedKey,
  externalUserId: "cus_123",
})
```

**Python**

```python
miosa.connections.set_key(
    "openrouter",
    key=user_supplied_key,
    external_user_id="cus_123",
)
```

**CLI**

```bash
miosa connections add models openrouter --external-user cus_123 --key-stdin <<< "$USER_KEY"
```

An end user's key is for agents only.
It is never offered to the AI Gateway.

### A Claude plan or a ChatGPT plan

Connecting a plan is a sign-in the user completes in their own browser.
Your code starts it, shows the user a link, and waits.
The call returns at once with what to show.
Nothing is connected yet.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const signin = await miosa.connections.connectSubscription({
  provider: "claude", // or "chatgpt", "kimi", "mistral"
  externalUserId: "cus_123",
})

// Show these in YOUR UI.
signin.verificationUrl // open this in the user's browser
signin.userCode        // ChatGPT and Kimi: the code they type there
signin.mode            // "paste_code" (Claude) or "device_code"
signin.expiresAt       // about 15 minutes

// Claude: the page shows a code after they approve. Your UI passes it back.
const connected = await signin.submitCode(codeTheyPasted)
console.log(connected.accountEmail, connected.accountPlan) // alice@example.com max

// ChatGPT, Kimi: they enter the code at the link. Wait until it lands.
const connected2 = await signin.wait({ onUpdate: (s) => console.log(s.status) })
```

**Python**

```python
signin = miosa.connections.connect_subscription(
    "claude",  # or "chatgpt", "kimi", "mistral"
    external_user_id="cus_123",
)

# Show these in YOUR UI.
signin.verification_url  # open this in the user's browser
signin.user_code         # ChatGPT and Kimi: the code they type there
signin.mode              # "paste_code" (Claude) or "device_code"
signin.expires_at        # about 15 minutes

# Claude: the page shows a code after they approve. Your UI passes it back.
connected = signin.submit_code(code_they_pasted)
print(connected["account_email"], connected["account_plan"])  # alice@example.com max

# ChatGPT, Kimi: they enter the code at the link. Wait until it lands.
connected = signin.wait(on_update=lambda s: print(s["status"]))
```

**CLI**

```bash
# Prints the link and the code, then returns. Your UI shows them.
miosa connections add models claude --external-user cus_123 --no-wait --json

# Claude: hand over the pasted code.
miosa connections signin code SIGNIN_ID --external-user cus_123 --code-stdin <<< "$PASTED_CODE"

# ChatGPT, Kimi: wait for the user to enter the code.
miosa connections signin wait SIGNIN_ID --external-user cus_123
```

There are two shapes of sign-in:

| Mode | Plans | What the user does | What you do |
|---|---|---|---|
| `paste_code` | Claude | Approves at the link, then copies the code the page shows. | Pass that code to `submitCode`. |
| `device_code` | ChatGPT, Kimi | Opens the link and types `userCode`. | Call `wait()`, or `poll()` on a timer. |

`wait()` resolves when the plan is connected.
It rejects with `SubscriptionSignInError` if the sign-in failed, expired or was cancelled.
`poll()` never rejects for a failed sign-in: read its `status`.
`cancel()` ends the sign-in.

A wrong or expired pasted code is rejected with `SIGNIN_CODE_REJECTED` (422).
The sign-in stays open, so the user can paste again.

The sign-in link and the code carry no credentials.
The plan's tokens are stored encrypted on the platform, refreshed in the background, and never returned by any call.

> **Caution**
>
> Show the link to the person who owns the plan, in your own UI.
> Do not open it for them from your server.
> The sign-in is the user's consent to connect their plan.

### Check, list and remove

**TypeScript**

```typescript
// Is it connected, and where does it come from?
const claude = await miosa.connections.get({ provider: "claude", externalUserId: "cus_123" })
claude.connected    // true
claude.scope        // "external_user", or "workspace" when it is inherited
claude.inherited    // true when it comes from a wider scope
claude.preview      // "sk-ant...1234" for a key. Never the secret.

// Everything this end user has, with the workspace's inherited connections marked
const all = await miosa.connections.list({ externalUserId: "cus_123", workspaceId })

// Does it work?
await miosa.connections.test({ provider: "claude", externalUserId: "cus_123" })

// Disconnect only the end user's own. The workspace's, if any, is untouched.
await miosa.connections.delete({ provider: "claude", externalUserId: "cus_123" })
```

**Python**

```python
claude = miosa.connections.get("claude", external_user_id="cus_123")
claude["connected"]   # True
claude["scope"]       # "external_user", or "workspace" when it is inherited
claude["inherited"]   # True when it comes from a wider scope

everything = miosa.connections.list(external_user_id="cus_123", workspace_id=workspace_id)

miosa.connections.test("claude", external_user_id="cus_123")
miosa.connections.delete("claude", external_user_id="cus_123")
```

**CLI**

```bash
miosa connections list --external-user cus_123 --workspace-id "$WORKSPACE_ID"
miosa connections test models claude --external-user cus_123
miosa connections rm models claude --external-user cus_123 --yes
```

`test` makes one cheap authenticated request to the provider, such as listing models.
For a plan it checks the stored state instead.
It answers `ok: true`, `ok: false` (the provider rejected the key) or `ok: null` (the provider did not answer, which is not the key's fault).
It never returns the key or the provider's response.

## Tool-server keys

A tool server is an MCP server your agents use: Apify, Refero, your own.
You define the server once, with its credential as a placeholder such as `{{secret:APIFY_TOKEN}}`.
Each end user then supplies their own value.
An agent run for that end user reaches the tool server with their key, and falls back to the workspace's.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
// Which keys do my tool servers need, and does this end user have them?
const keys = await miosa.connections.toolKeys.list({ workspaceId, externalUserId: "cus_123" })
// [{ name: "APIFY_TOKEN", connected: false, servers: [{ name: "Apify" }], ... }]

await miosa.connections.toolKeys.set({
  name: "APIFY_TOKEN",
  value: userApifyToken,
  workspaceId,
  externalUserId: "cus_123",
})

await miosa.connections.toolKeys.delete({ name: "APIFY_TOKEN", externalUserId: "cus_123" })
```

**Python**

```python
keys = miosa.connections.tool_keys.list(workspace_id=workspace_id, external_user_id="cus_123")

miosa.connections.tool_keys.set(
    "APIFY_TOKEN",
    user_apify_token,
    workspace_id=workspace_id,
    external_user_id="cus_123",
)
miosa.connections.tool_keys.delete("APIFY_TOKEN", external_user_id="cus_123")
```

**CLI**

```bash
miosa connections tool-keys list --external-user cus_123
miosa connections tool-keys set APIFY_TOKEN --external-user cus_123 --key-stdin <<< "$USER_TOKEN"
miosa connections tool-keys rm APIFY_TOKEN --external-user cus_123 --yes
```

Only a name that a tool server references can be set.
Anything else is `UNKNOWN_TOOL_KEY` (404), so this is not a general-purpose secret store.

## Which harness uses which connection

A harness is the agent that runs on the machine: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and the others.
Each accepts a set of connections.

| Harness (`runner`) | Accepts |
|---|---|
| Claude Code (`claude-code`) | Claude plan, Anthropic key, OpenRouter key, DeepSeek key, Amazon Bedrock |
| Codex (`codex`) | ChatGPT plan, OpenAI key, DeepSeek key, Amazon Bedrock |
| OpenCode (`opencode`) | ChatGPT plan, Anthropic key, OpenAI key, OpenRouter key, LLM Gateway key, Mistral key, Mistral Vibe plan |
| Pi (`pi`) and Prime Agent (`prime`) | Claude plan, ChatGPT plan, Anthropic key, OpenAI key, OpenRouter key, LLM Gateway key, Mistral key, Mistral Vibe plan |
| Hermes Agent (`hermes`) | ChatGPT plan, Claude plan, Anthropic key, OpenAI key, OpenRouter key |
| Kimi Code (`kimi`) | Kimi plan, Moonshot key |
| Mistral Vibe (`mistral`) | Mistral Vibe plan, Mistral key |
| OSA (`osa`) | An Anthropic, OpenAI or OpenRouter key, or the model key you set in Agent Studio |

Two limits come from the vendors, not from MIOSA:

- OpenCode does not take a Claude plan. Anthropic prohibits it, and OpenCode removed the support.
- Hermes takes a Claude plan only on a Claude Max plan with extra usage purchased. A Pro plan is refused by Anthropic.

You connect once, and any run on a compatible harness picks the connection up.
You do not pick a connection per run.

To see what a given user can run right now:

**TypeScript**

```typescript
for (const harness of await miosa.harnesses.list({ externalUserId: "cus_123" })) {
  const usable = harness.connections.filter((c) => c.usable).map((c) => c.credential)
  console.log(harness.id, harness.ready ? "ready" : "no credential", usable)
}
// claude-code ready ["claude_subscription"]
// opencode    ready ["chatgpt_subscription"]
// pi          no credential []
```

**Python**

```python
for harness in miosa.harnesses.list(external_user_id="cus_123"):
    usable = [c["credential"] for c in harness["connections"] if c["usable"]]
    print(harness["id"], "ready" if harness["ready"] else "no credential", usable)
```

**CLI**

```bash
miosa connections harnesses --external-user cus_123
```

The harness settings (which method is active, the default model) belong to you, the builder.
They are set per workspace and are the same for all of your end users.
The connections are theirs.
A key minted for an end user cannot change the harness settings.

## Choose which connection a harness uses

A harness that takes one method at a time (Claude Code, Codex) uses one connection.
A harness that takes several (OpenCode, pi, Prime Agent, Kimi Code, Mistral Vibe, Hermes Agent) uses the ones you enable.
These are the builder's settings, set per organization or per workspace.

**TypeScript**

```typescript
await miosa.agentSettings.updateHarness("claude-code", { authMethod: "claude_subscription", workspaceId })
await miosa.agentSettings.updateHarness("opencode", { enabledProviders: ["chatgpt_subscription", "openrouter"] })
```

**Python**

```python
miosa.agent_settings.update_harness("claude-code", auth_method="claude_subscription", workspace_id=workspace_id)
miosa.agent_settings.update_harness("opencode", enabled_providers=["chatgpt_subscription", "openrouter"])
```

**CLI**

```bash
miosa connections use claude-code claude                    # the Claude plan
miosa connections use opencode chatgpt openrouter           # several
miosa connections use opencode --all                        # every connected one
miosa connections use codex --model gpt-6.1-sol --effort high
```

Then run on any harness, with the model you want:

```bash
miosa prompt --harness opencode --model gpt-6.1-sol --sandbox my-box "add a health check"
```

`miosa prompt --harness` takes every harness the platform lists, including ones added after your CLI was released.
`miosa connections harnesses opencode` lists that harness's models and which are available with what is connected.

## Build it into your product

A "Connect your Claude plan" button in your settings page is two requests to your backend.
The sign-in id travels through the browser, and your backend names the end user from its own session.

```typescript
// 1. Start. Send the browser only what it needs.
app.post("/api/connect/claude", async (req, res) => {
  const signin = await miosa.connections.connectSubscription({
    provider: "claude",
    externalUserId: req.user.id, // from YOUR session, never from the request body
  })
  res.json({ signinId: signin.id, url: signin.verificationUrl })
})

// 2. The user approves in a new tab and pastes the code into your page.
app.post("/api/connect/claude/code", async (req, res) => {
  const signin = miosa.connections.resumeSubscription({
    id: req.body.signinId,
    provider: "claude",
    externalUserId: req.user.id,
  })
  const status = await signin.submitCode(req.body.code)
  res.json({ connected: status.connected, email: status.accountEmail, plan: status.accountPlan })
})
```

`resumeSubscription` picks a sign-in up by its id.
Because it carries the end user, a sign-in id belonging to someone else is `NOT_FOUND`, even with your organization-wide key.

The worked example, with a runnable server, is in the SDK repository under `examples/connect-agent-accounts`.
It connects a Claude plan, a ChatGPT plan, a key and a tool-server key for two customers, and shows that one customer's connection never reaches the other's runs.

## Security

- **Server only.** Call these methods from your backend with your `msk_*` key.
  Never put that key in a browser.
- **Mint an end-user key** for anything that runs near your customer's code. A key minted with an `externalUserId` always acts as that end user.
  It cannot read or change the workspace's or the organization's connections (`403 SCOPE_FORBIDDEN`), cannot change harness settings, and cannot see another end user's sign-ins.
- **No secret is returned**, by any call. Keys and plan tokens are encrypted at rest, bound to the end user they belong to, and decrypted only to start a run.
- **Audit.** Every connect, replace, remove and use is written to the [audit log](/docs/security/audit-log) with the end user's id and never the value.
- **Isolation.** A connection is checked against your organization on every read.
  An end user's id means nothing to another organization.
- **Scopes.** Reading needs `integrations:read` (plus `connections:read` for the connections list).
  Changing needs `integrations:write` (and `connections:write` for sign-ins).
- **Plans are the user's.** A plan connected for an end user is used only for runs on that end user's machines.
  It is never used to serve your other customers.
- **Rate limits** apply as everywhere ([Rate limits](/docs/rate-limits)).

## Errors

| Code | Status | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `SCOPE_FORBIDDEN` | 403 | The key acts for one end user and asked for something wider. |
| `MISSING_EXTERNAL_USER_ID` | 422 | `scope: "external_user"` without an `externalUserId`. |
| `CONFLICTING_SCOPE` | 422 | `scope` does not agree with the identifiers. |
| `INVALID_EXTERNAL_USER_ID` | 422 | The id is longer than 255 characters or has control characters. |
| `USE_SIGNIN` | 422 | A plan cannot be set; connect it with `connectSubscription`. |
| `VALIDATION_FAILED` | 422 | A field is missing or wrong, for example an empty key. |
| `SIGNIN_CODE_REJECTED` | 422 | The pasted code was wrong or expired. Paste again. |
| `SIGNIN_PROVIDER_ERROR` | 502 | The provider's sign-in service did not answer. Start again. |
| `NOT_FOUND` | 404 | Nothing is connected at exactly that scope. |
| `UNKNOWN_CREDENTIAL` | 404 | Not a credential MIOSA knows. |
| `UNKNOWN_TOOL_KEY` | 404 | No tool server references that secret name. |
| `OWN_CREDENTIALS_REQUIRED` | 422 | A run was started with nothing connected for its harness. |

## The API underneath

The SDK and CLI are thin wrappers.
Every route accepts `workspace_id`, `external_user_id` and an optional `scope`.

| Route | Does |
|---|---|
| `GET /agents/credentials` | Every credential and its state at the scope. |
| `PUT /agents/credentials/{credential}` | Set or replace a key. |
| `DELETE /agents/credentials/{credential}` | Remove it at exactly the scope. |
| `POST /agents/credentials/{credential}/test` | Does it work? |
| `POST /agent-signins` | Start a plan sign-in. Returns the link and the code. |
| `GET /agent-signins/{id}` | Poll it. |
| `POST /agent-signins/{id}/code` | Hand over a pasted code. |
| `DELETE /agent-signins/{id}` | Cancel it. |
| `GET /agents/tool-keys` | The keys your tool servers need. |
| `PUT /agents/tool-keys/{name}` | Set one. |
| `DELETE /agents/tool-keys/{name}` | Remove one. |
| `GET /connections` | Models, apps and tool servers in one list. |
| `GET /agents/settings` | Harness readiness at the scope. |

## Next

- [Agent-driven build](/docs/quickstart/agent-driven-build): Run an agent against a sandbox once an account is connected.
- [Ownership and attribution](/docs/platform/attribution): Tag every machine with your own customer ids.
- [Agents in your product](/docs/platform/agents-in-your-product): One machine per user, with an agent working in it.
- [Agent operating guide](/docs/guides/agent-operating-guide): Dispatch work and collect results.

pages.title: Agent devices
pages.description: MIOSA's device model for agent work: sandbox workers, computers, local devices, primary devices, persistence, and Docker Host boundaries.
pages.markdown:
Devices are the machines agents use to do real work. MIOSA has three active
device classes and one hosting target:

| Type | Product meaning |
|---|---|
| Sandbox Worker | Isolated code/file/build/preview/artifact workspace |
| Computer | Persistent cloud desktop/browser with screenshot and input APIs |
| Local Device / BYOC / OpenComputer | Paired user-owned host for local files, apps, private network access, or customer-owned capacity |
| Docker Host | Durable app-container host after development is finished |

Docker Host is not where an agent edits code. It is where a verified
sandbox-built app runs as a durable container.

---

## Choosing a device

Which runtime a task needs is a decision of its own. [Agent device selection](/docs/guides/agent-device-selection) covers the decision rule, per-role examples, the decision tree, and cost guidance. This page describes the device model  -  what each device class is and how they relate.

A single run can use more than one runtime. For example, a sandbox can build an
app, a computer can test the preview, and an OpenComputer can call a private
internal service before the final artifact is exported.

---

## How devices relate

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Agent] --> P[Device policy]
  P --> S[Sandbox Worker]
  P --> C[Computer]
  P --> L[Local Device]
  S --> Art[Artifacts and previews]
  C --> Shot[Screenshots and browser state]
  L --> Local[Private files and network]
  Art --> D[Deployment or Docker Host]
```

The agent can switch devices during a run. For example, a sandbox writes a web
app, a computer opens the preview and checks it visually, then the sandbox
publishes the verified result.

---

## Sandbox Worker

A sandbox is the normal runtime for coding agents.

### Sandbox capabilities

- persistent `/workspace`
- file read/write/list/delete
- Bash, Python, Node, package managers
- long-running dev servers
- public preview URLs
- snapshots and forks
- generated artifacts
- deploy and Docker Host publish prep
- scoped environment variables and connectors

Use a sandbox to build products like app builders, artifact factories, research
workspaces, evaluation runners, and code agents.

---

## Computer

A computer is a full desktop/browser runtime.

### Computer capabilities

- screenshot
- click, type, scroll, drag
- clipboard
- window control
- browser sessions
- visual QA
- terminal and shell
- persistent storage
- embeddable desktop stream

Use a computer when the job requires a visible browser, GUI automation, manual
handoff, or desktop-only software.

---

## Local Device / BYOC / OpenComputer

A local device is a paired machine owned by the user or tenant. In MIOSA docs
you will also see this path called BYOC or OpenComputers.

Use it when an agent needs:

- local files that cannot be uploaded
- private network access
- installed desktop apps
- local credentials that should not leave the machine
- customer-controlled hardware
- local GPUs or other host-specific capacity

Local devices are powerful but should be opt-in. The user should see exactly
which workspace and agent can reach the device. The device connects outbound to
MIOSA  -  no inbound ports are required.

---

## Primary device

Each workspace should have a primary device policy. Agents use it by default
when a task does not specify a runtime.

Recommended primary-device policies:

| Workspace type | Primary policy |
|---|---|
| App builder | Sandbox Worker |
| Browser automation workspace | Computer |
| Enterprise RPA | Computer, with BYOC/OpenComputer fallback |
| Customer-owned coding workspace | Persistent sandbox |
| Artifact factory | Sandbox Worker |

The primary device can change over time, but historical runs should still
record which device actually executed each action.

---

## Persistence

Agent work should survive normal stops.

| Runtime | Expected behavior |
|---|---|
| Persistent sandbox | Timeout stops compute and preserves state for resume |
| Non-persistent sandbox | Timeout destroys state |
| Computer | Stop/start preserves filesystem and desktop state |
| BYOC/OpenComputer | State stays on the customer-owned host unless the task exports it |
| Docker Host | App keeps running as a deployment until stopped or replaced |

For agent-building workflows, persistent sandbox should be the default. Use
non-persistent only for one-off untrusted jobs where the filesystem should be
discarded.

---

## Activity and timeout

Active agent work should reset the idle clock:

- exec calls
- file writes
- terminal input
- preview traffic
- browser/computer actions
- artifact generation
- deployment publish
- explicit extend calls

The UI and CLI should warn before a device is paused or destroyed. Long-running
workflows should create snapshots at stable checkpoints.

---

## Device permissions

Device access should be explicit:

| Permission | Example |
|---|---|
| `devices:use` | Run commands or browser actions on an assigned device |
| `devices:create` | Create child sandboxes or computers |
| `devices:destroy` | Permanently delete a device and saved state |
| `devices:connect-local` | Pair or use a local device |
| `devices:set-primary` | Change workspace default device policy |
| `deployments:publish` | Promote workspace output to durable hosting |

High-risk permissions should be gated by owner/admin roles or human approval.

---

## Building virtual-device products

With these primitives, you can build products that look like an always-on agent
workspace:

```text
Workspace
  -> primary sandbox for code and files
  -> optional computer for browser/desktop
  -> connected accounts and managed connectors
  -> jobs and schedules
  -> artifacts and previews
  -> deployment targets
```

This supports products like:

- 24/7 research agents
- browser automation workers
- AI app builders
- cofounder-style task operators
- artifact generation studios
- agent teams with shared files
- customer-owned coding workspaces

For Lovable/Replit/Genspark-style app builders, make the sandbox the primary
device and attach a computer only for browser QA or login-heavy checks. For a
Nebula-style virtual device, make the primary device visible in the UI so users
understand whether the current work is happening in a sandbox, a computer, or a
customer-owned OpenComputer.

---

## Related

- [Sandboxes](/docs/develop/sandboxes): Code, files, commands, previews, snapshots, and publish prep.
- [Computers](/docs/computers/overview): Desktop and browser automation for visual tasks.
- [What agents can do](/docs/guides/agent-capabilities): Built-in tools, app actions, permissions, and product surfaces.
- [Docker Host](/docs/docker-host/docker-deploy): Durable app containers on the workspace Docker Host host.

pages.title: Agent orchestration
pages.description: How to coordinate multiple agents across MIOSA sandboxes, computers, artifacts, previews, events, and deployments.
pages.markdown:
MIOSA lets you build agent systems where different agents use the right runtime
for each part of the job.

- A **sandbox agent** writes code, edits files, runs commands, builds packages,
  generates artifacts, and exposes preview ports.
- A **computer agent** uses a real browser or desktop for visual checks, clicks,
  form fills, screenshots, uploads, and human handoff.
- A **deployment agent** promotes a verified sandbox workspace into a production
  deployment or Docker Host app.
- Your **orchestrator** owns the task graph, model calls, permissions, retries,
  and user-facing progress stream.

The agents communicate through MIOSA-managed state: files, artifacts, events,
preview URLs, screenshots, snapshots, and deployment records.

If you are building an agent-company product, treat this as the platform layer:
agents are configured workers, devices are the execution substrate, connectors
grant tools, and events/artifacts make the work visible to users. See
[What MIOSA agents can do](/docs/guides/agent-capabilities),
[Configure an agent](/docs/guides/configure-agent), and
[Agent devices](/docs/guides/agent-devices) for the product model before
scaling the orchestration layer.

For the end-to-end product blueprint, including Polsia-style company operators,
Cofounder (cofounder.co)-style department agents, Nebula-style virtual devices,
Heuresis-style encoded workspaces, and prompt dispatch into devices, see
[Build an agent-company platform](/docs/guides/build-agent-company).

---

## Scale model: from one agent to thousands

The same primitives work for one agent, one hundred agents, or thousands of
agents, but the orchestration shape changes.

| Scale | Recommended shape |
|---|---|
| 1-10 agents | Direct agent loop creates/resumes sandboxes as needed |
| 10-100 agents | Queue-backed orchestrator with sandbox pools and per-workspace limits |
| 100-1,000 agents | Sharded job queues, regional sandbox pools, scoped tokens, explicit concurrency controls |
| 1,000+ agents | Dedicated tenant capacity, rate-limit contracts, batch APIs, event aggregation, and backpressure |

Do not start 10,000 independent sandboxes just because there are 10,000 logical
agents. Most products should distinguish:

- **Logical agent**: a model/tool loop or task worker in your application.
- **Runtime session**: a sandbox or computer doing actual work.
- **Workspace**: the persistent filesystem, secrets, snapshots, usage, and
  attribution boundary.

Many logical agents can share a queue and borrow runtime sessions from a pool.
Only the agents doing active code/browser work need a running sandbox or
computer at that moment.

---

---

## Mental model

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  U[User request] --> O[Your orchestrator]
  O --> SA[Sandbox agent]
  O --> CA[Computer agent]
  O --> DA[Deployment agent]

  SA --> S[MIOSA Sandbox]
  CA --> C[MIOSA Computer]
  DA --> D[MIOSA Deployment]

  S --> A[Artifacts and preview URLs]
  C --> A
  D --> A
  A --> O
  O --> UI[Your product UI]
```

The orchestrator should not make every agent share one messy machine. Instead,
each runtime does the work it is good at and emits durable outputs that the next
agent can consume.

---

---

## Runtime selection

| Job | Runtime | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Write app code | Sandbox | Fast headless Linux workspace with files and exec |
| Install dependencies | Sandbox | Dependency state stays in `/workspace` and snapshots |
| Run tests/builds | Sandbox | Deterministic command execution and streamed output |
| Serve a preview | Sandbox | Expose app ports as preview URLs |
| Inspect a browser UI | Computer | Real browser, screenshots, mouse, keyboard |
| Test signup/login flows | Computer | Cookies, popups, OAuth, uploads, and visual state |
| Generate PDFs/DOCX/images | Sandbox | Python/Node generators produce artifacts |
| Use private local systems | BYOC/OpenComputer | Data, network, apps, or local GPU capacity stays on the customer host |
| Publish production app | Deployment or Docker Host | Stable URL, versions, rollback, routing |

> **Note: Sandbox and Computer are different products**
>
> Do not collapse sandboxes and computers into one concept. Sandboxes are for
> headless code and artifacts. Computers are for GUI/browser work. Orchestration is
> the layer that lets them cooperate.

---

---

## Communication primitives

Use explicit handoffs instead of hidden shared memory.

| Primitive | Producer | Consumer | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| File | Sandbox agent | Sandbox agent, deployment agent | `/workspace/app/page.tsx` |
| Artifact | Sandbox agent | User, another agent | `proposal.pdf`, `chart.png` |
| Preview URL | Sandbox agent | Computer agent, user | `https://3000-...sandbox.miosa.ai` |
| Screenshot | Computer agent | Orchestrator, LLM | Browser QA finding |
| Event | Any runtime | UI, orchestrator | stdout, stderr, file changed, preview ready |
| Snapshot | Sandbox | Sandbox agent | checkpoint before risky refactor |
| Deployment | Deployment agent | User, support | durable production URL |

The orchestrator should store these as run state so the frontend can replay what
happened and the next agent has a clean input.

---

---

## Queue and pool architecture

For high-scale orchestration, put a queue in front of MIOSA runtimes.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  U[User/API request] --> Q[Task queue]
  Q --> O[Orchestrator workers]
  O --> P[Sandbox/computer pool]
  P --> S1[Sandbox session]
  P --> S2[Sandbox session]
  P --> C1[Computer session]
  S1 --> E[Event stream]
  S2 --> E
  C1 --> E
  E --> UI[Product UI and run store]
```

The queue owns backpressure. The runtime pool owns capacity. The orchestrator
owns task assignment. MIOSA owns isolated execution.

Use this pattern when:

- thousands of user tasks may arrive at once
- agents do bursty work
- you need to cap spend
- you need per-customer fairness
- you need reliable retries and dead-letter queues
- users need live progress without polling every runtime directly

---

---

## When to use ADK vs your own orchestrator

Use the [ADK](/docs/adk) when you want MIOSA's built-in tool catalog and a
simple agent loop.

Build your own orchestrator when you need:

- multiple agents with different responsibilities
- product-specific UI events
- custom approval steps
- background jobs and retries
- per-user quotas and billing
- white-label attribution
- durable run history in your product layer

The orchestrator is your product layer. MIOSA is the runtime layer.

---

---

## See also

- [Orchestration patterns](/docs/guides/agent-orchestration/patterns): Prompt dispatch, durable run groups, subagents, sandbox-hosted orchestrators, and permissions.
- [Orchestration examples](/docs/guides/agent-orchestration/examples): Worked flows: app builder with browser QA, sandbox-first code agent, minimal orchestrator shape.

pages.title: Runtime profiles and artifacts
pages.description: The end-to-end lane from runtime profile to artifact export, the prompt-to-device flow, how env and secrets are inherited, and how agent outputs become downloads.
pages.markdown:
This page covers the runtime mechanics of an agent product: how a run starts from a runtime profile, how a prompt reaches a device, how environment and secrets are inherited, and how generated files become user-facing downloads.

## E2E runtime profile to artifact export

This is the concrete end-to-end lane to implement first for a Polsia, Cofounder, Nebula, Heuresis, BusinessOS, Lovable, Replit, Genspark, Emergent, or Blackbox AI-style product:

```text
create runtime profile
  -> create or resume sandbox/computer
  -> dispatch Agent Run with profile id
  -> agent writes files in /workspace
  -> export approved artifact paths
  -> store download URL on your product run record
```

**CLI**

```bash
PROFILE_ID=$(miosa api POST /agent-runtime-profiles -d '{
  "workspace_id": "ws_123",
  "name": "Default app builder",
  "runtime": "claude-code",
  "tools": ["files", "exec", "previews", "artifacts"],
  "connectors": ["anthropic/workspace-claude"],
  "env": {"ANTHROPIC_MODEL": "claude-sonnet-4.6"},
  "is_default": true
}' | jq -r '.data.id')

SANDBOX_ID=$(miosa create builder-box \
  --template nextjs \
  --wait \
  --json | jq -r '.id // .data.id')

miosa prompt \
  --sandbox "$SANDBOX_ID" \
  --harness claude-code \
  "Build a lead-capture page, run tests, and write the final bundle to /workspace/dist."

miosa files cp -r "$SANDBOX_ID":/workspace/dist ./lead-capture --json
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const profile = await miosa.agentRuntimeProfiles.create({
  workspaceId: "ws_123",
  name: "Default app builder",
  runtime: "claude-code",
  tools: ["files", "exec", "previews", "artifacts"],
  connectors: ["anthropic/workspace-claude"],
  env: { ANTHROPIC_MODEL: "claude-sonnet-4.6" },
  isDefault: true,
})

const sandbox = await miosa.sandboxes.create({
  templateId: "nextjs",
  agentRuntimeProfileId: profile.id,
})

const run = await miosa.agentRuns.run({
  sandboxId: sandbox.id,
  agentRuntimeProfileId: profile.id,
  provider: "claude-code",
  cwd: "/workspace",
  prompt:
    "Build a lead-capture page, run tests, and write the final bundle to /workspace/dist.",
  metadata: { productRunId: "run_123" },
})

const exportInfo = await sandbox.createExport({
  paths: ["/workspace/dist"],
  label: "lead-capture-build",
})

await saveProductRunArtifact(run.id, exportInfo.archiveDownloadUrl)
```

**Python**

```python
profile = client.agent_runtime_profiles.create(
    workspace_id="ws_123",
    name="Default app builder",
    runtime="claude-code",
    tools=["files", "exec", "previews", "artifacts"],
    connectors=["anthropic/workspace-claude"],
    env={"ANTHROPIC_MODEL": "claude-sonnet-4.6"},
    is_default=True,
)

sandbox = client.sandboxes.create(
    template_id="nextjs",
    agent_runtime_profile_id=profile["id"],
)

run = client.agent_runs.run(
    sandbox_id=sandbox.id,
    agent_runtime_profile_id=profile["id"],
    provider="claude-code",
    cwd="/workspace",
    prompt=(
        "Build a lead-capture page, run tests, and write the final bundle "
        "to /workspace/dist."
    ),
    metadata={"product_run_id": "run_123"},
)

export_info = sandbox.create_export(
    ["/workspace/dist"],
    label="lead-capture-build",
)

save_product_run_artifact(run["id"], export_info["archive_download_url"])
```

**cURL**

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/agent-runtime-profiles \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "workspace_id": "ws_123",
    "name": "Default app builder",
    "runtime": "claude-code",
    "tools": ["files", "exec", "previews", "artifacts"],
    "connectors": ["anthropic/workspace-claude"],
    "is_default": true
  }'

curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/sandboxes \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"template_id":"nextjs","agent_runtime_profile_id":"arp_123"}'

curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/agent-runs \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "sandbox_id": "sbx_123",
    "agent_runtime_profile_id": "arp_123",
    "provider": "claude-code",
    "cwd": "/workspace",
    "prompt": "Build a lead-capture page, run tests, and write the final bundle to /workspace/dist."
  }'

curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/sandboxes/sbx_123/exports \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"paths":["/workspace/dist"],"label":"lead-capture-build"}'

curl "https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/sandboxes/sbx_123/exports/download?paths[]=/workspace/dist" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY" \
  --output lead-capture.tar.gz
```

Use a sandbox for generated files, reports, code, previews, and app bundles. Add
a computer step only when the run needs browser interaction, screenshots, or
visual QA. Use [Files, exec, and artifacts](/docs/develop/files-and-exec) to
promote approved paths into downloads, and [Agent Runtime Profiles](/docs/api-reference/agent-runtime-profiles)
for the reusable profile contract.

---

## Prompt-to-device flow

Use one product-level run model whether the user is building an app, generating
a report, or asking an operator to complete a business task.

```text
prompt
  -> resolve workspace and agent
  -> select runtime profile
  -> select sandbox, computer, or BYOC/OpenComputer target
  -> inject scoped env and secrets
  -> stream events while the device works
  -> save files, screenshots, artifacts, preview URLs, and deploy outputs
```

For Lovable, Replit, Genspark, Emergent, or Blackbox AI-style app builders, the default target should be a
persistent sandbox. The agent writes files into `/workspace`, runs install and
build commands there, starts a preview server, fixes errors in place, exports
deliverables, and publishes only after the user or browser QA approves the
result.

For Polsia or cofounder.co-style company operators, the same flow starts from a
business task instead of an app prompt. The orchestrator may use a sandbox for
documents and code, a computer for browser work, and BYOC/OpenComputer when the
task must run on customer-owned infrastructure.

## Runtime profiles and env inheritance

Runtime profiles keep the agent harness separate from the device. A profile
answers: which runtime starts, which tools are allowed, which non-secret env
defaults are present, and which connectors or secret groups can be requested.

Recommended resolution order:

| Source | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Tenant default profile | Platform-wide fallback for new workspaces |
| Workspace default profile | Customer/company-specific runtime choice |
| Agent profile | Role-specific tools, model, instructions, and connectors |
| Run override | One task's prompt, cwd, timeout, and non-secret env overrides |

Environment and secrets should be inherited narrowly:

| Value type | Inheritance rule |
|---|---|
| Non-secret env | Tenant defaults -> workspace defaults -> profile env -> run env |
| MIOSA runtime token | Minted per run or session with workspace/user/run attribution |
| Provider secrets | Resolved through managed secrets or connectors, never copied into chat |
| Browser-visible config | Only short-lived preview/share tokens and public config |
| BYOC/OpenComputer host secrets | Stay on the customer-owned host unless explicitly brokered |

If a value can spend money, access customer data, publish externally, or call a
provider API, treat it as a secret or connector grant instead of plain profile
env.

## Artifacts and downloads

Every agent run should end with named outputs, not just terminal text. Use
exports for files users should download and store the returned descriptor on
your product's run, task, or project record.

| Output | Device that produces it | User-facing surface |
|---|---|---|
| Generated app | Sandbox | Preview URL, deployment URL, source ZIP |
| PDF/DOCX/report | Sandbox | Artifact card with download button |
| Screenshot set | Computer | QA evidence and downloadable images |
| Research bundle | Sandbox | Markdown/CSV/ZIP artifact |
| Customer-local result | BYOC/OpenComputer | Host-side file plus brokered export if approved |

See [Files, exec, and artifacts](/docs/develop/files-and-exec) for the export
API shape.

> **Note: Related**
>
> [Build an agent-company platform](/docs/guides/build-agent-company) covers the orchestrator, runtime, and device modules this lane plugs into, and [Agent orchestration](/docs/guides/agent-orchestration) covers running many of these at once.

pages.title: Orchestration patterns
pages.description: Coordination patterns for MIOSA agent systems: prompt dispatch, durable run groups, subagents, sandbox-hosted orchestrators, self-configuring agents, artifact export, credentials, and permissions.
pages.markdown:
These are the coordination patterns that make an agent system work as it grows: how a prompt reaches the right device, how a task fans out into durable run groups, in-sandbox and sandbox-hosted topology, how generated work leaves the runtime, and how credentials and permissions stay scoped.

---

## Prompt dispatch

At runtime, orchestration mostly means dispatching prompts into the right
device and streaming the result back.

| Prompt target | Use it for | Example command |
|---|---|---|
| Sandbox | code, files, tests, builds, artifacts, preview servers | `miosa prompt --sandbox <id> "build the page"` |
| Computer | browser, screenshots, clicks, form fill, visual QA | `miosa prompt --computer <id> "test signup"` |
| BYOC/OpenComputer | private local files, apps, network, customer-controlled hardware | See [OpenComputers](/docs/opencomputers) for host-scoped work |

Create reusable runtime profiles for the agents your product supports. A
profile can be tenant-wide or workspace-specific, and it can apply to sandbox
workers, computer agents, or both.

Prompt-to-device flow should be explicit in your product backend:

```text
user prompt
  -> product run record
  -> runtime profile resolution
  -> sandbox, computer, or BYOC/OpenComputer target
  -> scoped env and secret injection
  -> event stream
  -> files, artifacts, screenshots, previews, deployments
```

This lets Polsia-style operators, cofounder.co-style company operating systems,
Nebula-style virtual devices, and Lovable/Replit/Genspark-style app builders
share one UI contract even when they use different runtimes underneath.

### Durable run groups

Use an Agent Run Group when one product task fans out into multiple child runs.
The group gives your UI one durable record for counts, status, cancellation,
child run lookup, and a group event stream.

```text
user task
  -> agent run group
    -> child run: sandbox coder
    -> child run: sandbox tester
    -> child run: computer browser QA
    -> child run: deployment verifier
  -> artifacts, events, previews, screenshots, deployment URL
```

Current dispatch batches are capped at 100 child runs per API call. For hundreds
or thousands of logical agents, queue the work in your backend and dispatch in
batches against one or more groups. Keep a separate concurrency policy per
tenant/workspace so one customer cannot consume the whole runtime pool.

The user-facing loop should be:

```text
create group
  -> dispatch child runs
  -> stream /agent-run-groups/{id}/events
  -> show child run status and output as it happens
  -> list artifacts from completed child runs
  -> expose download/preview/deploy actions in your UI
```

This avoids opening one browser stream per child agent. Your product backend can
subscribe to one group stream, normalize events into your own task timeline, and
keep the UI live while sandbox and computer agents work in parallel.

When a child run uses a sandbox process-backed runtime, cancellation stops the
recorded sandbox process instead of only changing run status. Use this for
longer build, test, scrape, or artifact-generation tasks where the user may
cancel from your UI.

**CLI**

```bash
miosa api POST /agent-runtime-profiles -d '{
  "name": "lumen-claude",
  "runtime": "claude-code",
  "workspace_id": "lumen",
  "tools": ["filesystem", "shell", "browser"],
  "connectors": ["anthropic/workspace"],
  "env": {"ANTHROPIC_MODEL": "claude-sonnet-4.6"},
  "is_default": true
}'

miosa agent run builder \
  --sandbox sbx_123 \
  --no-follow

miosa api POST /run-groups -d '{
  "name": "lumen-build-and-qa",
  "workspace_id": "ws_123",
  "concurrency_limit": 10,
  "expected_runs": 3
}'

miosa api POST /run-groups/grp_123/dispatch -d '{
  "runs": [
    {"sandbox_id": "sbx_code", "provider": "claude-code", "prompt": "Build the app", "orchestration_role": "coder"},
    {"sandbox_id": "sbx_test", "provider": "codex", "prompt": "Run tests", "orchestration_role": "tester"},
    {"computer_id": "cmp_browser", "provider": "osa", "prompt": "Verify signup in the browser", "orchestration_role": "browser-qa"}
  ],
  "async": true
}'

miosa api GET "/run-groups/grp_123/activity?stream=true&limit=100"
```

**TypeScript**

```typescript
const profile = await miosa.agentRuntimeProfiles.create({
  name: "lumen-claude",
  runtime: "claude-code",
  workspaceId: "ws_123",
  isDefault: true,
  appliesTo: { resources: ["sandbox", "computer"] },
  tools: ["filesystem", "shell", "browser"],
  connectors: ["anthropic/workspace"],
  env: { ANTHROPIC_MODEL: "claude-sonnet-4.6" },
})

const run = await miosa.agentRuns.run({
  sandboxId: "sbx_123",
  prompt: "Build the intake form and export the generated HTML.",
  agentRuntimeProfileId: profile.id,
  cwd: "/workspace",
})

const group = await miosa.agentRunGroups.create({
  name: "lumen-build-and-qa",
  workspaceId: "ws_123",
  concurrencyLimit: 10,
  expectedRuns: 3,
})

await miosa.agentRunGroups.dispatch(
  group.id,
  [
    {
      sandboxId: "sbx_code",
      provider: "claude-code",
      prompt: "Build the app",
      orchestrationRole: "coder",
    },
    {
      computerId: "cmp_browser",
      provider: "osa",
      prompt: "Verify signup in the browser",
      orchestrationRole: "browser-qa",
    },
  ],
  { async: true },
)

for await (const event of miosa.agentRunGroups.streamEvents(group.id)) {
  timeline.append({
    childRunId: event.agent_run_id,
    type: event.type,
    message: event.message,
  })
}
```

**Python**

```python
profile = client.agent_runtime_profiles.create(
    name="lumen-claude",
    runtime="claude-code",
    workspace_id="ws_123",
    is_default=True,
    applies_to={"resources": ["sandbox", "computer"]},
    tools=["filesystem", "shell", "browser"],
    connectors=["anthropic/workspace"],
    env={"ANTHROPIC_MODEL": "claude-sonnet-4.6"},
)

run = client.agent_runs.run(
    sandbox_id="sbx_123",
    agent_runtime_profile_id=profile["id"],
    cwd="/workspace",
    prompt="Build the intake form and export the generated HTML.",
)

group = client.agent_run_groups.create(
    name="lumen-build-and-qa",
    workspace_id="ws_123",
    concurrency_limit=10,
    expected_runs=3,
)

client.agent_run_groups.dispatch(
    group["id"],
    [
        {
            "sandbox_id": "sbx_code",
            "provider": "claude-code",
            "prompt": "Build the app",
            "orchestration_role": "coder",
        },
        {
            "computer_id": "cmp_browser",
            "provider": "osa",
            "prompt": "Verify signup in the browser",
            "orchestration_role": "browser-qa",
        },
    ],
    async_=True,
)

for event in client.agent_run_groups.stream_events(group["id"]):
    timeline.append(
        {
            "child_run_id": event["agent_run_id"],
            "type": event["type"],
            "message": event.get("message"),
        }
    )
```

If no explicit profile is passed, MIOSA resolves the workspace default profile
first, then the tenant default profile. Request-level `env` values override
non-secret profile defaults. Secret provider keys should come from managed
secrets or connectors, not from profile `env`.

Recommended inheritance order:

| Layer | Inherits into the run | Should not contain |
|---|---|---|
| Tenant default profile | Organization-wide runtime, tool, and non-secret env defaults | Customer-specific provider keys |
| Workspace default profile | Company/customer runtime choice, cwd defaults, allowed tools | Tenant admin keys |
| Agent profile | Role instructions, connectors, approval policy, model hints | Browser-visible secrets |
| Run request | Prompt, cwd, timeout, non-secret env overrides | Long-lived provider credentials |

Use managed secrets or connectors for anything that can spend money, access
customer data, publish externally, or call a provider API. The run should
receive a scoped MIOSA runtime token with tenant/workspace/user/run attribution,
plus brokered provider access only for the endpoints the profile allows.

Every dispatch should record:

- prompt
- runtime or harness
- device id
- scoped credentials and connectors
- approval policy
- streamed events
- files, artifacts, screenshots, previews, or deployment outputs

The user experience should be the same whether the prompt is handled by OSA,
Codex, Claude Code, Hermes, OpenCode, OpenClaw, or a custom runtime.

---

## Subagents inside sandboxes

You can also run subagents inside a sandbox. This is useful when the product
wants a primary orchestrator to delegate work into an isolated workspace.

```text
Account / tenant
  -> workspace
    -> orchestrator service
      -> sandbox
        -> subagent A: code editor
        -> subagent B: test runner
        -> subagent C: artifact generator
        -> subagent D: deploy verifier
```

The sandbox receives the environment and scoped credentials it needs. The
subagents run inside `/workspace`, communicate through files, local processes,
stdout, and MIOSA events, and report results back to the orchestrator.

Good uses for sandbox-hosted subagents:

- parallel code review agents inside one repo
- test generation plus test execution
- report generation workers
- artifact conversion workers
- dependency install/build/lint/test pipelines

Avoid using one sandbox as an uncontrolled multi-tenant process host. A sandbox
should belong to one tenant/workspace/security boundary.

---

---

## Sandbox-hosted orchestrators

The orchestrator does not always have to live in your backend. A MIOSA sandbox
can be the root orchestrator workspace.

```text
Tenant account
  -> workspace
    -> root orchestrator sandbox
      -> orchestration config
      -> local subagents
      -> child MIOSA sandboxes
      -> child MIOSA computers
      -> artifacts
      -> previews
      -> deployments
```

This pattern is useful for autonomous coding systems, research systems,
artifact factories, and customer-owned agent runtimes. The root sandbox keeps
the project files, agent configuration, run history, and local tooling. The
orchestrator process inside that sandbox can call MIOSA to launch additional
sandboxes or computers when it needs isolated workers.

Good examples of this pattern:

- root sandbox runs an agent manager
- child sandbox builds a web app
- child sandbox runs tests in parallel
- child computer opens the preview in a browser
- root sandbox collects screenshots, logs, and artifacts
- deploy agent publishes the verified result

The backend still owns tenant enforcement, billing, quotas, audit logging, and
token minting. The sandbox-hosted orchestrator owns the local plan and execution
strategy for that workspace.

---

---

## Self-configuring agents

A sandbox-hosted orchestrator can customize its own setup. It can write config
files, install packages, create worker scripts, generate task definitions, and
adjust its local workflow as the project evolves.

Typical files inside `/workspace`:

```text
/workspace
  agent.config.json
  miosa.runbook.md
  tasks/
    build.json
    test.json
    browser-qa.json
  agents/
    coder.ts
    tester.ts
    artifact-generator.py
  artifacts/
  logs/
```

Example `agent.config.json`:

```json
{
  "workspace": "lumen-demo",
  "defaultTemplate": "nextjs",
  "workers": {
    "coder": { "runtime": "local", "tools": ["files", "exec"] },
    "tester": { "runtime": "child-sandbox", "template": "miosa-sandbox" },
    "browserQa": { "runtime": "computer", "template": "ubuntu-browser" }
  },
  "limits": {
    "maxConcurrentWorkers": 8,
    "maxChildSandboxes": 4,
    "maxChildComputers": 1
  }
}
```

This lets an agent improve its own operating procedure without requiring every
change to be hard-coded in the parent application.

Use these guardrails:

- keep config files visible in `/workspace`
- require explicit approval for quota or permission increases
- validate generated config before applying it
- cap child sandbox/computer creation
- write run events back to the product UI
- snapshot before major self-modification
- keep tenant admin credentials outside the sandbox

The goal is controlled autonomy: the agent can code and configure its own
workspace, but MIOSA still enforces account boundaries and resource limits.

---

---

## Exporting generated work

Agents should leave concrete outputs behind. For app builders and agent-company
products, those outputs become the user's deliverable: HTML, PDFs, DOCX files,
CSV exports, screenshots, ZIPs, source patches, build logs, or deployment URLs.

Use declared artifact paths on Agent Runs when you expect a generated file:

```json
{
  "sandbox_id": "sbx_code",
  "provider": "claude-code",
  "prompt": "Build the landing page and export /workspace/artifacts/site.html",
  "metadata": {
    "artifact_paths": ["/workspace/artifacts/site.html"]
  }
}
```

When the run completes, list and download artifacts:

```bash
miosa run files <run-id> --json
miosa run download <run-id> <file-id> --output ./site.html
```

MIOSA captures artifact bytes into managed storage when possible. If an
artifact has `persisted: true`, your UI can keep showing a download button after
the runtime stops. If it is not persisted, keep the sandbox or computer running
until the file has been downloaded, published, or copied somewhere durable.

Use this split in your product UI:

| Output type | Best surface |
|---|---|
| HTML, PDF, DOCX, CSV, ZIP | Artifact download |
| Web app | Sandbox preview, then deployment |
| Screenshot or visual QA result | Artifact preview plus event timeline |
| Source code changes | Files panel, git diff, artifact ZIP |
| Long-running product | Deployment or Docker Host URL |

---

---

## Credentials and account connection

Large agent systems should use scoped credentials instead of sharing one tenant
admin key everywhere.

```text
Tenant key
  -> server-side orchestrator only
  -> mints scoped workspace/user tokens
  -> tokens injected into sandbox/computer runtime
  -> subagents call MIOSA within their allowed scope
```

Typical environment injected into a runtime:

```bash
MIOSA_API_KEY=msk_scoped_...
MIOSA_TENANT_ID=...
MIOSA_WORKSPACE_ID=...
MIOSA_PROJECT_ID=...
MIOSA_USER_ID=...
MIOSA_RUN_ID=...
```

This lets every subagent be connected to the correct account while still giving
the platform auditability, quotas, and revocation.

Important credential rules:

- Browser code never receives tenant admin keys.
- Sandboxes receive scoped runtime keys, not root account keys.
- Every token has workspace/project/user/run attribution.
- Every command, file write, preview, snapshot, and deploy is auditable.
- Quotas apply at tenant, workspace, user, and runtime-pool levels.

---

---

## Permissions and safety

Each agent should receive only the permissions it needs.

| Agent | Typical permissions |
|---|---|
| Sandbox code agent | sandbox files, exec, previews, snapshots |
| Artifact agent | sandbox files, exec, artifact export |
| Browser QA agent | computer screenshot, click, type, navigation |
| Deploy agent | deployment publish, domains, rollback |
| Billing/support agent | usage, credits, audit log |

Use scoped workspace keys or server-side tokens. Do not put tenant admin keys in
browser code.

---

---

## See also

- [Agent orchestration](/docs/guides/agent-orchestration): The concepts: scale model, runtime selection, communication primitives, and the queue and pool architecture.
- [Orchestration examples](/docs/guides/agent-orchestration/examples): Worked flows for app builders, sandbox-first code agents, and computer QA agents.

pages.title: Orchestration examples
pages.description: Worked orchestration flows on MIOSA: an app builder with browser QA, a sandbox-first code agent, a computer QA agent, a minimal orchestrator shape, and the product UI pattern.
pages.markdown:
Concrete flows that show the coordination patterns in action, from a full app builder with browser QA down to the minimal orchestrator shape and the UI it feeds.

---

## Example: app builder with browser QA

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant User
  participant O as Orchestrator
  participant S as Sandbox agent
  participant B as Browser agent
  participant D as Deploy agent

  User->>O: Build a signup landing page
  O->>S: create/resume nextjs sandbox
  S->>S: write files in /workspace
  S->>S: run npm install, tests, build
  S-->>O: preview_url + build log
```
