pages.title: Build a coding-agent product
pages.description: A branded coding-agent product: Wrap a harness in your own branded product. Build it on MIOSA with the exact resources, steps and commands.
pages.markdown:
`~25 min` `TypeScript` `Python`

> **What you're building**: Wrap a harness in your own branded product.
>
> **Primitives you'll use**: Sandbox, Agent and harness, Deployment (Docker Host)

## What you're building

your own product that wraps a coding harness (Claude Code, Codex, OSA, Hermes or your own) in your UI and billing Modelled on A branded coding-agent product, by You (built on an open harness).

Your product accepts a task from a customer, runs a harness inside an isolated MIOSA machine for that customer, streams progress to your UI and bills for usage.

Primitives you'll use: Sandbox · Agent and harness · Deployment (App Engine)

- Customers submit coding tasks in your UI
- A harness runs each task in isolation
- Live progress and a reviewable result
- Your branding and billing

Source: [/docs/build/run-agents](/docs/build/run-agents). A branded coding-agent product is a trademark of You (built on an open harness); this guide is not affiliated with or endorsed by them.

## What you need on MIOSA

Each row is one thing to create before you start. The number matches the step that uses it.

1. Organization and API key - Scopes every call; a workspace key is all a worker needs. - `miosa api-key create app-key --preset agent` [Docs](/docs/platform/api-keys)
2. Sandbox - The isolated Linux workspace the agent writes code and runs commands in. - `miosa create app-box --template nextjs --wait` [Docs](/docs/develop/sandboxes)
3. A workspace per customer - Isolates each customer’s machines, deployments, and data as they onboard. - `miosa workspace create customer-1` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
4. Branding and white-label - Your name and slug on previews, deployments, and the desktop; customers never see MIOSA. - `miosa org` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
5. Usage metering and bill-to - Usage per customer, and which account pays for new machines. - `miosa org bill` [Docs](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing)
6. Agent and harness - Turns a prompt into work: pick the harness and model a run uses. - `miosa agent harnesses` [Docs](/docs/api-reference/agent-runs)
7. Deployment (App Engine) - Publishes the app to an immutable, versioned URL with rollback. - `miosa deploy create --from-sandbox app-box --name app --wait` [Docs](/docs/docker-host/overview)

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant P as Your product
  participant S as Task sandbox
  participant A as Coding harness
  participant G as Git host

  U->>P: submit a task or an issue
  P->>S: create one sandbox per task
  P->>S: clone the repo, create a branch
  P->>A: dispatch the harness with the task
  A->>S: edit files, run the tests, commit
  S-->>P: events, diff and result files
  P->>G: push the branch and open a PR
  G-->>U: review the change
```

## How it maps onto MIOSA

A workspace the agent can break safely -> a MIOSA sandbox per task, with the repo cloned into /workspace

The agent edits files and runs commands -> agent runs (`miosa prompt`, client.runs) streaming events on that sandbox (`miosa prompt --sandbox ... --harness ...`)

Parallel tasks -> one sandbox per task or branch, sandbox snapshots and fork to try a second approach

Results you can review -> `miosa run files`, `miosa run outputs`, and the git diff inside the sandbox

Your customers stay separate -> a workspace per customer, usage metered and billed through bill-to

## Data and storage

Keep a tasks table in your own datastore: task id, repo, branch, sandbox id, run id, status, result links, and the user or customer it belongs to. The code itself lives in the sandbox and in Git, not in your database.

Per-customer usage (runs, minutes) feeds your billing; read it with `miosa run usage --group-by model`.

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash
miosa workspace create coding-agent-product-customer-1
```

Tag every machine and run with the customer id in `metadata`, and never query across customers. Meter usage per customer with GET /api/v1/usage and set who pays with PUT /api/v1/bill-to (/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Agent loop

Harness: OSA is MIOSA's own harness and works with any model provider you connect, including your own model.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (`miosa connections add models`); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

Sessions: one chat per project or conversation, so the agent keeps its context. The first `miosa prompt` on a sandbox uses `--new-chat` (a chat id is printed); every later turn passes `--chat <chat-id>`. `--reuse chat` keeps one new machine per chat so files persist.

Streaming: follow a run with `miosa run follow <run-id>` or client.runs.streamEvents(run.id), and steer or stop it with `miosa run steer` and `miosa run interrupt`.

The harness runs headless INSIDE the task sandbox with the repo checked out. It edits files, runs the project's own commands and commits; you never apply its edits from outside.

Parallel sessions are separate sandboxes (and separate chats). Snapshot before a risky change and fork to try a second approach.

## Steps

1. Create one sandbox per task or branch so parallel tasks never share state.
   ```bash
   miosa create coding-agent-product-task-1 --size medium --wait
   ```
   Check: The sandbox is running; two tasks have two sandboxes.
2. Clone the repository and create the task branch. Pass the Git token per exec or through the Secrets API; do not store it in the sandbox `env`.
   ```bash
   miosa exec coding-agent-product-task-1 -- git clone <repo-url> /workspace/repo
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa exec coding-agent-product-task-1 --cwd /workspace/repo -- git checkout -b task/<task-id>
   ```
   Check: The repo is in /workspace/repo on the task branch.
3. Dispatch the harness with the task.
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --sandbox coding-agent-product-task-1 --harness osa --model <anthropic-model-id> --chat <chat-id> "Do the task; run the tests; commit your work"
   ```
   Check: `miosa run list --status running` shows the run and events start streaming.
4. Follow the run, and steer or stop it from your UI.
   ```bash
   miosa run follow <run-id>
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa run steer --sandbox coding-agent-product-task-1 "also add tests"
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa run interrupt --sandbox coding-agent-product-task-1
   ```
   Check: The UI shows live events; a steer lands on the next turn; interrupt stops the agent.
5. Verify independently of the agent: run the test command yourself.
   ```bash
   miosa exec coding-agent-product-task-1 --cwd /workspace/repo -- npm test
   ```
   Check: Tests exit 0 in the sandbox, not just in the agent's summary.
6. Hand back the result: collect files and the diff, and push the branch if the task asks for it.
   ```bash
   miosa run files <run-id>
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa run download <run-id> <file-id> --output ./result
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa exec coding-agent-product-task-1 --cwd /workspace/repo -- git push origin task/<task-id>
   ```
   Check: The diff is reviewable outside the sandbox and the run id is attached to it.
7. Close out. For one-shot tasks let MIOSA do it (`miosa prompt --new-machine ... --after-run destroy`); keep or snapshot the sandbox when the user may continue.
   Check: No orphaned sandboxes remain after the task is closed.
8. Ship your product UI (a normal web app: task form, live events, diff viewer) as a deployment, built in its own sandbox.
   ```bash
   miosa create coding-agent-product-ui --template nextjs --wait
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa deploy create --from-sandbox coding-agent-product-ui --name coding-agent-product --dir /workspace --port 3000 --run-command "npm start" --wait
   ```
   Check: The public_url serves the task UI and submits a task end to end.

## Limits and costs

Set `--max-time` on every run so a stuck agent cannot run forever; use `--notify-email` or a webhook for long tasks.

Give the agent a token scoped to one repository, and only the permissions the task needs.

Parallel tasks multiply cost: cap concurrency per user or customer.

Prototype: keep it to one machine at the default size, skip replicas and custom hostnames you do not need, and delete everything when you are done.

## Acceptance checks

Two tasks run at the same time in two sandboxes without touching each other.

A finished task leaves a reviewable branch or diff and the run id.

Nothing was deployed or published: the deliverable is the diff.

Each customer is isolated in its own workspace and usage is metered against them.

Everything it created can be deleted with nothing left running.

## Next steps

- [Agent prompt builder Pick a product shape and hand the brief to your agent.](/docs/build)
- [Run coding agents Run Claude Code, Codex or Cursor in the cloud, or build a product on them.](/docs/build/run-agents)
- [Compare MIOSA How MIOSA compares to other sandbox and agent platforms.](/docs/compare)
- [What you can build Every product pattern MIOSA supports.](/docs/use-cases)

pages.title: Build a Manus-style agent
pages.description: Manus: A general agent with a desktop, browser, and files. Build it on MIOSA with the exact resources, steps and commands.
pages.markdown:
`~25 min` `TypeScript` `Python`

> **What you're building**: A general agent with a desktop, browser, and files.
>
> **Primitives you'll use**: Computer, Sandbox, Agent and harness

## What you're building

a general AI agent that takes a goal and works on it in a cloud computer Modelled on Manus, by Manus.

The user states a goal; the agent plans, then works in its own cloud environment (browser, files, code) and returns finished work, with the user able to watch or step in.

- Goal in, finished work out
- Its own cloud computer with a browser
- Writes and runs code and produces files
- Watch live or hand off

Source: [manus.im](https://manus.im/). Manus is a trademark of its owner; this guide is not affiliated with or endorsed by them.

Each row is one thing to create before you start. The number matches the step that uses it.

1. Organization and API key - Scopes every call; a workspace key is all a worker needs. - `miosa api-key create app-key --preset agent` [Docs](/docs/platform/api-keys)
2. Computer - A persistent Linux desktop for browser, mouse, and screenshot work. - `miosa computer create app-desktop` [Docs](/docs/computers/overview)
3. Sandbox - The isolated Linux workspace the agent writes code and runs commands in. - `miosa create app-box --template nextjs --wait` [Docs](/docs/develop/sandboxes)
4. A workspace per customer - Isolates each customer’s machines, deployments, and data as they onboard. - `miosa workspace create customer-1` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
5. Branding and white-label - Your name and slug on previews, deployments, and the desktop; customers never see MIOSA. - `miosa org` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
6. Usage metering and bill-to - Usage per customer, and which account pays for new machines. - `miosa org bill` [Docs](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing)
7. Agent and harness - Turns a prompt into work: pick the harness and model a run uses. - `miosa agent harnesses` [Docs](/docs/api-reference/agent-runs)

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant P as Your product
  participant C as MIOSA Computer
  participant A as Agent loop
  participant S as Work sandbox

  U->>P: state the goal
  P->>A: start a run on the computer
  A->>C: screenshot the desktop
  A->>C: click, type, launch apps
  A->>S: run code and write files
  P-->>U: live progress and screenshots
  U->>A: approve a consequential step
  A-->>P: finished files and a summary
```

## How it maps onto MIOSA

A real desktop and browser -> a MIOSA computer (persistent Linux desktop with a browser)

Sees and acts on the screen -> computer.screenshot(), click(), type(), key(), launch()

Code and files for the task -> a MIOSA sandbox for scripts and artifacts

Long-running work with a human in the loop -> agent runs (`miosa prompt`, client.runs) streaming events, approvals and `miosa run steer` / `interrupt`

## Data and storage

A tasks table in your datastore: task id, goal, plan, computer id, run id, status, approval records and artifact links. The desktop's own files and browser profile persist on the computer.

Code the agent writes and runs belongs in the work sandbox, not on the desktop.

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash
miosa workspace create manus-customer-1
```

Tag every machine and run with the customer id in `metadata`, and never query across customers. Meter usage per customer with GET /api/v1/usage and set who pays with PUT /api/v1/bill-to (/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Agent loop

Harness: OSA is MIOSA's own harness and works with any model provider you connect, including your own model.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (`miosa connections add models`); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

Sessions: one chat per project or conversation, so the agent keeps its context. The first `miosa prompt` on a computer uses `--new-chat` (a chat id is printed); every later turn passes `--chat <chat-id>`. `--reuse chat` keeps one new machine per chat so files persist.

Streaming: follow a run with `miosa run follow <run-id>` or client.runs.streamEvents(run.id), and steer or stop it with `miosa run steer` and `miosa run interrupt`.

The harness drives the computer: it looks (screenshot), decides and acts (click, type, key, launch), and repeats. Tell it explicitly which actions need approval.

One computer per user or per task keeps browser sessions and logged-in accounts from mixing.

## Steps

1. Create the computer the agent works on: a persistent Linux desktop with a real browser.
   ```bash
   miosa computer create manus-desktop
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa create manus-work --template python-data --wait
   ```
   Check: computer.screenshot() returns an image of the desktop and the work sandbox is running.
2. Plan before acting: have the agent write a short plan (steps and what "done" means) and keep it with the task so a human can read it.
   Check: The plan is stored and shown in the UI before the first action.
3. Dispatch the goal to the harness on the computer.
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --computer manus-desktop --harness osa --model <anthropic-model-id> --chat <chat-id> "Goal: <goal>. Plan first, then work in the browser and files, and save deliverables to /workspace/out"
   ```
   Check: The run starts and the first screenshot arrives within seconds.
4. The see-act loop: screenshot, decide, act, screenshot again. Store every screenshot as evidence.
   ```text
   computer.screenshot()
   ```
   ```text
   computer.click(x, y)
   ```
   ```text
   computer.type(text)
   ```
   ```text
   computer.key("Enter")
   ```
   ```text
   computer.launch(app)
   ```
   Check: Each action is followed by a stored screenshot you can replay.
5. Approvals and human takeover. Consequential actions (sending, buying, deleting, signing in) wait for a person; the person can take over the same live desktop for logins or CAPTCHAs and hand it back.
   ```bash
   miosa agent approvals
   ```
   Check: Nothing consequential runs without an approval record, and a takeover leaves the agent able to continue.
6. Long-running work: allow hours, watch progress, steer or stop.
   ```bash
   miosa run follow <run-id>
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa run steer --computer manus-desktop "focus on the pricing page"
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa run interrupt --computer manus-desktop
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa extend manus-desktop
   ```
   Check: Closing the UI does not stop the run, and reopening it shows current progress.
7. Collect the artifacts (files, documents, exports) and return them with a summary of what was done.

pages.description: Genspark Super Agent: A super-agent that plans and produces finished work. Build it on MIOSA with the exact resources, steps and commands.
pages.markdown:
`~25 min` `TypeScript` `Python`

> **What you're building**: A super-agent that plans and produces finished work.
>
> **Primitives you'll use**: Computer, Sandbox, Agent and harness, Deployment (Docker Host)

## What you're building

a super-agent that plans a task and produces finished work in a dedicated cloud machine Modelled on Genspark Super Agent, by Genspark.

The Super Agent breaks a request into steps, uses a browser and code execution in its own cloud machine, and returns deliverables such as documents, sheets and sites.

Primitives you'll use: Computer · Sandbox · Agent and harness · Deployment (App Engine)

- Plans and runs multi-step tasks
- Browser and code execution
- Produces finished deliverables
- Can publish the result

Source: [www.genspark.ai](https://www.genspark.ai/). Genspark Super Agent is a trademark of Genspark; this guide is not affiliated with or endorsed by them.

## What you need on MIOSA

Each row is one thing to create before you start. The number matches the step that uses it.

1. Organization and API key - Scopes every call; a workspace key is all a worker needs. - `miosa api-key create app-key --preset agent` [Docs](/docs/platform/api-keys)
2. Computer - A persistent Linux desktop for browser, mouse, and screenshot work. - `miosa computer create app-desktop` [Docs](/docs/computers/overview)
3. Sandbox - The isolated Linux workspace the agent writes code and runs commands in. - `miosa create app-box --template nextjs --wait` [Docs](/docs/develop/sandboxes)
4. A workspace per customer - Isolates each customer’s machines, deployments, and data as they onboard. - `miosa workspace create customer-1` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
5. Branding and white-label - Your name and slug on previews, deployments, and the desktop; customers never see MIOSA. - `miosa org` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
6. Usage metering and bill-to - Usage per customer, and which account pays for new machines. - `miosa org bill` [Docs](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing)
7. Agent and harness - Turns a prompt into work: pick the harness and model a run uses. - `miosa agent harnesses` [Docs](/docs/api-reference/agent-runs)
8. Deployment (App Engine) - Publishes the app to an immutable, versioned URL with rollback. - `miosa deploy create --from-sandbox app-box --name app --wait` [Docs](/docs/docker-host/overview)

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant P as Your product
  participant C as MIOSA Computer
  participant A as Agent loop
  participant S as Work sandbox

  U->>P: state the goal
  P->>A: start a run on the computer
  A->>C: screenshot the desktop
  A->>C: click, type, launch apps
  A->>S: run code and write files
  P-->>U: live progress and screenshots
  U->>A: approve a consequential step
  A-->>P: finished files and a summary
```

## How it maps onto MIOSA

A real desktop and browser -> a MIOSA computer (persistent Linux desktop with a browser)

Sees and acts on the screen -> computer.screenshot(), click(), type(), key(), launch()

Code and files for the task -> a MIOSA sandbox for scripts and artifacts

Long-running work with a human in the loop -> agent runs (`miosa prompt`, client.runs) streaming events, approvals and `miosa run steer` / `interrupt`

## Data and storage

A tasks table in your datastore: task id, goal, plan, computer id, run id, status, approval records and artifact links. The desktop's own files and browser profile persist on the computer.

Code the agent writes and runs belongs in the work sandbox, not on the desktop.

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash
miosa workspace create genspark-customer-1
```

Tag every machine and run with the customer id in `metadata`, and never query across customers. Meter usage per customer with GET /api/v1/usage and set who pays with PUT /api/v1/bill-to (/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Agent loop

Harness: OSA is MIOSA's own harness and works with any model provider you connect, including your own model.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (`miosa connections add models`); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

Sessions: one chat per project or conversation, so the agent keeps its context. The first `miosa prompt` on a computer uses `--new-chat` (a chat id is printed); every later turn passes `--chat <chat-id>`. `--reuse chat` keeps one new machine per chat so files persist.

Streaming: follow a run with `miosa run follow <run-id>` or client.runs.streamEvents(run.id), and steer or stop it with `miosa run steer` and `miosa run interrupt`.

The harness drives the computer: it looks (screenshot), decides and acts (click, type, key, launch), and repeats. Tell it explicitly which actions need approval.

One computer per user or per task keeps browser sessions and logged-in accounts from mixing.

## Steps

1. Create the computer the agent works on: a persistent Linux desktop with a real browser.
   ```bash
   miosa computer create genspark-desktop
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa create genspark-work --template python-data --wait
   ```
   Check: computer.screenshot() returns an image of the desktop and the work sandbox is running.
2. Plan before acting: have the agent write a short plan (steps and what "done" means) and keep it with the task so a human can read it.
   Check: The plan is stored and shown in the UI before the first action.
3. Dispatch the goal to the harness on the computer.
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --computer genspark-desktop --harness osa --model <anthropic-model-id> --chat <chat-id> "Goal: <goal>. Plan first, then work in the browser and files, and save deliverables to /workspace/out"
   ```
   Check: The run starts and the first screenshot arrives within seconds.
4. The see-act loop: screenshot, decide, act, screenshot again. Store every screenshot as evidence.
   ```text
   computer.screenshot()
   ```
   ```text
   computer.click(x, y)
   ```
   ```text
   computer.type(text)
   ```
   ```text
   computer.key("Enter")
   ```
   ```text
   computer.launch(app)
   ```
   Check: Each action is followed by a stored screenshot you can replay.
5. Approvals and human takeover. Consequential actions (sending, buying, deleting, signing in) wait for a person; the person can take over the same live desktop for logins or CAPTCHAs and hand it back.
   ```bash
   miosa agent approvals
   ```
   Check: Nothing consequential runs without an approval record, and a takeover leaves the agent able to continue.
6. Long-running work: allow hours, watch progress, steer or stop.
   ```bash
   miosa run follow <run-id>
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa run steer --computer genspark-desktop "focus on the pricing page"
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa run interrupt --computer genspark-desktop
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa extend genspark-desktop
   ```
   Check: Closing the UI does not stop the run, and reopening it shows current progress.
7. Collect the artifacts (files, documents, exports) and return them with a summary of what was done.
   ```bash
   miosa run files <run-id>
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa run download <run-id> <file-id> --output ./result
   ```
   Check: The user receives the finished files, not just a description of them.
8. The deliverable is a site or page: publish it.
   ```bash
   miosa deploy create --from-sandbox genspark-work --name genspark --dir /workspace/out --wait
   ```
   Check: The public_url serves the deliverable.

## Limits and costs

A computer bills while it runs: set a TTL, extend deliberately with `miosa extend`, and pause idle ones.

Set `--max-time` on runs; hours are normal, unbounded is not.

Never put long-lived credentials on the desktop; sign in through a human takeover so secrets stay with the user.

Prototype: keep it to one machine at the default size, skip replicas and custom hostnames you do not need, and delete everything when you are done.

## Acceptance checks

The agent completes a real browser task and the screenshots show the result.

A consequential action stopped for approval.

Artifacts were delivered and the computer persists across turns.

Each customer is isolated in its own workspace and usage is metered against them.

Everything it created can be deleted with nothing left running.

an autonomous software engineer that works in its own VM with a shell, editor and browser Modelled on Devin, by Cognition.

- Takes a whole engineering task
- Its own shell, editor and browser
- Long-running work with progress updates
- Delivers a pull request

6. Usage metering and bill-to - Usage per customer, and which account pays for new machines. - `miosa org bill` [Docs](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing)

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant P as Your product
  participant C as MIOSA Computer
  participant A as Agent loop
  participant S as Work sandbox

  U->>P: state the goal
  P->>A: start a run on the computer
  A->>C: screenshot the desktop
  A->>C: click, type, launch apps
  A->>S: run code and write files
  P-->>U: live progress and screenshots
  U->>A: approve a consequential step
  A-->>P: finished files and a summary
```

## How it maps onto MIOSA

Its own machine per task -> a MIOSA sandbox (long TTL, size large) per task

Long-running work, progress and steering -> agent runs (`miosa prompt`, client.runs) streaming events, `miosa run follow`, `miosa run steer`

Browser to verify its work -> a MIOSA computer (persistent Linux desktop with a browser) driven by computer.agent.run

Deliverables -> `miosa run files` plus a branch pushed from the sandbox

## Data and storage

A tasks table: ticket, repo, branch, sandbox id, run id, status, artifact links. The code lives in Git and the sandbox; the browser session lives on the computer.

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash
miosa workspace create devin-customer-1
```

Tag every machine and run with the customer id in `metadata`, and never query across customers. Meter usage per customer with GET /api/v1/usage and set who pays with PUT /api/v1/bill-to (/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Agent loop

Harness: OSA is MIOSA's own harness and works with any model provider you connect, including your own model.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (`miosa connections add models`); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

Sessions: one chat per project or conversation, so the agent keeps its context. The first `miosa prompt` on a computer uses `--new-chat` (a chat id is printed); every later turn passes `--chat <chat-id>`. `--reuse chat` keeps one new machine per chat so files persist.

Streaming: follow a run with `miosa run follow <run-id>` or client.runs.streamEvents(run.id), and steer or stop it with `miosa run steer` and `miosa run interrupt`.

The harness works in the sandbox like an engineer: read, edit, run, fix. The computer exists only to verify behaviour in a browser, so the agent sees what a user sees.

## Steps

1. Give each task its own large, long-lived sandbox: this is the agent's VM with a shell and editor.
   ```bash
   miosa create devin-swe-1 --template agent-node --size large --ttl 4h --wait
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa computer create devin-desktop
   ```
   Check: The sandbox is running with a 4h TTL, and the computer shows a desktop in computer.screenshot().
2. Clone the repository and create the task branch (pass the Git token per exec or via the Secrets API).
   ```bash
   miosa exec devin-swe-1 -- git clone <repo-url> /workspace/repo
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa exec devin-swe-1 --cwd /workspace/repo -- git checkout -b swe/<task-id>
   ```
   Check: The repo is on the task branch.
3. Dispatch the task to the harness on the sandbox. It plans, edits, runs tests and iterates on its own.
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --sandbox devin-swe-1 --harness osa --model <anthropic-model-id> --chat <chat-id> "Task: <ticket>. Plan, implement, run the tests, commit"
   ```
   Check: The run starts and events stream.
4. Watch and steer: the run may take hours.
   ```bash
   miosa run follow <run-id>
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa run steer --sandbox devin-swe-1 "prefer the existing logger"
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa run interrupt --sandbox devin-swe-1
   ```
   Check: Closing the UI does not stop the run; steering lands on the next turn.
5. Verify in a real browser: start the app in the sandbox, expose it with a preview, and have an agent click through the flow on the computer.
   ```bash
   miosa preview create devin-swe-1 3000 --name web
   ```
   ```text
   computer.agent.run("Open the preview URL and click through the signup flow")
   ```
   Check: A screenshot trail shows the flow working, or the exact step where it fails.
6. Deliver: push the branch, collect artifacts (test output, screenshots), and snapshot the sandbox for review.
   ```bash
   miosa exec devin-swe-1 --cwd /workspace/repo -- git push origin swe/<task-id>
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa run files <run-id>
   ```
   ```text
   sandbox.snapshots.create("ready for review")
   ```
   Check: A reviewer can open the branch, the artifacts and the snapshot.

Long tasks need a long TTL and `--max-time`; both bound cost.

Give the agent a token scoped to one repository.

One sandbox per task: cap concurrent tasks per user or customer.

Prototype: keep it to one machine at the default size, skip replicas and custom hostnames you do not need, and delete everything when you are done.

## Acceptance checks

A task goes from ticket to a pushed branch with passing tests.

The result was verified in a browser, with screenshots.

Closing the UI did not stop the run.

Each customer is isolated in its own workspace and usage is metered against them.

Everything it created can be deleted with nothing left running.

- [Run coding agents Run Claude Code, Codex or Cursor in the cloud, or build a product on them.](/docs/build/run-agents)
- [Compare MIOSA How MIOSA compares to other sandbox and agent platforms.](/docs/compare)

- Human takeover for logins and approvals
- Returns a summary and the files it produced

This is a pattern, not a copy of one product. Start from [the related MIOSA guide](/docs/computers/overview) and build the smallest version that does the capabilities above.

## What you need on MIOSA

Each row is one thing to create before you start. The number matches the step that uses it.

1. Organization and API key - Scopes every call; a workspace key is all a worker needs. - `miosa api-key create app-key --preset agent` [Docs](/docs/platform/api-keys)
2. Computer - A persistent Linux desktop for browser, mouse, and screenshot work. - `miosa computer create app-desktop` [Docs](/docs/computers/overview)
3. Sandbox - The isolated Linux workspace the agent writes code and runs commands in. - `miosa create app-box --template nextjs --wait` [Docs](/docs/develop/sandboxes)
4. A workspace per customer - Isolates each customer’s machines, deployments, and data as they onboard. - `miosa workspace create customer-1` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
5. Branding and white-label - Your name and slug on previews, deployments, and the desktop; customers never see MIOSA. - `miosa org` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
6. Usage metering and bill-to - Usage per customer, and which account pays for new machines. - `miosa org bill` [Docs](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing)
7. Agent and harness - Turns a prompt into work: pick the harness and model a run uses. - `miosa agent harnesses` [Docs](/docs/api-reference/agent-runs)

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant P as Your product
  participant C as MIOSA Computer
  participant A as Browser agent
  participant M as Model API

  U->>P: give the task
  P->>A: start a run on the computer
  A->>M: decide the next action
  A->>C: click, type, fill a form
  C-->>A: screenshot evidence
  P-->>U: live screenshots
  U->>C: take over for a login
  A-->>P: summary and extracted data
```

## How it maps onto MIOSA

A real desktop and browser -> a MIOSA computer (persistent Linux desktop with a browser)

Sees and acts on the screen -> computer.screenshot(), click(), type(), key(), launch()

The agent loop -> agent runs (`miosa prompt`, client.runs) streaming events that drive the computer

Approvals and takeover -> agent runs (`miosa prompt`, client.runs) streaming events, agent approvals, and a shared desktop a person can take over

## Data and storage

A tasks table in your datastore: task id, goal, plan, computer id, run id, status, approval records and artifact links. The desktop's own files and browser profile persist on the computer.

Code the agent writes and runs belongs in the work sandbox, not on the desktop.

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash
miosa workspace create chatgpt-agent-customer-1
```

Tag every machine and run with the customer id in `metadata`, and never query across customers. Meter usage per customer with GET /api/v1/usage and set who pays with PUT /api/v1/bill-to (/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Agent loop

Harness: OSA is MIOSA's own harness and works with any model provider you connect, including your own model.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (`miosa connections add models`); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

Sessions: one chat per project or conversation, so the agent keeps its context. The first `miosa prompt` on a computer uses `--new-chat` (a chat id is printed); every later turn passes `--chat <chat-id>`. `--reuse chat` keeps one new machine per chat so files persist.

Streaming: follow a run with `miosa run follow <run-id>` or client.runs.streamEvents(run.id), and steer or stop it with `miosa run steer` and `miosa run interrupt`.

The harness drives the computer: it looks (screenshot), decides and acts (click, type, key, launch), and repeats. Tell it explicitly which actions need approval.

One computer per user or per task keeps browser sessions and logged-in accounts from mixing.

## Steps

1. Create the computer the agent works on: a persistent Linux desktop with a real browser.
   ```bash
   miosa computer create chatgpt-agent-desktop
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa create chatgpt-agent-work --template python-data --wait
   ```
   Check: computer.screenshot() returns an image of the desktop and the work sandbox is running.
2. Plan before acting: have the agent write a short plan (steps and what "done" means) and keep it with the task so a human can read it.
   Check: The plan is stored and shown in the UI before the first action.
3. Dispatch the goal to the harness on the computer.
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --computer chatgpt-agent-desktop --harness osa --model <anthropic-model-id> --chat <chat-id> "Goal: <goal>. Plan first, then work in the browser and files, and save deliverables to /workspace/out"
   ```
   Check: The run starts and the first screenshot arrives within seconds.
4. The see-act loop: screenshot, decide, act, screenshot again. Store every screenshot as evidence.
   ```text
   computer.screenshot()
   ```
   ```text
   computer.click(x, y)
   ```
   ```text
   computer.type(text)
   ```
   ```text
   computer.key("Enter")
   ```
   ```text
   computer.launch(app)
   ```
   Check: Each action is followed by a stored screenshot you can replay.
5. Approvals and human takeover. Consequential actions (sending, buying, deleting, signing in) wait for a person; the person can take over the same live desktop for logins or CAPTCHAs and hand it back.
   ```bash
   miosa agent approvals
   ```
   Check: Nothing consequential runs without an approval record, and a takeover leaves the agent able to continue.
6. Long-running work: allow hours, watch progress, steer or stop.
   ```bash
   miosa run follow <run-id>
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa run steer --computer chatgpt-agent-desktop "focus on the pricing page"
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa run interrupt --computer chatgpt-agent-desktop
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa extend chatgpt-agent-desktop
   ```
   Check: Closing the UI does not stop the run, and reopening it shows current progress.
7. Collect the artifacts (files, documents, exports) and return them with a summary of what was done.
   ```bash
   miosa run files <run-id>
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa run download <run-id> <file-id> --output ./result
   ```
   Check: The user receives the finished files, not just a description of them.

## Limits and costs

A computer bills while it runs: set a TTL, extend deliberately with `miosa extend`, and pause idle ones.

Set `--max-time` on runs; hours are normal, unbounded is not.

Never put long-lived credentials on the desktop; sign in through a human takeover so secrets stay with the user.

Prototype: keep it to one machine at the default size, skip replicas and custom hostnames you do not need, and delete everything when you are done.

## Acceptance checks

The agent completes a real browser task and the screenshots show the result.

A consequential action stopped for approval.

Artifacts were delivered and the computer persists across turns.

Each customer is isolated in its own workspace and usage is metered against them.

Everything it created can be deleted with nothing left running.

## Next steps

- [Agent prompt builder Pick a product shape and hand the brief to your agent.](/docs/build)
- [Run coding agents Run Claude Code, Codex or Cursor in the cloud, or build a product on them.](/docs/build/run-agents)
- [Compare MIOSA How MIOSA compares to other sandbox and agent platforms.](/docs/compare)
- [What you can build Every product pattern MIOSA supports.](/docs/use-cases)

pages.title: Run Browser Use on MIOSA
pages.description: Browser Use: Install the open-source library and let an agent drive a real browser. Install and run it on a MIOSA sandbox or computer, then wrap it for your team or your customers.
pages.markdown:
`~15 min` `TypeScript` `Python`

> **What you're building**: Install the open-source library and let an agent drive a real browser.
>
> **Primitives you'll use**: Computer, Sandbox

> **Tip: Run theirs, or build your own**
>
> This guide runs **Browser Use** on MIOSA. You don't have to use it.
> You can build your own browser agent instead, on MIOSA alone: drive the [live browser inside a sandbox](/docs/browser-use) over CDP, or a full [computer](/docs/computer-use) with screenshots, clicks and typing.
> You own the loop, the prompts, the model and the product.
> See [Build a browser and computer-use agent](/docs/build/chatgpt-agent).

## What you're building

an open-source library that lets an AI agent drive a real browser Modelled on Browser Use, by Browser Use.

You give the library a task and a model; it controls a Chromium browser (pages, clicks, forms, extraction) in a loop until the task is done.

Primitives you'll use: Computer · Sandbox

- An agent that drives a real browser
- Extracts structured data from pages
- Works with your choice of model
- Open source and embeddable

You install and **run the real Browser Use** on MIOSA. Read the official docs first: [docs.browser-use.com](https://docs.browser-use.com/). Every install command below comes from them; if the docs and this guide disagree, the docs win. Browser Use is open source Python library.

## What you need on MIOSA

Each row is one thing to create before you start. The number matches the step that uses it.

1. Organization and API key - Scopes every call; a workspace key is all a worker needs. - `miosa api-key create app-key --preset agent` [Docs](/docs/platform/api-keys)
2. Computer - A persistent Linux desktop for browser, mouse, and screenshot work. - `miosa computer create app-desktop` [Docs](/docs/computers/overview)
3. Sandbox - The isolated Linux workspace the agent writes code and runs commands in. - `miosa create app-box --template nextjs --wait` [Docs](/docs/develop/sandboxes)
4. A workspace per customer - Isolates each customer’s machines, deployments, and data as they onboard. - `miosa workspace create customer-1` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
5. Branding and white-label - Your name and slug on previews, deployments, and the desktop; customers never see MIOSA. - `miosa org` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
6. Usage metering and bill-to - Usage per customer, and which account pays for new machines. - `miosa org bill` [Docs](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing)

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as You
  participant M as MIOSA Computer
  participant P as Model provider
  participant D as MIOSA Deploy

  U->>M: install the tool from its official docs
  M->>P: calls with your own provider key
  U->>M: run a real task
  M-->>U: output, files
  U->>D: publish it for your team or your customers
```

## How it runs on MIOSA

Where it runs -> a MIOSA computer (a persistent desktop with a browser)

State and files -> Scripts and outputs live in /workspace on the computer; browser profiles persist with the computer.

Model -> your own provider key, never a MIOSA platform key

Your customers -> one workspace each, isolated from each other

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash
miosa workspace create browser-use-customer-1
```

Tag every machine and run with the customer id in `metadata`, and never query across customers. Meter usage per customer with GET /api/v1/usage and set who pays with PUT /api/v1/bill-to (/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Install Browser Use

Run these inside the computer (its terminal), in order. The commands are from the official docs.

```text
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
```

```text
python3 --version   # Python >= 3.11 is required
```

```text
uv init --python 3.12
```

```text
uv add browser-use
```

Check: the install finishes without errors; the next sections configure and start it.

## Configure

Put your own model key in `.env` (the README example uses OPENAI_API_KEY). A MIOSA computer already has a desktop and Chrome for the agent to drive; use Browser Use's cloud browser only if you choose to.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="..."   # set it in the process environment, or the Secrets API; never write it into files you commit
```

## Run it

Start it and prove it works.

```text
uv run agent.py   # the README's agent.py with your task
```

Check: the tool starts without errors and responds.

## Persistence and access

Scripts and outputs live in /workspace on the computer; browser profiles persist with the computer.

Check: after the machine pauses and resumes, the tool starts again with its state intact.

## Make it a product

One computer per customer workspace; a queue in front; results and screenshots stored per customer.

## Limits and costs

Pin the version you tested and update deliberately; these tools change quickly.

Give the tool only the credentials it needs, as secrets, not baked into files.

Prototype: keep it to one machine at the default size, skip replicas and custom hostnames you do not need, and delete everything when you are done.

## Acceptance checks

Browser Use runs on a MIOSA computer and answers a real task.

State survives a pause and resume.

Each customer has its own workspace and its own instance; nothing is shared between them.

Everything it created can be deleted with nothing left running.

## Next steps

- [Run coding agents Run Claude Code, Codex or Cursor in the cloud, or build a product on them.](/docs/build/run-agents)
- [Compare MIOSA How MIOSA compares to other sandbox and agent platforms.](/docs/compare)

pages.title: Build a dots-style companion
pages.description: dots: Always-on companions, each with its own cloud computer. Build it on MIOSA with the exact resources, steps and commands.
pages.markdown:
`~25 min` `TypeScript` `Python`

> **What you're building**: Always-on companions, each with its own cloud computer.
>
> **Primitives you'll use**: Computer, Sandbox, Postgres, Agent and harness, Deployment (Docker Host)

## What you're building

always-on agents, each running in its own cloud computer with its own browser Modelled on dots, by OpenAI.

Each dot is a persistent agent with its own cloud computer; it keeps working between conversations and remembers the user.

Primitives you'll use: Computer · Sandbox · Postgres · Agent and harness · Deployment (App Engine)

- Always-on agents
- Each has its own cloud computer and browser
- Remembers context between sessions
- Does background work when idle

Source: [openai.com/index/introducing-dots/](https://openai.com/index/introducing-dots/). dots is a trademark of OpenAI; this guide is not affiliated with or endorsed by them.

## What you need on MIOSA

Each row is one thing to create before you start. The number matches the step that uses it.

1. Organization and API key - Scopes every call; a workspace key is all a worker needs. - `miosa api-key create app-key --preset agent` [Docs](/docs/platform/api-keys)
2. Computer - A persistent Linux desktop for browser, mouse, and screenshot work. - `miosa computer create app-desktop` [Docs](/docs/computers/overview)
3. Sandbox - The isolated Linux workspace the agent writes code and runs commands in. - `miosa create app-box --template nextjs --wait` [Docs](/docs/develop/sandboxes)
4. Postgres - Managed relational data, injected as DATABASE_URL in the machine and in production. - `miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"app-db","engine":"postgresql"}'` [Docs](/docs/data/postgres)
5. A workspace per customer - Isolates each customer’s machines, deployments, and data as they onboard. - `miosa workspace create customer-1` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
6. Branding and white-label - Your name and slug on previews, deployments, and the desktop; customers never see MIOSA. - `miosa org` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
7. Usage metering and bill-to - Usage per customer, and which account pays for new machines. - `miosa org bill` [Docs](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing)
8. Agent and harness - Turns a prompt into work: pick the harness and model a run uses. - `miosa agent harnesses` [Docs](/docs/api-reference/agent-runs)
9. Deployment (App Engine) - Publishes the app to an immutable, versioned URL with rollback. - `miosa deploy create --from-sandbox app-box --name app --wait` [Docs](/docs/docker-host/overview)

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant P as Your product
  participant DB as Managed Postgres
  participant V as Vector index
  participant A as Agent run

  U->>P: send a message
  P->>DB: load history and the persona
  P->>V: recall relevant memories
  P->>A: run a turn with tools
  A-->>P: streamed reply
  P->>DB: store both messages
  P-->>U: reply in the chat
```

## How it maps onto MIOSA

Remembers the user -> managed Postgres (`DATABASE_URL`) for messages, profile and memory

The model and tools behind each reply -> agent runs (`miosa prompt`, client.runs) streaming events in a sandbox, one run per user turn

One cloud computer per dot -> a MIOSA computer (persistent Linux desktop with a browser)

Stays alive between sessions -> a long TTL and `miosa extend`

## Data and storage

Postgres is the system of record: users, personas, conversations, messages (with role and timestamp), and memories (summary text, source message ids, importance).

Keep memory in Postgres as summaries plus key facts.

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash
miosa workspace create dots-customer-1
```

Tag every machine and run with the customer id in `metadata`, and never query across customers. Meter usage per customer with GET /api/v1/usage and set who pays with PUT /api/v1/bill-to (/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Agent loop

Harness: OSA is MIOSA's own harness and works with any model provider you connect, including your own model.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (`miosa connections add models`); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

Sessions: one chat per project or conversation, so the agent keeps its context. The first `miosa prompt` on a sandbox uses `--new-chat` (a chat id is printed); every later turn passes `--chat <chat-id>`. `--reuse chat` keeps one new machine per chat so files persist.

Streaming: follow a run with `miosa run follow <run-id>` or client.runs.streamEvents(run.id), and steer or stop it with `miosa run steer` and `miosa run interrupt`.

Each named agent is a saved agent that runs against a computer. State that must outlive a conversation (files, logged-in browser) lives on the computer; state about the person lives in Postgres.

## Steps

1. Create the database and schema: users, personas (or bots), conversations, messages, memories.
   ```bash
   miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"dots-memory","engine":"postgresql"}'
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa db connection dots-memory
   ```
   Check: You can insert and read a message through DATABASE_URL.
2. Create the backend sandbox that serves chat and your UI; give it DATABASE_URL. The agents themselves run on their computers, not here.
   ```bash
   miosa create dots-box --template agent-node --wait
   ```
   Check: The backend reads and writes messages in Postgres.
3. Create the computers: one computer per dot. They stay alive between conversations.
   ```bash
   miosa computer create dots-ada
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa extend dots-ada
   ```
   Check: A file created in one session is still there in the next; two bots (or dots) never see each other's files unless the computer is shared on purpose.
4. Define each named agent once, with its persona as instructions.
   ```bash
   miosa agent new dots-ada --harness osa --instructions-file persona.md
   ```
   Check: `miosa agent list` shows it, and a versioned definition exists per persona.
5. On every message, run the right agent against its computer and stream the reply into the chat.
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --computer dots-ada --agent dots-ada "<message>"
   ```
   Check: The reply streams, is written to messages, and the agent can use its browser and files.
6. Let the agent do read-only background work while idle, and report in the next conversation.
   Check: Idle work never sends, buys or deletes anything.
7. Memory: keep a rolling summary and key facts per user in Postgres, and put the summary in every turn.
   Check: Something said last week is recalled correctly this week.
8. Publish the chat UI and API.
   ```bash
   miosa deploy create --from-sandbox dots-box --name dots --dir /workspace --port 3000 --run-command "npm start" --wait
   ```
   Check: The public_url serves the chat and a new conversation works end to end.

## Limits and costs

Chat is high-volume and low-compute: keep the backend small and scale replicas before machine size; do not give every conversation its own machine unless it uses tools.

Cap memory growth: summarise and expire; embed summaries, not every message.

Computers bill while running: set TTLs, pause idle ones, and extend only for active users.

Prototype: keep it to one machine at the default size, skip replicas and custom hostnames you do not need, and delete everything when you are done.

## Acceptance checks

A conversation resumes days later with the right persona and remembered facts.

Users can delete their history and it is gone from Postgres and the index.

The product tells users they are talking to an AI.

Each agent keeps its own files and browser state between sessions.

Each customer is isolated in its own workspace and usage is metered against them.

Everything it created can be deleted with nothing left running.

- [Agent prompt builder Pick a product shape and hand the brief to your agent.](/docs/build)
- [Run coding agents Run Claude Code, Codex or Cursor in the cloud, or build a product on them.](/docs/build/run-agents)
- [Compare MIOSA How MIOSA compares to other sandbox and agent platforms.](/docs/compare)
- [What you can build Every product pattern MIOSA supports.](/docs/use-cases)

7. Usage metering and bill-to - Usage per customer, and which account pays for new machines. - `miosa org bill` [Docs](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing)
8. Agent and harness - Turns a prompt into work: pick the harness and model a run uses. - `miosa agent harnesses` [Docs](/docs/api-reference/agent-runs)
9. Deployment (App Engine) - Publishes the app to an immutable, versioned URL with rollback. - `miosa deploy create --from-sandbox app-box --name app --wait` [Docs](/docs/docker-host/overview)

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant P as Your product
  participant DB as Managed Postgres
  participant V as Vector index
  participant A as Agent run

  U->>P: send a message
  P->>DB: load history and the persona
  P->>V: recall relevant memories
  P->>A: run a turn with tools
  A-->>P: streamed reply
  P->>DB: store both messages
  P-->>U: reply in the chat
```

## How it maps onto MIOSA

Remembers the user -> managed Postgres (`DATABASE_URL`) for messages, profile and memory

The model and tools behind each reply -> agent runs (`miosa prompt`, client.runs) streaming events in a sandbox, one run per user turn

Character definitions and personas -> managed Postgres (`DATABASE_URL`) (a characters table with the system prompt)

Long-term memory -> managed Qdrant (`QDRANT_URL`) to recall earlier messages beyond the context window

Serving the app -> a MIOSA deployment (`miosa deploy create`), immutable and versioned

## Data and storage

Postgres is the system of record: users, personas, conversations, messages (with role and timestamp), and memories (summary text, source message ids, importance).

Qdrant holds embeddings of memories and, if you want recall of old messages, of message chunks. Store the Postgres id in the point payload.

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash
miosa workspace create character-ai-customer-1
```

Tag every machine and run with the customer id in `metadata`, and never query across customers. Meter usage per customer with GET /api/v1/usage and set who pays with PUT /api/v1/bill-to (/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Agent loop

Harness: OSA is MIOSA's own harness and works with any model provider you connect, including your own model.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (`miosa connections add models`); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

Sessions: one chat per project or conversation, so the agent keeps its context. The first `miosa prompt` on a sandbox uses `--new-chat` (a chat id is printed); every later turn passes `--chat <chat-id>`. `--reuse chat` keeps one new machine per chat so files persist.

Streaming: follow a run with `miosa run follow <run-id>` or client.runs.streamEvents(run.id), and steer or stop it with `miosa run steer` and `miosa run interrupt`.

Most turns are plain model calls from your backend with the persona and memories in the prompt. Tool turns (search, code, files) go to the harness inside the backend sandbox, so tools run in isolation.

## Steps

1. Create the database and schema: users, personas (or bots), conversations, messages, memories.
   ```bash
   miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"character-ai-memory","engine":"postgresql"}'
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa db connection character-ai-memory
   ```
   Check: You can insert and read a message through DATABASE_URL.
2. Create the vector index for memory recall.
   ```bash
   miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"character-ai-recall","engine":"qdrant"}'
   ```
   Check: QDRANT_URL and QDRANT_API_KEY are available to the backend.
3. Create the backend sandbox that serves chat and runs your tools; give it DATABASE_URL.
   ```bash
   miosa create character-ai-box --template agent-node --wait
   ```
   Check: The backend reads and writes messages in Postgres.
4. Store each persona (system prompt, style, boundaries) as a versioned row, and load it into every turn.
   Check: Editing a persona changes the next reply, not past ones.
5. Handle a turn: load the persona, recent messages and recalled memories, call the model, stream the reply, store both messages. Use the harness for turns that need tools; plain chat turns can call the provider directly.
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --sandbox character-ai-box --harness osa --model <anthropic-model-id> --chat <chat-id> "Reply to the user as the persona. Use tools only when the message needs them"
   ```
   Check: First token reaches the UI quickly and the whole exchange is stored.
6. Memory: after each session summarise it into memory rows, embed them into Qdrant, and recall the top few on every turn.
   Check: Something said last week is recalled correctly this week.
7. Publish the chat UI and API.
   ```bash
   miosa deploy create --from-sandbox character-ai-box --name character-ai --dir /workspace --port 3000 --run-command "npm start" --wait
   ```
   Check: The public_url serves the chat and a new conversation works end to end.

## Limits and costs

Chat is high-volume and low-compute: keep the backend small and scale replicas before machine size; do not give every conversation its own machine unless it uses tools.

Cap memory growth: summarise and expire; embed summaries, not every message.

Prototype: keep it to one machine at the default size, skip replicas and custom hostnames you do not need, and delete everything when you are done.

## Acceptance checks

A conversation resumes days later with the right persona and remembered facts.

Users can delete their history and it is gone from Postgres and the index.

The product tells users they are talking to an AI.

Each customer is isolated in its own workspace and usage is metered against them.

Everything it created can be deleted with nothing left running.

## Next steps

- [Run coding agents Run Claude Code, Codex or Cursor in the cloud, or build a product on them.](/docs/build/run-agents)
- [Compare MIOSA How MIOSA compares to other sandbox and agent platforms.](/docs/compare)
- [What you can build Every product pattern MIOSA supports.](/docs/use-cases)

pages.markdown:
`~15 min` `TypeScript` `Python`

> **What you're building**: Install the open-source assistant on a persistent computer that never sleeps.
>
> **Primitives you'll use**: Computer

## What you're building

an open-source personal AI assistant that runs on a machine you control and is reached through chat apps Modelled on OpenClaw, by OpenClaw Foundation.

OpenClaw runs on a persistent device, takes requests from chat apps (WhatsApp, Telegram and others) and works on email, calendar and the web while you are away.

Primitives you'll use: Computer

- Reached from the chat apps you already use
- Runs on a persistent device that never sleeps
- Works on inbox, calendar and web tasks
- Open source

You install and **run the real OpenClaw** on MIOSA. Read the official docs first: [docs.openclaw.ai/start/getting-started](https://docs.openclaw.ai/start/getting-started). Every install command below comes from them; if the docs and this guide disagree, the docs win. OpenClaw is open source, stewarded by the OpenClaw Foundation.

## What you need on MIOSA

Each row is one thing to create before you start. The number matches the step that uses it.

1. Organization and API key - Scopes every call; a workspace key is all a worker needs. - `miosa api-key create app-key --preset agent` [Docs](/docs/platform/api-keys)
2. Computer - A persistent Linux desktop for browser, mouse, and screenshot work. - `miosa computer create app-desktop` [Docs](/docs/computers/overview)
3. A workspace per customer - Isolates each customer’s machines, deployments, and data as they onboard. - `miosa workspace create customer-1` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
4. Branding and white-label - Your name and slug on previews, deployments, and the desktop; customers never see MIOSA. - `miosa org` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
5. Usage metering and bill-to - Usage per customer, and which account pays for new machines. - `miosa org bill` [Docs](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing)

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as You
  participant M as MIOSA Computer
  participant P as Model provider
  participant D as MIOSA Deploy

  U->>M: install the tool from its official docs
  M->>P: calls with your own provider key
  U->>M: run a real task
  M-->>U: output, files
  U->>D: publish it for your team or your customers
```

## How it runs on MIOSA

Where it runs -> a MIOSA computer (a persistent desktop with a browser)

State and files -> State, memory and credentials live on the machine. Use a MIOSA computer so the Gateway stays up between conversations, and extend its TTL (`miosa extend`).

Model -> your own provider key, never a MIOSA platform key

Your customers -> one workspace each, isolated from each other

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash
miosa workspace create openclaw-customer-1
```

Tag every machine and run with the customer id in `metadata`, and never query across customers. Meter usage per customer with GET /api/v1/usage and set who pays with PUT /api/v1/bill-to (/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Install OpenClaw

Run these inside the computer (its terminal), in order. The commands are from the official docs.

```text
curl -fsSL https://openclaw.ai/install.sh | bash
```

Check: the install finishes without errors; the next sections configure and start it.

## Configure

Node 24.16+ or 26.1+ is required; the installer provisions it when needed. The package route is `npm install -g openclaw@latest --allow-scripts=openclaw`.

Onboarding verifies model access, creates the workspace and configures the Gateway; it asks for your own model provider key.

Channels (WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack and others) are connected by you with each platform's own credentials.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (entered in the tool's own setup); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

## Run it

Start it and prove it works.

```text
openclaw onboard --install-daemon
```

```text
openclaw gateway status
```

Check: the tool starts without errors and responds.

## Persistence and access

State, memory and credentials live on the machine. Use a MIOSA computer so the Gateway stays up between conversations, and extend its TTL (`miosa extend`).

Check: after the machine pauses and resumes, the tool starts again with its state intact.

## Make it a product

Run one Gateway per customer on its own computer in that customer's workspace, so state, memory and credentials never mix.

## Limits and costs

Pin the version you tested and update deliberately; these tools change quickly.

Give the tool only the credentials it needs, as secrets, not baked into files.

Prototype: keep it to one machine at the default size, skip replicas and custom hostnames you do not need, and delete everything when you are done.

## Acceptance checks

pages.description: Perplexity: Search, read, and answer with citations. Build it on MIOSA with the exact resources, steps and commands.
pages.markdown:
`~25 min` `TypeScript` `Python`

> **What you're building**: Search, read, and answer with citations.
>
> **Primitives you'll use**: Sandbox, Agent and harness, Qdrant vectors, Deployment (Docker Host)

## What you're building

an answer engine that searches the web, reads sources and answers with citations Modelled on Perplexity, by Perplexity.

A question triggers a search, the top pages are fetched and read, and a model writes an answer that cites those sources.

Primitives you'll use: Sandbox · Agent and harness · Qdrant vectors · Deployment (App Engine)

- Searches the web and reads sources
- Answers with numbered citations
- Follow-up questions in a thread
- Focus modes for different domains

Source: [www.perplexity.ai](https://www.perplexity.ai/). Perplexity is a trademark of its owner; this guide is not affiliated with or endorsed by them.

## What you need on MIOSA

Each row is one thing to create before you start. The number matches the step that uses it.

1. Organization and API key - Scopes every call; a workspace key is all a worker needs. - `miosa api-key create app-key --preset agent` [Docs](/docs/platform/api-keys)
2. Sandbox - The isolated Linux workspace the agent writes code and runs commands in. - `miosa create app-box --template nextjs --wait` [Docs](/docs/develop/sandboxes)
3. Qdrant vectors - Managed vector store for search and embeddings, injected as QDRANT_URL. - `miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"app-index","engine":"qdrant"}'` [Docs](/docs/data/qdrant)
4. A workspace per customer - Isolates each customer’s machines, deployments, and data as they onboard. - `miosa workspace create customer-1` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
5. Branding and white-label - Your name and slug on previews, deployments, and the desktop; customers never see MIOSA. - `miosa org` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
6. Usage metering and bill-to - Usage per customer, and which account pays for new machines. - `miosa org bill` [Docs](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing)
7. Agent and harness - Turns a prompt into work: pick the harness and model a run uses. - `miosa agent harnesses` [Docs](/docs/api-reference/agent-runs)
8. Deployment (App Engine) - Publishes the app to an immutable, versioned URL with rollback. - `miosa deploy create --from-sandbox app-box --name app --wait` [Docs](/docs/docker-host/overview)

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant P as Your pipeline
  participant S as Sandbox
  participant V as Vector index
  participant M as Model

  U->>P: ask a question
  P->>S: fetch and extract the top pages
  S->>V: embed and store chunks
  P->>V: retrieve the best chunks
  P->>M: answer from those chunks only
  M-->>P: answer with citations
  P-->>U: answer and its sources
```

## How it maps onto MIOSA

Searches and reads sources -> a MIOSA sandbox running fetch/extract jobs (a computer when pages need a real browser)

Retrieval over what it read -> managed Qdrant (`QDRANT_URL`) for chunk embeddings

Answers with citations -> agent runs (`miosa prompt`, client.runs) streaming events that answer only from retrieved chunks and return source ids

Serves the answer UI or API -> a MIOSA deployment (`miosa deploy create`), immutable and versioned

## Data and storage

Qdrant holds chunk embeddings; the payload carries url, title, chunk id and fetched_at so every answer can cite a saved page.

Keep threads and answers in your own datastore, with their citations.

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash
miosa workspace create perplexity-customer-1
```

Tag every machine and run with the customer id in `metadata`, and never query across customers. Meter usage per customer with GET /api/v1/usage and set who pays with PUT /api/v1/bill-to (/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Agent loop

Harness: OSA is MIOSA's own harness and works with any model provider you connect, including your own model.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (`miosa connections add models`); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

Sessions: one chat per project or conversation, so the agent keeps its context. The first `miosa prompt` on a sandbox uses `--new-chat` (a chat id is printed); every later turn passes `--chat <chat-id>`. `--reuse chat` keeps one new machine per chat so files persist.

Streaming: follow a run with `miosa run follow <run-id>` or client.runs.streamEvents(run.id), and steer or stop it with `miosa run steer` and `miosa run interrupt`.

Retrieval comes first, generation second: the model sees only retrieved chunks and must cite them. The harness runs in the pipeline sandbox so fetching and extraction code is isolated.

## Steps

1. Create the vector index.
   ```bash
   miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"perplexity-index","engine":"qdrant"}'
   ```
   Check: QDRANT_URL and QDRANT_API_KEY are available to the pipeline.
2. Create the pipeline sandbox that fetches, extracts and indexes pages.
   ```bash
   miosa create perplexity-box --template agent-python --wait
   ```
   Check: The sandbox is running and can fetch a public URL.
3. Retrieve: for a question, call a search source you bring (a search API) or crawl a defined corpus, fetch the pages, and extract clean text with url, title and fetched_at.
   Check: Every stored page has a URL and a fetch time.
4. Chunk, embed and upsert into Qdrant with the url, title and chunk id in the payload.
   Check: The chunk count in Qdrant matches what you extracted.
5. Answer: give the model ONLY the retrieved chunks and instruct it to answer from them, citing chunk numbers; if the chunks do not contain the answer it must say so.
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --sandbox perplexity-box --harness osa --model <anthropic-model-id> --chat <chat-id> "Answer the question using only the provided chunks; cite them as [n]"
   ```
   Check: Every claim carries a citation that resolves to a saved page; an unanswerable question gets "I could not find this".
6. Follow-ups: keep a thread id and the last turns, and rewrite the follow-up into a standalone query before retrieval.
   Check: "And what about its price?" retrieves about the right product.
7. Publish the answer UI: stream the answer text first, then the citations.
   ```bash
   miosa deploy create --from-sandbox perplexity-box --name perplexity --dir /workspace --port 3000 --run-command "npm start" --wait
   ```
   Check: The public_url answers a question end to end.

## Limits and costs

Respect robots.txt and rate limits when crawling; cache fetched pages so repeated questions do not refetch.

Bound retrieval: a fixed number of chunks per answer keeps latency and cost predictable.

Prototype: keep it to one machine at the default size, skip replicas and custom hostnames you do not need, and delete everything when you are done.

## Acceptance checks

Answers cite sources and the citations resolve to saved pages.

A question the index cannot answer is declined, not invented.

Each customer is isolated in its own workspace and usage is metered against them.

Everything it created can be deleted with nothing left running.

- [Run coding agents Run Claude Code, Codex or Cursor in the cloud, or build a product on them.](/docs/build/run-agents)
- [Compare MIOSA How MIOSA compares to other sandbox and agent platforms.](/docs/compare)
- [What you can build Every product pattern MIOSA supports.](/docs/use-cases)

Harness: OSA is MIOSA's own harness and works with any model provider you connect, including your own model.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (`miosa connections add models`); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

Sessions: one chat per project or conversation, so the agent keeps its context. The first `miosa prompt` on a sandbox uses `--new-chat` (a chat id is printed); every later turn passes `--chat <chat-id>`. `--reuse chat` keeps one new machine per chat so files persist.

Streaming: follow a run with `miosa run follow <run-id>` or client.runs.streamEvents(run.id), and steer or stop it with `miosa run steer` and `miosa run interrupt`.

Retrieval comes first, generation second: the model sees only retrieved chunks and must cite them. The harness runs in the pipeline sandbox so fetching and extraction code is isolated.

## Steps

1. Create the vector index.
   ```bash
   miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"phind-index","engine":"qdrant"}'
   ```
   Check: QDRANT_URL and QDRANT_API_KEY are available to the pipeline.
2. Create the pipeline sandbox that fetches, extracts and indexes pages.
   ```bash
   miosa create phind-box --template agent-python --wait
   ```
   Check: The sandbox is running and can fetch a public URL.
3. Retrieve: for a question, call a search source you bring (a search API) or crawl a defined corpus, fetch the pages, and extract clean text with url, title and fetched_at.
   Check: Every stored page has a URL and a fetch time.
4. Chunk, embed and upsert into Qdrant with the url, title and chunk id in the payload.
   Check: The chunk count in Qdrant matches what you extracted.
5. Answer as an artifact: give the model ONLY the retrieved chunks and ask for a small self-contained app (a chart, a calculator, a runnable code sample) plus a one-line summary, citing chunk numbers. Do not ask for an essay.
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --sandbox phind-box --harness osa --model <anthropic-model-id> --chat <chat-id> "Answer the question using only the provided chunks; cite them as [n]"
   ```
   Check: Every claim carries a citation that resolves to a saved page; an unanswerable question gets "I could not find this".
6. Render the artifact: the sandbox builds the returned app and your UI embeds it in a sandboxed iframe next to the sources, so the answer is something the reader can run, not just read.
   ```bash
   miosa preview create phind-box 3000 --name answer
   ```
   Check: The answer renders as a live artifact, and re-running the same question from the stored spec renders the same thing.
7. Follow-ups: keep a thread id and the last turns, and rewrite the follow-up into a standalone query before retrieval.
   Check: "And what about its price?" retrieves about the right product.
8. Publish the answer UI: stream the answer text first, then the citations.
   ```bash
   miosa deploy create --from-sandbox phind-box --name phind --dir /workspace --port 3000 --run-command "npm start" --wait
   ```
   Check: The public_url answers a question end to end.

## Limits and costs

Respect robots.txt and rate limits when crawling; cache fetched pages so repeated questions do not refetch.

Bound retrieval: a fixed number of chunks per answer keeps latency and cost predictable.

Prototype: keep it to one machine at the default size, skip replicas and custom hostnames you do not need, and delete everything when you are done.

## Acceptance checks

Answers cite sources and the citations resolve to saved pages.

A question the index cannot answer is declined, not invented.

Each customer is isolated in its own workspace and usage is metered against them.

Everything it created can be deleted with nothing left running.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant P as Your pipeline
  participant S as Sandbox
  participant V as Vector index
  participant M as Model

  U->>P: ask a question
  P->>S: fetch and extract the top pages
```

Answers with citations -> agent runs (`miosa prompt`, client.runs) streaming events that answer only from retrieved chunks and return source ids

Serves the answer UI or API -> a MIOSA deployment (`miosa deploy create`), immutable and versioned

## Data and storage

Qdrant holds chunk embeddings; the payload carries url, title, chunk id and fetched_at so every answer can cite a saved page.

Keep threads and answers in your own datastore, with their citations.

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash

```

Tag every machine and run with the customer id in `metadata`, and never query across customers. Meter usage per customer with GET /api/v1/usage and set who pays with PUT /api/v1/bill-to (/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Agent loop

Retrieval comes first, generation second: the model sees only retrieved chunks and must cite them. The harness runs in the pipeline sandbox so fetching and extraction code is isolated.

## Steps

1. Create the vector index.
   ```bash
   miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"deep-research-index","engine":"qdrant"}'
   ```
   Check: QDRANT_URL and QDRANT_API_KEY are available to the pipeline.
2. Create the pipeline sandbox that fetches, extracts and indexes pages.
   ```bash
   miosa create deep-research-box --template agent-python --wait
   ```
   Check: The sandbox is running and can fetch a public URL.
3. Retrieve: for a question, call a search source you bring (a search API) or crawl a defined corpus, fetch the pages, and extract clean text with url, title and fetched_at.
   Check: Every stored page has a URL and a fetch time.
4. Chunk, embed and upsert into Qdrant with the url, title and chunk id in the payload.
   Check: The chunk count in Qdrant matches what you extracted.
5. Research run: plan sub-questions, search and read many sources, and write a structured report with citations. This takes minutes, so run it long and report progress.
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --sandbox deep-research-box --harness osa --model <anthropic-model-id> --chat <chat-id> "Research: <question>. Plan, read sources, write report.md with numbered citations"
   ```

