pages.title: Build an OpenSwarm-style multi-agent app
pages.description: OpenSwarm: An AI desktop built around running several agents in parallel. Build it on MIOSA with the exact resources, steps and commands.
pages.markdown:
`~25 min` `TypeScript` `Python`

> **What you're building**: An AI desktop built around running several agents in parallel.
>
> **Primitives you'll use**: Sandbox, Computer, Agent and harness, Deployment (Docker Host)

## What you're building

an AI desktop app built around running several agents in parallel (proprietary; distributed as signed builds) Modelled on OpenSwarm, by OpenSwarm.

An orchestrator breaks a goal into parts and runs agents on them at the same time, then combines what they return.

Primitives you'll use: Sandbox · Computer · Agent and harness · Deployment (App Engine)

- An orchestrator that runs agents in parallel
- Each agent works on a part of the goal
- A combined result
- A desktop to watch and steer it

Source: [openswarm.com](https://openswarm.com/). OpenSwarm is a trademark of its owner; this guide is not affiliated with or endorsed by them.

## What you need on MIOSA

Each row is one thing to create before you start. The number matches the step that uses it.

1. Organization and API key - Scopes every call; a workspace key is all a worker needs. - `miosa api-key create app-key --preset agent` [Docs](/docs/platform/api-keys)
2. Sandbox - The isolated Linux workspace the agent writes code and runs commands in. - `miosa create app-box --template nextjs --wait` [Docs](/docs/develop/sandboxes)
3. Computer - A persistent Linux desktop for browser, mouse, and screenshot work. - `miosa computer create app-desktop` [Docs](/docs/computers/overview)
4. A workspace per customer - Isolates each customer’s machines, deployments, and data as they onboard. - `miosa workspace create customer-1` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
5. Branding and white-label - Your name and slug on previews, deployments, and the desktop; customers never see MIOSA. - `miosa org` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
6. Usage metering and bill-to - Usage per customer, and which account pays for new machines. - `miosa org bill` [Docs](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing)
7. Agent and harness - Turns a prompt into work: pick the harness and model a run uses. - `miosa agent harnesses` [Docs](/docs/api-reference/agent-runs)
8. Deployment (App Engine) - Publishes the app to an immutable, versioned URL with rollback. - `miosa deploy create --from-sandbox app-box --name app --wait` [Docs](/docs/docker-host/overview)

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant O as Orchestrator
  participant W1 as Worker 1
  participant W2 as Worker 2

  U->>O: give the goal
  O->>O: plan and split the work
  O->>W1: dispatch subtask, group id, role
  O->>W2: dispatch subtask, group id, role
  W1-->>O: result and artifacts
  W2-->>O: result and artifacts
  O->>O: join the results
  O-->>U: one combined answer
```

## How it maps onto MIOSA

An orchestrator that plans and delegates -> agent runs (`miosa prompt`, client.runs) streaming events from your orchestrator process in its own sandbox

Workers that run in parallel -> one sandbox per worker (`orchestration_role`, `agent_run_group_id` tie them together)

Shared starting state -> sandbox snapshots and fork: snapshot once, restore into each worker

Joined result -> client.runs.waitForCompletion, then run outputs and files from every worker

## Data and storage

Keep the plan (subtasks, owners, status) and each worker's result keyed by the run group id, so a failed join can resume and the UI can show who did what.

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash
miosa workspace create openswarm-customer-1
```

Tag every machine and run with the customer id in `metadata`, and never query across customers. Meter usage per customer with GET /api/v1/usage and set who pays with PUT /api/v1/bill-to (/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Agent loop

Harness: OSA is MIOSA's own harness and works with any model provider you connect, including your own model.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (`miosa connections add models`); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

Sessions: one chat per project or conversation, so the agent keeps its context. The first `miosa prompt` on a sandbox uses `--new-chat` (a chat id is printed); every later turn passes `--chat <chat-id>`. `--reuse chat` keeps one new machine per chat so files persist.

Streaming: follow a run with `miosa run follow <run-id>` or client.runs.streamEvents(run.id), and steer or stop it with `miosa run steer` and `miosa run interrupt`.

The orchestrator is an agent that decides the subtasks; workers are separate harness runs, each on its own machine. Give each worker a narrow role and only the tools it needs. Cap the number of workers and the depth of delegation.

## Steps

1. Create the orchestrator's own sandbox. It plans and delegates; it does not do the work.
   ```bash
   miosa create openswarm-orchestrator --wait
   ```
   Check: The orchestrator can create other sandboxes with the SDK.
2. Create one worker sandbox per child agent (a fresh, isolated machine each).
   ```bash
   miosa create openswarm-worker-1 --wait
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa create openswarm-worker-2 --wait
   ```
   Check: Two workers are running and cannot see each other's files.
3. Create ONE shared computer for children that need a desktop or browser.
   ```bash
   miosa computer create openswarm-desktop
   ```
   Check: A desktop child can open a browser; code children never touch it.
4. Snapshot the orchestrator workspace once and restore it into each worker so they start from the same state.
   ```text
   sandbox.snapshots.create("shared start")
   ```
   Check: Every worker begins with identical files.
5. Fan out: dispatch one run per worker, tied together by a group id and a role.
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --sandbox openswarm-worker-1 --harness osa --model <anthropic-model-id> --chat <chat-id> "<subtask>"
   ```
   ```text
   client.agentRuns.run({ provider: "osa", targetKind: "sandbox", targetId: worker1.id, orchestration_role: "researcher", agent_run_group_id: "grp_1", prompt: "<subtask>" })
   ```
   Check: The runs execute in parallel and show the same group id.
6. Join: wait for every run, collect each output and files, and let the orchestrator merge them. Retry only the worker that failed.
   ```text
   client.runs.waitForCompletion(run.id)
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa run outputs <run-id>
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa run files <run-id>
   ```
   Check: One failed worker is retried without rerunning the others.
7. Publish the joined report or the orchestrator UI.
   ```bash
   miosa deploy create --from-sandbox openswarm-orchestrator --name openswarm --dir /workspace --wait
   ```
   Check: The public_url shows the joined result.

## Limits and costs

Parallelism multiplies cost: cap workers per job and give every run `--max-time`.

Use `idempotency_key` on `sandboxes.create` in retry loops so a retried fan-out does not create duplicates.

Prefer fewer, better-scoped workers over many shallow ones.

Prototype: keep it to one machine at the default size, skip replicas and custom hostnames you do not need, and delete everything when you are done.

## Acceptance checks

Every child run completes and its output is collected.

Children are isolated from each other; only desktop children share the computer.

The orchestrator's final answer cites which worker produced what.

Each customer is isolated in its own workspace and usage is metered against them.

Everything it created can be deleted with nothing left running.

## Next steps

- [Agent prompt builder Pick a product shape and hand the brief to your agent.](/docs/build)
- [Run coding agents Run Claude Code, Codex or Cursor in the cloud, or build a product on them.](/docs/build/run-agents)
- [Compare MIOSA How MIOSA compares to other sandbox and agent platforms.](/docs/compare)
- [What you can build Every product pattern MIOSA supports.](/docs/use-cases)

## Install Hermes Agent

Run these inside the sandbox (for example `miosa exec hermes-agent-box -- bash -lc '<command>'`), in order. The commands are from the official docs.

```text

```

Check: the install finishes without errors; the next sections configure and start it.

5. Branding and white-label - Your name and slug on previews, deployments, and the desktop; customers never see MIOSA. - `miosa org` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)

7. Agent and harness - Turns a prompt into work: pick the harness and model a run uses. - `miosa agent harnesses` [Docs](/docs/api-reference/agent-runs)
8. Deployment (App Engine) - Publishes the app to an immutable, versioned URL with rollback. - `miosa deploy create --from-sandbox app-box --name app --wait` [Docs](/docs/docker-host/overview)

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant O as Orchestrator
  participant W1 as Worker 1
  participant W2 as Worker 2

  U->>O: give the goal
  O->>O: plan and split the work
  O->>W1: dispatch subtask, group id, role
  O->>W2: dispatch subtask, group id, role
  W1-->>O: result and artifacts
  W2-->>O: result and artifacts
  O->>O: join the results
  O-->>U: one combined answer
```

## How it maps onto MIOSA

An orchestrator that plans and delegates -> agent runs (`miosa prompt`, client.runs) streaming events from your orchestrator process in its own sandbox

Workers that run in parallel -> one sandbox per worker (`orchestration_role`, `agent_run_group_id` tie them together)

Shared starting state -> sandbox snapshots and fork: snapshot once, restore into each worker

Joined result -> client.runs.waitForCompletion, then run outputs and files from every worker

## Data and storage

Keep the plan (subtasks, owners, status) and each worker's result keyed by the run group id, so a failed join can resume and the UI can show who did what.

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash
miosa workspace create gemini-agent-customer-1
```

Tag every machine and run with the customer id in `metadata`, and never query across customers. Meter usage per customer with GET /api/v1/usage and set who pays with PUT /api/v1/bill-to (/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Agent loop

Harness: OSA is MIOSA's own harness and works with any model provider you connect, including your own model.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (`miosa connections add models`); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

Sessions: one chat per project or conversation, so the agent keeps its context. The first `miosa prompt` on a sandbox uses `--new-chat` (a chat id is printed); every later turn passes `--chat <chat-id>`. `--reuse chat` keeps one new machine per chat so files persist.

Streaming: follow a run with `miosa run follow <run-id>` or client.runs.streamEvents(run.id), and steer or stop it with `miosa run steer` and `miosa run interrupt`.

The orchestrator is an agent that decides the subtasks; workers are separate harness runs, each on its own machine. Give each worker a narrow role and only the tools it needs. Cap the number of workers and the depth of delegation.

## Steps

1. Create the orchestrator's own sandbox. It plans and delegates; it does not do the work.
   ```bash
   miosa create gemini-agent-orchestrator --wait
   ```
   Check: The orchestrator can create other sandboxes with the SDK.
2. Create one worker sandbox per child agent (a fresh, isolated machine each).
   ```bash
   miosa create gemini-agent-worker-1 --wait
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa create gemini-agent-worker-2 --wait
   ```
   Check: Two workers are running and cannot see each other's files.
3. Connect the business systems the sub-agents act on as tool servers, one connection per system, scoped to what each sub-agent needs.
   ```bash
   miosa connections add models anthropic --key-stdin <<< "$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa connections add tools --name <system> --url <mcp-server-url> --header-env Authorization=<ENV_VAR>
   ```
   Check: Each sub-agent can call only its own system's tools.
4. Snapshot the orchestrator workspace once and restore it into each worker so they start from the same state.
   ```text
   sandbox.snapshots.create("shared start")
   ```
   Check: Every worker begins with identical files.
5. Fan out: dispatch one run per worker, tied together by a group id and a role.
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --sandbox gemini-agent-worker-1 --harness osa --model <anthropic-model-id> --chat <chat-id> "<subtask>"
   ```
   ```text
   client.agentRuns.run({ provider: "osa", targetKind: "sandbox", targetId: worker1.id, orchestration_role: "researcher", agent_run_group_id: "grp_1", prompt: "<subtask>" })
   ```
   Check: The runs execute in parallel and show the same group id.
6. Join: wait for every run, collect each output and files, and let the orchestrator merge them. Retry only the worker that failed.
   ```text
   client.runs.waitForCompletion(run.id)
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa run outputs <run-id>
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa run files <run-id>
   ```
   Check: One failed worker is retried without rerunning the others.
7. Persist the plan and every worker result in Postgres so a crashed orchestrator can resume.
   ```bash
   miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"gemini-agent-state","engine":"postgresql"}'
   ```
   Check: Killing the orchestrator mid-run and restarting it resumes from stored state.
8. Publish the joined report or the orchestrator UI.
   ```bash
   miosa deploy create --from-sandbox gemini-agent-orchestrator --name gemini-agent --dir /workspace --wait
   ```
   Check: The public_url shows the joined result.

## Limits and costs

Parallelism multiplies cost: cap workers per job and give every run `--max-time`.

Use `idempotency_key` on `sandboxes.create` in retry loops so a retried fan-out does not create duplicates.

Prefer fewer, better-scoped workers over many shallow ones.

Prototype: keep it to one machine at the default size, skip replicas and custom hostnames you do not need, and delete everything when you are done.

## Acceptance checks

Every child run completes and its output is collected.

Children are isolated from each other.

The orchestrator's final answer cites which worker produced what.

Each customer is isolated in its own workspace and usage is metered against them.

Everything it created can be deleted with nothing left running.

## Next steps

- [Agent prompt builder Pick a product shape and hand the brief to your agent.](/docs/build)
- [Run coding agents Run Claude Code, Codex or Cursor in the cloud, or build a product on them.](/docs/build/run-agents)
- [Compare MIOSA How MIOSA compares to other sandbox and agent platforms.](/docs/compare)
- [What you can build Every product pattern MIOSA supports.](/docs/use-cases)

pages.markdown:

> **What you're building**: A voice agent that talks and takes real actions.
>
> **Primitives you'll use**: Sandbox, Agent and harness, Redis, Deployment (Docker Host)

## What you're building

a platform for building voice agents that talk and take actions Modelled on ElevenLabs Agents, by ElevenLabs.

2. Sandbox - The isolated Linux workspace the agent writes code and runs commands in. - `miosa create app-box --template nextjs --wait` [Docs](/docs/develop/sandboxes)
3. Redis - Managed cache and session store, injected as REDIS_URL. - `miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"app-cache","engine":"redis"}'` [Docs](/docs/data/redis)
4. A workspace per customer - Isolates each customer’s machines, deployments, and data as they onboard. - `miosa workspace create customer-1` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
5. Branding and white-label - Your name and slug on previews, deployments, and the desktop; customers never see MIOSA. - `miosa org` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
6. Usage metering and bill-to - Usage per customer, and which account pays for new machines. - `miosa org bill` [Docs](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing)
7. Agent and harness - Turns a prompt into work: pick the harness and model a run uses. - `miosa agent harnesses` [Docs](/docs/api-reference/agent-runs)
8. Deployment (App Engine) - Publishes the app to an immutable, versioned URL with rollback. - `miosa deploy create --from-sandbox app-box --name app --wait` [Docs](/docs/docker-host/overview)

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Caller
  participant V as Voice provider
  participant P as Your service
  participant R as Managed Redis
  participant T as Your systems

  C->>V: speak
  V->>P: transcript and call id
  P->>R: load per-call session state
  P->>T: call a tool mid-call
  T-->>P: result
  P->>R: save the turn
  P->>V: text to speak
  V-->>C: spoken reply
```

## How it maps onto MIOSA

Real-time conversation loop -> a MIOSA sandbox running the pipeline (speech-to-text, LLM, text-to-speech) as a background process

Per-call session state -> managed Redis (`REDIS_URL`) keyed by call id

Tools the agent can call mid-call -> agent runs (`miosa prompt`, client.runs) streaming events in a sandbox that holds your tool code

A stable endpoint for the telephony or web client -> a MIOSA deployment (`miosa deploy create`), immutable and versioned

## Data and storage

Redis holds live per-call session state (it is read on every turn, so it must be fast). Transcripts and outcomes are durable records.

Write transcripts and outcomes to your own durable store after each call.

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash
miosa workspace create elevenlabs-customer-1
```

Tag every machine and run with the customer id in `metadata`, and never query across customers. Meter usage per customer with GET /api/v1/usage and set who pays with PUT /api/v1/bill-to (/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Agent loop

Harness: OSA is MIOSA's own harness and works with any model provider you connect, including your own model.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (`miosa connections add models`); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

Sessions: one chat per project or conversation, so the agent keeps its context. The first `miosa prompt` on a sandbox uses `--new-chat` (a chat id is printed); every later turn passes `--chat <chat-id>`. `--reuse chat` keeps one new machine per chat so files persist.

Streaming: follow a run with `miosa run follow <run-id>` or client.runs.streamEvents(run.id), and steer or stop it with `miosa run steer` and `miosa run interrupt`.

The real-time audio loop (speech-to-text, model, text-to-speech) is run by your voice provider. Your side is the brain and the hands: a low-latency decision per turn plus tools that act on your systems.

Use the harness for tool work and post-call analysis, not for each spoken turn: a spoken turn must answer in about a second.

## Steps

1. Create the session store.
   ```bash
   miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"elevenlabs-sessions","engine":"redis"}'
   ```
   Check: REDIS_URL is available; a key set with a TTL expires.
2. Create the sandbox that runs your agent service and tool handlers.
   ```bash
   miosa create elevenlabs-box --template agent-node --wait
   ```
   Check: The sandbox is running.
3. Bring the telephony and voice providers. MIOSA does not provide phone numbers, speech-to-text or voice models: connect your own provider keys (ElevenLabs, Vapi, Retell, Twilio, or similar) and point their webhooks at your deployment.
   Check: A provider webhook test reaches your service, and the keys are stored with the Secrets API, never in the sandbox `env`.
4. Implement the tools the agent may call mid-call (look up an order, book a slot) as HTTP handlers in the sandbox. Keep each under a second; for slow work, acknowledge and finish asynchronously.
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --sandbox elevenlabs-box --harness osa --model <anthropic-model-id> --chat <chat-id> "Handle tool call <name> with args <json>; reply with JSON only"
   ```
   Check: A tool call returns within the latency budget and the caller hears no long silence.

   Check: A dropped and rejoined call resumes with its state.
6. Publish the webhook and tool endpoints; providers need a public, stable URL.
   ```bash
   miosa deploy create --from-sandbox elevenlabs-box --name elevenlabs --dir /workspace --port 3000 --run-command "npm start" --wait
   ```
   Check: The public_url answers the provider's health check.

## Limits and costs

Latency is the product: keep tool handlers fast, keep the sandbox warm (not paused), and put the deployment in the region closest to your telephony provider.

Telephony minutes and voice models are billed by your providers, separately from MIOSA.

Record calls only where the caller has been told and has consented.

Prototype: keep it to one machine at the default size, skip replicas and custom hostnames you do not need, and delete everything when you are done.

## Acceptance checks

A test call completes: greeting, a tool call, and a clean hang-up.

The transcript and outcome are stored.

The agent hands off to a human when it cannot continue.

Each customer is isolated in its own workspace and usage is metered against them.

Everything it created can be deleted with nothing left running.

## Next steps

- [Agent prompt builder Pick a product shape and hand the brief to your agent.](/docs/build)
- [Run coding agents Run Claude Code, Codex or Cursor in the cloud, or build a product on them.](/docs/build/run-agents)
- [Compare MIOSA How MIOSA compares to other sandbox and agent platforms.](/docs/compare)
- [What you can build Every product pattern MIOSA supports.](/docs/use-cases)

pages.markdown:
`~25 min` `TypeScript` `Python`

> **What you're building**: Programmable phone agents at scale.
>
> **Primitives you'll use**: Sandbox, Agent and harness, Redis, Deployment (Docker Host)

## What you're building

programmable phone agents that run calls at scale Modelled on Bland AI, by Bland AI.

You define a call task and tools; the platform places many calls in parallel and returns transcripts and outcomes.

Primitives you'll use: Sandbox · Agent and harness · Redis · Deployment (App Engine)

- Programmable phone agents
- Calls at scale
- Tools and transfers
- Transcripts and outcomes

Source: [bland.ai](https://bland.ai/). Bland AI is a trademark of its owner; this guide is not affiliated with or endorsed by them.

## What you need on MIOSA

Each row is one thing to create before you start. The number matches the step that uses it.

1. Organization and API key - Scopes every call; a workspace key is all a worker needs. - `miosa api-key create app-key --preset agent` [Docs](/docs/platform/api-keys)
2. Sandbox - The isolated Linux workspace the agent writes code and runs commands in. - `miosa create app-box --template nextjs --wait` [Docs](/docs/develop/sandboxes)
3. Redis - Managed cache and session store, injected as REDIS_URL. - `miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"app-cache","engine":"redis"}'` [Docs](/docs/data/redis)
4. A workspace per customer - Isolates each customer’s machines, deployments, and data as they onboard. - `miosa workspace create customer-1` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
5. Branding and white-label - Your name and slug on previews, deployments, and the desktop; customers never see MIOSA. - `miosa org` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
6. Usage metering and bill-to - Usage per customer, and which account pays for new machines. - `miosa org bill` [Docs](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing)
7. Agent and harness - Turns a prompt into work: pick the harness and model a run uses. - `miosa agent harnesses` [Docs](/docs/api-reference/agent-runs)
8. Deployment (App Engine) - Publishes the app to an immutable, versioned URL with rollback. - `miosa deploy create --from-sandbox app-box --name app --wait` [Docs](/docs/docker-host/overview)

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Caller
  participant V as Voice provider
  participant P as Your service
  participant R as Managed Redis
  participant T as Your systems

  C->>V: speak
  V->>P: transcript and call id
  P->>R: load per-call session state
  P->>T: call a tool mid-call
  T-->>P: result
  P->>R: save the turn
  P->>V: text to speak
  V-->>C: spoken reply
```

## How it maps onto MIOSA

Real-time conversation loop -> a MIOSA sandbox running the pipeline (speech-to-text, LLM, text-to-speech) as a background process

Per-call session state -> managed Redis (`REDIS_URL`) keyed by call id

Tools the agent can call mid-call -> agent runs (`miosa prompt`, client.runs) streaming events in a sandbox that holds your tool code

A stable endpoint for the telephony or web client -> a MIOSA deployment (`miosa deploy create`), immutable and versioned

Batches of calls -> one run per call in a queue, concurrency capped to your limits

## Data and storage

Redis holds live per-call session state (it is read on every turn, so it must be fast). Transcripts and outcomes are durable records.

Write transcripts and outcomes to your own durable store after each call.

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash
miosa workspace create bland-customer-1
```

Tag every machine and run with the customer id in `metadata`, and never query across customers. Meter usage per customer with GET /api/v1/usage and set who pays with PUT /api/v1/bill-to (/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Agent loop

Harness: OSA is MIOSA's own harness and works with any model provider you connect, including your own model.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (`miosa connections add models`); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

Sessions: one chat per project or conversation, so the agent keeps its context. The first `miosa prompt` on a sandbox uses `--new-chat` (a chat id is printed); every later turn passes `--chat <chat-id>`. `--reuse chat` keeps one new machine per chat so files persist.

Streaming: follow a run with `miosa run follow <run-id>` or client.runs.streamEvents(run.id), and steer or stop it with `miosa run steer` and `miosa run interrupt`.

The real-time audio loop (speech-to-text, model, text-to-speech) is run by your voice provider. Your side is the brain and the hands: a low-latency decision per turn plus tools that act on your systems.

Use the harness for tool work and post-call analysis, not for each spoken turn: a spoken turn must answer in about a second.

## Steps

1. Create the session store.
   ```bash
   miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"bland-sessions","engine":"redis"}'
   ```
   Check: REDIS_URL is available; a key set with a TTL expires.
2. Create the sandbox that runs your agent service and tool handlers.
   ```bash
   miosa create bland-box --template agent-node --wait
   ```
   Check: The sandbox is running.
3. Bring the telephony and voice providers. MIOSA does not provide phone numbers, speech-to-text or voice models: connect your own provider keys (ElevenLabs, Vapi, Retell, Twilio, or similar) and point their webhooks at your deployment.
   Check: A provider webhook test reaches your service, and the keys are stored with the Secrets API, never in the sandbox `env`.
4. Implement the tools the agent may call mid-call (look up an order, book a slot) as HTTP handlers in the sandbox. Keep each under a second; for slow work, acknowledge and finish asynchronously.
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --sandbox bland-box --harness osa --model <anthropic-model-id> --chat <chat-id> "Handle tool call <name> with args <json>; reply with JSON only"
   ```
   Check: A tool call returns within the latency budget and the caller hears no long silence.
5. Keep per-call state in Redis keyed by call id with a TTL (turns so far, collected fields, handoff flags).
   Check: A dropped and rejoined call resumes with its state.
6. Batch calling: queue numbers, run calls with a concurrency cap, respect calling windows and consent, and record outcomes per number.
   Check: Concurrency never exceeds the cap, and do-not-call numbers are skipped.
7. Publish the webhook and tool endpoints; providers need a public, stable URL.
   ```bash
   miosa deploy create --from-sandbox bland-box --name bland --dir /workspace --port 3000 --run-command "npm start" --wait
   ```
   Check: The public_url answers the provider's health check.

## Limits and costs

Latency is the product: keep tool handlers fast, keep the sandbox warm (not paused), and put the deployment in the region closest to your telephony provider.

Telephony minutes and voice models are billed by your providers, separately from MIOSA.

Record calls only where the caller has been told and has consented.

Prototype: keep it to one machine at the default size, skip replicas and custom hostnames you do not need, and delete everything when you are done.

## Acceptance checks

A test call completes: greeting, a tool call, and a clean hang-up.

The transcript and outcome are stored.

The agent hands off to a human when it cannot continue.

Each customer is isolated in its own workspace and usage is metered against them.

Everything it created can be deleted with nothing left running.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
```

Your customers -> one workspace each, isolated from each other


## Install Pipecat

Run these inside the sandbox (for example `miosa exec pipecat-box -- bash -lc '<command>'`), in order. The commands are from the official docs.

```text
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
```

```text
uv tool install "pipecat-ai[cli]"
```

```text
pipecat init
```

```text
# or, by hand: uv init my-pipecat-app && cd my-pipecat-app && uv add pipecat-ai
```

Check: the install finishes without errors; the next sections configure and start it.

## Configure

Add the provider extras you use (`uv add "pipecat-ai[option,...]"`) and put your own speech-to-text, LLM and text-to-speech keys in `.env`. Telephony and WebRTC transports are external providers you bring.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="..."   # set it in the process environment, or the Secrets API; never write it into files you commit
```

Start it and prove it works.

```text
uv run bot.py
```

```bash
miosa preview create pipecat-box 7860 --name web
```

Check: the preview URL answers, and still answers after the machine pauses and resumes (previews wake it on request).

One bot process per customer workspace (or a pool with a session router); session state in Redis keyed by call id.

## Limits and costs

Pin the version you tested and update deliberately; these tools change quickly.

Give the tool only the credentials it needs, as secrets, not baked into files.

Pipecat runs on a MIOSA sandbox and answers a real task.

State survives a pause and resume.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
```

```mermaid
  participant P as Your tool
  participant S as Project sandbox
```

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant P as Your app
  participant Q as Job queue
  participant G as Generation API
  participant S as Render sandbox

  U->>P: submit a prompt or a script
  P->>Q: create a job
  Q->>G: call the model provider you bring
  G-->>Q: clip or voice track
  Q->>S: compose and encode with ffmpeg
  S-->>P: finished media file
  P-->>U: progress, then the result
  U->>P: publish or download
```

## How it maps onto MIOSA

Prompt to asset -> agent runs (`miosa prompt`, client.runs) streaming events that call your generation provider and write results into the sandbox

Heavy rendering and encoding -> a MIOSA sandbox jobs (ffmpeg or headless rendering), sized up with `--size`

Projects and assets -> managed Postgres (`DATABASE_URL`) for job metadata; files and volumes for the media

Preview before export -> a sandbox preview URL (`miosa preview create`)

## Data and storage

Jobs (status, inputs, output path) are metadata; the media itself is large, so keep it as files in the render sandbox and a volume, not in Postgres.

Assets are content-addressed by hash so identical inputs are never regenerated.

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash

```

Tag every machine and run with the customer id in `metadata`, and never query across customers. Meter usage per customer with GET /api/v1/usage and set who pays with PUT /api/v1/bill-to (/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Agent loop

Harness: OSA is MIOSA's own harness and works with any model provider you connect, including your own model.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (`miosa connections add models`); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

Streaming: follow a run with `miosa run follow <run-id>` or client.runs.streamEvents(run.id), and steer or stop it with `miosa run steer` and `miosa run interrupt`.

The generation model is a provider you bring; the harness orchestrates the job in a sandbox and runs ffmpeg for everything deterministic. Keep generation and rendering as separate, retryable steps.

## Steps

1. Create the render worker: a larger sandbox for encoding and compositing.
   ```bash
   miosa create runway-box --size large --wait
   ```
   Check: The sandbox is running.
2. Call the generation model you bring (your provider's API) with the prompt or image; store the returned clip.
   Check: The provider returns a clip or transcript and you store its job id.
3. Post-process in the sandbox: trim, stitch, add captions and audio, and encode with ffmpeg (install it in your template once, not per job).
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --sandbox runway-box --harness osa --model <anthropic-model-id> --chat <chat-id> "Assemble the final video from /workspace/jobs/<id> with ffmpeg and write it to /workspace/out"
   ```

   ```bash
   miosa run follow <run-id>
   ```
   Check: The UI shows progress while the job runs and the final file when done.
5. Preview and export: serve the output for playback, and offer a download.
   ```bash
   miosa preview create runway-box 3000 --name web
   ```
   Check: The preview plays the clip; the download has the right size and format.
6. Publish the app that accepts jobs and plays results.
   ```bash
   miosa deploy create --from-sandbox runway-box --name runway --dir /workspace --port 3000 --run-command "npm start" --wait
   ```

A job runs from input to a playable output file.

```mermaid

  U->>P: submit a prompt or a script
```

Decks, images and templates -> managed Postgres (`DATABASE_URL`) for deck metadata, object storage for the rendered assets

2. Generate the deck structure with the text model you bring: first an outline, then one record per slide (title, bullets, speaker notes). Return JSON, not HTML; the layout is yours.
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --sandbox gamma-box --harness osa --model <anthropic-model-id> --chat <chat-id> "Turn <document> into slide JSON: outline first, then one object per slide; no markup"
   ```

3. Render in the sandbox: your templates turn the slide JSON into HTML, and the headless browser renders images and a PDF. Images come from the image model you bring, cached by prompt.


3. A workspace per customer - Isolates each customer’s machines, deployments, and data as they onboard. - `miosa workspace create customer-1` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
4. Branding and white-label - Your name and slug on previews, deployments, and the desktop; customers never see MIOSA. - `miosa org` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
5. Usage metering and bill-to - Usage per customer, and which account pays for new machines. - `miosa org bill` [Docs](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing)
6. Agent and harness - Turns a prompt into work: pick the harness and model a run uses. - `miosa agent harnesses` [Docs](/docs/api-reference/agent-runs)
7. Deployment (App Engine) - Publishes the app to an immutable, versioned URL with rollback. - `miosa deploy create --from-sandbox app-box --name app --wait` [Docs](/docs/docker-host/overview)

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant P as Your app
  participant Q as Job queue
  participant G as Generation API
  participant S as Render sandbox

  U->>P: submit a prompt or a script
  P->>Q: create a job
  Q->>G: call the model provider you bring
  G-->>Q: clip or voice track
  Q->>S: compose and encode with ffmpeg
  S-->>P: finished media file
  P-->>U: progress, then the result
  U->>P: publish or download
```

## How it maps onto MIOSA

Prompt to asset -> agent runs (`miosa prompt`, client.runs) streaming events that call your generation provider and write results into the sandbox

Heavy rendering and encoding -> a MIOSA sandbox jobs (ffmpeg or headless rendering), sized up with `--size`

Projects and assets -> managed Postgres (`DATABASE_URL`) for job metadata; files and volumes for the media

Preview before export -> a sandbox preview URL (`miosa preview create`)

## Data and storage

Jobs (status, inputs, output path) are metadata; the media itself is large, so keep it as files in the render sandbox and a volume, not in Postgres.

Assets are content-addressed by hash so identical inputs are never regenerated.

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash
miosa workspace create descript-customer-1
```

Tag every machine and run with the customer id in `metadata`, and never query across customers. Meter usage per customer with GET /api/v1/usage and set who pays with PUT /api/v1/bill-to (/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Agent loop

Harness: OSA is MIOSA's own harness and works with any model provider you connect, including your own model.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (`miosa connections add models`); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

Sessions: one chat per project or conversation, so the agent keeps its context. The first `miosa prompt` on a sandbox uses `--new-chat` (a chat id is printed); every later turn passes `--chat <chat-id>`. `--reuse chat` keeps one new machine per chat so files persist.

Streaming: follow a run with `miosa run follow <run-id>` or client.runs.streamEvents(run.id), and steer or stop it with `miosa run steer` and `miosa run interrupt`.

The generation model is a provider you bring; the harness orchestrates the job in a sandbox and runs ffmpeg for everything deterministic. Keep generation and rendering as separate, retryable steps.

## Steps

1. Create the render worker: a larger sandbox for encoding and compositing.
   ```bash
   miosa create descript-box --size large --wait
   ```
   Check: The sandbox is running.
2. Ingest: transcribe the media with a speech-to-text provider you bring, and store the transcript with word timestamps.
   Check: The provider returns a clip or transcript and you store its job id.
3. Apply edits: deleting or moving words becomes a list of cuts that ffmpeg applies to the original media.
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --sandbox descript-box --harness osa --model <anthropic-model-id> --chat <chat-id> "Assemble the final video from /workspace/jobs/<id> with ffmpeg and write it to /workspace/out"
   ```
   Check: The output plays, has the right duration, and the job row points to it.
4. Show progress: stream run events to the UI so a long render never looks hung.
   ```bash
   miosa run follow <run-id>
   ```
   Check: The UI shows progress while the job runs and the final file when done.
5. Preview and export: serve the output for playback, and offer a download.
   ```bash
   miosa preview create descript-box 3000 --name web
   ```
   Check: The preview plays the clip; the download has the right size and format.
6. Publish the app that accepts jobs and plays results.
   ```bash
   miosa deploy create --from-sandbox descript-box --name descript --dir /workspace --port 3000 --run-command "npm start" --wait
   ```
   Check: The public_url accepts a job and plays the finished result.

## Limits and costs

Rendering is the cost: size the sandbox to the job, set `timeout_sec` up to the longest render, and pause or destroy workers when the queue is empty.

Provider usage (generation, speech) is billed by those providers; store your own job-level cost.

Prototype: keep it to one machine at the default size, skip replicas and custom hostnames you do not need, and delete everything when you are done.

## Acceptance checks

A job runs from input to a playable output file.

A failed provider call leaves the job retryable, not stuck.

Progress is visible while a job runs.

Each customer is isolated in its own workspace and usage is metered against them.

Everything it created can be deleted with nothing left running.

- [Run coding agents Run Claude Code, Codex or Cursor in the cloud, or build a product on them.](/docs/build/run-agents)
- [Compare MIOSA How MIOSA compares to other sandbox and agent platforms.](/docs/compare)
- [What you can build Every product pattern MIOSA supports.](/docs/use-cases)

## What you're building

- Answers from your help center

- Hands off to a human

4. A workspace per customer - Isolates each customer’s machines, deployments, and data as they onboard. - `miosa workspace create customer-1` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
5. Branding and white-label - Your name and slug on previews, deployments, and the desktop; customers never see MIOSA. - `miosa org` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
6. Usage metering and bill-to - Usage per customer, and which account pays for new machines. - `miosa org bill` [Docs](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing)
7. Agent and harness - Turns a prompt into work: pick the harness and model a run uses. - `miosa agent harnesses` [Docs](/docs/api-reference/agent-runs)
8. Deployment (App Engine) - Publishes the app to an immutable, versioned URL with rollback. - `miosa deploy create --from-sandbox app-box --name app --wait` [Docs](/docs/docker-host/overview)

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant P as Your app
  participant A as Agent sandbox
  participant T as Systems and index
  participant H as Human reviewer

  U->>P: open a case
  P->>A: run the agent with scoped tools
  A->>T: read records and retrieve sources
  T-->>A: facts with their sources
  A-->>P: a proposal with citations
  P->>H: request approval when it matters
  H-->>P: approve or edit
  P->>T: apply the change, write the audit row
```

## How it maps onto MIOSA

The agent that does the domain work -> agent runs (`miosa prompt`, client.runs) streaming events in a sandbox, with the tools it may call defined by you

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash

```

## Agent loop

Harness: OSA is MIOSA's own harness and works with any model provider you connect, including your own model.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (`miosa connections add models`); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

Sessions: one chat per project or conversation, so the agent keeps its context. The first `miosa prompt` on a sandbox uses `--new-chat` (a chat id is printed); every later turn passes `--chat <chat-id>`. `--reuse chat` keeps one new machine per chat so files persist.

The agent runs inside the sandbox with only the tools you defined. It proposes; your code enforces limits (refund caps, allowed recipients) so the model cannot talk its way past them.

## Steps

1. Create the domain database.
   ```bash
   miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"intercom-fin-db","engine":"postgresql"}'
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa db connection intercom-fin-db
   ```
   Check: Domain tables exist: customers, tickets, messages, actions.
2. Create the agent sandbox.
   ```bash
   miosa create intercom-fin-box --template agent-python --wait
   ```
   Check: The sandbox is running with DATABASE_URL set.
3. Load the knowledge base (help center, policies) into a vector index so answers cite policy.
   ```bash
   miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"intercom-fin-knowledge","engine":"qdrant"}'
   ```
   Check: A policy, document or article question retrieves the right passage.
4. Define the tools the agent may call on real systems (look up an order, refund within a limit, change an address) as narrow functions with typed arguments.
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --sandbox intercom-fin-box --harness osa --model <anthropic-model-id> --chat <chat-id> "Resolve ticket <id> using only the defined tools and the cited policy; escalate if unsure"
   ```
   Check: The agent completes the case using only those tools.

   ```bash
   miosa agent approvals
   ```
   Check: A refund over the limit, a send, or a filing waits for approval.


   ```bash

   ```
   Check: The public_url serves the review queue.

Customer data is personal data: store only what the task needs, honour deletion requests, and keep an audit trail.

Keep tenant data separate: a workspace per customer, and every query filtered by tenant.

Set `--max-time` on runs and cap tool calls per case.

Prototype: keep it to one machine at the default size, skip replicas and custom hostnames you do not need, and delete everything when you are done.

## Acceptance checks

The agent resolves a representative case end to end using only the defined tools.

A high-stakes action waited for human approval.

The audit trail reconstructs the decision.

Each customer is isolated in its own workspace and usage is metered against them.

Everything it created can be deleted with nothing left running.

- [Run coding agents Run Claude Code, Codex or Cursor in the cloud, or build a product on them.](/docs/build/run-agents)

pages.markdown:

> **What you're building**: Turn call transcripts into sourced insights and next steps.
>

## What you're building

a post-call analysis agent: call transcripts in, sourced insights and next steps out Modelled on Gong, by Gong.

Call and email transcripts are analysed by an agent that extracts commitments, objections and next steps, attaching a timestamped quote to every claim, and surfaces them to the rep.

Primitives you'll use: Sandbox · Agent and harness · Postgres · Deployment (App Engine)

- Post-call analysis over transcripts
- Every insight quotes the moment it came from
- Suggested next steps
- A per-deal history

Source: [www.gong.io](https://www.gong.io/). Gong is a trademark of its owner; this guide is not affiliated with or endorsed by them.

## What you need on MIOSA

Each row is one thing to create before you start. The number matches the step that uses it.

1. Organization and API key - Scopes every call; a workspace key is all a worker needs. - `miosa api-key create app-key --preset agent` [Docs](/docs/platform/api-keys)
2. Sandbox - The isolated Linux workspace the agent writes code and runs commands in. - `miosa create app-box --template nextjs --wait` [Docs](/docs/develop/sandboxes)
3. Postgres - Managed relational data, injected as DATABASE_URL in the machine and in production. - `miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"app-db","engine":"postgresql"}'` [Docs](/docs/data/postgres)
4. A workspace per customer - Isolates each customer’s machines, deployments, and data as they onboard. - `miosa workspace create customer-1` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
5. Branding and white-label - Your name and slug on previews, deployments, and the desktop; customers never see MIOSA. - `miosa org` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
6. Usage metering and bill-to - Usage per customer, and which account pays for new machines. - `miosa org bill` [Docs](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing)
7. Agent and harness - Turns a prompt into work: pick the harness and model a run uses. - `miosa agent harnesses` [Docs](/docs/api-reference/agent-runs)
8. Deployment (App Engine) - Publishes the app to an immutable, versioned URL with rollback. - `miosa deploy create --from-sandbox app-box --name app --wait` [Docs](/docs/docker-host/overview)

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant P as Your app
  participant A as Agent sandbox
  participant T as Systems and index
  participant H as Human reviewer

  U->>P: open a case
  P->>A: run the agent with scoped tools
  A->>T: read records and retrieve sources
  T-->>A: facts with their sources
  A-->>P: a proposal with citations
  P->>H: request approval when it matters
  H-->>P: approve or edit
  P->>T: apply the change, write the audit row
```

## How it maps onto MIOSA

The agent that does the domain work -> agent runs (`miosa prompt`, client.runs) streaming events in a sandbox, with the tools it may call defined by you

Domain records and history -> managed Postgres (`DATABASE_URL`) for records, citations and an audit trail

Each customer is isolated -> a workspace per customer (`miosa workspace create`)

Human review and escalation -> agent approvals (`miosa agent approvals`) and a review queue in your product

## Data and storage

Postgres is the system of record with an append-only audit table; nothing the agent decides exists only in a prompt.

Keep sources with every stored field so a human can check them.

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash
miosa workspace create gong-customer-1
```

Tag every machine and run with the customer id in `metadata`, and never query across customers. Meter usage per customer with GET /api/v1/usage and set who pays with PUT /api/v1/bill-to (/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Agent loop

Harness: OSA is MIOSA's own harness and works with any model provider you connect, including your own model.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (`miosa connections add models`); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

Sessions: one chat per project or conversation, so the agent keeps its context. The first `miosa prompt` on a sandbox uses `--new-chat` (a chat id is printed); every later turn passes `--chat <chat-id>`. `--reuse chat` keeps one new machine per chat so files persist.

Streaming: follow a run with `miosa run follow <run-id>` or client.runs.streamEvents(run.id), and steer or stop it with `miosa run steer` and `miosa run interrupt`.

The agent runs inside the sandbox with only the tools you defined. It proposes; your code enforces limits (refund caps, allowed recipients) so the model cannot talk its way past them.

## Steps

1. Create the domain database.
   ```bash
   miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"gong-db","engine":"postgresql"}'
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa db connection gong-db
   ```
   Check: Domain tables exist: accounts, people, enrichment fields with their sources, drafts.
2. Create the agent sandbox.
   ```bash
   miosa create gong-box --template agent-python --wait
   ```
   Check: The sandbox is running with DATABASE_URL set.
3. Define the enrichment tools (company data, people data, web research); every returned field must carry its source URL.
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --sandbox gong-box --harness osa --model <anthropic-model-id> --chat <chat-id> "Enrich account <id>: find the people and facts, attach a source URL to every field, draft the first email"
   ```
   Check: The agent completes the case using only those tools.
4. Put a human in the loop where it matters: the agent proposes, a person approves anything irreversible or high-stakes, and low-confidence cases escalate with context.
   ```bash
   miosa agent approvals
   ```
   Check: A refund over the limit, a send, or a filing waits for approval.
5. Write an audit record for every agent action: who, what, inputs, outputs, and the run id.
   ```bash
   miosa audit
   ```
   Check: Any decision can be reconstructed from the audit trail.
6. Publish the agent API and the review UI.
   ```bash
   miosa deploy create --from-sandbox gong-box --name gong --dir /workspace --port 3000 --run-command "npm start" --wait
   ```
   Check: The public_url serves the review queue.

## Limits and costs

Customer data is personal data: store only what the task needs, honour deletion requests, and keep an audit trail.

Keep tenant data separate: a workspace per customer, and every query filtered by tenant.

Set `--max-time` on runs and cap tool calls per case.

Prototype: keep it to one machine at the default size, skip replicas and custom hostnames you do not need, and delete everything when you are done.

## Acceptance checks

The agent resolves a representative case end to end using only the defined tools.

A high-stakes action waited for human approval.

The audit trail reconstructs the decision.

Each customer is isolated in its own workspace and usage is metered against them.

Everything it created can be deleted with nothing left running.

## What you're building

a medical evidence engine: clinician questions answered from a trusted corpus, with citations back to the source article Modelled on OpenEvidence, by OpenEvidence.

A question is answered by retrieval first: the app searches a licensed or public corpus, reads the passages, and a model writes an answer that cites the source article; figures and tables come from the retrieved passage.

9. Deployment (App Engine) - Publishes the app to an immutable, versioned URL with rollback. - `miosa deploy create --from-sandbox app-box --name app --wait` [Docs](/docs/docker-host/overview)

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant P as Your app
  participant A as Agent sandbox
  participant T as Systems and index
  participant H as Human reviewer

  U->>P: open a case
  P->>A: run the agent with scoped tools
  A->>T: read records and retrieve sources
  T-->>A: facts with their sources
  A-->>P: a proposal with citations
  P->>H: request approval when it matters
```

Source documents -> object storage (S3-compatible buckets)

Ingestion and re-embedding -> agent runs in a sandbox, on a schedule (`miosa schedule`)

Answer synthesis -> a model API you bring; no proprietary model or search index of our own

## Data and storage

Postgres is the system of record with an append-only audit table; nothing the agent decides exists only in a prompt.

A vector index backs retrieval; keep source ids so every cited passage resolves.

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash
miosa workspace create openevidence-customer-1
```

## Steps

   ```bash
   miosa create openevidence-box --template agent-python --wait
   ```
   Check: The sandbox is running with DATABASE_URL set.
3. Ingest the corpus into a vector index: split each source into passages and keep the article id, section and page in the payload so an answer can cite the exact passage it used.
   ```bash
   miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"openevidence-corpus","engine":"qdrant"}'
   ```
   Check: A policy, document or article question retrieves the right passage.
4. Define read-only retrieval over the corpus. The agent answers only from retrieved passages and must cite the passage it used; if the corpus does not answer the question it says so.
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --sandbox openevidence-box --harness osa --model <anthropic-model-id> --chat <chat-id> "Handle the case using only the defined tools; cite sources; escalate if unsure"
   ```

pages.title: Build an internal Business OS
pages.description: BusinessOS is MIOSA's own Apache-2.0 internal company OS. Clone the real repo, run it on a MIOSA sandbox or computer, preview it, customize the modules, and publish it behind your own domain.
pages.markdown:
`~15 min` `TypeScript` `Python`

> **What you're building**: MIOSA's own BusinessOS template, Apache 2.0 - one private internal company OS where your team's agents, apps, and data live together.
>
> **Primitives you'll use**: Organization and API key, Sandbox, Computer, Postgres, Deployment (Docker Host), Custom domain

![The BusinessOS desktop: draggable module windows, a real local terminal, and the OSA assistant](https://miosa.ai/docs-assets/build/business-os.png)

*The BusinessOS desktop - draggable module windows, a real local terminal, and the OSA assistant. Screenshot from the BusinessOS repository (Apache-2.0).*

## What you're building

an open-source operating layer for running a business: workspaces, modules, a terminal and agents

A local-first desktop and web app: a Go backend with PostgreSQL and Redis, a SvelteKit frontend, an optional Electron shell, and a bundled Optimal Engine for knowledge and agent context.

Primitives you'll use: Organization and API key · Sandbox · Computer · Postgres · Deployment (App Engine) · Custom domain

- Draggable, persistent module windows
- Workspaces, roles and teams
- A real terminal (PTY) surface
- Governed knowledge and memory through Optimal Engine
- A custom-module builder

You install and **run the real BusinessOS** on MIOSA. Read the official docs first: [github.com/Miosa-osa/BusinessOS](https://github.com/Miosa-osa/BusinessOS). Every install command below comes from them; if the docs and this guide disagree, the docs win. BusinessOS is open source (Apache-2.0), from MIOSA.

## What you need on MIOSA

Each row is one thing to create before you start. The number matches the step that uses it.

1. Organization and API key - Scopes every call; a workspace key is all a worker needs. - `miosa api-key create app-key --preset agent` [Docs](/docs/platform/api-keys)
2. Sandbox - The isolated Linux workspace the agent writes code and runs commands in. - `miosa create app-box --template nextjs --wait` [Docs](/docs/develop/sandboxes)
3. Computer - A persistent Linux desktop for browser, mouse, and screenshot work. - `miosa computer create app-desktop` [Docs](/docs/computers/overview)
4. Postgres - Managed relational data, injected as DATABASE_URL in the machine and in production. - `miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"app-db","engine":"postgresql"}'` [Docs](/docs/data/postgres)
5. A workspace per customer - Isolates each customer’s machines, deployments, and data as they onboard. - `miosa workspace create customer-1` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
6. Branding and white-label - Your name and slug on previews, deployments, and the desktop; customers never see MIOSA. - `miosa org` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
7. Usage metering and bill-to - Usage per customer, and which account pays for new machines. - `miosa org bill` [Docs](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing)
8. Deployment (App Engine) - Publishes the app to an immutable, versioned URL with rollback. - `miosa deploy create --from-sandbox app-box --name app --wait` [Docs](/docs/docker-host/overview)
9. Custom domain - Puts the app on a hostname you own, with HTTPS. - `miosa deploy domain-add app app.example.com` [Docs](/docs/docker-host/domains)

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant T as Your team
  participant B as BusinessOS (Go + SvelteKit)
  participant S as MIOSA Sandbox
  participant D as MIOSA Deploy

  T->>S: clone Miosa-osa/BusinessOS and run make onboard
  S->>B: start Go backend, SvelteKit frontend, Postgres and Redis
  B-->>T: the internal OS on a preview URL
  T->>B: work in modules, then customize them in the clone
  T->>D: publish the web frontend
  D-->>T: https os.example.net
```

## How it runs on MIOSA

Where it runs -> a MIOSA sandbox (an isolated Linux workspace)

State and files -> Do not delete `.run/pgdata`; it is the local database. A persistent sandbox keeps it across pauses.

Model -> your own provider key, never a MIOSA platform key

Its web port 5273 -> a MIOSA preview URL (`miosa preview create`)

Your customers -> one workspace each, isolated from each other

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash
miosa workspace create business-os-customer-1
```

Tag every machine and run with the customer id in `metadata`, and never query across customers. Meter usage per customer with GET /api/v1/usage and set who pays with PUT /api/v1/bill-to (/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Install BusinessOS

Run these inside the sandbox (for example `miosa exec business-os-box -- bash -lc '<command>'`), in order. The commands are from the official docs.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Miosa-osa/BusinessOS.git /workspace/BusinessOS
```

```bash
cd /workspace/BusinessOS
```

```text
make onboard
```

Check: the install finishes without errors; the next sections configure and start it.

## Configure

`make onboard` checks tools, creates local env files, initialises an isolated PostgreSQL cluster and Redis under `.run/`, starts the bundled Optimal Engine, installs dependencies and starts the backend, frontend and (unless `BUSINESSOS_HEADLESS=1`) the Electron shell. It needs Node 22+, pnpm 9.15.4, Go 1.26.2, PostgreSQL 14+, Redis 7+, Elixir/Mix and Python 3.

Model: chosen by your agent. Use a current model from a provider I have connected; ask which if none is.

## Run it

Start it and prove it works.

```text
make dev-local-verify
```

```text
make dev-local-status
```

Check: the tool starts without errors and responds.

## Persistence and access

Do not delete `.run/pgdata`; it is the local database. A persistent sandbox keeps it across pauses.

It listens on port 5273. Run it as a background process so it outlives your shell, then open a preview:

```bash
miosa preview create business-os-box 5273 --name web
```

Check: the preview URL answers, and still answers after the machine pauses and resumes (previews wake it on request).

## Make it a product

It is an internal-company OS; do not resell it as a multi-tenant product without reading its licence and README.

## Limits and costs

Pin the version you tested and update deliberately; these tools change quickly.

Give the tool only the credentials it needs, as secrets, not baked into files.

Prototype: keep it to one machine at the default size, skip replicas and custom hostnames you do not need, and delete everything when you are done.

## Acceptance checks

BusinessOS runs on a MIOSA sandbox and answers a real task.

State survives a pause and resume.

Each customer has its own workspace and its own instance; nothing is shared between them.

Everything it created can be deleted with nothing left running.

## Next steps

- [Agent prompt builder Pick a product shape and hand the brief to your agent.](/docs/build)
- [Run coding agents Run Claude Code, Codex or Cursor in the cloud, or build a product on them.](/docs/build/run-agents)
- [Compare MIOSA How MIOSA compares to other sandbox and agent platforms.](/docs/compare)
- [What you can build Every product pattern MIOSA supports.](/docs/use-cases)

## Customizing it

BusinessOS is a template, not a fixed product: the meaning of a module comes from your company, not from the repo. A fresh install shows an intentional unshaped-module screen until you give it shape. Everything you edit lives in the clone you already have:

- **Frontend and modules** live in `frontend/` (SvelteKit). A module is a route plus the people, agents, records, states, and policies it owns; start from an existing foundational route as a template.
- **Go backend** lives in `desktop/`: the API your modules call for their data.
- **Knowledge and agents** come from the bundled Optimal Engine in `optimal-engine/`, which gives the assistant memory, search, and agent context over your own data.
- **Workspace shape** lives in `workspaces/`: teams, roles, and the private projections a workspace starts from.

Change code in the running machine and restart the stack to see it:

```bash
miosa exec business-os-box --cwd /workspace/BusinessOS -- make dev-local-restart
```

The repository's own [docs/](https://github.com/Miosa-osa/BusinessOS/tree/main/docs) cover the architecture, module authoring, and operations in depth.

5. Usage metering and bill-to - Usage per customer, and which account pays for new machines. - `miosa org bill` [Docs](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing)

7. Deployment (App Engine) - Publishes the app to an immutable, versioned URL with rollback. - `miosa deploy create --from-sandbox app-box --name app --wait` [Docs](/docs/docker-host/overview)

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant M as Teammate
  participant O as One organization
  participant W as Team workspace
  participant S as Sandbox
  participant A as Agent run

  M->>O: sign in with a role
  O->>W: scope machines and data to the team
  M->>A: ask for something
  A->>S: work inside the team sandbox
  A-->>M: a result, a draft or a built tool
  M->>M: approve anything consequential
```

## How it maps onto MIOSA

One organization for the company -> the MIOSA organization, with teammates as members (`miosa member add`)

A workspace per team -> `miosa workspace create`

Agents that do work -> agent runs (`miosa prompt`, client.runs) streaming events in a sandbox

Audit -> `miosa audit`

## Data and storage

Keep application data in managed Postgres with a row-level owner (member id or team), and keep an append-only audit table for agent actions.

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash
miosa workspace create team-ai-workspace-customer-1
```

Tag every machine and run with the customer id in `metadata`, and never query across customers. Meter usage per customer with GET /api/v1/usage and set who pays with PUT /api/v1/bill-to (/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Agent loop

Harness: OSA is MIOSA's own harness and works with any model provider you connect, including your own model.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (`miosa connections add models`); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

Sessions: one chat per project or conversation, so the agent keeps its context. The first `miosa prompt` on a sandbox uses `--new-chat` (a chat id is printed); every later turn passes `--chat <chat-id>`. `--reuse chat` keeps one new machine per chat so files persist.

Streaming: follow a run with `miosa run follow <run-id>` or client.runs.streamEvents(run.id), and steer or stop it with `miosa run steer` and `miosa run interrupt`.

Agents act as members: every run carries the asking member's id in `metadata`, uses credentials scoped to that member or team, and cannot exceed what the member may do.

## Steps

1. Create a workspace per team inside the one organization, and invite members.
   ```bash
   miosa workspace create team-ai-workspace-ops
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa org invite dana@team-ai-workspace.com
   ```
   Check: A member of one team cannot see another team's machines.
2. Run the chat backend and agent runner in a sandbox in each team workspace.
   ```bash
   miosa create team-ai-workspace-box --template agent-node --wait
   ```
   Check: Each team has its own backend.
3. Dispatch agent work from the chat, on the team's sandbox, with the member's id in run metadata.
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --sandbox team-ai-workspace-box --harness osa --model <anthropic-model-id> --chat <chat-id> "<request from the member>"
   ```
   Check: Every run shows who asked and which team it ran for.
4. Control access: members and roles, and an audit trail of what agents did.
   ```bash
   miosa member add dana@team-ai-workspace.com --role member
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa audit
   ```
   Check: A removed member loses access immediately.
5. Publish the internal UI.
   ```bash
   miosa deploy create --from-sandbox team-ai-workspace-box --name team-ai-workspace --dir /workspace --port 3000 --run-command "npm start" --wait
   ```
   Check: Members can open it and nobody else can.

## Limits and costs

Connectors are the real work: budget time for each source system's auth, rate limits and data shape.

Set `idle_timeout_sec` so unused team sandboxes pause.

Prefer read-only access by default; grant writes per task.

Prototype: keep it to one machine at the default size, skip replicas and custom hostnames you do not need, and delete everything when you are done.

## Acceptance checks

Members see only their team's data and tools.

Every agent action is attributable to a member in the audit log.

Nothing consequential happens without the approval the guide describes.

Each customer is isolated in its own workspace and usage is metered against them.

Everything it created can be deleted with nothing left running.

## What you need on MIOSA

Each row is one thing to create before you start. The number matches the step that uses it.

1. Organization and API key - Scopes every call; a workspace key is all a worker needs. - `miosa api-key create app-key --preset agent` [Docs](/docs/platform/api-keys)
2. Sandbox - The isolated Linux workspace the agent writes code and runs commands in. - `miosa create app-box --template nextjs --wait` [Docs](/docs/develop/sandboxes)
3. Qdrant vectors - Managed vector store for search and embeddings, injected as QDRANT_URL. - `miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"app-index","engine":"qdrant"}'` [Docs](/docs/data/qdrant)
4. A workspace per customer - Isolates each customer’s machines, deployments, and data as they onboard. - `miosa workspace create customer-1` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
5. Branding and white-label - Your name and slug on previews, deployments, and the desktop; customers never see MIOSA. - `miosa org` [Docs](/docs/platform/white-label)
6. Usage metering and bill-to - Usage per customer, and which account pays for new machines. - `miosa org bill` [Docs](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing)
7. Agent and harness - Turns a prompt into work: pick the harness and model a run uses. - `miosa agent harnesses` [Docs](/docs/api-reference/agent-runs)
8. Deployment (App Engine) - Publishes the app to an immutable, versioned URL with rollback. - `miosa deploy create --from-sandbox app-box --name app --wait` [Docs](/docs/docker-host/overview)

## Architecture

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant M as Teammate
  participant O as One organization
  participant W as Team workspace
  participant S as Sandbox
  participant A as Agent run

  M->>O: sign in with a role
  O->>W: scope machines and data to the team
  M->>A: ask for something
  A->>S: work inside the team sandbox
  A-->>M: a result, a draft or a built tool
  M->>M: approve anything consequential
```

## How it maps onto MIOSA

Provisioning in isolation -> a MIOSA sandbox with scoped credentials

Answers from the handbook -> managed Qdrant (`QDRANT_URL`)

Checklist state per hire -> managed Postgres (`DATABASE_URL`)

Org membership -> `miosa org invite`, `miosa member add`

## Data and storage

Keep application data in managed Postgres with a row-level owner (member id or team), and keep an append-only audit table for agent actions.

## Auth and tenancy

Your organization is the platform; customers never get a MIOSA account, they sign into YOUR product. One workspace per customer, created as they onboard, isolates their machines, runs and data.

```bash
miosa workspace create employee-onboarding-agent-customer-1
```

Tag every machine and run with the customer id in `metadata`, and never query across customers. Meter usage per customer with GET /api/v1/usage and set who pays with PUT /api/v1/bill-to (/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Agent loop

Harness: OSA is MIOSA's own harness and works with any model provider you connect, including your own model.

Model: Anthropic (Claude). Calls use my own provider key (`miosa connections add models`); MIOSA platform keys are never used.

Sessions: one chat per project or conversation, so the agent keeps its context. The first `miosa prompt` on a sandbox uses `--new-chat` (a chat id is printed); every later turn passes `--chat <chat-id>`. `--reuse chat` keeps one new machine per chat so files persist.

Streaming: follow a run with `miosa run follow <run-id>` or client.runs.streamEvents(run.id), and steer or stop it with `miosa run steer` and `miosa run interrupt`.

Agents act as members: every run carries the asking member's id in `metadata`, uses credentials scoped to that member or team, and cannot exceed what the member may do.

## Steps

1. Store the checklist and each hire's progress.
   ```bash
   miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"employee-onboarding-agent-onboarding","engine":"postgresql"}'
   ```
   Check: A new hire has a checklist with item states.
2. Provision what each item needs in a sandbox with scoped credentials (repos, accounts, access), recording each grant.
   ```bash
   miosa create employee-onboarding-agent-box --template agent-node --wait
   ```
   Check: Every grant is logged and revocable.
3. Answer questions from the handbook with citations.
   ```bash
   miosa api POST /databases -d '{"name":"employee-onboarding-agent-handbook","engine":"qdrant"}'
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa prompt --sandbox employee-onboarding-agent-box --harness osa --model <anthropic-model-id> --chat <chat-id> "Answer from the handbook chunks; cite them"
   ```
   Check: A policy question is answered with a link to the handbook page.
4. Report progress to the manager and escalate blocked items.
   Check: The manager sees what is done and what is stuck.
5. Control access: members and roles, and an audit trail of what agents did.
   ```bash
   miosa member add dana@employee-onboarding-agent.com --role member
   ```
   ```bash
   miosa audit
   ```
   Check: A removed member loses access immediately.
6. Publish the internal UI.
   ```bash
   miosa deploy create --from-sandbox employee-onboarding-agent-box --name employee-onboarding-agent --dir /workspace --port 3000 --run-command "npm start" --wait
   ```
   Check: Members can open it and nobody else can.

## Limits and costs

Connectors are the real work: budget time for each source system's auth, rate limits and data shape.

Set `idle_timeout_sec` so unused team sandboxes pause.

Prefer read-only access by default; grant writes per task.

Prototype: keep it to one machine at the default size, skip replicas and custom hostnames you do not need, and delete everything when you are done.

## Acceptance checks

Members see only their team's data and tools.

Every agent action is attributable to a member in the audit log.

Nothing consequential happens without the approval the guide describes.

Each customer is isolated in its own workspace and usage is metered against them.

Everything it created can be deleted with nothing left running.

## Next steps

- [Agent prompt builder Pick a product shape and hand the brief to your agent.](/docs/build)
- [Run coding agents Run Claude Code, Codex or Cursor in the cloud, or build a product on them.](/docs/build/run-agents)
- [Compare MIOSA How MIOSA compares to other sandbox and agent platforms.](/docs/compare)
- [What you can build Every product pattern MIOSA supports.](/docs/use-cases)

pages.title: CLI or MCP: which to use
pages.description: The miosa CLI is for humans and scripts in a terminal; MCP gives AI clients the same capabilities as tools. Both use the same API key and scopes.
pages.markdown:
CLI & MCP

Two ways into the same platform, with the same API key and the same scopes. Pick the one your client can run.

[CLI overview](/docs/cli)[MCP overview](/docs/mcp)[Install the CLI](/docs/cli/install)[MCP tools](/docs/mcp/tools)

- The **CLI** (`miosa`) is for humans, scripts and agents with a shell. You type commands, read text or JSON, and branch on exit codes.
- **MCP** gives AI clients (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Claude Desktop) the same capabilities as tools. The model calls tools by name instead of running shell commands.

Both use the **same API key and the same scopes**. A key that can create a sandbox from the CLI can create one over MCP, and the reverse. The only difference is the surface.

## Which should an agent use?

- **Has a shell? Use the CLI.** Claude Code, Codex, Cursor's terminal and any CI job can run `miosa`. The CLI is often the better choice: it reaches the whole platform, not just one tool surface; output is scriptable; and it composes with `jq`, pipes and files.
- **No shell? Use MCP.** Claude Desktop chat and other hosted chat products have no shell, so tools are the only path. MCP lets the model call capabilities by name.

Nothing is lost either way, because the key, the scopes and the resources are identical.

## Comparison

| | CLI | MCP |
|---|---|---|
| Who drives it | A person, a script, or an agent with a shell | An AI client without a shell (Claude Desktop), or one that prefers tools |
| Interface | `miosa <command> [flags]` | JSON-RPC tools over Streamable HTTP or stdio |
| Install | npm, Homebrew, install script, Releases | Hosted endpoint, no install, or `pip install miosa-mcp` |
| Output | Text or JSON, with exit codes | Structured tool results and images |
| Coverage | The whole platform, plus `miosa api` for any endpoint | The MCP tool surface |
| Best for | Agents with shell access, build loops, CI, one-off operations | Clients without a shell |
| Auth | `msk_u_*` key or a profile | `msk_u_*` key as a Bearer token |
| Scope model | Same key scopes | Same key scopes |

## Use both

A common split: an agent with a shell drives the platform with the CLI, and a client without a shell reaches the same account over MCP with the same key.

```bash
ID=$(miosa create agent-box --size small --wait --json | jq -r .id)   # CLI, from a shell agent
miosa exec "$ID" -- npm test
# the same account over MCP: exec(sandbox_id=ID, command="npm run build")
miosa list --json | jq -r '.data[].name'                              # CLI, read back
```

- [CLI overview](/docs/cli): Install, command groups, global flags and exit codes.
- [MCP overview](/docs/mcp): Connect Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or Claude Desktop.

> **Note**
>
> Both surfaces inherit the same tenant scoping, plan limits, credit checks and audit logging, because both sit in front of the MIOSA REST API.

pages.title: CLI overview
pages.description: The miosa command line tool. Install, sign in, and drive sandboxes, computers, agents, deployments and every platform resource from the terminal.
pages.markdown:
CLI & MCP

The fastest way to control all of MIOSA, for you and your agents. Everything the console does, scriptable, with JSON output.

`npm i -g @miosa/cli`

The miosa CLI on macOS, Linux and Windows. The fastest path inside a container or CI job.

- [Install and authenticate](/docs/cli/install): npm, Homebrew, script or release archive, then sign in.
- [Use from agents](/docs/cli#use-the-cli-from-agents): Let OSA or any agent with a shell drive the platform.
- [Command reference](/docs/cli#command-groups): Every command group, flag and exit code.
- [CLI or MCP](/docs/cli/cli-vs-mcp): Which one to give an agent, and why both work.
