pages.title: MIOSA vs boat
pages.description: A factual comparison of MIOSA and boat (boat.dev), cloud sandboxes for AI agents, using boat's public documentation as of 2026-10-23.
pages.markdown:
Compare

boat and MIOSA both give AI agents their own Linux machines. This page compares what each documents, including where boat is ahead.

Every boat statement below is from boat's own public site and documentation ([boat.dev](https://boat.dev/), [docs.boat.dev](https://docs.boat.dev/)), read on 2026-10-23.
MIOSA statements link to the page that documents them.

## What boat is

boat is a cloud sandbox product for AI agents: persistent Ubuntu VMs with SSH, Docker inside, a desktop, and disk-level forks from snapshots ([boat.dev](https://boat.dev/)).
It was called Box until 2026-09-15; the old `box` CLI and endpoints still work until 2026-10-31 ([migrating from Box](https://docs.boat.dev/migrating-from-box.md)).
It is a sandbox product, not a deploy platform: there is no deploy, custom domain, rollback, or managed database command ([always-on services](https://docs.boat.dev/long-running-tasks/always-on-services.md), [host CLI](https://docs.boat.dev/hosting/host-cli.md)).

boat does not appear in the ComputeSDK runs our [benchmark page](/docs/benchmarks) reports, so this page has no measured comparison.

## Capabilities side by side

| Capability | MIOSA | boat | boat source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Persistent Linux machines | [Yes, sandboxes and computers](/docs/sandboxes-or-computers) | Yes, Ubuntu VMs with SSH | [boat.dev](https://boat.dev/) |
| Docker inside the machine | [Yes](/docs/develop/sandboxes/docker) | Yes | [boat.dev](https://boat.dev/) |
| Full desktop | [Yes, Computers](/docs/computers/overview) | Yes | [boat.dev](https://boat.dev/) |
| Snapshots and forks | [Yes: snapshots, restore, fork, pause and resume](/docs/develop/snapshots) | Yes: stop snapshots the disk, resume and fork from it | [CLI reference](https://docs.boat.dev/cli-reference.md) |
| Fan-out from one snapshot | [Yes, `miosa batch new --count`](/docs/cli/platform) | `boat new --from <snapshot> --count` up to 1000 | [CLI reference](https://docs.boat.dev/cli-reference.md) |
| Resize a running machine | [Yes, in place while running](/docs/develop/sandboxes/sizing) | Stop first, then resume with a new size | [CLI reference](https://docs.boat.dev/cli-reference.md) |
| Public URL for a port | [Yes, previews](/docs/develop/previews) | Yes, `<sandbox>-<port>.on.boat.dev`, token-gated by default | [host CLI](https://docs.boat.dev/hosting/host-cli.md) |
| Deploy to a production URL | [Yes, with releases and rollback](/docs/services/overview) | No; always-on means a systemd unit you write | [always-on services](https://docs.boat.dev/long-running-tasks/always-on-services.md) |
| Custom domains | [Yes](/docs/services/domains) | No | [host CLI](https://docs.boat.dev/hosting/host-cli.md) |
| Managed databases | [Postgres, MySQL, Redis, MongoDB, Qdrant](/docs/data/overview) | Not in the docs index | [llms.txt](https://docs.boat.dev/llms.txt) |
| SDKs | [TypeScript, Python, Go, Elixir, Java, Rust](/docs/sdks) | Python, TypeScript | [quickstart](https://docs.boat.dev/quickstart.md) |
| CLI | [Yes](/docs/cli) | Yes | [CLI reference](https://docs.boat.dev/cli-reference.md) |
| Billing | [Per second while running, one price per size](/docs/pricing) | Per second while running; plans from $20 to $2000 a month come back as compute | [pricing](https://docs.boat.dev/pricing) |
| Regions | [us-east, us-west, us-mia](/docs/regions) | EU only | [pricing](https://docs.boat.dev/pricing) |

## Where boat leads

These are real differences, from boat's documentation:

- **Install signs you in.** The install script opens sign-in and checkout in one step ([quickstart](https://docs.boat.dev/quickstart.md)); MIOSA installs the CLI, then `miosa login` is a second step.
- **Agent self-sign-up is a documented protocol**, with a split start-then-wait login for agents ([agent auth](https://docs.boat.dev/agent-auth.md)).
- **Long commands.** `boat exec --timeout 0` runs without a limit and can detach and re-attach.
- **JSON output switches on when output is piped** ([CLI reference](https://docs.boat.dev/cli-reference.md)); MIOSA needs `--json`.
- **Fan-out from a snapshot** with `--count` up to 1000, and **per-sandbox variables** on create (`-e KEY=VALUE`).
- **Command history** with output, per sandbox (`boat history`).

## Where MIOSA differs

- **Deploy is a product**, not a recipe: deploy from a repository, a directory, or a sandbox, with releases, promote and rollback. See [Services](/docs/services/overview).
- **Custom domains** with DNS verification. See [Domains](/docs/services/domains).
- **Managed databases** with backups and connection strings. See [Databases](/docs/data/overview).
- **Live resize** of a running sandbox, and **checkpoints and restore**. See [Sizing](/docs/develop/sandboxes/sizing) and [Snapshots](/docs/develop/snapshots).
- **One interface for everyone**: MCP, a CLI, and six SDKs. See [MCP](/docs/mcp), [CLI](/docs/cli), [SDKs](/docs/sdks).
- **US regions**, and bring your own cloud on AWS and Google Cloud. See [Regions](/docs/regions) and [BYOC](/docs/infrastructure/byoc/overview).

## When to choose each

- **Choose boat** if you want EU-hosted sandboxes with SSH, unlimited-length commands, and a one-step agent sign-up, and you do not need deploys, domains, or databases from the same product.
- **Choose MIOSA** if you want sandboxes, full computers, deployments, domains, and managed data on one platform, in US regions.

> **Note: boat's own comparison**
>
> boat's compare page lists MIOSA once, as "full VMs with /dev/kvm and no 24-hour timeout" ([boat.dev/compare](https://boat.dev/compare)).
> boat also builds [battleships.dev](https://battleships.dev/), a third-party-looking comparison site; see [the Compare overview](/docs/compare#independent-comparisons).

## Sources

- boat site and docs: https://boat.dev and https://docs.boat.dev (read on 2026-10-23).
- MIOSA capabilities, as documented on this site.

- [MIOSA vs CodeSandbox](/docs/compare/codesandbox): The next comparison.
- [All comparisons](/docs/compare): Every provider MIOSA is measured against.

pages.title: MIOSA vs CodeSandbox
pages.description: A factual comparison of MIOSA and CodeSandbox, using the independent ComputeSDK benchmark and CodeSandbox's public documentation as of October 2026.
pages.markdown:
Compare

CodeSandbox and MIOSA both run code in managed cloud environments. This page compares them on the independent ComputeSDK benchmark and on the capabilities MIOSA documents.

## What CodeSandbox is

CodeSandbox provides instant cloud development environments and sandboxes, described in its public documentation at ([codesandbox.io](https://codesandbox.io/), as of October 2026).

## Measured performance

The independent ComputeSDK benchmark runs the same workload against every provider. That is the only apples-to-apples number here.

| Metric | MIOSA | CodeSandbox | As of |
|---|---|---|---|
| Burst startup, median time-to-interactive | **57.09 ms (#1 of 32)** | 33771.52 ms (#29) | 2026-10-23 |
| DAX full build, 2026-08-28 | **39.3 s (#1 of 19)** | 81.2 s (#13) | 2026-08-28 |
| DAX full build, 2026-10-23 | **38.8 s (#3 of 22)** | no result | 2026-10-23 |

Source: ComputeSDK, via [our benchmark page](/docs/benchmarks). Burst startup is the time from a create request to the first successful command inside a fresh sandbox, under 100 concurrent creates. Where a run is not listed, the provider did not appear in that run.

> **Note: Fair reading**
>
> The burst number here is under heavy concurrency; CodeSandbox is a mature product for interactive development that this benchmark does not fully represent.

## Capabilities side by side

Each CodeSandbox answer comes from CodeSandbox's own documentation, linked in the last column. codesandbox.io blocks automated fetches, so these answers were read from the archived copy of 2026-04-21 and may be out of date.
Each MIOSA answer links the page that documents it.
"Not documented" means the vendor's docs do not say, not that the feature is missing.

| Capability | MIOSA | CodeSandbox | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Isolation | [Firecracker microVM by default](/docs/develop/sandboxes) | Firecracker microVM | [CodeSandbox docs](https://codesandbox.io/docs/sdk/core-concepts) |
| Sandbox lifetime | [Idle timeout, 1 hour by default and up to 24 hours, extendable; computers persist](/docs/develop/sandboxes/timeouts) | Hibernates after 1 minute to 24 hours of inactivity | [CodeSandbox docs](https://codesandbox.io/docs/sdk/hibernate) |
| Pause, snapshots, forks | [Yes: pause and resume, snapshots, restore and fork](/docs/develop/snapshots) | Yes: hibernate and resume with memory, forks | [CodeSandbox docs](https://codesandbox.io/docs/sdk/hibernate) |
| Full Linux desktop and computer use | [Yes, Computers](/docs/computers/overview) | Not documented | [CodeSandbox docs](https://codesandbox.io/docs/sdk) |
| Public preview URL for a port | [Yes](/docs/develop/previews) | Yes | [CodeSandbox docs](https://codesandbox.io/docs/sdk/hosts) |
| Deploy to a production URL | [Yes, Services and Docker Host, with releases and rollback](/docs/services/overview) | Not documented | [CodeSandbox docs](https://codesandbox.io/docs/sdk) |
| Managed databases | [Postgres, MySQL, Redis, MongoDB, Qdrant](/docs/data/overview) | Not documented | [CodeSandbox docs](https://codesandbox.io/docs/sdk) |
| SDKs | [TypeScript, Python, Go, Elixir, Java, Rust](/docs/sdks) | JavaScript/TypeScript | [CodeSandbox docs](https://codesandbox.io/docs/sdk) |
| CLI | [Yes](/docs/cli) | Yes | [CodeSandbox docs](https://codesandbox.io/docs/sdk/cli) |
| MCP server | [Yes, hosted](/docs/mcp) | Not documented | [CodeSandbox docs](https://codesandbox.io/docs/sdk) |
| Bring your own cloud | [Yes, AWS and Google Cloud](/docs/infrastructure/byoc/overview) | No self-hosting | [CodeSandbox docs](https://codesandbox.io/docs/sdk/faq) |
| Billing | [Per second while running, one price per size](/docs/pricing) | Per minute, in VM credits | [CodeSandbox docs](https://codesandbox.io/docs/sdk/pricing) |
| Regions | [us-east, us-west, us-mia](/docs/regions) | Not documented | [CodeSandbox docs](https://codesandbox.io/docs/sdk) |

## Where MIOSA differs

These capabilities are documented for MIOSA on this site:

- **Persistent computers with a full Linux desktop**, not only headless sandboxes. See [Computers](/docs/computers/overview).
- **Deployments and Docker Host**, so a machine becomes a versioned URL or a containerized app. See [Deployments](/docs/docker-host/overview).
- **White-label platform**, so your customers see your brand and domains. See [White-label setup](/docs/platform/white-label).
- **One interface for everyone**: MCP, a CLI, and six SDKs. See [MCP](/docs/mcp), [CLI](/docs/cli), [SDKs](/docs/sdks).
- **Managed data** with connection injection: Postgres, MySQL, Redis, MongoDB, Qdrant. See [Data](/docs/data/overview).
- **Regions and OpenComputers** for machines you own. See [Regions](/docs/regions) and [OpenComputers](/docs/opencomputers).

## When to choose each

- **Choose CodeSandbox** if you want instant, interactive cloud development environments for people as well as agents.
- **Choose MIOSA** if you want a runtime built for agents and apps: sandboxes, computers, agent runs, deployments, and managed data, with the measured startup figures above.

## Sources

- CodeSandbox public documentation: https://codesandbox.io (as of October 2026).
- ComputeSDK benchmark results, via [our Benchmark page](/docs/benchmarks) (2026-10-23).
- MIOSA capabilities, as documented on this site.

- [All comparisons](/docs/compare): Every provider MIOSA is measured against.

pages.title: Changelog
pages.description: Customer-facing updates to MIOSA products, platform capabilities, SDKs, CLI tools, and documentation.
pages.markdown:
This page highlights meaningful improvements after they are available to customers.

Entries focus on the product result, affected workflow, and any action customers should take.

Internal infrastructure details, private identifiers, security-sensitive implementation notes, and routine maintenance are intentionally excluded.

Planned work belongs in [Availability & Roadmap](/docs/availability), not in the changelog.

> **Note: No action usually required**
>
> Unless an entry includes an action notice, existing projects and integrations continue working without changes.

---

## Rolling out

In progress

Merged and rolling out. Each bullet moves under its date once it is live.

- Flat pricing: one flat hourly price per machine size for sandboxes and computers, with apps and databases billed on use up to that size's price.
- A deployment guest is isolated per customer rather than by the host session.
- A sandbox copy cold boots the scrubbed disk when memory is withheld.
- Docker Engine 29.9 with the `docker compose` and `docker buildx` plugins in the default `miosa-sandbox` template and the templates built on it.
- SOMA at `small`, `medium` and `large`, with live vCPU and memory resize.
- SSH certificates scoped to a single sandbox, alongside the existing authorized keys.

## October 2026

### October 18, 2026

New

- Deployments: a Next.js standalone build ships and runs as built - only the top-level dependency folder is stripped from the artifact, and the standalone server is started directly, so an app whose build output carries its own dependencies runs in a guest with no package-registry access.
- Deployments: `PORT` is set for the app unless the app sets its own.

Improved

- Deployments on managed hosts: a release starts, stays up and serves its app on the port it listens on, and readiness is checked inside the host against that port, so an app that reported listening is no longer left unreported.
- Deployments: a managed instance records the shape its guest actually got.

Fixed

- Deployments on managed hosts: the platform's own sweepers no longer kill a deployment's guest while it is still starting, and a guest survives a restart of the host agent.
- Deployments on managed hosts: a guest is published at its host's mesh address, so a deployment's hostname reaches the app.
- Deployments: a release that cannot install, cannot launch, or never answers on its port fails the launch with a named reason - `release_install_failed`, `app_launch_failed` or `app_not_listening` - instead of leaving a guest that cannot work.
- Deployments: a Next.js release that produced no application build is refused with `build_output_missing` naming the missing output, instead of a guest that restarts forever.
- Databases: backup retention restamps completed backups only, and only when the plan's date is at least a minute later, so a completed backup keeps its full window.

pages.title: Moving from Vercel
pages.description: Import a Vercel project with miosa import vercel, review the plan, and what carries over.
pages.markdown:
`miosa import vercel` reads a Vercel project's `vercel.json` and writes a plan.
The plan names the MIOSA project, the `production` environment, one service, and the environment variable names the file declares.
Review the plan, then apply it.
Nothing is created until you apply.

## Import a project

```bash
npm i -g @miosa/cli
miosa import vercel --from-file vercel.json --name shop --repo https://github.com/acme/shop
miosa import vercel --from-file vercel.json --out plan.json
miosa import vercel --apply --plan plan.json
```

| Flag | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--from-file` | The `vercel.json` to read |
| `--name` | The MIOSA project name |
| `--service` | The service name inside the project (default `web`) |
| `--repo` | The Git URL of the service's source |
| `--region` | `us-east`, `us-west` or `us-mia`; overrides the file |
| `--into` | Import into an existing MIOSA project |
| `--apply` | Create what the plan says |
| `--resume` | Continue an interrupted apply |

## What carries over

| Vercel | MIOSA |
|---|---|
| The app | A [service](/docs/services/overview) built from the repository |
| Region | The service region, when the file names one MIOSA has |
| Environment variable names | [Variables](/docs/services/variables) with no values |

Values are never copied.
Set each value on the service, then deploy.

## What does not carry over

The plan lists each of these with the reason: rewrites, redirects, headers, builds, the `functions` block, `cleanUrls`, `trailingSlash`, `buildCommand`, `installCommand`, `outputDirectory` and `crons`.
Recreate what you need as [service settings](/docs/services/services).

## Where to go next

- [Services quick start](/docs/services/quickstart)
- [Moving from Railway](/docs/migrate/railway)

pages.title: Migrating from miosa-sandbox
pages.description: Move off the deprecated @miosa/sandbox, miosa-sandbox, and sandboxes-go packages onto the canonical MIOSA SDKs.
pages.markdown:
The standalone sandbox packages are deprecated compatibility wrappers. Each one now delegates to the canonical MIOSA SDK, so the fastest migration is often to install the canonical package and change one import.

| Deprecated package | Canonical replacement |
|---|---|
| `@miosa/sandbox` (JavaScript) | `@miosa/sdk` |
| `miosa-sandbox` (Python) | `miosa` |
| `sandboxes-go` (Go) | `github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa-go/v2` |

## JavaScript

```bash
npm install @miosa/sdk
```

```typescript
// Before
import { MIOSA } from '@miosa/sandbox';
const client = new MIOSA({ apiKey: process.env.MIOSA_API_KEY! });

// After
import { Miosa } from '@miosa/sdk';
const client = new Miosa({ apiKey: process.env.MIOSA_API_KEY! });
```

`@miosa/sandbox` re-exports the canonical client, so it keeps installing while you migrate, but new code should import `@miosa/sdk` directly. The renamed classes map as:

| Old import | Canonical replacement |
|---|---|
| `MIOSA` | `Miosa` |
| `SandboxClient` | `Sandboxes` |
| `ComputerClient` | `Computers` |
| `CreateSandboxOptions` | `SandboxCreateParams` |
| `CreateComputerOptions` | `ComputerCreateParams` |

## Python

```bash
pip install miosa
```

```python
# Before
from miosa_sandbox import MIOSA
with MIOSA(api_key="msk_...") as client:
    with client.sandboxes.create() as sandbox:
        print(sandbox.exec("python3 -c 'print(1 + 1)'").stdout)

# After
from miosa import Miosa
with Miosa(api_key="msk_...") as client:
    with client.sandboxes.create() as sandbox:
        print(sandbox.exec("python3 -c 'print(1 + 1)'").stdout)
```

`MIOSA` and `AsyncMIOSA` are preserved in the compatibility package and return the canonical `miosa` resource classes; the async class becomes `AsyncMiosa`.

## Go

```bash
go get github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa-go/v2
```

```go
// Before
import sandboxes "github.com/miosa-ai/sandboxes-go"
client, _ := sandboxes.New(sandboxes.Config{APIKey: os.Getenv("MIOSA_API_KEY")})

// After
import miosa "github.com/Miosa-osa/miosa-go/v2"
client := miosa.NewClient("msk_...")
```

> **Note: Sunset window**
>
> The `sandboxes-go` package receives bug fixes but no new features, with a sunset date of 2026-11-08. The JavaScript and Python compatibility packages exist only so older integrations keep installing while they migrate.

## Behavior differences to expect

- **One client, one surface.** In the canonical SDKs, sandboxes live on the client (`client.sandboxes`) alongside computers, files, snapshots, and agent runs. Code that reached for a separate sandbox client now goes through the single client.
- **Ownership selectors are first-class.** `workspace_id`, `project_id`, and `external_user_id` can be passed directly on create, and are exposed on the returned handle.
- **`size` and `resource_contract`.** When no size is supplied, the compatibility packages request the canonical `small` contract: 2 vCPU, 4096 MiB memory, and 10240 MiB disk. The response exposes `size`, `resource_contract`, and `usage()` on both sync and async handles.
- **Canonical names.** Use `client.sandboxes` on the sandbox image, `client.computers` with `miosa-desktop`, and `client.dockerDeploy` for the Docker Host appliance. `computer` is the user-facing product name; `miosa-desktop` is the template it boots from.

## Verify the migration

The compatibility packages and the canonical SDKs hit the same API, so the check is behavioral:

```python
from miosa import Miosa

with Miosa(api_key="msk_...") as client:
    sbx = client.sandboxes.create(template_id="miosa-sandbox", size="small")
    print(sbx.state, sbx.resource_contract)
    print(sbx.exec("python3 -c 'print(1 + 1)'").stdout)   # 2
    sbx.destroy()
```

If that prints `2` and a `small` contract, the migration is complete.

## See also

- [TypeScript SDK](/docs/sdks/typescript): The canonical JavaScript and TypeScript client.
- [Python SDK](/docs/sdks/python): The canonical Python client, sync and async.
- [Go SDK](/docs/sdks/go): The canonical Go client, version 2.

pages.title: Availability & Roadmap
pages.description: Current MIOSA product availability, what is generally available, what is in hardening, and what is planned next.
pages.markdown:
This page gives customers a clean read on what is ready for production today, what is available for selected partners, and what is still on the roadmap.

> **Note**
>
> Last updated: 2026-07-25.
> We update this page when a platform capability changes release stage.

## Release stages

| Stage | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Generally available** | Supported for production use with documented APIs and normal support paths. |
| **Partner preview** | Available to approved customers while we finish polish, SDK parity, or operating runbooks. |
| **In hardening** | Built or partially available, but not ready to promise as a stable public surface. |
| **Planned** | On the roadmap, not available for production use yet. |

## Generally available

- **Sandboxes**: Create isolated Linux workspaces for code generation, build steps, test runs, long-running commands, file operations, and live previews.
- **Live previews**: Expose a running process on a public preview URL, with private preview tokens for embedded product experiences.
- **Publishing and rollback**: Turn a sandbox into a durable deployment version, promote it, list versions, and roll back when needed.
- **Managed data services**: Use Postgres, MySQL, Redis, Qdrant, object storage, per-project auth, and persistent volumes with credentials injected into runtime.
- **White-label platform**: Use external IDs, browser tokens, custom branding, preview domains, webhooks, and usage rollups to build MIOSA into your own product.

## Partner preview

These surfaces are being used with selected customers while we continue polishing public docs and SDK parity.

| Surface | Current scope |
|---|---|
| **Computers** | Full Linux desktops for browser automation, screenshot loops, and computer-use agents. |
| **Dynamic deployments** | Production server processes created from a sandbox publish. |
| **Docker Host** | Workspace-scoped container runtime for apps that need Docker, server processes, background workers, or database-backed production hosting. |
| **Tenant deployment domains** | Branded app domains for generated apps, separate from sandbox preview domains. Routing exists; tenant-level self-service remains operator-assisted while exact deployment domains are self-service. |
| **External computer providers** | Bring third-party computer providers into the same MIOSA computer abstraction. |
| **Evaluations** | Desktop and agent workflow benchmarks using reproducible tasks, traces, and scoring. |

## In hardening

| Area | Status |
|---|---|
| **Desktop computer provisioning** | Computers preserve disks and snapshots across stop, resume, and failed recovery. Start latency and stream readiness continue to be hardened. |
| **Dynamic runtime routing** | Dynamic runtimes keep the active healthy version serving while candidates build. Route evidence and automated recovery continue to be hardened. |
| **Docker Host fleet maintenance** | Host upgrades preserve deployment records and desired state, restore desired-running apps, and verify workloads before returning a host to active service. |
| **Customer-cloud regions** | AWS and Google Cloud foundations exist, but production placement remains gated on a real provider canary and per-host acceptance evidence. |
| **Managed data recovery** | Database IDs, credentials, volumes, bindings, and desired state survive host maintenance. Recovery visibility continues to be expanded across product surfaces. |
| **Deployment proof** | CLI, TypeScript SDK, Python SDK, and Go SDK expose proof checks. Java and Elixir parity is still in progress. |
| **SDK parity** | Python and TypeScript are deepest today. Go, Java, Elixir, and UI packages are being brought to the same coverage over time. |
| **Cross-workspace analytics** | Resource attribution is live. Higher-level dashboards and billing views are expanding. |

## What is live in Release 4

Recent platform changes customers can rely on now.
Each is a result, not a promise of future work.

| Change | Result |
|---|---|
| Disk corruption guard | Restoring a memory snapshot onto a disk that grew after the snapshot is refused instead of corrupting the filesystem. Live on the control plane and all hosts. |
| Guest isolation from the internal network | A sandbox cannot reach the platform's own network except the managed-database proxy range. The Firecracker rule ordering that stops an older allow rule from shadowing the deny is live fleet-wide, and SOMA already enforced it. |
| Preview fallback for white-label staff | Preview access for a white-label organization's own staff falls back to the authenticated console path instead of failing. |
| Disk larger than the pre-built slot | A request for a disk larger than the pre-built slot boots at the requested size instead of failing or returning the wrong size. |
| Learn credits cooldown | An expired Learn attempt is timed from its expiry, and an expired attempt with no answers no longer counts as a failure. |
| Function pool | The per-host function pool is deployed but dark: it is not a customer surface yet. |
| SOMA catalog accuracy | The runtime catalog no longer advertises pause or snapshots for SOMA, which has neither. |

## Planned

| Capability | Notes |
|---|---|
| Native GPU sandboxes | Targeted early 2027, for workloads that need accelerated inference or rendering. |
| Edge functions | Targeted Q1 2027, as a deployment target separate from origin runtimes. |
| Native nameservers | Targeted Q4 2026, for customers who want MIOSA to manage more of the domain lifecycle. |
| OTLP export | Planned for teams that want platform traces in their own observability stack. |
| Test-mode API keys | Planned to separate production billing from integration testing. |

## Deliberate product boundaries

MIOSA is focused on AI-generated software, isolated execution, live previews, desktop automation, white-label SaaS infrastructure, and durable deployment. It is deliberately not:

- **Managed Kubernetes**. Sandboxes and Deployments cover the workloads people would otherwise use K8s for.
- **Generic VPS hosting**. Compute is always tied to a tenant identity (workspace or `external_workspace_id`).
- **Cryptocurrency or blockchain primitives**.

## See also

- [Benchmarks](/docs/benchmarks) for verified performance results.
- [Evaluations](/docs/evaluations) for agent task scoring and desktop workflow benchmarks.
- [Provider comparison](/docs/integrations/comparison) for the compute-provider landscape.
- [Customer infrastructure](/docs/infrastructure/byoc/overview) for MIOSA-managed, connected-machine, AWS, Google Cloud, and hybrid placement.
- [Known limitations](/docs/known-limitations) for the concrete gaps and gotchas behind these stages.
- [Changelog](/docs/changelog) for shipped product changes.

pages.title: Known Limitations
pages.description: An honest list of what doesn't work yet, what's in progress, and what's intentionally out of scope. Updated continuously.
pages.markdown:
We document what doesn't work, on purpose. If you hit something here, it isn't a bug in your code. It is a known gap. For release stages and the roadmap, see [Availability & Roadmap](/docs/availability); this page lists the concrete gaps and gotchas you can hit today.

> **Note**
>
> Last updated: 2026-10-11. We update this page on every release.

## Sandboxes `Public V1`

- **Availability is catalog-driven**. A named size, including `xs`, can be selected only when the template catalog and tenant policy admit it. A published contract is not a guarantee of immediate capacity in every environment.
- **The default is `small`**. It resolves to 2 vCPU, 4096 MiB RAM, and 10240 MiB disk. Raw CPU, memory, and disk fields must form a complete exact match for a published contract.
- **Timeouts are bounded**. `timeout_sec` defaults to 3600 and has a maximum of 86400. The extend endpoint replaces the timeout instead of adding duration. `always_on` is policy-dependent.
- **Usage can be incomplete**. Active CPU and network values can be `null` with `measurement_status` set to `unavailable`, or retained with status `stale`. Clients must not treat unavailable values as zero or stale values as current.
- **Snapshots are supported**. Public V1 includes customer-managed snapshot create, list, show, delete, and restore (`/sandboxes/{id}/snapshots` and `/sandboxes/{id}/restore/{snap_id}`), plus pause, resume, and fork.
- **AWS BYOC sandbox capacity is a gated private preview**. Managed and enabled BYOC environments share the sandbox contract, but BYOC placement is unavailable until the customer environment is accepted.
- **No GPU sandboxes**. The public sandbox create contract does not accept, persist, or schedule GPU requests; GPU runtime infrastructure exists behind a feature flag but is not productized, and no GPU rate is billable.
- **No nested virtualization**. KVM and QEMU cannot run inside a sandbox.

## Deployments `Phase 3/4 complete; dynamic runtime in hardening`

- **Custom domain apex records require ALIAS / ANAME**. DNS providers that do not support flattening, such as GoDaddy, require a workaround.
- **No edge functions yet**. Only origin compute is available.
- **Rollback is per-deployment, not per-route**. You cannot pin one URL path to version 1 and another to version 2 within the same deployment.
- **Containerized deployments publish through Docker Host**. Every sandbox ships Docker with the `docker compose` and `docker buildx` plugins, so you can build and test a container image there. A durable deployment of a containerized app is published through [Docker Host](/docs/docker-host/docker-deploy); the standard runtime builder builds from source and does not build OCI images into a deployment.
- **Railpack / Nixpacks framework detection** exists but dynamic generation from buildpacks is not complete.
- **Docker Host is a separate runtime path**. It publishes into the workspace Docker Host appliance and proves readiness through the `docker_deploy_app` row, container route, host health, and public URL. Standard MIOSA deployments and Docker Host deployments share the deployment API surface, but they do not use the same runtime substrate.

## Data Services

- **Managed Postgres** `Beta`. Provisioning lifecycle and credential injection exist. PgBouncer connection pooling and off-box backup drills are in progress.
- **Redis** `Beta`. Single-node only. Multi-zone replication is planned.
- **Object Storage** `Beta`. S3-compatible API is live; pre-signed browser uploads work. CDN distribution and geo-replication rollout are operational work in progress.
- **Auth-as-a-Service** `Beta`. Per-project email/password signup, login, JWT verify, password reset, and email confirmation endpoints are live. Refresh tokens, magic links, OAuth providers, MFA, and passkeys are still planned.
- **Volumes** `Beta`. Persistent local-backend volumes can be created, attached to computers, detached, deleted, and metered. Local volumes live on one host, so cross-host attach returns an error rather than moving the volume automatically.
- **Usage / audit query views grouped by `external_workspace_id`** have no API view. Raw audit events exist; aggregate them per workspace in your own code.

## Computers (Desktop) `GA`

- **Headed-only**: no headless mode for Computers. You boot a real Xfce desktop. For headless workloads, use Sandboxes.
- **Browser cookies do not persist** across sessions by default. Use a volume mount or browser profile snapshot to carry cookies across reboots.
- **No multi-monitor virtualization**. Single 1920 × 1080 frame buffer.
- **Audio not exposed**. The stream is video-only; system audio is dropped at the host.

## Computer-Use API

- **No managed agent loop**. You bring your own agent (Anthropic SDK, OpenAI computer-use API, or custom). A built-in `computer.prompt()` convenience will ship when the hosted Optimal session endpoint is publicly available.
- **Approval gating is not enforced server-side**. The approve / reject action protocol is a client-side convention only. Gate sensitive operations in your own agent code.
- **Computer sub-resources** (auto_stop, vnc_credentials, apps, stream_token, metrics, ports, volume attach/detach, clone) have full coverage in the Python SDK. TypeScript, Go, and Java parity is targeted Q3 2026.

## SDKs

| SDK | P1 + P2 resources | P3 / P4 resources | Computer depth |
|---|---|---|---|
| Python | Full | Full | Full |
| TypeScript | Full | Full | Partial |
| Go | Full | Partial | Partial |
| Java | Full | Partial | Partial |
| Elixir | Full | Partial | Partial |

- **Deployment proof parity is still uneven**. CLI, TypeScript SDK, Python SDK, and Go SDK expose proof checks. Java and Elixir proof helpers are still pending.
- **`embeddings`, `provider_defaults`, `benchmarks`, `command_center`, `community`, `email`, `builder_sessions`, `snapshots_standalone`** are Python-only today. Other SDK languages are pending.
- **Python sync client uses long-poll fallback** for streaming events. Use the async client or the TypeScript SDK for proper SSE.
- **Tab-synced language preference** persists in `localStorage`, not your user account. Switching language on one device does not propagate to another.

## API

- **No GraphQL endpoint**. REST + SSE by design.
- **Webhook delivery retries run for roughly 15.5 hours (within a 24-hour window)**. After eight attempts the event is dropped. Use the audit log to backfill missed events.
- **Rate limits**: 60 to 30,000 requests per minute per API key by tier, and 2,500/25,000/100,000 per minute per workspace on Developer/Business/Enterprise. Higher limits are available on request.
- **Browser tokens have a 1-hour default TTL** (60 seconds to 7 days). Refresh server-side; do not attempt client-side extension.
- **One sandbox per browser token**. A single token cannot scope across multiple sandboxes.

## Pricing and Billing

- **No per-tenant usage budgets yet**. You set a workspace cap today; tenant-level caps tied to `external_workspace_id` roll out with the billing attribution extension.
- **All traffic is billable** against the account’s spendable credit balance today. See [Availability & Roadmap](/docs/availability) for test-mode keys.

## Observability

- **No native log aggregation across workspaces**. Query per-resource today.
- **No OTLP trace export yet**. The `/events` SSE streams provide raw events; bring your own collector.

## See Also

- [Changelog](/docs/changelog) - what we just shipped
- [Concepts](/docs/concepts) - the resource model

pages.title: Recovery Playbooks
pages.description: Symptom-first recovery procedures for deployments, domains, TLS, Docker Host hosts, sandboxes, and production rollback.
pages.markdown:
Use these playbooks when a customer-visible workflow is unhealthy.

Diagnose before mutating anything, preserve the last known-good version, and make one bounded recovery change at a time.

## First five minutes

1. Resolve the exact Organization, Workspace, Project, and affected resource.
2. Record the public URL, deployment ID, active version ID, and current health state.
3. Test the public route from outside the runtime.
4. Separate build, runtime, route, DNS, and TLS failures.
5. Preserve the previous ready Version and any operation or idempotency ID.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Public URL fails"] --> B["DNS resolves?"]
  B -->|no| DNS["Correct records and verify propagation"]
  B -->|yes| C["TLS active?"]
  C -->|no| TLS["Inspect validation and certificate state"]
  C -->|yes| D["Route targets active Version?"]
  D -->|no| ROUTE["Repair route reconciliation"]
  D -->|yes| E["Healthy Runtime Instance?"]
  E -->|no| RUN["Reconcile from immutable Release"]
  E -->|yes| APP["Inspect application logs and health contract"]
```

## Deployment is down

| Check | Healthy proof | Recovery |
|---|---|---|
| Active Version | Exact expected version ID | Promote the last verified ready Version |
| Artifact | Running digest matches Release | Replace the runtime from the immutable Release |
| Runtime | Required instances are ready | Reconcile or replace failed instances |
| Route | Public URL reaches active Version | Reconcile routing after runtime readiness |
| Application | Health endpoint succeeds | Fix configuration or publish a corrected Release |

Do not rebuild an old Release to recover it.

Rollback should select an already verified Version while preserving the Deployment and domain identities.

## Domain remains pending

1. Copy the exact record type, host, target, and ownership token returned by MIOSA.
2. Remove conflicting records at the same hostname.
3. Disable DNS proxying until ownership verification completes.
4. Query the authoritative DNS provider, then public resolvers.
5. Retry verification only after the expected answer is visible.

For a wildcard such as `*.apps.example.com`, most providers expect the host field `*.apps`, not the complete hostname.

For an apex hostname, use the provider's supported ALIAS, ANAME, or flattened CNAME behavior when a normal CNAME is not permitted.

## TLS is not active

- Confirm DNS already resolves to the MIOSA verification target.
- Confirm the hostname is attached to only one Organization and Deployment.
- Check whether a restrictive CAA record blocks the certificate authority.
- Keep proxying disabled until verification and certificate provisioning finish.
- Do not repeatedly detach and reattach the hostname because that restarts validation.

## Docker Host host is unhealthy

1. Confirm the host record points to the expected appliance and organization.
2. Confirm the appliance agent, Docker Engine, and required persistent storage are healthy.
3. Confirm the immutable Release is available to the appliance.
4. Check the last deployment operation before starting another one.
5. Reconcile the desired Deployment instead of creating a duplicate Deployment.

> **Caution: Avoid duplicate builds**
>
> If a request times out, first determine whether the remote build is still running.
> Recover with the recorded operation ID or idempotency key instead of submitting the same build again.

## Sandbox preview fails

- Confirm the Sandbox is running.
- Confirm the application listens on `0.0.0.0`, not only `localhost`.
- Confirm the requested preview port matches the application port.
- Confirm the development process is still alive.
- Recreate the Preview only after proving the Sandbox process and port are healthy.

## Escalation evidence

Provide support with resource IDs, UTC timestamps, operation IDs, expected and observed states, the public hostname, and redacted error output.

Never include API keys, cookies, database credentials, private source, customer personal data, or raw environment files.

## See also

- [Deployment domains](/docs/docker-host/domains)
- [Rollback](/docs/docker-host/rollback)
- [Docker Host hosts](/docs/docker-host/docker-deploy)
- [Known limitations](/docs/known-limitations)

pages.title: Evaluations
pages.description: Measure sandbox, desktop, and agent workflows with reproducible tasks, traces, and desktop-readiness benchmarks.
pages.markdown:
Evaluations help you answer a simple question: is your agent actually getting work done on a real computer or sandbox, and how long does the work take?

MIOSA evaluations cover three layers:

| Layer | What it measures |
|---|---|
| **Sandbox workflow** | create, write files, run commands, expose a preview, publish, and clean up |
| **Desktop workflow** | boot a Computer, open a browser, screenshot, click, type, scroll, and observe the result |
| **Agent task** | give an agent a goal, collect the trace, score whether the final state matches the expected outcome |

> **Note**
>
> The public docs describe the measurement model, task shape, and customer-facing outputs. The internal runner, scheduling, and scoring implementation are intentionally abstracted.

## Why evaluations matter

For app-builder products and computer-use agents, normal API uptime is not enough. You need to know:

- How quickly a workspace becomes usable.
- Whether the desktop stream is ready before the agent acts.
- Whether screenshots and actions stay responsive during real tasks.
- Whether a generated app can move from prompt to preview to publish.
- Whether a model, tool loop, or provider change improves task success.

## OSWorld-compatible benchmark direction

OSWorld is a public benchmark for multimodal agents in real computer environments. It defines real desktop tasks, setup state, agent interaction, and execution-based scoring across open-ended workflows. The public OSWorld site describes 369 real-world computer tasks, with 361 tasks commonly used when excluding Google Drive tasks that need manual configuration.

MIOSA uses the same idea for product benchmarking:

- Start from a known computer state.
- Run a task through screenshot and action APIs.
- Capture every observation and action.
- Score the final state with a deterministic evaluator where possible.
- Save the trace so failures can be replayed and compared.

## Evaluation flow

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Task suite] --> B[Provision sandbox or computer]
  B --> C[Run agent loop]
  C --> D[Capture trace]
  D --> E[Score result]
  E --> F[Report success, latency, and cost]
```

## Desktop readiness metrics

These are the computer desktop metrics we track for V1 quality:

| Metric | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Provision time** | Time from create request to assigned machine. |
| **Desktop ready** | Time until the desktop stream accepts a real connection. |
| **First screenshot** | Time until the agent can observe the screen. |
| **First action** | Time until click, type, or key events are accepted. |
| **Screenshot latency** | Round-trip time for repeated screenshots during a task. |
| **Action latency** | Round-trip time for click, type, scroll, and key events. |
| **Task success** | Whether the final desktop state matches the evaluator. |
| **Trace completeness** | Whether every observation and action is captured for replay. |

## Sandbox workflow metrics

For AI app builders, the main path is:

1. Create a sandbox.
2. Write generated files.
3. Install and run the app.
4. Expose a live preview.
5. Iterate on feedback.
6. Publish to a durable deployment.
7. Destroy or pause the workspace.

MIOSA tracks timing and failure rates across that whole path, not just isolated endpoint latency.

## What customers see

- **Run summaries**: Success rate, total time, p50 and p95 latency, failed step, and resource usage.
- **Trace replay**: Screenshots, commands, preview URLs, action events, and final result state.
- **Provider comparison**: Compare native MIOSA Computers, BYOC machines, and external providers through one task shape.
- **Regression checks**: Re-run the same task suite after image, SDK, agent, or provider changes.

## V1 scope

| Capability | Status |
|---|---|
| Desktop readiness benchmark | Available as a V1 quality target. |
| OSWorld-style task scoring | In hardening for partner use. |
| Public leaderboard | Planned after the runner and reporting format stabilize. |

## Use cases

- Validate that a Lumen lead magnet builder can create, preview, and publish a generated app.
- Compare two agent prompts against the same browser task.
- Check whether a desktop image change affected first screenshot time.
- Prove that a full-stack app builder still works after SDK or deploy changes.

## See also

- [Benchmarks](/docs/benchmarks) for current production timing data.
- [Computers](/docs/computers/overview) for desktop automation.
- [Where compute runs](/docs/integrations/external-computers) for MIOSA-managed, OpenComputers and BYOC capacity.
- [Provider Comparison](/docs/integrations/comparison) for the wider compute landscape.

## Method and reproduction

- **Independent and open source**: The benchmark code, runner and every result file are public. ComputeSDK states that sponsors cannot influence results. [github.com/computesdk/benchmarks](https://github.com/computesdk/benchmarks)
- **Same code, every provider**: The same open code against every provider, with fixed workloads and a fixed scoring ceiling. Each metric reports min, max, median, p95 and p99, and burst TTI also reports a composite score that rewards speed and reliability together.
- **Automated**: Runs execute on GitHub Actions on Namespace runners, and every result is committed to the repository as JSON. The repository lists the schedule as daily at 5pm Pacific, 00:00 UTC. In practice the burst TTI history is daily through 2026-07-13 and then weekly on Fridays, with extra runs on 2026-09-10 and 2026-09-16.
- **Live leaderboards and methodology**: Live leaderboards and the full methodology are published by ComputeSDK. [computesdk.com/benchmarks](https://www.computesdk.com/benchmarks)

```bash
git clone https://github.com/computesdk/benchmarks
cd benchmarks

# MIOSA's burst TTI row, latest run
jq '.results[] | select(.provider=="miosa")' results/burst_tti/2026-10-23.json

# Every provider, sorted by median
jq -r '.results[] | "\(.summary.ttiMs.median)\t\(.provider)"' results/burst_tti/2026-10-23.json | sort -n
```

- [Burst TTI results](https://github.com/computesdk/benchmarks/tree/main/results/burst_tti): Every dated burst time-to-interactive result file.
- [DAX results](https://github.com/computesdk/benchmarks/tree/main/results/sandbox-dax): Every dated DAX sandbox build result file.

pages.title: Getting started
pages.description: Where to start, how to authenticate, install the CLI, get an API key, attach IDs to a sandbox, and pick a region.
pages.markdown:
Short answers on the first steps with MIOSA.

Open a category, or use Expand all and Collapse all above the list.
Every question has its own link - the icon on the right - so you can share an answer directly.

## Where do I start?

The [Quickstart](/docs/quickstart) recommends **Track 1: sandbox to deployment** first.
Your first success is a site live at the production URL MIOSA returns, verified end to end.
The full walkthrough is [Build and deploy a Next.js app](/docs/learn/first-production-app).

## How do I authenticate?

With a MIOSA API key in an `Authorization: Bearer` header, or with a JWT from `POST /auth/login`.
See [Authentication](/docs/authentication) and [API keys](/docs/platform/api-keys).

## How do I install the CLI and sign in?

Install the `miosa` CLI (v2.2) from npm, Homebrew, the install script, or a release archive.
Then run `miosa login` for the device-code flow and `miosa whoami` to confirm the active organization and workspace.
See [Install the CLI](/docs/cli/install).

```bash
miosa login     # device-code flow
miosa whoami    # confirm the active organization and workspace
```

## How do I get an API key?

Create one under **Workspace → Settings → API Keys**.
The plaintext is shown once and only the hash is stored.
Key families are `msk_u_` (user), `msk_p_` (tenant platform), and `msk_a_` (operator admin, not self-service).
Default rates are 600 requests per minute for a user key and 30,000 for a platform key; rotate every 90 days.
See [API keys](/docs/platform/api-keys).

## Is there a test mode?

No.
There are no dedicated test-mode keys: `msk_u_*` and `msk_p_*` keys hit the billable production substrate.
Use a sandbox or a separate workspace for experiments.

## What IDs can I attach to a sandbox?

Free-form `metadata`, plus the queryable `external_user_id`, `external_workspace_id`, and `external_project_id`.
See [Metadata and labels](/docs/develop/sandboxes/metadata).

## Which regions exist, and can a sandbox move between them?

`us-west` (default), `us-east`, and `us-mia`, all generally available.
A resource lives in one region for its lifetime, so create one per region.
EU and APAC are on the roadmap.
See [Regions](/docs/regions).

pages.title: Sandboxes and computers
pages.description: Sandbox vs Computer, the default sandbox, run length, states, pausing, and snapshots.
pages.markdown:
## Sandbox or Computer?

Use a [Sandbox](/docs/develop/sandboxes) for code, files, and processes.
Use a [Computer](/docs/computers/overview) when you need a visible desktop, a browser login, or human takeover.
Use **Docker Host** when you need a durable, always-on URL.

```bash
miosa create my-box --wait     # provision a sandbox and wait until it is ready
miosa list                     # see all your sandboxes
```

## What do I get in a default sandbox?

A headless microVM that is persistent by default, with `/workspace` as the editable root, booted from a template (usually `miosa-sandbox`).
The default size `small` is 2 vCPU, 4096 MiB RAM, and 10240 MiB disk, and responses carry a versioned `resource_contract`.
See [Sandboxes](/docs/develop/sandboxes) and [Sizing and limits](/docs/develop/sandboxes/sizing).

## What is different about a Computer?

A Computer is a durable cloud Linux desktop (Xfce and Firefox) with screenshot, click, type, and streaming, plus human takeover.
You embed or share it through `computer.urls()["desktop_url"]`.
See [Computers](/docs/computers/overview) and [Embed a live desktop](/docs/computers/embedding).

## How long can a sandbox run?

`timeout_sec` is 1 to 86400 seconds, default 3600.
`always_on` disables timeout enforcement subject to tenant policy.
The timeout counts from the last activity, and expiry stops a persistent sandbox and destroys a non-persistent one.
A sandbox also stops after 30 minutes idle by default on accounts created on or after October 11, 2026 (set `idle_timeout_sec` to `0` to disable), and a stopped sandbox wakes on the next request.
See [Timeouts and auto-stop](/docs/develop/sandboxes/timeouts).

## What are the sandbox states?

`creating`, `running`, `stopped`, `paused`, `error`, and `destroyed`.
`paused` exists only on a runtime that advertises pause, which is Firecracker today; SOMA has no pause.
See [Sandbox lifecycle](/docs/develop/sandboxes/lifecycle).

## Does stopping a sandbox lose my files?

No. Stop keeps the sandbox id and the disk, including files, installed packages, and enabled services; resume brings it back.
Stop never keeps running processes.
Pause (Firecracker only) keeps processes for up to 30 minutes, then behaves like a stop.
Persistent means the sandbox survives a stop, not the loss of its host; the `durability` field says how many hosts hold the saved state.
SOMA does not support persistence, pause, or snapshots yet.
Destroy is what removes saved state.
See [Snapshots and persistence](/docs/develop/snapshots).

## What is the difference between a snapshot and a fork?

Restore builds a new sandbox from a checkpoint; fork branches a running sandbox into an independent one.
Both leave the source unchanged.
See [Snapshots and persistence](/docs/develop/snapshots).

```bash
miosa snapshot save my-box before-upgrade   # pin a named restore point
miosa snapshot fork before-upgrade          # branch it into an independent sandbox
```

## Does a snapshot save my database?

No. A snapshot captures the sandbox disk and, where the runtime advertises it, memory only.
External databases, object storage, connectors, and third-party services are not rolled back with it.
Keep durable state in a data service.
See [Data overview](/docs/data/overview).

pages.title: Browser and computer use
pages.description: Where browser automation runs, what starting a browser returns, CDP, live takeover, and billing.
pages.markdown:
Short answers on browser automation, the computer-use loop, and live takeover.

## Where does browser automation run?

Inside a sandbox. The browser is part of the sandbox and starts lazily on the first browser request, then survives pause and resume.
See [Browser use](/docs/browser-use).

## What does starting a browser return?

A `stream_url` (live view), a `cdp_url` (Chrome DevTools Protocol), a one-hour `stream_auth` token, and a 1280x720 viewport.
Every sandbox image includes Chromium and Node, so any sandbox works.
See [Browser use quickstart](/docs/browser-use/quickstart).

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.miosa.ai/api/v1/sandboxes/$SANDBOX_ID/browser \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MIOSA_API_KEY"
```

## How does an agent attach to the browser?

Connect over CDP to the same browser a human can watch, so cookies and logins are shared.
Detach when you are done rather than calling `browser.close()`.
See [Drive the browser over CDP](/docs/browser-use/cdp).

## Can a human watch or take over a session?

Yes. Share a live viewer link for browser sessions, or take over a Computer desktop directly.
The live viewer needs the sandbox's virtual display, which a SOMA sandbox does not have yet.
See [Live viewer](/docs/browser-use/live-viewer) and [Embed a live desktop](/docs/computers/embedding).

## What is the computer-use loop?

Screenshot, decide, take one action, screenshot again.
Coordinates are screen pixels with the origin at the top left.
See [Computer use quickstart](/docs/computer-use/quickstart).

## How is browser and computer use billed?

Browser use bills as ordinary sandbox usage.
See [Browser use limits](/docs/browser-use/limits) and [Pricing and limits](/docs/pricing).

pages.title: Agents
pages.description: Supported harnesses, creating and running an agent, OSA, model keys, and where agents run.
pages.markdown:
Short answers on agent harnesses, model keys, and where agents run.

## Which agent harnesses are supported?

`claude-code`, `codex`, `osa`, and `custom`, set with `miosa agent new --harness`.
Agent Run providers also include `claude`, `pi`, and `hermes`.
See [Agents CLI](/docs/cli/agents) and [Configure an agent](/docs/guides/configure-agent).

## How do I create and run an agent?

```bash
miosa agent new reviewer --harness claude-code --instructions-file review.md
miosa agent run reviewer "review PR 42" --sandbox my-box
miosa run list                 # follow, stop
```

See [Agents CLI](/docs/cli/agents).

## What is OSA?

OSA is MIOSA's open-source agent.
It installs on your machine, runs as an MCP client, and runs headless with `osa run "..."` when you do not want the terminal UI.
See [MCP](/docs/mcp) and the [CLI reference](/docs/cli).

## Do agents use MIOSA platform keys?

No. Agents use your own model connections, never MIOSA platform keys.
Create an agent-scoped key and add a model connection before the first run.
See [Agents CLI](/docs/cli/agents).

## Where do agents run?

Agents work against a device: a Sandbox Worker, a Computer, or a local/BYOC device.
Docker Host is a hosting target, not an agent device.
See [Agent devices](/docs/guides/agent-devices) and [Choose an agent device](/docs/guides/agent-device-selection).

## Can I drive MIOSA from my own agent loop?

Yes. Call the primitives from your own backend, or start with the [Agent Development Kit (ADK)](/docs/adk).
See [Integrating an AI agent](/docs/guides/agent).

pages.title: SOMA and runtimes
pages.description: What SOMA is, the default runtime, how to select one, access requests, and availability.
pages.markdown:
Short answers on the runtime you boot a sandbox on.

## What is SOMA?

SOMA (Secure Optimized Machine Architecture) is MIOSA's own open-source Rust VMM on Linux KVM, giving each sandbox one hardware-isolated VM with its own kernel.
See [SOMA](/docs/soma).

## How do I select a runtime?

Pass `runtime_profile: "standard" | "soma" | "auto"` when creating a sandbox, from the REST API, the SDKs (`runtime`), the CLI (`miosa create --runtime`), or the console.
An invalid value returns `INVALID_SANDBOX_RUNTIME_PROFILE`; there is no silent fallback.
`GET /api/v1/sandboxes/runtimes` lists the runtimes your organization can select.
See [Choosing a runtime](/docs/soma/choosing-a-runtime).

```bash
miosa create --runtime soma --size small
```

## Is SOMA available to everyone?

Yes. SOMA is available to every customer, at `small`, `medium`, and `large`, with live vCPU and memory resize.
`GET /api/v1/sandboxes/runtimes` reports what each runtime supports today.
See [SOMA](/docs/soma).

## What is generally available and what is in preview?

Sandboxes, previews, publishing, data, white-label, SOMA, and the sandbox browser are generally available.
Computers, dynamic deployments, Docker Host, and tenant deployment domains are in partner preview; GPU-backed sandboxes are not productized and remain on the roadmap.
See [Availability and roadmap](/docs/availability).

pages.title: White-label and platform builders
pages.description: White-label architecture, branded URLs, end-user auth, billing your customers, and branding.
pages.markdown:
Short answers on running MIOSA under your own brand for your customers.

## How does white-label work on MIOSA?

Your platform maps to one MIOSA organization, with a workspace per downstream customer and a project per thing they build.
End users never need a MIOSA account.
See [White-label platform architecture](/docs/platform/overview).

## What branded URLs can I use?

A preview domain (`https://{port}-{slug}.sandbox.{preview_domain}`), a deployment domain (`https://{slug}.{deployment_domain}`), and a MIOSA fallback (`https://{slug}.{organization_slug}.miosa.app`).
See [Branding and domain setup](/docs/platform/white-label).

## How do my end users authenticate?

Never put an `msk_*` key in a browser.
Your backend mints short-lived scoped tokens, and end-user-scoped secrets and OAuth are keyed on `external_user_id`.
See [Attribution](/docs/platform/attribution) and [White-label credentials](/docs/security/white-label).

## How do I bill my customers through MIOSA?

MIOSA charges the organization owner for all usage in one bill.
Charge back to customers by grouping the Usage Rollup on `workspace_id` or the `external_*` fields.
See [Usage and billing](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Can I brand the console and desktop?

Yes. Set `custom_app_name`, `custom_logo_url`, `support_url`, `desktop_wallpaper_url`, and `powered_by_visible` through `PUT /api/v1/tenant/branding`.
See [Branding and domain setup](/docs/platform/white-label).

pages.title: Business OS and internal use
pages.description: Running your own company on MIOSA, connectors, device choice, and platform checklists.
pages.markdown:
Short answers on running your own company on MIOSA and building an internal platform.

## Can I run my own company on MIOSA?

Yes. The reference map includes MIOSA BusinessOS, a self-hosted business workspace you run internally rather than launch as a product.
See [Agent company reference map](/docs/guides/agent-company-reference-map).

## How do agents reach my internal tools?

Managed connectors attach in-VM tools without shipping you vendor tokens; the sandbox gets a placeholder swapped only for that provider's endpoint.
See [Managed connectors](/docs/guides/managed-connectors).

## How do I pick a device for each job?

Pure reasoning needs no device; files and code use a Sandbox; browser and desktop work use a Computer; private customer resources use a local device; serving traffic uses Docker Host.
See [Choose an agent device](/docs/guides/agent-device-selection).

## Where do I start building an internal platform?

Follow the build-your-own-platform checklist: workspace, credentials, runtime profile, primary device, dispatch, stream, export, snapshot, publish, scale.
See [Build an agent-company platform](/docs/guides/build-agent-company).

pages.title: Security and compliance
pages.description: SOC 2, HIPAA, where data lives, how secrets are stored, retention, and publishable keys.
pages.markdown:
Short answers on certifications, data location, secrets, and retention.

## Are you SOC 2 compliant?

Not yet. Our SOC 2 audit is in progress and not complete, so there is no report to share today.
Until it is issued, we can share our security questionnaire and controls documentation under NDA.
See [Trust](https://miosa.ai/trust) for the current status.

## Do you support HIPAA?

MIOSA runs HIPAA-compliant infrastructure for healthcare workloads, and business associate agreements (BAAs) are available for Enterprise customers.
See [Trust](https://miosa.ai/trust).

## Where does my data live?

In United States data centers we provision, network, and manage directly; MIOSA is not a reseller of a hyperscaler.
The three live regions are all in the US, and a resource cannot move between them after creation.
See [Regions](/docs/regions) and [Trust](https://miosa.ai/trust).

## How are secrets stored?

Values are encrypted with ChaCha20-Poly1305.
Sandboxes see an opaque `miosa-tok-<hex>` placeholder that is swapped at egress, so no one - including MIOSA engineers - can re-read a stored value.
See [Secrets](/docs/security/secrets).

## How long is data retained?

Egress audit events are retained 90 days.
Usage and credit records are kept separately.
There is no published zero-retention mode.
See [Data retention](/docs/data-retention).

## Are there publishable keys for the browser?

No. There are no `pk_*` publishable keys: API keys are server-only.
Browser and embed access uses short-lived scoped tokens instead (`mp_` preview, `ms_` share, and browser tokens).
See [API keys](/docs/platform/api-keys) and [Browser tokens](/docs/platform/browser-tokens).

pages.title: Pricing and limits
pages.description: What you are billed for, paused cost, named sizes, hard caps, rate limits, and credits.
pages.markdown:
Short answers on what is billable, the sizes and caps, and how credits work.

## What am I billed for?

Running sandboxes and computers at the hourly price of their size, apps and databases on what they use (never more than the price of their size), paused storage, storage and egress, and builds.
The full list is on [Pricing and limits](/docs/pricing).

```bash
miosa usage my-box           # runtime, time left and estimated cost
```

## Do paused sandboxes cost anything?

Storage only. Billing for compute stops when the sandbox leaves `running`.
See [Sizing and limits](/docs/develop/sandboxes/sizing).

## What are the named sizes?

`xs` (1 vCPU, 2 GiB, 10 GiB) through `xl` (16 vCPU, 32 GiB, 80 GiB), with `small` as the default.
See [Sizing and limits](/docs/develop/sandboxes/sizing).

## What are the hard caps?

Concurrent sandboxes per plan (Developer 10, Business 250, Enterprise 500; upgrade or raise it through support), `timeout_sec` 1 to 86400, an 86,400 second maximum exec timeout, a 500 MB maximum upload, and a 1 hour browser token TTL.
See [Pricing and limits](/docs/pricing).

## What are the rate limits?

60 to 30,000 requests per minute per API key by tier, and 2,500/25,000/100,000 per minute per workspace on Developer/Business/Enterprise, with `429` and `Retry-After` on overrun.
See [Rate limits](/docs/rate-limits).

## How do I cap what one end user can spend?

The [Quotas API](/docs/api-reference/quotas) sets `max_sandboxes`, `max_concurrent`, `max_storage_gb`, and `max_credit_cents` per `external_user_id`, enforced at create time.

## How do I charge my own customers?

MIOSA bills you once; you charge your customers using attribution.
The [Usage Rollup API](/docs/api-reference/usage-rollup) groups by `external_user_id`, `external_project_id`, or `workspace_id`.
See [Usage and billing](/docs/platform/usage-and-billing).

## Do credits expire?

It depends on the grant.
Credits you add do not expire.
Recurring plan credits expire at the start of the UTC day after the 30-day billing period.
Promotional credits (the one-time welcome grant and promo-code redemptions) expire 180 days after they are granted.
The nearest expiry is reported as `credit_expiry_at` on `GET /api/v1/credits/balance`.
See [Pricing and limits](/docs/pricing).

pages.title: Support
pages.description: How to get help, what to include in a request, status and changes, and the community.
pages.markdown:
Short answers on reaching the team and following platform changes.

## How do I get help?

Open an in-product ticket from the dashboard - the fastest path for anything involving a resource - or email support@miosa.ai for non-resource questions.
See [Support](/docs/support).

## What should I include in a request?

The resource id, the operation you ran, a timestamp with timezone, the `x-request-id`, and the exact error message.
See [Support](/docs/support).

## Where can I see status and changes?

The status page for live health, the [changelog](/docs/changelog) for shipped changes, and [Known limitations](/docs/known-limitations) for current gaps.
See [Support](/docs/support).

## Where is the community?

Join the MIOSA Discord for questions and announcements.

## Still stuck?

- [Ask OSA](/docs/support): Ask OSA is built into every docs page - use the button in the header for instant answers grounded in these docs.
- [Email support](mailto:support@miosa.ai): Open a ticket from the dashboard, or email the support address. Include the resource id, operation, timestamp, x-request-id, and exact error.
- [Join Discord](https://discord.gg/miosa): Ask in the MIOSA Discord, where the team and other builders hang out.

pages.title: Troubleshooting
pages.description: The front door for things that are not working: sandbox, exec, preview, secret, network, and deploy failures, and where to look for each.
pages.markdown:
Start with the exact resource id and the operation that failed. Most requests also return an `x-request-id` header  -  include it in any support request.

```bash
miosa doctor   # checks CLI version, config, endpoint, key, and clock skew
```

A skewed clock breaks signed webhooks and expiring tokens, so `miosa doctor` is a fast first check.

## Sandbox will not start

- **Still `provisioning`.** The runtime is not ready yet. Poll `GET /api/v1/sandboxes/{id}` and wait for `state` to become `running` and `ready` to be `true`.
- **`error`.** A boot or runtime failure. Check `sbx.data["metadata"]` for `last_error`, then destroy and create a new sandbox.
- **`exec` is refused.** A sandbox that is still starting rejects commands. The CLI's `exec` retries with backoff for up to 90 seconds; SDK callers should do the same or wait for `ready`.

## Commands fail or hang

- **A command returns non-zero.** The sandbox exits with the remote command's status. Read `stderr`; nothing is silently swallowed.
- **`exec` times out.** The sandbox `exec` endpoint accepts a `timeout` of 1 to 86,400 seconds (default 3,600) regardless of the sandbox's own timeout. For long work, start a [background process](/docs/develop/sandboxes/long-running-tasks) and poll its logs instead.
- **A file upload fails.** The maximum file upload is 500 MB. Split larger artifacts or write them from inside the sandbox.
- **HTTP `429`.** You hit a rate limit. Wait for the seconds in the `Retry-After` header. See [Rate limits](/docs/rate-limits).

## Previews do not load

- **`404` or connection refused.** Nothing is listening on the port you exposed. Confirm the server is bound to `0.0.0.0`, not just `127.0.0.1`, and that the port number matches.
- **A private preview needs a token.** Private previews require a valid token. See [Previews](/docs/develop/previews) for visibility and sharing.

## A secret is not working

Secrets are covered in depth in [Security troubleshooting](/docs/security/troubleshooting). That page catalogs the most common issues  -  a placeholder that is not swapped, an unbound or mismatched scope, and rotation that seems not to take effect  -  with root causes and fixes, alongside Connect Accounts, the Network Allowlist, the Audit Log, and white-label credentials.

## The network is blocked

A sandbox starts in audit-only mode, so nothing is blocked until you enforce an allowlist. If a call is blocked, check the pending queue (`sandbox.network.pending()`) or filter the audit log by `action=reject`; each row names the rule in `rejected_by`. Common gaps (`pip`, `npm`, CDNs) are listed in [Internet access and egress](/docs/develop/sandboxes/internet-access).

## A deployment failed

- **Build fails.** Read the build logs for the deployment version; see the [Docker Host deploy guide](/docs/docker-host/docker-deploy) for container build paths.
- **A custom domain does not resolve.** Apex records need ALIAS / ANAME support in your DNS provider.
- **You need the previous version back.** Roll back to a prior release; see [Releases](/docs/docker-host/releases) and [Rollback](/docs/docker-host/rollback).

For host, tunnel, and bring-your-own-cloud problems, see [OpenComputers troubleshooting](/docs/opencomputers/troubleshooting).

## SSH and connections

There is no public SSH endpoint. `miosa ssh`, the SDK SSH tunnel, and preview URLs are the only ways in. See [Connecting to a running sandbox](/docs/develop/sandboxes/connect).

## Still stuck

Open a support ticket from the MIOSA dashboard and include the resource id, the operation, a timestamp with timezone, and the `x-request-id`. Remove API keys, tokens, and private URLs from anything you paste. See [Support](/docs/support) for other channels.

- [Security troubleshooting](/docs/security/troubleshooting): Secrets, OAuth, network allowlist, audit log, and white-label issues.
- [OpenComputers troubleshooting](/docs/opencomputers/troubleshooting): OpenComputer connectivity, failed commands, desktops, and tunnels.
- [Known limitations](/docs/known-limitations): What does not work yet, and what is intentionally out of scope.

pages.title: Support
pages.description: How to reach the MIOSA team, what to include so a ticket resolves fast, and where to check status and what has shipped.
pages.markdown:
## Get in touch

- **In-product ticket.** Open a support ticket from the MIOSA dashboard. This is the fastest path for account-specific issues because it carries your tenant context.
- **Email.** Write to `platform@miosa.ai` for anything that is not tied to a live resource, such as roadmap questions or a limitation you need lifted.

## What to include

A precise report resolves in one round trip. Include:

- The **resource id** (sandbox, computer, deployment, secret) and your tenant or workspace.
- The **operation** that failed and how you invoked it (SDK call, CLI command, raw request).
- A **timestamp with timezone**, and the request's **`x-request-id`** header if you have it.
- The **error text** exactly as it came back, including the status code.
- What you already checked, such as the pending network queue or build logs.

> **Caution: Redact secrets before you send**
>
> Remove API keys, tokens, host keys, private URLs that contain tokens, and any sensitive command output. Never paste a live `msk_*` key or a secret value into a ticket.

## Before you open a ticket

Many issues have a documented fix:

- [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting) is the front door for sandbox, exec, preview, network, and deploy problems.
- [Security troubleshooting](/docs/security/troubleshooting) covers secrets, OAuth, the network allowlist, and the audit log.
- `miosa doctor` checks your CLI version, config, endpoint, key, and clock skew in one command.

## Status and changes

- **Status page.** The status page shows current platform health and recent incidents. Check it first if something looks broadly broken rather than scoped to your tenant.
- **Changelog.** The [changelog](/docs/changelog) lists what shipped, and [Known limitations](/docs/known-limitations) lists what has not.

## Raising a limit

Concurrency, rate limits, and volume terms can be raised for a plan. Ask through the same channels and include your expected scale; see [Pricing and limits](/docs/pricing) for the current defaults.

- [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting): Common failures and where to look for each.
- [Known limitations](/docs/known-limitations): What does not work yet, updated every release.
- [Status](https://miosa.ai/status): Current platform health and incident history.
